10291-in-the-fourth-year-anticipations-o:
H. G. Wells wrote this book in 1918, in the fourth year of the First World War, to argue for a peace that would last. Wells, already famous for novels and for books on social questions, turned here to the League of Nations idea then taking shape. He writes as a public thinker, not as a novelist.

Wells urges that peace must rest on open talks, disarmament, and a world body able to settle quarrels by law. He warns against a patched-up peace that leaves old rivalries intact. Readers get a clear, hopeful wartime plea for world order, written before the peace treaties were made.
10418-the-money-moon-a-romance:
Jeffery Farnol published this romance in 1911, dedicating it to Jennifer, whose faith and generosity inspired him. Farnol, author of The Broad Highway, writes of George Bellew, a young man seeking counsel of his valet. Small Porges looks for a fortune for another and finds an uncle instead. The tone is playful and romantic.

A haycart, a belligerent wagoner, a move to Arcadia, peaches, gooseberries, and Sergeant Appleby fill the comic road. Bellew and Adam make a solemn league, and a man with a tiger mark adds mystery. Readers get a warm, whimsical romance of England, money, and love.
10455-a-golden-book-of-venice:
Mrs. Lawrence Turnbull published this historical romance in 1900, set in sixteenth-century Venice. Turnbull calls Venice the noblest city, a city of moods, floating like a mirage between blue water and sky, its gold dim on palace fronts but its splendor still alive. She dedicates the book to her father's vivid historic tales.

A sunny November day opens the story, with sea and sky one glory of warmth and color. Love, politics, and Venetian custom drive the plot through palaces and canals. Readers get a rich, romantic portrait of Renaissance Venice, written with affection and color.
10476-the-vanishing-man-a-detective-roma:
R. Austin Freeman published this detective romance in 1911. It introduces Dr. John Thorndyke, a teacher of forensic medicine at St. Margaret's Hospital. Thorndyke knows every famous legal-medical case. He twists facts from chemistry, physics, and history into proof. The book is a classic of science-based detection.

A vanishing man, an eavesdropper, a watercress bed, a museum idyll, and John Bellingham's will carry the plot. The case moves through probate court and proof by circumstance. An accusing finger and a strange symposium close the case. Readers get a clever, learned mystery, praised for fair, scientific clues.
10511-a-rogue-by-compulsion-an-affair-of:
Victor Bridges published this secret-service thriller in 1915, with a frontispiece by John H. Cassel. Its hero, a rogue by compulsion rather than by choice, bolts for freedom, dons overalls and a bicycle, and finds a dubious refuge. An offer without alternative draws him into secret work he cannot refuse.

A kiss and a confession, Sir George Frinton, a man with a scar, Mademoiselle Vivien the palmist, and a summons from Dr. McMurtrie carry the plot through three years of separation. Bridges writes with pace and romance. Readers get a stylish, early spy tale of compulsion, love, and danger.
10519-mercy-philbrick-s-choice:
This novel, published in 1876, opens with two sonnets on gratitude to those who save souls from moral night, as well as bodies from peril. Mercy Philbrick's choice, the title promises, will turn on truth, faith, and duty, not merely on love or fortune. The tone is earnest, moral, and Victorian.

A late November afternoon, with leaden gray sky and dull red sunset, opens chapter one, as Mercy faces a dangerous way full of hidden pitfalls. Light, in the sonnets' image, shows the safe path. Readers get a thoughtful, old-style novel of a woman's moral choice, faith, and thankfulness.
10555-the-life-of-marie-antoinette-queen:
Charles Duke Yonge published this life of Marie Antoinette in 1876, drawing chiefly on letters published by Arneth and Feuillet de Conches. Arneth's volumes hold letters between the queen, her mother Maria Theresa, and her brothers Joseph and Leopold, with reports from Count Mercy d'Argenteau that form a near history of the French court.

Yonge warns that some Feuillet letters may be clever forgeries, chiefly early ones, but holds most genuine, especially later, more important ones. The book follows Marie Antoinette from dauphiness to queen and revolution. Readers get a detailed, source-based biography of a tragic queen.
10642-towards-the-great-peace:
Ralph Adams Cram, an American architect and writer, published Towards the Great Peace in 1922, in the years just after the First World War. The book gathers lectures built around a prayer by Bishop Hacket, which Cram uses to argue for a peace deeper than treaties. He calls for narrow, selfish thinking to give way to a shared care for justice and the common good.

Cram writes that great peace will come not from machines of power but from the daily conduct of ordinary people, and from replacing hatred and fear with a generous heart. His language is earnest and religious, shaped by the shock of war. Readers get a hopeful, idealistic plea for moral renewal after a devastating conflict.
10740-the-way-of-peace:
James Allen, author of As a Man Thinketh, wrote The Way of Peace as a guide to inner calm through spiritual practice. Its chapters treat the power of meditation, the two masters of self and truth, the gain of spiritual power, selfless love, and the realization of perfect peace. Saints, sages, and saviors appear as examples of the law of service.

Allen calls meditation a ladder from error to truth and from pain to peace, climbed by saints and sought sooner or later by every sinner. His prose is simple, earnest, and aphoristic. Readers looking for quiet, devotional counsel on letting go of self will find this short book direct and encouraging.
10769-a-wanderer-in-florence:
E. V. Lucas published A Wanderer in Florence in May 1912 as a companion for visitors to the Tuscan city. A historical chart from 1296 to 1564 opens the book, followed by colored views of the Duomo and Campanile, the Palazzo Vecchio, the Uffizi loggia, the Ponte Vecchio, and Santa Croce. Lucas walks the reader street by street.

His text mixes history, art notes, and personal observation, pointing out what to see and why it matters. The tone is friendly and well-informed, never academic. Travelers, then and now, get a graceful guide to Florence's churches, palaces, and squares.
10942-the-claim-jumpers-a-romance:
Stewart Edward White set this 1901 romance in the mining West. Bennington, a young Easterner, leaves a New York boarding house for gold country, where he hunts for a claim, meets a swift-footed girl in the brush. Chapters move from a letter and a story-book West to a pioneer's picnic, a girl on a train, and masks off.

White writes the West as both real and romantic: rough camps, mountain spires, and sudden violence, alongside courtship and honour. Bennington learns that girls of the West run faster than his Eastern notions allow, and that business and bravery must go together. The novel gives readers a spirited adventure of mining, love, and frontier justice.
11053-minnie-s-sacrifice:
Frances E. W. Harper wrote this rediscovered novel about slavery, family, and freedom, edited by Frances Smith Foster. Miriam, a mother in a lowly cabin, mourns her daughter Agnes, an enslaved young woman who fell victim to her master's power and died early. The novel follows what that loss means for the next generation.

Minnie, raised amid struggle, works at a wash-tub day after day to keep her children at school, and her eldest daughter graduates from high school and seeks a teaching post. Harper links personal sacrifice to education and civil rights, writing with anger at slavery and hope for Black advancement.
11127-the-case-of-jennie-brice:
Mary Roberts Rinehart published this 1913 mystery, The Case of Jennie Brice, illustrated by M. Leone Bracker. The narrator, calling herself Pitman, keeps boarders in lower Allegheny, where rents are cheap because houses flood every spring. After a flood, mud shovelled from the cellar reveals Peter, the spaniel Mr. Ladley left when he went away, recalling a worse flood five years earlier that brought mystery and sudden death.

Pitman, born on Penn Avenue, ran away from school to marry Mr. Pitman, and returned to Pittsburgh after twenty years' wandering. The case turns on Jennie Brice's coat, found across the river on a cake of ice: either her body, wrapped in the coat, was thrown into the current. Rinehart builds a domestic mystery from floods, boarders, and a vanished wife.
1114-the-merchant-of-venice:
Antonio, a Venetian merchant, borrows from Shylock the moneylender to help his friend Bassanio woo Portia, pledging a pound of his own flesh if he fails. When his ships are lost, Shylock demands his bond, and Portia, disguised as a lawyer, saves Antonio with a quibble. William Shakespeare's comedy mixes romance and courtroom drama.

Shylock's famous plea for common humanity complicates a play long staged as simple comedy, and modern audiences weigh its mercy against its prejudice. The trial scene and the casket test still grip the stage. The play endures as both a crowd-pleaser and a hard moral problem.
11144-somewhere-in-france:
Richard Harding Davis published this 1915 collection of six stories set in France during the First World War. The title story follows Marie Gessler, a German woman trained as a nurse, who passes as French among Parisians, learns French from her mother,.

Other stories include Playing Dead, The Card-Sharp, Billy and the Big Stick, The Boy Scout, and The Frame-Up. One narrator describes a man who claims that had he said his name was Cohen, Selmsky, or Meyer, instead of Craig Talbot, he would have been taken for a Jew. Davis, a famous war correspondent, wrote these tales from close observation of wartime France, mixing espionage, humour, and adventure.
11211-a-minstrel-in-france:
Harry Lauder's wartime memoir is dedicated to his only son, Captain John Lauder of the Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders, killed in France on December 28, 1916. Lauder, Scotland's famous music-hall entertainer, recounts recruiting tours, concerts for troops, and visits to the front, carrying his son's bonnet home from where he fell. A poem opening the book mourns the boy while insisting he played his part.

The memoir mixes show business with grief: jokes, songs, and backstage stories sit beside accounts of mud, loss, and Scottish regiments under fire. Lauder's voice is plain and sentimental, and the book's power comes from that combination. It offers a performer's view of the First World War, shaped by personal bereavement.
11269-virgie-s-inheritance:
Mrs. Georgie Sheldon's 1887 novel introduces Virgie, a young woman caring for a dying father whose strength, breath, and health are failing fast. In a small, cozy room hung with her own pen-and-ink and crayon pictures, he tells her he must set his house in order and provide for her future. The inheritance of the title, and the secrets around it, drive the chapters that follow.

Sheldon, a best-selling author of domestic sensation fiction, builds the plot on family mystery, virtue tested, and eventual reward. The novel's sentimental machinery is frank: good characters suffer, villains scheme, and providence sorts them out. It remains a representative sample of the popular fiction American women read in large numbers.
11345-education-as-service:
J. Krishnamurti, writing as Alcyone, published Education as Service in Chicago in 1912, applying his teacher's instructions from At the Feet of the Master to schooling. The book takes four qualifications, love, discrimination, desirelessness, and good conduct, and shows how teachers and students should live them. Good conduct divides into self-control of mind and action, tolerance, cheerfulness, one-pointedness, and confidence.

Krishnamurti argues that teaching is among the noblest forms of work, yet modern days have not ranked it with other learned professions. Love comes first, he insists, before method. The book belongs to early Theosophical educational writing, earnest and idealistic, and it still speaks to teachers who see their work as service rather than employment.
11357-jimgrim-and-allah-s-peace:
Talbot Mundy's Jimgrim and Allah's Peace follows a journalist narrator sent to Jerusalem in 1920. who seeks a man named Grim, a shadowy British officer whose real name and rank Mundy promised never to reveal. Chapters move through escorts, stipulations, outlaws, and desert politics, with Grim manipulating enemies by leaving them free to make mistakes. The narrator, knowing enough Arabic to misunderstand it fluently, learns Jerusalem again after prewar visits.

Mundy writes adventure with a political edge, set in the Mandate's early years among Arabs, Jews, and British officials. Jimgrim, resourceful and secretive, anchors the action. The novel appeals to readers of imperial adventure who want desert intrigue rather than simple heroics.
11379-round-anvil-rock-a-romance:
Nancy Huston Banks's 1903 romance Round Anvil Rock weaves fiction around a real Kentucky rock and actual events, with a preface admitting only slight liberties. the Wilderness Road drawn nearer the Ohio, the Sisters of Charity anticipated, and Philip Alston's death disregarded, since his influence outlived him. Chapters follow a girl and a boy, the house of cedar, Philip Alston gentleman, a night ride, the Wilderness Road, a camp meeting, and a dance in the forest.

Banks, author of Oldfield, writes southern Kentucky a century earlier as a world of log chapels, justice temples, and hunter's moons. The romance balances local history with love story. Readers of regional historical fiction will find its preface as interesting as its plot, honest about fiction's claims.
11402-the-sky-line-of-spruce:
Edison Marshall's 1922 novel The Sky Line of Spruce, in three parts titled The Wakening, The Wolf-Man, and The Taming. opens with a convict road gang working near Walla Walla among barley fields, meadow larks, and Northern Pacific rails. The gang seems ordinary labor except for one wind-tanned, towering figure who demands individual consideration from the warden. Plug Spanos, a notorious gunman, looks like an artless plow-boy, a contrast Marshall enjoys.

The novel follows its hero from prison labor into northern forests, wolf country, and a struggle to master himself and his surroundings. Marshall, author of The Voice of the Pack, writes outdoor adventure with strong landscape feeling. The book suits readers who enjoy early twentieth-century wilderness fiction.
11417-french-mediaeval-romances-from-the:
Eugene Mason's 1911 translation, French Mediaeval Romances from the Lays of Marie de France, brings seventeen lays into English. Contents include Gugemar, the Dolorous Knight, Eliduc, the Nightingale, Sir Launfal, the Two Lovers, the Were-Wolf, the Ash Tree. the Honeysuckle, Equitan, Milon, Yonec, the Thorn, Graelent, a story from beyond the sea, and the Chatelaine of Vergi. Marie's prologue urges those given comely speech not to hide their light.

Marie, writing in Anglo-Norman France, shaped short romances of love, magic, and loyalty that influenced later literature. Mason's versions are clear and readable, preserving the lays' brevity. Readers new to medieval romance will find this collection an ideal starting point.
11520-the-obstacle-race:
Ethel M. Dell's 1921 novel, dedicated to her dear half-sister Mary, opens with a verse on running a race to obtain the prize. Four parts follow: London and sacrifice, the wand of office and midsummer madness, birds of a feather and Saltash, and at last a free gift, friendship, and confession.

A young woman and Dick, prowling round a fairground tent, give the book its centre, with days of supreme happiness spun out second by second. The obstacle race of the title is love itself, run through honour, pride, and the price of choosing well.
11602-the-world-of-ice:
Robert Michael Ballantyne's 1893 boys' book, The World of Ice, follows the whaling cruise of the Dolphin and her crew in the polar regions. A preface hopes only for profit and amusement, in short compass.

Chapters introduce the crew, a pirate fight, and a search that sends the Dolphin north after the Pole Star. Ice, whales, and polar scenes follow, with dogs, walrus meat, and a ship at sea in all but name. Meetuck the Inuit, O'Riley, and the captain's men give the tale its humour and its hardships. The book is a Victorian adventure of ice and whaling.
1167-a-strange-disappearance:
Anna Katharine Green, America's first great woman detective writer, tells of a young woman who vanishes from a New York house, leaving only a ring and a mystery. A detective and his aide trace her through boarding houses, false names, and a villain's plot, with the law and love both in play.

Green, who wrote The Leavenworth Case, builds the puzzle with care and keeps the solution hidden to the last chapter. The novel mixes sensation with courtroom sense. It suits readers who like classic detection and the New York of the gaslight age.
11774-international-finance:
Hartley Withers wrote International Finance in May 1916, reprinted in June 1918, opening with capital and its reward. Finance, he says, is the machinery of money dealing, joining lenders and borrowers, and capital claims reward as stored-up work.

Chapters follow banking machinery, bills of exchange, the Bank of England, and the great joint stock banks, then investments, securities, and the Stock Exchange. A later passage notes picture palaces crammed nightly and furs selling well, while international finance lies stricken and gasping from war. The book explains money at war to a general reader.
1185-history-of-the-conflict-between-rel:
John William Draper was an American scientist of the nineteenth century. He argues that science and the Roman Church fought a long war. The fight ran from the fate of Greek learning to Galileo, Darwin, and the Vatican Council. He tells the tale as a clash between inquiry and dogma, with libraries burned and thinkers silenced.

Draper writes as a partisan of science, and his history is one-sided by modern lights, but it shaped a whole generation's view of faith and reason. The book's famous "conflict thesis" still frames popular debate. It serves as both history and a document of Victorian science at war.
12029-george-washington-s-rules-of-civil:
Moncure D. Conway's 1890 book George Washington's Rules of Civility, traced to their sources and restored, is inscribed to his son Eustace Conway. Among Washington's manuscript books preserved in the State Archives at Washington City, the earliest bears a date written in it by Washington himself. That date is 1745, when the future president was still a boy copying maxims.

Conway traces the 110 rules of civility to their French and English sources, showing how a young Virginian learned manners from a conduct book. The rules, on behavior at table, in conversation, and in company, reveal the discipline behind Washington's later dignity. Conway's restoration made a schoolboy's copybook into a document of American character.
12188-the-key-to-peace:
A. Marie Miles wrote The Key to Peace as a short devotional work in letter form, addressed to a grandson who asked how anyone knows right from wrong. The answer, Miles says, lies in the Bible, read with care.

Letters list what scripture teaches about right and wrong conduct, urging salvation, prayer, Bible study, and life filled with the Holy Spirit. The tone is grandmotherly and direct, quoting the psalm that great peace have they which love thy law. The book belongs to plain evangelical devotion: short chapters, personal address, and a steady claim that peace follows obedience to God word. It reads as a family gift rather than a work of theology.
12321-rudimental-divine-science:
Mary Baker Eddy published Rudimental Divine Science in 1891, revised in 1908 by trustees under her will. Eddy, founder of Christian Science, dedicates the little book to loyal students working and waiting for the science of mind healing.

Contents define Christian Science, its principle, the personality and individuality of God, healing sickness and sin, and the non-existence of matter. A mid-book passage warns that untruthfulness, pride, envy, and lust weigh against healing power, since the science of healing is the truth of healing. The book is a primer, not a system: short definitions for students of Eddy church. It shows Christian Science in its founder own compressed terms.
12361-the-mother-s-recompense-volume-1-a:
Grace Aguilar published The Mother Recompense, volume one, as a sequel to Home Influence, in a Tauchnitz edition of 1859. Aguilar wrote the domestic story and its sequel in 1836, when she was little above nineteen, with little later alteration.

The preface, by her mother, notes the unceasing labors of her dear child. The story follows Caroline, a girl who feels herself a slave to her mother coldness and severity, longing to throw aside galling bondage. Aguilar, a Jewish writer in Victorian England, writes of family duty, faith, and a mother love tested by misunderstanding. The novel is earnest domestic fiction, valued for its moral seriousness and its early woman voice.
12362-the-mother-s-recompense-volume-2-a:
Grace Aguilar's second volume, published in 1859 as a sequel to Home Influence, returns to Mrs. Hamilton and her circle at Oakwood. Emmeline, Ellen and their young friends fill their days with drawing and embroidery, while Mrs. Hamilton turns them toward charity work for a family in distress. The household mixes ease, kindness and watchful moral care.

Guests, excursions and the long-awaited return of Edward give the volume its movement, as Ellen's new cheerfulness puzzles her friends. Aguilar uses talk, letters and small domestic crises to test duty, affection and self-command. The recompense of the title is moral rather than material: a mother's influence repaid in grown children who choose good conduct for themselves.
12375-masters-of-space:
Walter Kellogg Towers published Masters of Space in 1917, a book for young readers about inventors and their networks. Morse and the telegraph, Thompson and the cable, Bell and the telephone, Marconi and the wireless telegraph, and Carty and the wireless telephone all appear. Towers dedicates the book to his collaborator Berenice Laura Towers.

Chapters follow each inventor from workshop to world network, with illustrations. A mid-book passage shows Professor Henry, fifty years Bell senior, spending a day over Bell apparatus, as he had aided Morse a generation earlier. Towers writes hero stories of invention, stressing patience, experiment, and public use. The book is a period piece of popular science, confident that wires and waves were shrinking the world.
12520-deadham-hard-a-romance:
Lucas Malet's 1919 romance, Deadham Hard, opens in the House of the Tamarisks, where a humanist turned hermit lives under stress of circumstance. A young scholar and gentleman of happy disposition enters, and the past lays an ominous hand on the present. A Bulgarian proverb fronts the book: youth has no boundaries, age has the grave.

Book two, The Hard School of Things as They Are, follows Damaris through maiden meditation, parish life, freedom sampled on the bar, and acquaintance with the hidden ways of men. Malet writes in a rich, psychological manner about faith, desire and duty. The novel is a late Victorian study of a young woman growing up between a sheltered house and a hard world.
12529-quiet-talks-on-service:
S. D. Gordon's 1906 Quiet Talks on Service, companion to his talks on power and prayer, treats Christian service as friendship with Jesus. Contents run from personal contact with Jesus, the beginning of service, through the triple life and yokefellows. A passion for winning men, deep-sea fishing, money as a golden channel, worry as a hindrance, and Gideon's band sifted for service follow.

Personal contact opens with three young men on a road at a quarter past three, and follows John chapter one. Gordon writes in a gentle, devotional voice, practical and warm. The book belongs to popular evangelical literature of its time, urging readers to serve through friendship, not duty alone, and to let outlook change with contact.
12535-witness-for-the-defence:
A. E. W. Mason's 1914 novel, The Witness for the Defence, opens with Henry Thresk and a little speech his mother made a habit of repeating to her son. Chapters move from Bignor Hill and Bombay to Jane Repton, a quest, and a tent at Chitipur. A photograph, a rifle, an episode in Ballantyne's life and news from Chitipur follow.

Thresk intervenes and gives evidence. The Hazlewoods, a great crusade, consequences, trouble, advice, Pettifer's plan, a letter, a trap, methods from France, a witness in the library, two strangers and a verdict follow. Mason builds a courtroom and Indian mystery with care. The novel is a classic Edwardian thriller, where one witness can turn a trial and a life.
12609-back-to-the-woods-the-story-of-a-f:
Hugh McHugh's 1902 John Henry book, Back to the Woods, tells a fall from grace in comic sketches. Chapters promise John Henry's lucky days, ghost story, burglar, country cop, telegram, two queens and happy home. Illustrations name Clara J., a dream of peaches, Uncle Peter the original trust tamer, Aunt Martha, Tacks the boy disaster and Bunch Jefferson.

Chapter one opens at the races, after John Henry promised Clara J. never again to light a pipe at the track. Seven, come eleven, he cries, and the fall begins. McHugh writes in the same slangy voice as his other John Henry tales. The book is a light, episodic comedy of gambling, friends and domestic trouble.
1266-lavender-and-old-lace:
Myrtle Reed tells of two old maids, Jane and Mary, who keep a prim house full of lavender and old lace. Young lovers whose romance stirs their own buried pasts come to stay. A niece's visit, a lost letter, and a garden's secrets bring old loves back to light.

Reed writes with sentiment and a light, old-style charm, and the tale ends in weddings and reconciliations. The book was a bestseller in its day, and it suits readers who like gentle romance, pretty detail, and a story that believes in second chances.
13005-representative-plays-by-american-d:
This volume of Representative Plays by American Dramatists opens with George Henry Boker's Francesca da Rimini, a tragedy in five acts. An editor's introduction places Boker among friends such as Bayard Taylor, Richard Henry Stoddard, and Charles Godfrey Leland, a close literary circle. The play text follows the second edition, checked against the actor Lawrence Barrett's copy.

Boker takes his tale from Dante: Francesca, wife of Lanciotto Malatesta, loves his brother Paolo, and the lovers pay with their lives. The cast list recalls an 1882 Chicago staging at McVicker's Theatre. A second play in the volume turns to politics and reform, with a would-be reformer eager for martyrdom. Together they show American drama reaching for both old legend and new causes.
13044-the-idler-in-france:
Marguerite Gardiner, Countess of Blessington, published The Idler in France in 1841 as a record of travel and society. She notes cleaner towns and new business in the south, save Marseilles and Toulon, which were always busy. At Nîmes she praises the amphitheatre and the Maison Carrée, and claims Italy has nothing to equal the latter pair.

Later chapters visit picture galleries, where Gérard, Delacroix, and Isabey gave works to a famed actress, and libraries of presentation copies. Blessington also records cooks whose skill at meatless dinners was said to keep Catholicism flourishing. The book is a lively, gossipy tour, half guidebook and half salon diary, from a well-placed traveler.
13172-true-stories-of-crime-from-the-dis:
Arthur Train, formerly district attorney of New York County, published these true crime stories in 1908 from his own office experience. Contents run from The Woman in the Case and Five Hundred Million Dollars to The Lost Stradivarius and later tales of fraud and murder. Train writes as a lawyer who has seen the courtroom from the inside.

One trial turns on violins, and dull talk of violin structure bores the jury until a German maker, asked if a fiddle is a Strad, grunts in disgust. Another tale follows a dandy in a tall silk hat who steps in to go bond for a prisoner, just to best a policeman. Train's stories mix law, humor, and human folly, and they show how real cases often outdo fiction.
13261-jason-a-romance:
Justus Miles Forman's 1909 Jason, a romance published by Harper, follows Ste. Marie, a young American in Paris, through mystery, vows, and a dark lady. Chapters run from a ladder to the stars and a pair of haunting eyes to old David Stewart, a brave gentleman hurt in a good cause. Then Jason sets forth on the great adventure. Forman writes romantic adventure with polish.

Ste. Marie, sworn not to see the woman he loves, fears she will think only one thing of him, while Hartley offers to explain, knowing Miss Benham will not laugh it off. Later, Hartley asks a niece about her uncle's party on the night Ste. Marie vanished, recalling galloping pigs at Captain Stewart's flat. The novel is a Paris romance of honor, love, and intrigue.
1331-abc-s-of-science:
Charles Oliver offers an ABC of science for young or beginning readers, taking topics in alphabetical order and explaining each in short, clear terms. The book aims to make science friendly, not fearsome. Oliver's ABC form lets a child dip in anywhere, learning a new fact on each page.

Simple entries cover common facts and ideas, with examples a child can grasp. As an early popular science primer, it shows how Victorians and Edwardians tried to open the world of science to everyone. The book's simple language suits early readers, who can sound out science words with help.
13403-english-travellers-of-the-renaissa:
Clare Howard, of Barnard College, traces English travel in the Renaissance from pilgrimage to study, diplomacy, and language learning. Her 1914 book follows the beginnings of travel for culture, the high purpose of the Elizabethan traveller, and the cynical sneers at the Italianate Englishman who came home changed.

Perils awaited Protestant travellers: the Inquisition, Jesuits, and penalties for recusancy, with licences that barred some countries and left men unsure whether they might pass through Venetian or Florentine lands. Howard also weighs manners, arguing that a scholar without good breeding is a pedant and a philosopher without it a cynic. Travel, in her account, made the Englishman and sometimes unmade him.
13448-the-pleasures-of-ignorance:
Robert Lynd's 1921 essays take pleasure in not knowing, and in looking closely at common things. Chapters run from the herring fleet and the betting man to cats, May, June, insects, trains, weeds, and the daredevil barber. Lynd asks why we hate insects, what virtue means, and how a quiet hill road can feel remote from war.

Butterflies get a patient passage: most people know the tortoiseshell and the little blues, but not the Camberwell Beauty, the Dingy Skipper, or the Pearl-bordered Fritillary. Lynd writes in an easy, talkative style, finding wit in eggs at Easter, catkins like falling rain, and the old indifference that lets life go on. The book charms by praising attention over expertise.
1353-off-on-a-comet-a-journey-through-pl:
Jules Verne's adventure begins on the coast of Algeria, where Captain Hector Servadac and his orderly wake to find the land itself changed overnight. A comet has grazed the earth and carried away a whole region, with its people, animals, and sea, on a wild ride through planetary space.

Aboard their flying fragment, Servadac and his companions map new shores, meet other castaways, and reckon the comet's course among the planets. Verne mixes astronomy lessons with jokes, quarrels, and peril. It is a bold, cheerful voyage tale about science, courage, and life on a world adrift.
13886-rhymes-of-the-rookies-sunny-side-o:
W. E. Christian published Rhymes of the Rookies in 1917, verses on the sunny side of soldier service. Dedicated to Theodore Roosevelt, colonel of the Rough Riders, the book opens with a toast to the colours. Contents include My Bunkie, Our Officers, Pay Day, The Army Grouch, and The Hike. A soldier's primer and an A-B-C of army life teach in rhyme.

Christian writes of hiking in the Philippines, mountain batteries, and cavalry songs. A marine's hymn and a tale of a rookie add humour. One poem urges men to prepare and hike, lest liberty fall. The verses keep morale high with jokes and pride. They offer a cheerful view of American training camps in wartime.
14020-the-works-of-horace:
C. Smart translated Horace literally into English prose in this handy volume, revised by Theodore Alois Buckley. The first book of Odes opens with an ode to Maecenas, descended from royal ancestors, both protection and darling honour. Other odes praise Olympic dust, chariot races, and the palm of victory. Crowds of Quirites raise men to high dignities.

Later odes urge ending grief and life's toils by mellow wine, whether camp banners or Tibur's shade detain the reader. Teucer, fleeing Salamis and his father, offers a model of endurance. Smart's literal prose aids students reading Latin alongside English. The volume suits classical students. It preserves a standard Victorian school translation.
14029-chateau-and-country-life-in-france:
Mary King Waddington's 1909 memoir recalls French country life from inside its châteaux. Chapters visit Lafayette's home, winter households, Norman towns, and Boulogne-sur-Mer. Weddings, hunts, festivals, and Christmas in the Valois fill the calendar. Guests arrive in muddy boots for the chase, linger over long pauses at table, and gather for music after dinner.

Kindness toward village children stands out. Waddington and her friends serve soup from a keeper's cottage to schoolchildren on cold days, and later watch a Christmas procession where little ones kiss the foot of the infant Jesus. A Racine celebration and country visits add literary color. The book charms as a diplomat's wife's notebook: observant, social, and fond of France, with the pleasures and limits of château society shown side by side.
14085-partners-of-chance:
Henry Herbert Knibbs published this western novel in 1921, following a boy named Little Jim after his father sells the family cattle, team, and tools. Cast loose, Jim falls in with riders, horse traders, and drifters. Chapters move from water holes and pony tracks to the town of San Andreas, where a loaded gun and a mescal punch raise the stakes.

Friendship drives the plot more than gunplay. Jim learns to read men and horses, to stand by a partner in a saloon showdown, and to hold his nerve on rough trails. Cheyenne, Bartley, and the men of the Box-S ranch test him in turn. Knibbs writes the range in plain, sunlit prose, and the book keeps the pace of a trail drive: steady work, sudden trouble, and loyalty that has to be earned.
1411-domestic-peace:
Balzac sets this brief sketch on a November night in 1809, when Napoleon's empire stands at its height and Paris is full of balls and uniforms. At one such ball, a married couple's peace is tested by flirtation, gossip, and the sharp eyes of a crowded room, all within the space of a single evening.

The tale turns on glances, dances, and words that mean more than they say, and on how quickly a small slight can grow into a quarrel. Told with brisk economy, it shows Balzac's gift for reading a marriage in one social scene. It is a miniature of pride, jealousy, and forgiveness.
14154-the-tale-of-terror-a-study-of-the-:
Edith Birkhead's 1921 study traces the tale of terror from ancient myth and medieval romance to the Gothic novel. An opening chapter follows fear through ballads, folk tales, Elizabethan drama, and the credulous age of reason. Walpole's Castle of Otranto then launches the Gothic proper, with its medieval revival, stage machinery, and bequest to later writers.

Author portraits fill the middle chapters. Maturin, flamboyant in blue coat and silk stockings, loved emphasis in life and in fiction, and his Fatal Revenge stands as his true horror tale. Mary Shelley receives cooler treatment: her Castruccio, sketched from records, slides from open-hearted youth to crafty tyrant, while the prophetess Beatrice dies in Inquisition dungeons. Birkhead writes as a scholar with a storyteller's pace, and her history still guides readers through haunted castles and villains.
14249-half-a-chance:
Frederic S. Isham's 1909 novel opens with Mr. Gillett's charge and a message to the Admiralty, then follows wheels of justice through opera, botany lessons, tides varying, and a park conference. Part two moves from incidents and a change of front to festivities, the princess suite, currents and countercurrents, flight, and the unexpected. A paper, a condition, and a riverbank close the run.

London bookshops and sudden violence anchor the middle. A book-worms' row between thoroughfares hides rare Horaces, Ovids, Greek tragedies, and golden-age poets behind cobwebs, where truth nestles in dark corners. A girl fingers a coin left by a fellow who sacrificed his life for hers, wonders if he drowned at all, and drops it as shots ring from the park. Spiral Row winds near Regent's Park, curving away from Camden Town's hum. Romance and intrigue share the novel evenly.
14262-the-shadow-of-a-crime-a-cumbrian-r:
Hall Caine wrote this Cumbrian romance in 1885, set round the town of Wythburn. A crime in the night sets the plot moving, and an outcast, an empty saddle, and a house on the moss follow. The tale moves through the Red Lion inn, Sim's Cave, and the high fells. Ralph, the hero, bears a shadow that tests his love and his honor. Caine writes in a warm, earnest voice, full of moorland color.

Ralph seeks a Christian burial for the dead when the parish has no parson. He begs the clerk to dig a grave at once, and slips coins into his hand to soften the refusal. The clerk fears a penalty, yet agrees to give what burial needs no book. Later chapters follow flight on the fells, a betrothal, and Ralph's sacrifice at sunrise on the Raise. The novel joins crime, faith, and love in a northern landscape.
14371-the-portland-peerage-romance:
Charles J. Archard wrote this 1907 romance of the Portland peerage, built from letters and family lore. It follows the Bentincks from the first hero of the line through dukes, weddings, and wild sons. A farmer duke weds a rich Miss Scott, and dukes grow eccentric at Welbeck. The book leans on letters, such as Fanny Kemble's notes to dearest Hal. Archard tells the tale as a family chronicle, half history and half gossip.

One house, with stabling fit for a monarch's stud, was gambled away at cards by the third Duke and Earl Harcourt. The fifth Duke walled his garden with a screen of ground glass, 200 feet on each side and 80 feet high, so no neighbor could glimpse him at ease. Letters about a bust for Lord Titchfield show the family's care for likenesses and gifts. The book charms as a peerage tale of pride, luck, and building whims.
1447-the-illustrious-prince:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's thriller follows Hamilton Fynes, an Englishman drawn into a web of state secrets, and Penelope Morse, an American girl caught between East and West. A fatal despatch, an interrupted theatre party, and a duel of wits with a foreign agent drive the plot through London and beyond.

Oppenheim's hero moves among diplomats, inspectors, and spies, where a word out of place can cost a life or a treaty. The pace is swift and the setting is polished. It is a classic Edwardian tale of espionage, romance, and the hidden wars fought in drawing rooms.
14477-the-inside-story-of-the-peace-conf:
Dr. E. J. Dillon, a journalist long based in Europe, published this insider account of the Paris Peace Conference in February 1920, barely a year after the talks began. He had watched the delegates at close range.

Dillon describes the city, the secrecy and censorship, and the aims of the great powers, then turns to Poland, Italy, Japan, Russia, and the new states of Europe. He criticizes the Treaty of Versailles and the Covenant of the League with sharp insider detail. The book remains a vivid, partisan first draft of how the postwar settlement was made.
14779-mr-fortescue-an-andean-romance:
William Westall opens in a quiet Essex village, where cottages, a green and a parish dinner set the pace of life. One morning the place wakes to crowds, carriages and horsemen in scarlet coats and top boots, all gathering for an event that breaks the usual sleepy round.

From that English start, the romance moves toward the Andes, as its title promises. Fortescue's story joins adventure, travel and love in South American mountains and valleys, far from the village green. Westall balances local colour at home with the larger dangers abroad, making the novel a Victorian tale of a man drawn out of a small world into a wider one.
1505-the-rape-of-lucrece:
Shakespeare's narrative poem, dedicated to the Earl of Southampton, tells of Tarquin's assault on Lucrece, the chaste wife of Collatine, and of her grief, her accusation, and her death. In long, ornate stanzas the poem dwells on Lucrece's lament, her plea to night and opportunity, and her final appeal to her husband and father.

Her death sparks the revolt that ends the Tarquins' rule in Rome, turning a private crime into a public revolution. The poem's rhetoric is rich and its feeling is intense. It is a major early Shakespeare work, prized for its verse and its tragic power.
1515-the-merchant-of-venice:
Shakespeare's Venice comedy follows Antonio, a merchant who borrows from Shylock the moneylender to help his friend Bassanio woo Portia of Belmont. Shylock's bond demands a pound of flesh if the loan fails, and when Antonio's ships are lost, the bond is called in a Venetian court.

Portia, disguised as a young lawyer, saves Antonio by the letter of the law, and the play's comedy darkens around Shylock's forced conversion. Modern readers debate its treatment of Jews with good reason. The Merchant remains a brilliant, troubling play about money, mercy, and law.
15194-out-to-win-the-story-of-america-in:
Coningsby Dawson's 1918 book tells the story of America in France during the First World War, dedicated to his American friends and brothers-in-arms. Chapters include We've Got Four Years, War as a Job, The War of Compassion, and The Last War. A preface for fools only opens the book with a sting.

Dawson writes as a participant and witness, praising American effort while chiding stay-at-home talkers who gave little but mean views. His prose is warm, direct, and wartime in tone. The book serves as both tribute and firsthand record of how Americans saw their war in France.
15243-over-paradise-ridge-a-romance:
Maria Thompson Daviess's Paradise Ridge romance, in four books of food, shelter, laughter, and love, opens with a young woman feeling sap rise in her nature. Samuel Foster Crittenden sparks the change, and a seed basket and garden hoe wake her grandmother's country blood. A land call, she says, had to be answered.

Through farm work, a child in miniature overalls, and love's growth, Daviess builds a Southern romance of home and soil. The book is dedicated to Bernice Lanier Dickinson. Readers who like country romance will enjoy its warmth, humor, and garden-fresh feeling.
15317-the-baronet-s-bride-or-a-woman-s-v:
May Agnes Fleming's 1910 novel, The Baronet's Bride, subtitled A Woman's Vengeance, opens with Whittier verses on clouds, thunder, and wrongs that make God's love plain. A second poem on shadow, light's constant companion, follows. Fleming, author of Lady Evelyn and Queen of the Isle, writes in the sensation style.

A baronet, a bride, and a woman's vengeance drive a plot of love, wrong, and retribution through drawing rooms and secrets. The novel trades on emotion, suspense, and moral payoff. Fans of Victorian melodrama will find the book earnest, plot-heavy, and full of period feeling.
1553-the-hidden-masterpiece:
Balzac's Hidden Masterpiece opens on a cold December morning in 1612, when a poor young painter stands before a house in the Rue des Grands-Augustins in Paris. Inside, the aged master Frenhofer guards a portrait he has laboured over for ten years, a work no eye has seen and which may be genius or madness.

Two younger painters, Porbus and Poussin, bargain for a glimpse, offering a beautiful model in exchange, and the unveiling shocks them all. Balzac's tale asks what art is for, and what perfection costs. It is a profound, brief masterpiece about creation, obsession, and the limits of sight.
15534-children-of-the-market-place:
Edgar Lee Masters published this novel in 1922, dedicated to George P. Brett. Its narrator opens with a striking birth: he was born in London on June 18, 1815, while the battle of Waterloo was being fought. Thousands gave up their lives as life was bestowed on him. His father fought in that battle, and his mother, only eighteen, died as he was being born.

The narrator keeps his mother's picture beside him, bound to her by a tender, mystical love, though he never knew her in daily life. Her wistful eyes, gentle smile, dark hair in elfin disorder, and slender throat rise from a drawing made four months before his birth. Masters builds a long life story from that loss, following a child of Waterloo through a changing America. The novel blends personal memory with history, in the reflective voice of Spoon River's author.
15763-count-hannibal-a-romance-of-the-co:
A romance of the French court by Stanley J. Weyman, in the 1922 John Murray edition used here. Weyman, a master of historical adventure, sets his tale among courtiers, duels, and diplomacy. Hannibal de Saulx, Comte de Tavannes, dominates the action from the first chapter. Crimson favours and a rough wooing open a story of love and peril.

Tavannes moves through the Louvre, the amphitheatre, and the Orleannais, bargaining, fighting, and guarding his lady. A duel, a bargain, and close quarters test his honour. Weyman writes with pace and period colour, letting swordplay serve character. The novel delights as old-style romance: bold men, brave women, and a court where a word can kill.
15776-the-economic-consequences-of-the-p:
A famous protest against the Versailles Treaty by John Maynard Keynes, Fellow of King's College, Cambridge. Harcourt, Brace and Howe issued it in New York in 1920. Keynes, a British delegate at the Paris conference, resigned in disgust at the terms. His book argues that a harsh peace would ruin Europe, not heal it.

Chapters move from Europe before the war, through the conference and the treaty, to reparation in detail. Keynes shows how debts and payments would crush Germany and starve trade. Europe after the treaty, and remedies, close the argument. The book changed debate at once, and still stands as a warning about victors' justice.
15978-the-broken-soldier-and-the-maid-of:
A wartime story by Henry Van Dyke, issued by Harper and Brothers in New York. Van Dyke, author of The Story of the Other Wise Man, writes of France in the Great War. A broken soldier, wounded in body and spirit, meets a maid of France whose courage mends him. Pictures join the text.

The soldier's road through ruined villages and kind homes forms the tale. The maid, young and steadfast, offers food, shelter, and faith. Van Dyke writes with warmth for French endurance and American sympathy. The story stands as a small tribute: war breaks men, and a stranger's kindness helps set them whole.
15979-miss-caprice:
A romance by St. George Rathborne, author of Dr. Jack and Miss Pauline of New York, issued in 1893. The first chapter, called Coward, opens with tourists on a lovely January day, on the hill back of Valletta, on Malta, gem of the Mediterranean. Blue water dotted with sails, a hazy African coast, and a double harbour fill the view.

Quarantine harbour serves general trade, while Great Harbour serves government vessels. Maltese streets, quaint and sunlit, frame the heroine's arrival. Miss Caprice, wilful and charming, stirs love and quarrels among her party. Rathborne writes with brisk, popular skill. The novel delights as a Mediterranean romance: a capricious heroine, a storied island, and love under a southern sun.
16100-marietta-a-maid-of-venice:
F. Marion Crawford's 1901 novel takes readers to Venice and the glass island of Murano, where Angelo Beroviero runs a glass furnace. His only daughter Marietta is the maid of the title, and the household distrusts a Dalmatian servant called Zorzi, a waif old Angelo keeps on despite talk. Servants and workmen whisper that Zorzi may be a heretic and that he may love Marietta.

From those whispers grows a romance of craft, class, and jealousy in a city of furnaces, canals, and old families. Crawford, a popular novelist of his day, fills the book with Venetian color and careful detail about glassmaking. The novel suits readers who like historical romance with a strong sense of place.
16114-the-knight-of-the-golden-melice-a-:
John Turvill Adams published this historical romance in New York in 1857, taking his cue from Winthrop's History of New England. Winthrop records a man who called himself the Knight of the Golden Melice, and Adams builds a tale of early New England around that strange figure. A dedication to a young student, signed J. T. A., opens the book with praise for useful learning over frivolous pursuits.

The romance mixes colonial governors, settlers, and native peoples with love, honor, and adventure in a raw new colony. Adams writes in the earnest, old-fashioned style of mid-century historical fiction, with long scenes and high feeling. Readers who like early American settings will enjoy its blend of real chronicle and invented chivalry.
1614-the-golden-fleece-a-romance:
Julian Hawthorne's Golden Fleece opens with a professor on a hot veranda, thermometer at eighty-seven degrees, punching pipe ash with his finger while nature woos the soul to languor. From this languid start the romance follows the professor and his companions, including a general, through talk, travel, and romantic entanglement.

Hawthorne, son of Nathaniel, writes in a romantic manner of his own, full of colour and adventure, and the tale's energy never quite abates. The Golden Fleece is a period romance, less famous than its author's name, but full of old-fashioned charm.
16215-jack-sheppard-a-romance:
W. Harrison Ainsworth's Jack Sheppard, in a 1922 Berlin English Library edition, romances the famous London thief. Its first epoch, dated 1703, opens with Jonathan Wild, the thief-taker who ruled the underworld, and follows Sheppard from apprentice days toward escapes, robberies, and the gallows. An epigraph from Guzman d'Alfarache teases the art of robbery and the price of hanging.

Ainsworth, the Victorian master of Newgate romance, writes with pace, color, and a taste for low life and high drama. Sheppard's daring made him a folk hero, and the novel helped fix his legend. Readers who like historical adventure with a rogue hero will enjoy this brisk classic.
16224-a-bibliographical-antiquarian-and-:
Rev. Thomas Frognall Dibdin's Bibliographical, Antiquarian, and Picturesque Tour in France and Germany, in a second edition of 1829, records a book lover's continental journey. Volume one, printed by William Nicol at the Shakespeare Press, opens with a letter to Rev. John Lodge, librarian at Cambridge, recalling pleasant talks about continental libraries. Dibdin promises libraries, manuscripts, bindings, and scenery in equal measure.

His tour visits great collections, describes rare books, and paints towns and roads with an antiquary's delight. Dibdin, a famous bibliographer, writes with enthusiasm that made book collecting fashionable. Readers who love old books and old Europe will enjoy this gossipy, learned travelogue.
16252-jan-a-dog-and-a-romance:
A. J. Dawson's Jan, published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1915 by arrangement with Harper, tells a dog's life as a romance. Contents follow Finn coming home, Nuthill and Shaws, the lady Desdemona, her wanderings and her nest, and a lone mother with family life and death. Jan goes to Nuthill, learns his first steps, fights his first fight, stands before judges, and travels from Sussex to Saskatchewan.

Murder, discipline, and a sourdough character deepen the tale, which treats dogs as full persons with pride and loyalty. Dawson writes warm, outdoor fiction for animal lovers. Readers who enjoy dog stories with adventure and feeling will find Jan a faithful companion.
16258-the-squire-of-sandal-side-a-pastor:
Amelia E. Barr's 1886 pastoral romance takes its name from Seat-Sandal, a Lake District mountain between Dunmail Raise and Grisedale Pass. From its summit, walkers see Grasmere vale and lake at their feet, with Windermere, Esthwaite, and Coniston and a brotherhood of mountains all around. An old grey manor house below gives the story its home ground.

Contents run from the sheep shearing and Julius Sandal through Charlotte, the day before Christmas, wooing and wedding, an enemy in the household, Esau, and a new squire. Barr writes warm, rural fiction of family, land, and love. Readers who like English country romance will enjoy its Lakeland color and gentle plot.
16283-idolatry-a-romance:
Julian Hawthorne's Idolatry, published in Boston by James R. Osgood in 1874, is a romance of enchantment, Egypt, and spiritual danger. Contents move from The Enchanted Ring and Out of Egypt through a May morning, a Brahman, a new man with an old face, and the vagaries of Helwyse. A quarrel, a collision imminent, the voice of darkness, and Helwyse resisting the devil deepen the plot, with a chapter called The Tower of Babel along the way.

Later chapters cross Charon's ferry, weigh legend and chronicle, and follow betrothal, marriage, and a black cloud toward peace and good-will. Hawthorne, son of Nathaniel, writes lush, mystical romance. Readers who like Victorian tales of fate, occult lore, and love will find this a rich, strange novel.
16593-general-science:
Bertha M. Clark, head of science at William Penn High School for Girls in Philadelphia, wrote this 1912 general science textbook for school use. Chapters run from heat, temperature, and burning through food, water, and air to light, refraction, photography, and color. Later chapters treat pumps, city water, fermentation, bleaching, dyeing, and drugs.

Clark writes clearly for girls' high school classes, with practical examples at every step. The principal and librarian of her school helped shape the book. Students of science education will find a well-made early textbook, broad, plain, and hands-on.
16705-a-wanderer-in-venice:
E. V. Lucas wanders Venice in this 1914 Macmillan volume, with sixteen color plates by Harry Morley and photographs from paintings. Chapters run from the Bride of the Adriatic through St. Mark's, the Piazza and Campanile, and the Doges' Palace to the Grand Canal, Browning and Wagner, and palaces along the water. A preface quotes an old traveler who prized Venice above four rich manors.

Lucas writes as a charming, learned companion, mixing art, history, and street life. The book suits travelers and armchair wanderers alike. It remains a beloved guide to Venice, rich in pictures and gentle wisdom.
16801-horace-and-his-influence:
Grant Showerman wrote this book on Horace and his influence for the Our Debt to Greece and Rome series, edited by Hadzsits and Robinson. The front matter lists many donors whose gifts made the library possible, from Philadelphia lawyers and doctors to collectors and scholars. The series aims to show what modern life owes to Greece and Rome, book by book.

Showerman traces Horace's verse, wit, and good sense through later ages, showing how a Roman poet shaped schools, letters, and taste. He writes for general readers, not just classicists. The book gives a clear, short guide to Horace's afterlife, and a fine entry to the whole debt series for readers new to Latin letters.
16859-woman-s-endurance:
A. D. L., chaplain in the concentration camp at Bethulie in the Orange River Colony in 1901, wrote this diary of South African women in the Boer War, printed at Cape Town in 1904. A preface by D. de Villiers of the Boer Relief Committee says the diary should convince any reader that these women were heroines, and that its proceeds will aid the orphanage at Bethulie.

The diary tells of camp life, loss, faith, and devotion under harsh rule, in a true and touching voice. Its editor frames it as a legacy of pure faith for all women to follow. The book gives a rare, first-hand account of war as borne by women and children, sober, sad, and full of quiet courage.
16910-a-short-history-of-france:
Mary Platt Parmele wrote this short history of France, illustrated, issued by Scribner's in New York in 1907, with copyrights in 1894, 1898, 1905, and 1906. A frontispiece shows Gambetta proclaiming the Republic, from a painting by Howard Pyle. Chapters run from early Gaul and Caesar's conquest, through Christianity, Franks, Clovis, Charles Martel, Charlemagne, Northmen, feudalism, Hugh Capet, crusades, Philip Augustus, Abelard, and Louis IX, onward.

Parmele gives a brisk, schoolroom survey of France from Gaul to modern times, in plain, narrative prose. Her book suits young readers and general readers who want France in one volume. It gives a clear, old-style outline, useful as a first history, though modern readers will seek later books for depth and balance.
16974-the-story-of-the-9th-king-s-in-fra:
Enos Herbert Glynne Roberts traces a Liverpool regiment from its volunteer roots to war in France. Newspaper and print workers formed the corps in 1861, took their oath at St. George's Hall, and grew through mergers into the King's Liverpool Regiment. Early chapters cover parades, reviews, and drill at home before the move abroad.

The heart of the book follows the 9th King's with the 1st, 55th, and 57th Divisions in France, closing with a list of honors won. Roberts writes as a regimental historian, plain and proud, with dates and places kept clear. Readers keen on local units and the Western Front will find a steady, detailed unit story here.
16999-servia-youngest-member-of-the-euro:
Andrew Archibald Paton's 1845 travel book follows a stay in Belgrade and rides through the highlands and woods of Serbia in 1843 and 1844. The road in runs from Beirut by sea to Varna and up the Danube, with stops at Widdin, Semlin, and the Iron Gates. Once in Serbia, Paton sketches forts, towns, codes, and the men who framed them.

Paton checked his history against Ranke, Engel, and men on the spot, including the framer of the Serbian code. The mix of travel chat and state history gives a lively view of a young state between empires. Readers keen on the Balkans will find a fresh, firsthand picture of Serbia finding its feet.
170-the-haunted-hotel-a-mystery-of-moder:
A London doctor dies under strange circumstances, and his widow remarries in Venice. Wilkie Collins's Haunted Hotel, a mystery of modern Venice, follows Countess Narona to a hotel built on a palace with a dark past. Guests sense a presence, and a headless horror walks the rooms.

Collins divides the tale into four parts, moving from London salons to Venetian canals. A postscript ties the ghost to murder, opium, and a hidden crime. The novel mixes sensation fiction with a modern setting. It remains a chilling lesser-known Collins mystery.
17107-a-bibliographical-antiquarian-and-:
Thomas Frognall Dibdin's second volume of his bibliographical tour, in its 1829 second edition, writes home in letters from France and Germany. Letter One walks Paris boulevards, buildings, and fountains. Later letters describe the Royal Library and its librarians, early printed and rare books, the Arsenal library, Ste. Genevieve, the Mazarine, and the king's private library.

Booksellers, printers, binders, and men of letters fill the later letters, with a Roxburghe banquet for book lovers. Dibdin writes with gusto for fellow collectors, naming books, bindings, and owners at length. Bibliophiles will enjoy a chatty, learned tour of Paris libraries as they stood in the 1820s, before many treasures moved.
17128-noteworthy-families-modern-science:
Francis Galton and Edgar Schuster compiled this 1906 index of kinship among persons of note in modern science. Brief notices cover sixty-six living Fellows of the Royal Society in 1904, drawn from replies to Galton's circular of that spring. Chapters set out general remarks, orders of ability, counts of kin in each degree, and conclusions on marked and unmarked noteworthiness.

The book belongs to the Eugenics Record Office series, and its views on heredity belong firmly to its age. As a record, it gives a dense, factual map of scientific families and their ties. Historians of science will find a useful, if dated, source on who knew whom, and how talent ran in families.
17159-women-of-modern-france:
Hugo P. Thieme's study traces French women from the 1500s to the 1800s, through politics, family, letters, faith, and salons. Chapters pair queens and mistresses of Louis XIV with salon leaders such as Mme. de Sevigne, Mme. Geoffrin, and Mme. du Chatelet, then move to Marie Antoinette, the Revolution, the Empire, and the nineteenth century. The book belongs to a series on woman in all ages and lands.

Thieme sorts his subjects into three kinds: virtuous wives, intriguing mistresses, and women of letters, a frame of its own age. His sketches are short, vivid, and full of names. Modern readers will find a useful, if dated, survey of how French women shaped courts, salons, and books.
17175-the-tapestry-room-a-child-s-romanc:
Mrs. Molesworth's 1899 child's romance, pictured by Walter Crane, opens on a cold terrace where an old raven hobbles in the frost. Inside, children meet Mademoiselle Jeanne and Prince Cheri, and on a moonlit night they step into a tapestry world. A forest of rainbows, frog land, a swan song, and the brown bull of Norrowa fill their night tales.

Dudu, the old storyteller, spins yarns that blend wonder with gentle lessons. The book suits children who like quiet magic and kind endings, told in soft, old-style prose. With Crane's pictures, it remains a charming Victorian fantasy, best read at bedtime or by a winter fire.
17183-atma-a-romance:
Caroline Augusta Frazer, writing as A. C. F., published this Montreal romance in 1891 under the name Atma. The title draws on atman, a word Max Muller notes is often rendered as soul, mind, or spirit, yet best kept as Self. An opening sonnet on decay sets the tone: fading days, fallen faiths, and a hope that old power may return.

The romance turns on faith in its wane and the search for a living spirit beneath dead forms. Its verse-like prose and philosophic bent suit readers who like Victorian tales of religion and the inner life. Short and earnest, the book offers a period meditation on self, loss, and renewal rather than a fast plot.
17287-history-of-france:
Charlotte M. Yonge's History of France, in J. R. Green's History Primers, gives school readers the French story in eight short chapters. Earlier kings open the tale, then the Hundred Years' War, the struggle with Burgundy, Italian wars, wars of religion, power of the crown, the Revolution, and France since the Revolution. Maps of provinces and departments aid the text.

Yonge writes in plain, orderly prose, with Celts, Romans, Goths, Burgundians, and Franks each placed in turn. The primer suits young students and general readers who want a first frame for French history. Its Victorian tone is firm and clear, and its short chapters make a long story easy to follow.
17293-fre-de-ric-mistral-poet-and-leader:
Charles Alfred Downer's 1901 Columbia study treats Frederic Mistral as poet and leader in Provence. Part One covers the revival of Provencal speech: Mistral's life, the Felibrige founded in 1854, the modern Provencal tongue, its verse forms, and Mistral's great dictionary, Lou Tresor dou Felibrige. Part Two reads his long poems Mireio, Calendau, Nerto, and the Rhone poem, plus lyrics and a tragedy.

Downer writes as a scholar of French letters, with a bibliography and index for students. His study shows how a poet saved a language and gave it books. Readers keen on Provence, minority tongues, or French poetry will find a thorough, readable introduction to Mistral's work and cause.
17315-abe-lincoln-gets-his-chance:
Frances Cavanah wrote this children's life of Abraham Lincoln for the Weekly Reader Children's Book Club, published by Rand McNally in 1959 with pictures by Paula Hutchison. Cavanah states that she leaned chiefly on Lincoln's own words and on accounts from family and friends who knew his daily life at first hand. Where talk had to be imagined, she shaped it to fit what is known of the circumstances.

The book follows the young Lincoln toward the chances that made his career, in short chapters suited to young readers. Its tone is plain and encouraging, built to give children a first, human picture of the future president. Readers get a mid-century school book biography, honest about its invented dialogue and warm toward its subject.
17624-a-bibliographical-antiquarian-and-:
Thomas Frognall Dibdin, doctor of divinity and member of academies at Rouen and Utrecht, wrote this bibliographical, antiquarian, and picturesque tour in France and Germany. This third volume, in a second edition printed by William Nicol at the Shakespeare Press, carries the motto that all things are full of God. Its letters run from Strasbourg to Stuttgart and beyond.

Letter one covers Baden, the elder Schweighaeuser, and Stuttgart's public and royal libraries. Letter two covers the royal palace, a bibliographical negotiation, and Dannecker the sculptor. Letter three leaves Stuttgart for Ulm and Augsbourg, with the picture gallery there. Readers get a book lover's tour of libraries and art.
17642-romance:
Joseph Conrad and F. M. Hueffer wrote this novel together, published in 1903 by Doubleday, Page and Company and printed at the Country Life Press in Garden City, New York. The book is divided into five parts: The Quarry and the Beach, The Girl with the Lizard, Casa Riego, Blade and Guitar, and The Lot of Man. Its opening bids a polite farewell to yesterday and today.

What matters is a far-off day of romance, when the narrator's story begins. Readers get a collaboration between two major writers, blending Conrad's sea feeling with Hueffer's romantic invention. The novel suits readers of Conrad and of Ford Madox Ford, Hueffer's later name.
17718-infelice:
Augusta J. Evans Wilson, author of At the Mercy of Tiberius and St. Elmo, published this novel in London in 1902 with James Nisbet and Company. An epigraph from Vanini warns against laying rough hands on any man's opinion, since opinions are venerable properties, and those showing most decrepitude deserve the gentlest handling. That plea for tolerance frames the tale.

The first chapter opens on a stormy night, when a woman waits to see Dr. Hargrove, who is absent, and Hannah the servant cannot say when he will return. Readers get a late Victorian Southern romance of feeling, faith, and endurance, in Wilson's earnest style. The book suits readers of Evans Wilson's popular fiction.
178-confidence:
Bernard Longueville lingers in Siena, sketching and watching two women who will shape his life. Henry James's Confidence follows Bernard, his friend Gordon, and Angela Vivian through Italy and beyond. Gordon asks Bernard to judge Angela's character, a trust that tangles all three.

James studies confidence itself: who deserves it, who betrays it, and how lovers test it. Italian springs, Paris rooms, and American returns set the comedy of manners. The novel's talk and observation matter more than plot twists. It shows James refining the international theme. James's talk of trust and betrayal anticipates the subtler novels of his middle years.
17913-clemence:
Retta B. Babcock wrote Clemence, the Schoolmistress of Waveland, in Cleveland in 1870, after her earlier book Graham Lodge won a kind public. She says she built this work on facts, not wild fancy, since truth from the heart reaches the heart best.

The tale opens with a daughter kneeling by her grieving mother, urging trust in God through hard days. Clemence then takes up school work and the cares of a small town, with loss, faith, and duty close at hand. It is a plain, earnest novel of a woman's life, written for readers who liked tales with a moral core.
18010-marie-gourdon-a-romance-of-the-low:
Maud Ogilvy wrote Marie Gourdon in Montreal in 1890, printed by John Lovell and Son, and dedicated to Lady Helen Munro-Ferguson of Raith. Ogilvy sets her little story on the banks of the lower St. Lawrence, where she spent happy days.

The tale opens on a bright August afternoon at Rimouski, where old French Canadian women nod over spinning-wheels in the heat. Tide, sand, and maple trees frame a romance of the river country, with French songs on the air. Ogilvy writes with a visitor's fond eye. It is a sweet, short Canadian romance, full of sun, river, and old ways.
18097-public-school-domestic-science:
Mrs. J. Hoodless wrote Public School Domestic Science in Toronto in 1898, printed by Copp, Clark, as a text for high and public schools. Hoodless led the School of Domestic Science at Hamilton, and her book could be used by any school whose trustees so ordered.

Chapters teach the link of food to the body, food classes, nutrition, economy, and protein foods, with notes from Atwater on cost and value. A quote from Sir Henry Thompson warns that bad diet breeds more ills than drink. The book is a plain, early home-economics text, and a window on how Canada once taught girls to feed a home well.
18225-the-shield-of-silence:
Harriet T. Comstock wrote The Shield of Silence, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap, copyright 1921 by Doubleday, Page. Comstock, author of Joyce of the North Woods, dedicates the book to her son Philip.

The tale opens with a calm in the soul, like calm in ocean depths, while waves of unrest surge round it. Meredith Thornton wakes at last, her faculties long drugged by training, and Joan rises from her task, torn between hate and pity. Comstock writes of silence, love, and moral choice with earnest warmth. It is a thoughtful, old novel of women's hearts and hidden strength.
18325-with-our-soldiers-in-france:
Sherwood Eddy, author of Suffering and the War, wrote this 1917 account of work with American soldiers in France, published by the Association Press in New York for the YMCA. Eddy dedicates the book to the real heroes of the war: mothers who gave sons and wives who gave husbands. A frontispiece shows the American YMCA headquarters in Paris.

Chapters take readers to the front, with General Pershing's force, through a day in the bull ring, and with the British army. Life in a base camp, the camp of the prodigals, and religion at the front follow. The book opens with a sudden call up the line, over paved French roads crowded with motor transports. Readers get the war behind the guns: huts, singing, refreshments, and chaplains among men far from home.
18361-operation-outer-space:
Murray Leinster wrote this science fiction novel of a crowded Earth looking outward. It opens with Jed Cochrane riding a helicab through the night over a city of fourteen million people. Lighted buildings soar from street canyons, and rooftops serve as recreation space, the only space left. Cochrane, cynical and self-aware, counts other cities of eight, ten, and twelve million.

Cochrane is sent to the rocket port at once, with his secretary, two technical men, and a writer, to take instructions from Dr. William Holden on the way. He rages at the mix-up, insisting he must talk to Hopkins, since the Dikkipatti Hour depends on him. Readers get Leinster's answer to overcrowding: a mission to the Moon, or beyond, sold to a public that must learn to want the stars again.
18369-westminster-sermons-with-a-preface:
Charles Kingsley published this volume of Westminster sermons with Macmillan in London in 1881, prefaced by a paper read at Sion College in 1871. Kingsley says the sermons comment on one idea. They were preached at Westminster Abbey or at a Chapel Royal. Facts of nature, the human heart, and reason do not contradict Church of England doctrine, he says. They coincide with it.

Kingsley calls natural theology more important and more forgotten than it should be, and offers suggestions rather than teaching. He believes a natural theology is possible, and that it should keep pace in every age with doctrinal theology, following Bishop Butler's Analogy of Religion, Natural and Revealed. Readers get a Victorian churchman arguing that science and faith, rightly read, speak the same language.
18390-letters-from-france:
C. E. W. Bean, war correspondent for the Commonwealth of Australia, wrote these letters from France, published by Cassell in London, New York, Toronto, and Melbourne in 1917, with a map and eight plates. Bean dedicates the book to Australians who fell at Fromelles on July 19, 1916, in the sharpest action their force had known. A plate shows Australians watching the bombardment of Pozieres while their mates lay beneath it.

Chapters move to the front, through a country with eyes, the road to Lille, the differences, the Germans, the planes, and the coming struggle. Later letters give Fricourt and La Boisselle, the dugouts, a raid, Pozieres, an abysm of desolation, Pozieres Ridge, and the green country. The book opens with a padre speaking rightly to sunburnt troops aboard a liner. Readers get the Australian war in letters: mud, battle, and mates, written by the man who became Australia's official historian.
18483-fighting-france:
Stéphane Lauzanne, lieutenant in the French army, chevalier of the Legion of Honor, and editor in chief of Le Matin, wrote this war book, published by D. Appleton in New York and London in 1918, with an introduction by James M. Beck and translation by John L. B. Williams. Lauzanne was a member of the French mission to the United States.

He dedicates the book to his chiefs, his comrades, and his men, who fight for the great cause of liberty and civilization. The book gives a French officer's view of the Great War, written while the fighting still went on, and meant to carry France's case to American readers.
18493-introduction-to-non-violence:
Theodore Paullin wrote this pamphlet for the Pacifist Research Bureau in Philadelphia in July 1944, as number one in series three of Non-Violent Action in Tension Areas. The bureau's members included Dorothy Day, A. J. Muste, Clarence Pickett, and many other pacifist leaders of the day.

Chapters move from an introduction on terms to violence without hate, non-violence by necessity, non-violent coercion, and satyagraha, or non-violent direct action. Later sections take up non-resistance, active goodwill and reconciliation, and conclusions, offering a wartime case for action that refuses hate while still resisting wrong.
18507-angelic-wisdom-about-divine-provid:
Emanuel Swedenborg wrote this work on divine providence, first published in Latin at Amsterdam in 1764, here in William Frederic Wunsch's standard translation for the Swedenborg Foundation of New York. The first English translation in the United States appeared in 1851, and this printing is the fifty-first, from 1975. Swedenborg writes as a theologian of the inner sense of Scripture, setting out how God's care governs the world.

Contents ask what divine providence is, its goal and outlook, and its laws, with regard for human freedom and reason. Later chapters treat the struggle against evil, noncompulsion, overt and hidden guidance, human prudence, time and eternity, profanation, tolerance, and why evil is permitted. Readers get Swedenborg's system in order: a providence that attends the evil and the good alike, without forcing the will it seeks to save.
18515-police:
Robert W. Chambers wrote this book of linked stories, published by D. Appleton in New York and London in 1915, with pictures by Henry Hutt. Chambers dedicates the volume to Louise Jocelyn in verse, praising the pretty things she says and does, turning autumn into May. The book's title, Police, with three exclamation marks, points to its comic, fantastic strain rather than to a police procedural.

Contents give The Third Eye, The Immortal, The Ladies of the Lake, One Over, Un Peu d'Amour, and The Eggs of the Silver Moon. Illustrations promise dainty noses to the wind, climbing among mangroves, a concertina played to lure a cave girl down a hill, and coquina slabs. Readers get Chambers in his fanciful mode: strange peoples, lost worlds, and romance, told with the light touch that made his early books popular.
18520-sabotage-in-space:
Carey Rockwell wrote this Tom Corbett Space Cadet adventure, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York in 1955, with Willy Ley as technical adviser and pictures by Louis Glanzman. Sabotage in Space stands among the Space Cadet books. It follows Stand by for Mars, Danger in Deep Space, and On the Trail of the Space Pirates. The Space Pioneers, The Revolt on Venus, and Treachery in Outer Space came before it as well.

The book opens at nine in the evening, when an electronic time tone booms from the Tower of Galileo over Space Academy, U.S.A. Lights wink out in cadet dormitories and slidewalks crisscross the campus. Tom Corbett and his fellow cadets face sabotage that threatens ships, crews, and the academy's name. Young readers get a space academy mystery: drills, rockets, and a saboteur hidden among the very people trained to stop him.
18555-a-chance-acquaintance:
W. D. Howells published this novel with James R. Osgood in Boston in 1873, printed by the University Press at Cambridge. The story opens on the forward promenade of a Saguenay boat leaving Quebec on a Tuesday morning, where Miss Kitty Ellison waits for departure.

Kitty watches the St. Lawrence and Quebec in warm yellow light, with the citadel flag above the Upper Town and tinned roofs below. The novel follows a chance meeting on a pleasure trip, where a young woman's hopes, manners, and judgments meet a stranger's, and a brief acquaintance tests what each takes for character.
18651-a-cigarette-maker-s-romance:
F. Marion Crawford published this romance at New York and London in 1894, after an 1890 copyright. It opens in the inner room of a Munich tobacconist's shop, a place Crawford admits few novelists would pick for a stage. His opening pages compare life to a play, with Fate as manager and each person cast for a leading part, a walk-on, or a supernumerary.

From that curious stage the romance unfolds, with Munich streets and shop life at the fore. Crawford, known for Mr. Isaacs and Dr. Claudius, writes in a rich, reflective style. The novel is a charming, offbeat love story from a popular writer of the day.
18786-treachery-in-outer-space:
Carey Rockwell wrote this Tom Corbett Space Cadet tale, published at New York by Grosset and Dunlap in 1954, technical advice by Willy Ley, pictures by Louis Glanzman. It opens in a dormitory where Astro, the giant Venusian cadet, hazes three frightened newcomers, Coglin, Spears, and Duke, while Tom Corbett and Roger Manning watch, trying not to laugh. Correct address, Astro insists, is Very well, not sir.
