Henry H. Saylor, author of Bungalows and Making a Rose Garden, published this practical book with McBride, Nast and Company at New York in January 1913. Saylor argues that a good fireplace is not simply a large one with a strong draft. Colonial ancestors built cavernous openings and generous flues, losing perhaps ninety percent of the heat up the chimney while blistering toes and chilling backs.

Chapters cover construction, odd forms, facings and mantels, mending poor fireplaces, accessories, and building the fire. Illustrations show an English basket grate in brass, an inglenook with stone hearth, a Caen stone mantel, and a craftsman-style brick fireplace with a copper hood. Saylor wants a steady blaze whose heat the back and sides reflect into the room.
26847-a-pessimist-in-theory-and-practice:
Robert Timsol published this novel with John B. Alden of New York in 1888. Its narrator, Bob, has seen little of his college friend Hartman since their student days, when Hartman counted as a youth of eminent promise. Last May, fishing and resting after a year of close business, Bob stumbles on Hartman in a secluded woodland region and is taken home to a comfortable bachelor establishment. Hartman reads, fishes, climbs, rides several hobbies, and meditates on man, nature, and human fate.

Thirty-four chapters follow. They run from Wisdom in the Woods and Worse Yet through complications, a wilful princess, and a stay at Newport. They close with conspiracy, apology for lying, and a family conclave. Hartman's dogs, the neighborhood hens, and a few small farmers are his company, and his wit, in Bob's phrase, has a nasty nagging fashion. The book closes with advice to persons about to marry.
2685-the-way-to-peace:
Margaret Deland sets this novel in Kennebunkport, Maine, in August 1910, opening with Athalia Hall pausing for breath on a steep road above a covered bridge. Dawn air, bay scent, and dew drenched leaves fill the valley as night still hangs like gauze below.

Athalia's way to peace runs through family duty, love, and the quiet choices of a New England life. Deland writes with warmth and moral clarity, in the tradition of the village novel. The book offers a gentle story of a woman finding calm after storm, and of a town that watches her.
26889-the-pools-of-silence:
De Vere Stacpoole, author of The Blue Lagoon, published this novel with Duffield and Company in 1910. Forty-two chapters in four parts open in Paris on January 4, at the last post-graduate lecture of Thénard, the Beaujon Hospital's famous neurologist. Among the crowded benches sits Dr. Paul Quincy Adams, a six-foot-two Vermonter who walked from his rooms in the Rue Dijon because omnibuses were slow and cabs dear.

From Paris the story moves to Matadi and Yandjali, into the voice of the Congo forest, big game country, and the pools that give the book its name. There an antelope vanishes from the foggy margin, and a leopard's roaring head is jerked under the surface by something beneath the water. Later chapters promise elephant land, the great herd, the feast of vultures, and Captain Berselius beholding his other self.
26902-the-rover-boys-in-alaska-or-lost-i:
Arthur M. Winfield, the pen name of Edward Stratemeyer, published this Rover Boys book with Grosset and Dunlap in 1914. It belongs to the first Rover Boys series. Earlier titles run from the Rover Boys at school and on the ocean through the jungle, out west, and on the great lakes. They continue in the mountains, in camp, and on treasure isle. Thirty chapters carry Tom, Dick, and Sam Rover from college days to Alaska and back.

The book opens with Tom and Sam back at college life's grind. Tom is still dizzy from Pelter's footstool whack. Tom disappears. Dick and Sam chase clues through Chicago and Seattle to Juneau and Skagway, and the trail leads into the mountains of Alaska. A slide down the mountainside, a shelter under the cliff, the grip of a tornado, and the fields of ice stand between the brothers and good-bye to Alaska.
26945-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for December 1878 opens with Danubian Days, a steamer journey from Belgrade to Pesth past cliffs, forests, and moss-grown ruins. The writer watches the Servian people with sympathy, noting their hard lot, their pride in cannon taken from the Turks, and their love of their native land.

The rest of the number carries the magazine's usual mix: a serialized novel running into its late chapters, with engagements hostile and otherwise, plus popular literature and science for the general reader. The issue shows a Victorian monthly doing what it did best, pairing travel, fiction, and instruction.
26967-the-coming-of-the-ice:
G. Peyton Wertenbaker's 1926 story from Amazing Stories opens with the last man on earth, alone in endless snow and twilight. The narrator, cut off from every human voice, looks back to 1930, when the surgeon Sir John Granden began the operations that would stretch his life across ages.

As the ice creeps over the world and the years blur into thousands, the narrator keeps asking one question: what year is it now? The tale mixes early science fiction with a lonely meditation on time, love, and what remains of a man when everyone he knew is gone.
2706-the-bravo-of-venice-a-romance:
This romance of Venice, translated from the German by M. G. Lewis, comes with an introduction on Lewis himself. Lewis professed to have translated the tale out of German, much as Horace Walpole once framed his own romance, and the introduction weighs that claim with amusement.

The story follows a bravo, a hired swordsman, through Venetian canals, conspiracies, and midnight rescues. Daggers, masks, and noble villains crowd a city built for intrigue. The book delights as gothic melodrama, and as a sample of the tales that fed English readers' hunger for Italy.
27232-the-white-mice:
Richard Harding Davis's The White Mice, published by Scribner's in 1912 with illustrations by George Gibbs, opens with the lion and the mouse. The mouse begs life, then gnaws the hunter's net and frees the lion. The fable sets the novel's theme of small helpers and great debts.

Peter de Peyster hears the call of the White Mice, Roddy shifts reins to his revolver, and a masked man staggers under a blow. The action runs to Venezuela, where a hero cries that now he knows why he came, in Davis's brisk adventure of rescue and revolution.
27325-my-sword-s-my-fortune-a-story-of-o:
Herbert Hayens's My Sword's My Fortune, a story of old France from Collins' Clear-Type Press in 1904, sends its hero to Paris, to La Boule d'Or, and into the astrologer's house. He meets the Cardinal, attends the reception at the Luxembourg, and discovers the plot.

Pillot comes to the rescue, escapes narrow, a trap leads to the Bastille, and freedom brings a fight on the staircase. The Queen's friends in Paris are few, yet the country stands ready to fight for the King. A timid coachman leaves the hero to drive the escape coach, through the mob's rising to Mazarin triumphant.
27368-the-cult-of-incompetence:
Emile Faguet of the French Academy wrote this sharp critique of democratic government, translated from the French by Beatrice Barstow with an introduction by Thomas Mackay, and published by E. P. Dutton in 1912. Faguet argues that modern states hand public work to people unfit for it, and that the fault lies in the system itself rather than in any one party.

His chapters take up confusion of functions, the competence of legislators, laws under democracy, judicial incompetence, and attempted remedies, closing with a chapter called The Dream. Even in translation, the argument keeps its force and bite. Readers interested in why governments fail will find a provocative, old-fashioned polemic here.
27395-the-slave-of-silence:
F. M. White, author of Tregarthen's Wife and The Robe of Lucifer, published this novel of mystery and pursuit with Little, Brown in Boston in November 1906, from a 1904 copyright. Forty short chapters carry the action forward at speed, with illustrations that catch its most violent moments.

The frontispiece shows a pair rushing at Berrington, who fires right and left, while later pictures show Richford shaking and quivering with passion and a police officer eyeing a figure with suspicion. Silence, and what it costs to keep it, drives the plot. Readers of Edwardian thrillers will find a brisk, eventful example of the kind.
27508-the-king-s-warrant-a-story-of-old-:
Alfred H. Engelbach, author of Poor Little Gaspard's Drum, published this historical novel in London with the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge in 1878. It came under the direction of its Committee of General Literature and Education, with a New York edition from E. and J. B. Young. Its three parts are The Two Orphans, The Lettre de Cachet, and The Fall of New France.

The story opens as England and France formally draw the sword sheathed since Aix-la-Chapelle, eight years earlier. The Seven Years' War begins in earnest, though their American dependencies have fought for two years already. A girl pleads softly for news of the missing, and a fiery little king of the kitchen seizes a man by the throat. Engelbach tells old and new France in one tale.
2761-benita-an-african-romance:
H. Rider Haggard wrote this African romance from a tale he believed had a foundation in fact. Some twenty five or thirty years earlier, an adventurous trader heard from natives behind Quilimane a legend of treasure buried in the sixteenth century by a party of Portuguese.

Benita, a young Englishwoman, is drawn into the search, with love, danger, and a ghostly past guiding her steps. Haggard writes with his usual African color and supernatural hints. The novel offers a treasure hunt with a heroine at its heart, and a past that refuses to stay buried.
27705-the-golden-face-a-great-crook-roma:
William Le Queux, author of Mademoiselle of Monte Carlo and The Stretton Street Affair, published this great crook romance with the Macaulay Company of New York in 1922. An illustration shows the narrator slipping a pendant into Lady Lydbrook's soft hand at her half-open bedroom door.

The narrator opens by easing his conscience and disclosing facts that puzzled newspaper readers for a year or two. After much perplexity, he resolves to make a clean breast of curious and sensational circumstances. Chapters run from Private and Personal and Room Number 88 through the man with the hump, the four false fingers, and the painted envelope, to Abdul Hamid's jewels. The sign of ninety-nine closes the list.
27709-five-o-clock-tea-farce:
W. D. Howells wrote this one-act farce about a five o'clock tea, first published in 1894 by Harper and Brothers with illustrations. The scene is Mrs. Amy Somers's drawing room, where guests gather and talk over tea.

The comedy turns on social maneuvering: Mrs. Somers rehearses poses before her mirror, then spars with Mr. Willis Campbell over a question she will not answer directly. Light, witty, and brief, the play shows Howells's gift for drawing character out of polite conversation. The frontispiece shows Campbell pressing his question on Amy Somers.
27766-romance-of-roman-villas-the-renais:
Elizabeth W. Champney wrote this 1908 volume on the romance of Roman villas in the Renaissance, published by G. P. Putnam's Sons with illustrations in photogravure. It follows her books on Italian villas, feudal châteaux, and French abbeys.

Chapters visit the Vatican's Villa of the Belvedere, the Villa Farnesina, the Villa Madama, the Villa d'Este with Tasso, and Hadrian's Villa. Champney blends history, art, and anecdote, from the finding of the Apollo Belvedere to the ladies of Palliano, for readers who loved Rome through its stories. The frontispiece shows Pope Julius II viewing the newly found Apollo Belvedere, after a painting by Carl Becker.
27880-evening-dress-farce:
W. D. Howells wrote Evening Dress, a farce published by Harper and Brothers in 1893 in their Black and White Series, illustrated and priced at fifty cents. The play opens with Mrs. Edward Roberts urging her husband to reach a party in time for at least the last half, though he is dead tired from a night train.

Illustrations show a trust scene, sleeves a trifle short, and that little supper, marking the comedy of clothes and social obligation. Howells's farce turns evening dress into a small domestic crisis, with the manners and misunderstandings of polite society supplying the laughs.
2793-flip-a-california-romance:
Bret Harte sets this romance where the Los Gatos road climbs like a fiery rocket's trail into the blue shadows of the Coast Range. Near the summit lies an embayed terrace hedged by dwarf firs, wistfully eyed by every traveler on the heat laden road.

Flip, a wild girl of the mountains, meets a stranger from the world below, and love grows between freedom and convention. Harte writes with pastoral charm and a light hand. The novella offers a California idyll, where a girl as free as the hills must choose her road.
28004-a-little-tour-in-france:
Henry James published A Little Tour in France with William Heinemann in London in 1900, with ninety-four illustrations by Joseph Pennell. The tour moves from Tours and its cathedral through Blois, Chambord, Amboise, Chenonceaux, and Loches to Bourges, Le Mans, Angers, and Nantes.

Later chapters visit La Rochelle, Poitiers, Toulouse, Carcassonne, Nîmes, Arles, Avignon, and Dijon, with the Pont du Gard and the Palace of the Popes among the sights. James writes as a literary traveler, attentive to architecture, history, and atmosphere, and the book is a classic of travel writing.
28047-strange-alliance:
Bryce Walton wrote Strange Alliance, a science-fiction story opening with Doctor Spechaug running down a narrow road at nine in the morning with fresh blood on his hands and brown serge suit. He does not react emotionally to the blood, and he realizes he has lost minutes from his memory.

Spechaug hates the silent ignorance of the peasants around Glen Oaks, and his wife, taken from a local barnyard, most of all. He sees a chance to escape the place he has wanted to leave for five years. The tale, haunted by a dark heritage, turns a professor's blackout into a story of fate and a strange alliance.
28053-celebration-in-baltimore-of-the-tr:
William Wirt delivered this address in Baltimore on Monday, October 25, 1830, at a public celebration of liberty in France. The city had gathered to mark the July Revolution, which had driven Charles X from the French throne and set Louis-Philippe in his place. The volume, printed by John D. Toy, preserves the day's proceedings by order of its committee.

Wirt's speech praises free government, links the French rising to America's own revolution, and urges citizens to guard liberty at home. The book gives historians a clear record of how Americans in 1830 greeted news from Paris. It reads as both a civic oration and a snapshot of Jacksonian-era public feeling.
28241-a-padre-in-france:
George A. Birmingham wrote A Padre in France as a chaplain's memoir of the First World War. Birmingham, author of General John Regan and Spanish Gold, served with troops in France, moving from camp to camp, hut to hut, and convalescent camp to backwater. Chapters cover khaki, leisure hours, Woodbine Hut, and the daily round of a padre's work.

Birmingham opens with Balak and Balaam, on kings who seek spiritual help against invasion, and tells his own work with humour and plain faith. He meets soldiers, nurses, and French villagers, and learns the war zone by foot. The book gives a warm, first-hand view of chaplain life.
28540-bibliomania-or-book-madness-a-bibl:
Thomas Frognall Dibdin's Bibliomania, or Book-Madness, first published in 1809, returns here in the new and improved edition of 1876 from Chatto and Windus. The bibliographical romance, illustrated with cuts, carries the motto that books led some men to knowledge and others to madness. A supplement adds preliminary observations and a key to the assumed characters in the drama.

Dibdin dedicates the edition to the Earl of Powis, president of the Roxburgh Club, and fills footnotes with book catalogues, descriptions, and prices. Collectors, auctions, and rival bibliophiles drive the comedy. Readers get a book about book lovers, learned, gossipy, and fond of its own madness.
28613-pioneers-of-science:
Oliver Lodge's Pioneers of Science, published by Macmillan and Company in 1893 with portraits and illustrations, lectures on astronomy's makers. Lodge, professor of physics at Victoria University College, Liverpool, begins with Copernicus and the motion of the Earth. Tycho Brahé and the earliest observatory, Kepler and planetary laws, and Galileo with telescope and Inquisition follow.

Descartes and his vortices lead to Newton's Principia, then Roemer and Bradley on the velocity of light. Lagrange and Laplace, Herschel, asteroids, Bessel, Neptune, comets, meteors, and the tides complete the course. Readers get the solar system explained through the lives that unlocked it, lecture by lecture.
28631-amabel-channice:
Anne Douglas Sedgwick's Amabel Channice, published by the Century Company of New York in October 1908, opens at Charlock House. Lady Channice waits for her son Augustine to come in from the garden, with tea ready and the kettle steaming. The grey stone house stands low and solid, its lawn sloping to a sunken wall, a sluggish stream, and flat meadows beyond.

Inside, the drawing-room is wainscotted in ancient oak, lit by four high windows yet dark, with cracked maroon leather chairs. Lady Channice has quietly removed the ugliest ornaments, from gilt footstools to birds under glass. Readers get a restrained novel of a lonely house and the peace its mistress seeks.
28832-the-sargasso-of-space:
Edmond Hamilton wrote this science fiction story, first printed in Astounding Stories in September 1931. The freighter Pallas, bound from Jupiter toward Neptune, loses its fuel through leaking tanks and drifts helplessly toward a dead area of space, a graveyard where wrecked ships gather. Captain Crain tells his twenty-odd officers and men the plain facts: the main radio is dead, the auxiliary set cannot reach Neptune, and the rockets cannot fire without fuel.

The tale follows the crew's debate over abandoning ship in space suits or waiting for rescue that may never come. Hamilton, a pioneer of space opera, builds dread from simple arithmetic: fuel, distance, and drift. Readers get a tense early example of the stranded-spaceship story, with a captain's calm and a crew's fear carrying the plot.
28877-penelope-s-progress-being-such-ext:
Kate Douglas Wiggin wrote this 1897 travel story, Penelope's Progress, drawn from the commonplace book of Penelope Hamilton and her experiences in Scotland. Penelope, already known from Penelope's English Experiences, now tours Scotland with her friends, recording what she sees and hears in witty, observant entries. Houghton, Mifflin published it in Boston and New York, in a binding meant to look Scottish.

Wiggin, author of The Birds' Christmas Carol and Timothy's Quest, writes light travel humor with a warm eye for people and places. The book suits readers who like old-fashioned travel writing: anecdotes, dialogue, and description rather than guidebook facts. It remains a charming record of how an American woman of the 1890s saw Scotland, and of the friendships that made the journey.
29007-the-skilful-cook-a-practical-manua:
Mary Harrison wrote this practical manual of modern cookery, The Skilful Cook, in an eighth edition of 1905 from J. M. Dent in London. Harrison, a first-class diplomée of South Kensington and lecturer on hygiene, domestic economy, and cookery, dedicates the book by permission to Princess Christian. Its contents run from hints to young housekeepers, food and diet, and the table, to how to cook and how to clean.

The book belongs to a series that also offered a guide to modern cookery, three hundred sixty-six menus, and twelve hundred recipes of Baron Brisse. Harrison writes for housekeepers who want sound, modern practice rather than show. Readers get a solid Edwardian cookery manual, practical in tone and broad in coverage, from the table to the kitchen's daily work.
2911-justice:
John Galsworthy's Justice follows William Falder, a junior clerk in a solicitor's office, whose forgery and love for Ruth Honeywill lead him to prison. The cast includes the solicitors James and Walter How, their managing clerk Cokeson, a judge, advocates, a prison governor, a chaplain, a doctor, and warders. The action moves from office to courtroom to cell.

The play's force lies in its attack on a system that breaks the men it punishes, as Ruth describes a fate hanging over Falder. Her advocate asks whether her danger and unhappiness affect his balance, his control, and even his reason, and she answers yes. Justice helped change British attitudes toward solitary confinement and remains Galsworthy's most influential play.
29224-the-group-a-farce:
Mercy Warren wrote this farce in two acts, extracted here from Representative Plays by American Dramatists, volume one. Warren, who lived from 1728 to 1814, wrote in a Revolutionary America where most literature was satirical and where Congress had urged patriots to shun the theatre. Her play turns that satire to the stage.

The Group mocks its targets through named types: Crusty Crowbar, Hector Mushroom, Beau Trumps, and Hum Humbug. Warren, a leading woman writer of the Revolution, uses comedy as political argument. Readers get a rare early American political farce, sharp and partisan, from a woman who watched the Revolution's leaders at close range.
29256-high-finance:
Otto H. Kahn delivered this address, High Finance, at the annual dinner of the American Newspaper Publishers Association on April 27, 1916, at the Waldorf-Astoria in New York. Kahn begins with the term itself, from the French haute finance, which in Europe named the most respectable and trustworthy financial houses. In America, he notes, the term had come to suggest something different.

Kahn asks why the United States alone among great nations shows widespread suspicion, even hostility, toward finance and especially toward New York, the country's financial capital. Finance cannot be absolved, he admits, but deeper causes lie beneath. Readers get a banker's public defense of his calling, frank about its faults and impatient with its critics, on the eve of American entry into war.
29272-no-hiding-place:
Richard R. Smith wrote this space war story about a reversal of fortune. Earth lies enveloped in atomic fire, and a ship becomes a prize of war. Disaster, the story says, may make victory mandatory. The ship leaps toward the stars, engines roaring and bulkheads protesting, while Emmett Corbin in the control room endures heat, fumes, and the screech of tormented metal.

Smith's foes, the Agronians, are destructive and malicious. The magazine's introduction says readers will forgive the hero for turning a victory technique back on its makers, in a move almost too ghastly to contemplate. He fills their ship with that unexpected reversal. Readers get a hard, exciting tale of conflict in space, where human heroism becomes the cornerstone of a desperate fight.
29273-a-complete-edition-of-the-works-of:
Nancy Luce of West Tisbury, Dukes County, Massachusetts, published this complete edition of her works in New Bedford in 1875, printed by the Mercury Job Press. Luce, a poor island woman who kept hens as companions, wrote poems and prose pieces with plain, urgent feeling. Her titles show her concerns: God's Words, Sickness, Poor Little Hearts, Milk, No Comfort, and Prayers.

Luce's central theme is kindness to helpless creatures. God, she writes, forbids all cruelty to dumb creatures and to helpless humans, and will hear the cry of the afflicted. Her hen's names, including Poor Little Tweedle and Pinky, fill the pages with affection. Readers get a rare voice from the margins of nineteenth-century America, devout, eccentric, and tender toward animals.
29276-morals-in-trade-and-commerce:
Frank B. Anderson, president of the Bank of California National Association, delivered this lecture before students of the University of California at Berkeley on February 15, 1911, under the Barbara Weinstock Foundation. Anderson speaks to young people about ideals and commerce, asking what picture of service or goal they carry into the world.

Youth's power and eagerness to make ideals, Anderson says, is its most beautiful thing, and the unfortunate person goes out without some goal to attain. Ideals change with changing needs, but the making of them does not. Readers get a banker's address on business ethics, plain and earnest, urging students to let conscience shape careers in trade and commerce.
29283-salvage-in-space:
Jack Williamson published this story in Astounding Stories in March 1933. Thad Allen, a meteor miner, works a lump of iron he calls his planet, the smallest and loneliest in the solar system. In bulky Osprey space armor and magnetic boots, he secures a meteorite the size of his head to the mass he has built up over five perilous weeks.

Allen's dangerous bonanza arrives as a derelict rocket-flier, manned, the magazine says, by death invisible. Williamson turns salvage into suspense: a lone miner, a dead ship, and a prize that may kill him. Readers get a classic space-mining tale about hard work, isolation, and a find that is worth more than its metal.
29331-the-crevice:
William J. Burns and Isabel Ostrander published this mystery novel in New York in 1915 with Grosset and Dunlap, illustrated by Will Grefe. Its chapters open with Pennington Lawton and the Grim Reaper, then revelations, Henry Blaine taking a hand, the search, and the will. A first counter-move, a letter, and Guy Morrow facing a problem follow.

Later chapters bring a disappearance, Margaret Hefferman's failure, the confidence of Emily, and a cipher. An empty house, checkmate, a library chair, a rescue, and a trap close the plot. Burns, the famous detective, lends the book its investigative air. Readers get an early twentieth-century detective novel, plotted through wills, ciphers, and counter-moves.
29335-a-gold-hunter-s-experience:
Chalkley J. Hambleton published this gold-hunting memoir in Chicago in 1898, printed for private circulation. Hambleton writes from memory and from old letters to his sister in the east, answering friends who often asked him to write up his Pike's Peak expedition. The book is a personal account, not a guide.

Early in the summer of 1860, Hambleton caught gold fever. Chicago, after the panic of 1857, lay in depression, money scarce and business dull. Gold found near Pike's Peak in the fall of 1858 by Georgian prospectors drew hundreds west. Readers get a firsthand gold-rush memoir, modest and direct, about hope, hardship, and a young man's gamble on the frontier.
29353-vampires-of-space:
Sewell Peaslee Wright published this story in Astounding Stories in March 1932, with Commander John Hanson telling of a terrifying encounter with the Electites of space. Hanson, now called old John Hanson by youngsters in blue-and-silver uniforms, insists the joke is not always on him. He takes amusement in watching cocky young officers of the Special Patrol Service.

Young Clippen, a nice clean youngster and third officer on the Caliobre, one of the newest patrol ships, drops in to see Hanson whenever he has leave. Hanson's tale then turns to the Electites, whose attack meets the patrol's sprays in midair, as the illustration shows. Readers get a space adventure of strange, draining foes, told by a veteran commander with a storyteller's relish.
29375-manufacturing-cost-data-on-artific:
Otto Luhr, consulting engineer, and Herman Friedl, architect, published this cost study in Chicago for their ice-making system, patent applied for. The pamphlet argues that artificial ice, frozen from pure clean water by refrigeration, is more sanitary than natural ice cut from lakes and rivers in winter. In time, the authors say, natural ice will be banned except where its source is beyond doubt.

Numbered sections break down costs: engine room labor, ice plant labor, office expense, overhead, power, and sales assumptions. Luhr and Friedl claim their method cuts labor to the minimum and lets artificial ice sell at natural ice prices. Readers get a practical early business pamphlet, useful for historians of refrigeration and for anyone tracing how ice became a manufactured product.
29378-pinafore-palace:
Kate Douglas Wiggin and Nora Archibald Smith made this 1907 verse book for very young children, drawn from the idea that every home with a young child counts as a Pinafore Palace. Grosset and Dunlap printed it in the Children's Crimson Series, with two main parts: The Royal Baby and Little Prince and Princess. Rhymes cover baby's plays, hush-a-byes, journeys, friends, heroes, and nonsense, plus grandmother's wisdom.

The verse is soft, playful, and meant to be read aloud to toddlers in pinafores or kilts. Wiggin and Smith speak straight to the small court of listeners, with warmth and a light comic touch. Parents, teachers, and students of children's verse will find a sweet, period-perfect sample of nursery poetry from a century ago.
29399-clairvoyance:
C. W. Leadbeater's 1903 book, second edition from the Theosophical Publishing Society in London, sets out the Theosophical view of clairvoyance, or clear sight beyond the senses. Chapters define the power, then divide it with care: simple clairvoyance, full and partial; clairvoyance in space, intentional, semi-intentional, and unintentional; and clairvoyance in time, toward past and future. Leadbeater writes for readers who know some occult terms, and he apologizes to those who do not.

The book claims to map powers that science of its day could not test, in calm, systematic prose. Its interest now lies in what it reveals about Theosophy at its height. Students of esoteric thought, psychical research, and Edwardian occultism will find a full, earnest primer on a once-fashionable art.
29462-the-house-under-the-sea-a-romance:
Max Pemberton, author of Kronstadt and The Phantom Army, set this 1902 romance in the Pacific, printed by D. Appleton and Company of New York. A plain seaman tells the story of Ken's Island at the request of many gentlemen, as best his ability allows. Jasper Begg commissions the steamship Southern Cross through Philips, Westbury, and Company for a voyage whose purpose unfolds chapter by chapter.

The crew goes ashore, learns strange things, goes aboard, and returns again, while a picture asks the tale's question: shall we go, or stay? Pemberton writes a sea yarn of mystery and daring. Readers of Edwardian adventure will enjoy a brisk romance of islands, ships, and secrets under the sea.
29475-under-arctic-ice:
H. G. Winter's novelette, printed in Astounding Stories in January 1933 as a follow-up to Seed of the Arctic Ice, races to the aid of the submarine Peary, lost beneath polar ice. Ken Torrance heads poleward through eight short chapters, from an empty room and a crash to the fate of the Peary, a last assault, and a duel. Search planes, the tale reports, have come back with no clue to the lost boat.

Winter mixes real polar peril with pulp wonder: a trapped crew, an icy limbo, and avenging sealmen who guard the deep. The pace is brisk, the chapters short, and the stakes plain. Fans of early science adventure will enjoy a taut rescue yarn where cold, dark water and strange foes press hard on brave men.
29548-warrior-race:
Robert Sheckley's short tale opens with a survey note: three planets, intelligent human-type life on the second, a unique social structure, and a population stable at three billion. Its tag line claims that breaking the foe's spirit is war's true aim, and the aliens knew the best method. Fannia and Donnaught, stranded twenty light-years from Thetis with only a cup of emergency fuel, blame each other for the tanks.

Fannia points out that Donnaught, with the build of an ox, should have checked the tanks, while Donnaught blames Fannia's nose for blocking his gauge reading. They can squeeze three light-years from the fuel before falling back on atomics. Fans of Sheckley will enjoy a sharp, funny tale of war, blame, and alien ways.
29573-the-o-ruddy-a-romance:
Stephen Crane, author of The Red Badge of Courage, and Robert Barr, author of Tekla, wrote The O'Ruddy together, printed in 1903 by Frederick A. Stokes Company of New York. Its hero tells of chieftain ancestors at Glandore for many centuries. They were so well known that hardly a vessel could pass the Old Head of Kinsale, since boats put off to exchange greetings. The family name, he says, was spoken in half the seaports of Europe.

The romance that follows mixes Irish swagger, swords, and love, with two swords left by a father: a grand one given by King Louis and a plain one. Readers of romantic adventure will find a high-spirited tale, finished after Crane's death, full of Irish wit and daring.
298-the-market-place:
A financier sits alone after a sweeping victory, sensing its shapeless scale. Harold Frederic's Market-Place opens with a victor who holds his enemies at mercy and wonders when to stop grinding their faces. Vistas of conquest stretch in every direction.

The novel follows market battles, ruined rivals, and the moral weight of winning without limit. Frederic, who also wrote Theron Ware, studies ambition in the age of trusts. The opening's fascinated pain sets the book's tone. It remains a sharp novel of money and power. Frederic died before finishing his market novel's full design.
29810-the-girl-scouts-their-history-and-:
Girl Scouts, Incorporated, printed this handbook as Series Number 6, from national headquarters at 189 Lexington Avenue, New York City. Its motto is Be Prepared, and its slogan is Do a Good Turn Daily. The promise binds a scout to do her duty to God and country, help other people at all times, and obey the Scout Laws. Ten laws follow, from honor to be trusted through loyalty, courtesy, thrift, and cleanliness in thought, word, and deed.

The history opens with Sir Robert Baden-Powell, whose Boy Scout movement in England proved too attractive to limit to boys. The Girl Guides, its sister organization, quickly followed. Juliette Low, an American visiting England and a personal friend of Scouting's father, saw the movement's future for her country. The handbook tells how she brought it home and built its practice.
29820-the-cathedrals-of-northern-france:
Francis Miltoun wrote The Cathedrals of Northern France for the Cathedral Series, with eighty pictures, plans, and diagrams by Blanche McManus. L. C. Page and Company of Boston printed it in 1903, in October of that year. Miltoun and McManus dedicate the book to the genius of race that made possible these architectural glories of France. An apologia opens on two ways of writing travel: recounting the journey or giving its results.

Four parts order the tour: transition examples at Laon, Noyon, and Soissons, then the grand group of Amiens, Beauvais, Rouen, St. Denis, Paris, Le Mans, Chartres, and Reims. The Loire cathedrals and central France follow. The book gives history, plan, and picture together, for readers who want to know the great churches rather than merely admire them.
29838-common-science:
Carleton W. Washburne, superintendent of schools at Winnetka, Illinois, wrote Common Science for the New-World Science Series, edited by John W. Ritchie. Washburne had taught physical science and educational psychology at the State Normal School in San Francisco. His book, illustrated with photographs, sits beside Delos Fall's Science for Beginners and Moseley's Trees, Stars, and Birds in the same series.

The book gives science for beginners in plain, schoolroom style, with experiments and review work for young students. A transcriber's note warns modern readers that much of the science has been superseded, and that some experiments are hazardous and should not be tried at home. Advice on toxic substances and electrical apparatus, it says, should not be followed. Read with that caution, the book is a window on 1920s school science.
29889-life-sentence:
James McConnell wrote this short tale with pictures by Dick Francis. Its epigraph asks a strange question: how often should one hear Happy New Year said in a single lifetime? Outside, bells ring and crowds shout the greeting, while music waxes and wanes in wild symphony. Oliver Symmes hears the raucous music of the crowd, feels it give him life, and then feels it pass, leaving him empty.

A young woman in a pleasant green uniform enters his room and turns up the light. She wears the badge of a geriatrician, with the motto To Care for the Aged. She watches the crowd outside and wishes she could join it. Inside her prison, as she thinks of it, the only function of living is the awaiting of death. The tale is a somber, tender science fiction piece.
29910-the-second-voice:
Mann Rubin wrote The Second Voice as his first appearance in the science fiction field. He had sold to the television show Tales of Tomorrow. He had won the Stephen Vincent Benet Award for one-act plays at Stanford University. The headnote calls Spud, the world-famous dummy, the heart of the tale: Spud talks to Mars with surprising results. Crawford, the showman, runs a rehearsal at Harlow Field in under an hour.

He hears the orchestra, approves the guest vocalist's song, and finishes a long dialogue between Spud and himself. He checks timing and changes a few script lines. Harlow Field, the largest experimental base in the world, is a garden of atoms and a proving ground for secret weapons, and its guards and rules give Crawford the jitters. Rubin keeps the show-business frame tight and the Mars twist strange.
29989-the-outbreak-of-peace:
H. B. Fyfe wrote The Outbreak of Peace for Analog Science Fact and Fiction in February 1961, with pictures by van Dongen. Its headnote claims that a well-run diplomatic mission can turn the most smashing battle success into a fabulous Pyrrhic victory. Space Marshal Wilbur Hennings gazes through a one-way glass at a square before the capitol on Pollux V, decorated with a spaceship's hulk.

The hulk is the first spaceship ever to have landed on Pollux V, a hundred and fifty years before. To the locals that seems impressive, amid the spread of Terran colonies and federations. To Hennings it is merely antiquated, not yet historically precious. Commodore Miller, his aide, plans a march past the heap, down an outer stairway, to heighten the pomp of opening a conference. Fyfe keeps the diplomacy dry and the irony sharp.
300-united-states-declaration-of-indepen:
When a people must dissolve political bands, decency requires them to declare their causes. The Declaration of Independence, adopted in 1776, opens with that claim and the self-evident truths of equality and unalienable rights. Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness head the list.

Governments derive just powers from the consent of the governed, the text argues, and a destructive government may be altered or abolished. A long list of grievances against the king follows. The Declaration founded American political language. Its sentences still anchor debates on rights. Jefferson's draft, revised by Congress, became America's founding creed.
30283-the-sound-of-silence:
Barbara Constant tells a quiet science fiction tale of loneliness in a crowd, from Analog, June 1962, with pictures by Schelling. Most people call being alone in a crowd the ultimate loneliness, the story notes, and one slight difference can make a person forever alone in the crowd. At Hoskins, Haskell and Chapman, nobody knows why Lucilla Brown, secretary to G. G. Hoskins, arrives half an hour before work every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday.

Even Hoskins himself could hardly explain how his exasperated wish for someone to beat him to the office set her early habit going, months before, on a gloomy March day. Paul Chapman, the very junior partner, showed interest in Lucilla through fall and winter, then little interest all spring and summer. Nobody asks where Lucilla goes at half past four on her early days, and the story keeps that secret close.
30367-old-quebec-the-fortress-of-new-fra:
Gilbert Parker and Claude G. Bryan tell the story of Old Quebec, the fortress of New France. A Macmillan volume from New York and London in 1903, set up, electrotyped, and published in September and reprinted in November, carries it. An illustration gives Major General James Wolfe from a scarce contemporary print engraved by R. Houston. A note and prelude open, followed by early voyages, the era of Champlain, and the heroic age of New France.

Ad majorem Dei gloriam, royal government, the noblesse and the people, and Frontenac and La Salle follow. Fire, massacre, and siege, the close of the century, border warfare, and the beginning of the end follow. Parker and Bryan write the fortress town as the seat of French power in Canada, from first voyages to the long struggle that closed the French regime.
30380-pipe-of-peace:
James McKimmey, Jr., tells Pipe of Peace, a short tale introduced by a song's warning that it is later than you think, lamentably unsung for Henry on a beautiful morning. The farmer refuses to work, while his wife, a short thin woman with worried eyes, watches him sit before the kitchen table, thin himself, tall and tough-skinned, his leather-look face immobile. Why, she asks, and he answers with good reasons, pouring yellow cream into coffee.

Henry lifts his cup at last, tasting, and answers her fear that they will starve with not likely, not until everybody else does. She circles the room in quick, aimless bird steps, fingers clutching the table's edge, calling him crazy in a half-question and half-pronouncement. He leans back, allows he might have gone crazy, and gives his ground plainly: each man in his own turn, and this is his turn.
30381-prelude-to-space:
Robert W. Haseltine opens a science fiction story on a steep central Wisconsin hill, where a bow hunter climbs holding his bow away from his body for balance. At the crest sits a stranger on a stump, watching the climb, greeting the hunter cheerfully, and asking to look at the bow.

He admires its workmanship and asks if it is all the hunter uses. The hunter replies that he never cared much for guns, since a bow gives an animal a fairer chance for its life. Their talk sets up a survey the hunter may not recognize as one, with stakes larger than a hillside meeting. Haseltine uses a plain outdoor encounter to open a wider space story.
30445-the-flamp-the-ameliorator-and-the-:
E. V. Lucas gathers three stories in a volume first printed in 1897 and reprinted through 1900, opening with a verse dedication to Molly and Hilda. The title pieces follow children who slip away on a sunny May afternoon, creeping past apple trees and bluebells toward a shared patch of yellow gorse.

Lucas writes with light humor and close attention to games, small plots, and the secret codes of childhood. The Flamp, The Ameliorator, and The Schoolboy's Apprentice each turn on a young hero trying to improve, impress, or outwit the adult world. Together they form a gentle, old-fashioned set of tales about play, pride, and learning by doing.
30458-novice:
James H. Schmitz sets a science fiction story from Analog, June 1962, around Telzey Amberdon, a young woman who senses a hidden presence in a garden of flowering native shrubs. Her companion Tick-Tock acts spooked, her own nerves stir without visible cause, and neither Aunt Halet in the house nor a servant explains the feeling.

Telzey plucks a blade of grass, chews it thoughtfully, and puzzles over the odd morning, though she is not ordinarily nervous. Schmitz defines a novice as one who is inexperienced, not incompetent and not stupid, and the tale tests that claim. It turns on perception, hidden watchers, and a heroine learning to trust her own alertness.
30475-with-a-vengeance:
J. B. Woodley writes With a Vengeance, a future tale dated 10 October 2119 in New San Francisco, where Kyle becomes First Imperator of Terra at precisely 9:50 in the morning. His coup is fantastically direct and facile, tempting the narrator to believe the old cliché that the time was right.

The narrator resents the new aristocracy of politics, and resents Kyle in particular, noting how elections once swung by huge majorities and historians then claimed the time was right. A swing to absolute monarchy follows, complete with a Kyle dynasty. Woodley opens with a warning for apprentices, who are future journeymen and even masters.
30477-the-sign-of-silence:
William Le Queux writes The Sign of Silence, published in London, Melbourne, and Toronto in 1917 by Ward, Lock, with a frontispiece asking, well, are you ready. Le Queux, author of If Sinners Entice Thee and The Room of Secrets, is praised in the front matter as the master of mystery.

Reviewers say he whirls readers from incident to incident, holding attention from first page to close, and call him no better companion on a railway journey. World opinions from Paris to London stress his skill, speed, and fame. The novel fits his run of enthralling romances, built on secrets, suspense, and a silence that hides danger.
30507-right-above-race:
Otto H. Kahn writes Right Above Race, published in London, New York, and Toronto in 1918. Its epigraph vows that blood shall not drown conscience, and that honor shall be heeded beyond race.

Contents open with Americans of German origin and the war. Later essays cover Prussianized Germany, the poison growth of Prussianism, frenzied liberty, and the myth of a rich man's war. A letter to a German closes the named pieces. Kahn argues for loyalty to conscience and country over ethnic ties, defending German Americans while condemning Prussian militarism. Kahn writes with plain force, and his plea still speaks to later wars.
30542-berenice:
E. Phillips Oppenheim writes Berenice, copyrighted in 1907 and published in Boston in January 1911, with illustrations by Howard Chandler Christy and Howard Somerville. Oppenheim's long list of novels includes A Prince of Sinners, A Lost Leader, Anna the Adventuress, The Great Secret, and The Master Mummer.

Later titles add The Avenger, A Maker of History, Mysterious Mr. Sabin, The Missioner, The Yellow Crayon, and The Betrayal, showing a prolific career in romance and intrigue. Berenice fits that run of fashionable thrillers, with society, secrets, and strong heroines. The Boston edition, second printing, presents the novel in a handsome illustrated form.
30640-anything-once:
Douglas Grant writes Anything Once, copyrighted in 1920 by W. J. Watt of New York, with a frontispiece by Paul Stahr showing a man drinking deeply, then struggling to sit, face whitening beneath its tan. Grant, author of The Single Track, Booty, and The Fifth Ace, opens with a roadside meeting, partners, and the vendor of everything.

Later chapters add under the big top, concerning an omelet, the red notebook, revelations, and journey's end. The long, long trail closes the book. Chapter one opens with white dust lying thick on a broad road through ripe grain fields, rising in spirals beneath farm horses drawing an empty hay wagon. Grant writes a road tale of chance, trade, and adventure.
30681-nanny-merry-or-what-made-the-diffe:
Published in London, Edinburgh, and New York in 1872, this children's story follows a small girl called Nannie and an old blind woman, Grannie Burt. Grannie lives in a little brown house under an old elm tree, and she keeps her Bible by her even though she cannot read it. She says she likes the feeling of it, and that touching it calms her troubles.

Nannie comes down the path, often with gifts from her mother, and reads the good book aloud until tears run down Grannie's face. The tale's question, what made the difference, points to that simple kindness and faith at work in a child's daily life. Young readers get a gentle Victorian moral story, with a warm home, a kind old neighbor, and a girl learning to care for others.
30889-the-mechanism-of-the-human-voice:
Emil Behnke, late lecturer on vocal physiology at the Tonic Sol-fa College and teacher of voice production, wrote this book on the mechanism of the human voice. It is held here in a fifteenth edition from J. Curwen and Sons in London. It was edited, with a new chapter on voice failure, by Mrs. Emil Behnke, and it sold for one shilling and sixpence. Behnke dedicates the essay affectionately to his dear wife.

A preface to the ninth edition, by his widow, thanks readers for kind words on the book's usefulness since her husband's death. She says she and her daughter proved the Behnke system of voice training with pupils, speakers and singers alike, to gratifying effect. The new chapter on voice failure aims to prevent breakdowns from which many students suffer. It is a concise, practical guide to how the voice works and how to keep it sound.
3096-beatrice:
Haggard published this novel in 1893. Its heroine, Beatrice, moves through love, faith, and family pressure. Chapter titles trace her course: a mist wraith, a confession of faith, appointments, appeals, and a night of storm. Geoffrey, Lady Honoria, and Elizabeth circle her, arranging and resisting while she tries to choose for herself.

Vows carry the plot. What Beatrice dreamed, what she swore, and what she will stand by once the cost is plain decide everything. The scenes shift between country houses and London rooms. A woman's word becomes the hinge on which the whole story swings.
3097-the-wanderer-s-necklace:
H. Rider Haggard wrote The Wanderer's Necklace, first published in 1914, as a romance of ninth-century Byzantium, dedicated to Sir Edgar Vincent. An editor's note claims the recovery of a bygone life ending in the early ninth century, fixed by the part played by the Empress Irene. The narrator, a Northman at court, serves as captain of the Augusta's guard.

Martina's favor brings him a commission worth more than random kisses, and he reads it in a little private room on the palace wall, struggling with Greek. He is made governor of a province, and the story follows war, love, and exile across the Byzantine world. The novel shows Haggard's late taste for historical romance told through reincarnation's frame.
31138-the-so-called-human-race:
Bert Leston Taylor's 1922 collection, published by Alfred A. Knopf in New York and arranged with an introduction by Henry B. Fuller, gathers the humorist's pieces on human folly. It opens with Taylor's own verse on Puck, the mischief-making sprite who still finds mortals playing blind man's buff under an older moon, laughing at the same old game.

The title says the theme: men and women, for all their airs, remain gloriously foolish, and Taylor's light verse and prose catch them at it. Published in March 1922 with a second printing the next month, the book shows why Taylor was a favorite wit of his generation.
31286-let-em-breathe-space:
Lester del Rey's story, printed in Space Science Fiction in July 1953, follows a Saturn expedition five months out from Earth, halfway to its goal. Eighteen men and two women are sealed in a spaceship. The narrator, Paul, a broad former fullback roughed up by an old explosion, is sick of feuding, bad food, and the eternal smell of people. He is also sick of whole-wheat pancakes served for the ninth morning running as punishment for griping about the coffee.

As the magazine's note warns, the atmosphere aboard is literally poisoned, and tension edges toward murder among scientists who cannot escape one another. Taut and wry, the tale turns a life-support failure into a study of tempers fraying in deep space.
31380-bred-of-the-desert-a-horse-and-a-r:
Marcus Horton's 1915 romance, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York by arrangement with Harper and Brothers, follows a desert horse from birth to reunion in twenty-three chapters. It opens at high noon in a yellow-pink twilight before a Southwestern sandstorm, with dust-devils swirling and sand clouds billowing down the slopes. The storm hurtles across the swollen Rio Grande into town.

Later chapters bring Felipe's celebration, a surprise, a new home, loneliness, a first great lesson, a stranger, a second lesson, and love rejected. They go on to adventure in the waste places, changes of masters, Pat turning thief, a running fight, fidelity, life and death, quiescence, and reunion. Dedicated to one who taught consideration for the dumb, the book tells its horse's life with sympathy and desert color.
31504-concerning-justice:
Lucilius A. Emery's Concerning Justice, published by Yale University Press in 1914, gathers addresses delivered in the William L. Storrs Lecture Series of 1914 before the law school of Yale University. Emery, writing for lawyers and general readers, opens with the problem stated: theories as to the source of justice, and definitions of justice. A second chapter takes up the problem of rights and different theories about them.

The lectures ask what justice is, where it comes from, and what rights it protects. Emery's treatment is philosophical rather than technical, and his Yale audience gives the book its tone of public reasoning. Readers of legal philosophy will find a concise, early twentieth-century statement of questions that still divide lawyers: whether justice is found, made, or agreed.
31519-narakan-rifles-about-face:
Jan Smith's science-fiction story Narakan Rifles, About Face, opens with Lieutenant Terrence O'Mara lying flat on his back on a cot. He tries to keep his big body still in the humid heat of Naraka. Stripped to his regulation shorts, he drags on a cigarette and watches smoke mingle with water beading on the command post's concrete. In disgust he damns Naraka as an outpost of civilization, fit only, he asks, for the Rumi.

The headnote presents the Narakans as undisciplined troops, survivors of the Suzi swamps, until the four-fisted O'Mara moves among them with a steady, dangerous purpose. Smith's story follows that transformation, as O'Mara drills a sloppy outfit into rifles that can stand and fight. Readers of military science fiction will find a brisk tale of leadership under alien suns.
31542-pierre-and-luce:
Romain Rolland's Pierre and Luce was translated by Charles de Kay and published by Henry Holt and Company of New York in 1922. It is a short novel of young love in wartime Paris. Rolland, author of Jean-Christophe and Colas Breugnon, opens with a passage called "The Isle of Calms." It compares the lovers to the Sargasso Sea, into which the Gulf Stream drifts the odds and ends carried by marine currents. The image sets the tone for a love apart from the war around it.

Pierre and Luce meet, love, and face a world at war that has little room for their happiness. Rolland writes with lyric tenderness, making the lovers' brief idyll stand against the violence of their time. Readers will find a compact, moving novel, famous as one of Rolland's most delicate works, and a portrait of youth caught in the Great War.
31661-exile-from-space:
Judith Merril's story Exile from Space opens with a headnote about a strange girl who worried her keepers over the impression she would make. She fell in love passionately, as others of her blood must have done, the headnote says. The narrator does not know where they got the car, but a plate had to be forged for it, since its own was wrong. They sewed her a skirt, blouse, and shoes copied from television.

They could not make her a lipstick, since they could not work out its chemical composition. They decided she was as well off without a driver's license or automobile registration as with imperfect papers. They worried about her hair, and even thought of cutting it short. Merril's tale follows a girl born in a place that still is not her home.
31662-their-son-the-necklace:
Eduardo Zamacois's Their Son, The Necklace, translated by George Allan England and published in New York by Boni and Liveright in 1919, gathers stories by the Spanish author. The translator dedicates the volume to his sister, and thanks her for valuable help with local terms and obscure passages in these stories. Zamacois, a popular Spanish novelist and short-story writer, writes of family, love, and social life with a direct, humane touch.

The title stories give the volume its shape: a son, a necklace, and the human complications that gather around them. England's translation aims to keep Zamacois's local color without losing his clarity. Readers of Spanish fiction in English will find a readable, early twentieth-century collection, where domestic drama carries larger questions of honor and affection.
31705-the-social-direction-of-evolution-:
William E. Kellicott, professor of biology at Goucher College, published The Social Direction of Human Evolution, an outline of the science of eugenics, with D. Appleton and Company at New York and London in 1919, with copyright in 1911. Its three chapters cover the sources and aims of the science of eugenics, its biological foundations, and human heredity and the eugenic program.

Kellicott's book sets out eugenic thought as it stood in the early twentieth century, with population figures and illustrations to carry its argument. It is a historical document of a movement that later fell into disrepute, and it shows how its advocates joined biology to social policy.
31768-the-economic-functions-of-vice:
John McElroy's 1906 essay was published in Washington by the National Tribune. It argues that nature is wasteful in generation and that human vice must be judged by its effects, not only by moral labels. He opens with the cod, which casts millions of eggs for the few that survive, and the oak, which showers down seed to the same end.

From that picture of waste, McElroy builds an economic case: activities condemned as vice may still serve functions in society, and condemning them without counting their results misses the point. Readers get a provocative early twentieth-century argument that mixes biology, economics, and social criticism.
31787-the-bird-and-insects-post-office:
Robert Bloomfield's Bird and Insects' Post-Office, with thirty-five illustrations and published by E. P. Dutton in New York, is a children's book in letters. Bloomfield, author of The Farmer's Boy, wrote all but letters eight, ten, eleven, and sixteen, which are by his eldest son Charles.

The letters pass between birds and insects. They run from the magpie to the sparrow and the sparrow's reply. Others run from a young garden-spider to her mother, a young nightingale to a wren, and an earwig deploring the loss of all her children. Readers get a charming early children's classic, rescued from Bloomfield's posthumous Remains of 1824 and reissued for the little ones for whom it was written.
31835-prisoners-of-conscience:
Amelia E. Barr's 1897 novel Prisoners of Conscience, copyrighted in 1896 and 1897 by The Century Company, is set among the people of the northern isles. Book first follows Liot Borson through the weaving of doom, jealousy cruel as the grave, a sentence for life, and a door wide open.

Book second follows David Borson through a new life, kindred quick and dead, the justification of death, a sacrifice accepted, and at last it is peace. Readers get a stern, religious novel of guilt, conscience, and forgiveness, illustrated with scenes of Lerwick men, peat-gatherers, and the kirk.
3187-christian-science:
Mark Twain divides this volume into two books. Book One holds matter written about four years earlier, never before published in book form, and now corrected where judgment or fact had erred. Book Two, written at the start of 1903 and new in print, presents a character portrait of Mary Baker Eddy, drawn from her own writings.

Twain's target is Christian Science as a system and Mrs Eddy as its prophet. He quotes her at length, then applies his own logic to her claims about mind, matter, and healing. The book is polemical Twain at full power: funny, relentless, and convinced that a popular faith deserves the same plain scrutiny as a popular fraud.
32029-seed-of-the-arctic-ice:
H. G. Winter's short story Seed of the Arctic Ice was printed in Astounding Stories in February 1932. It opens in a submarine beneath the ice-roofed Arctic sea, where a sleepy lookout watches ghostly fish and pale sunlight filtering through breaks in the ice-floes. The four other men on duty sit motionless and silent.

Its sidenote promises that killer whales and seal-creatures tangle Ken Torrance in an amazing adventure under the ice. When something on the scope-screen brings the lookout to alert attention, the monotony breaks. Readers get a pulp underwater adventure of Arctic creatures and a submarine crew, told in brisk, atmospheric prose.
32109-tales-of-the-caravan-inn-and-palac:
William Hauff's tales, translated from the German by Edward L. Stowell and published in Chicago in 1882, gather the German author's best-known fairy stories in three framed groups. Stowell's preface introduces Hauff for American readers: born at Stuttgart in 1802, educated at Tuebingen, graduated in 1824 with a doctorate, and a tutor in a nobleman's family for two years. In his leisure hours as a tutor, Hauff composed most of the works on which his fame rests.

Part one, Tales of the Caravan, opens with a caravan crossing the desert and includes The Caliph Stork, The Rescue of Fatima, Little Muck, and The False Prince. Part two, Tales of the Inn, offers The Marble Heart and Said's Adventures. Part three, Tales of the Palace, gives The Dwarf Nosey and The Story of Almansor. Readers get classic German fairy tales, told with Eastern colour and moral turns.
32133-the-graveyard-of-space:
Milton Lesser's short story, printed in Imagination in April 1956, is set in the Sargasso area of the void, a region about which nobody knows very much. One thing is certain, its introduction warns: if a ship is caught there, it is doomed. The story follows Ralph and his wife Diane aboard the battered old Gormann 87, a small ship watching asteroids pass like tiny, slow-moving flashes of light at the viewport.

Ralph lights what may be their last cigarette and offers to share it. Diane, hunched at the viewport, has aged through three years on asteroid 4712, a tiny rock between Jupiter and Mars, where the couple worked a mine with high uranium potential. The mine was a failure, as everything in their life together had been, Ralph reflects. Readers get a grim, intimate space story about a married couple, a failed mine, and a ship drifting toward a graveyard.
32443-saga-of-halfred-the-sigskald-a-nor:
Felix Dahn's Saga of Halfred the Sigskald, translated by Sophie F. E. Veitch and published in Paisley and London in 1886, tells a northern tale of the tenth century. It opens nearly fifty winters before its telling, with a boy named Halfred growing up in Iceland, where his father Hamund's splendid hall stood on Hamund Fjord. Heathen folk, the tale says, believed elves and goblins still moved freely among northern nations.

One friendly elf, the story adds, laid wild honey on the infant Halfred's lips at his shield cradle. The elf promised victory in harping and singing, so all nations would name him Sigskald, or victory poet. Dahn calls that tale idle, yet Halfred grows strong and beautiful, sitting alone on cliffs listening to wind in the crags and longing to tune his harp. The saga follows a poet-hero shaped by music, myth, and the north.
32485-the-giants-from-outer-space:
Geoff St. Reynard's tale, printed in Imagination in May 1954, opens in the ninetieth star system explored by curious men of Earth, where seven planets circle a star. Between the fourth and fifth planets lies an asteroid belt of some three or four thousand tiny bodies, once a single planet shattered by an unimaginable explosion. Its largest fragment now measures no more than four hundred and forty miles across.

Aboard an exploring ship, Pinkham and his men argue over a life-scanner that cannot be wrong. It reports no water, no air, and no gravity worth mentioning on a silly-looking little apple of a world, yet insists somebody is sitting on it. Reynard builds grim terror in the void from that paradox, as explorers face giants from outer space on a world that should hold no life at all.
32692-a-day-s-ride-a-life-s-romance:
Charles James Lever tells of Algernon Sydney Potts, heir to a long line of apothecaries in Dublin. His father, Launcelot Peter Potts, scorned senna and black drop and dreamed of honors no chemist ever won, from general's stars to the woolsack. The son sets out to seek adventures and a grander life.

Potts rides with a horse named Blondel, falls in with vagabonds, and poses as a man of fortune at inns such as the Pig. Wine, doubt, and a poor girl's sorrows test his pose, and the tale follows a dreamer learning that the world's judgment, like a court's, weighs every man by his peers.
3281-cy-whittaker-s-place:
Joseph C Lincoln sets this Cape Cod novel around Cy Whittaker's place. The perfect boarding house opens the chapters, with the wanderer's return and a fixing over. Bailey Bangs's experiment, a front door caller, and icicles and dust follow. Captain Cy proves delinquent, and the cow lady, politics and birthdays, and a letter and a visitor keep the village busy.

A bargain off, town meeting, and the repulse lead to a clue, with Debby Beasley to the rescue and a remarkable drive. Lincoln writes his village with a native's ear for talk and a humorist's eye for pride. Boarding houses, town meetings, and plans that rarely survive contact with neighbors: Lincoln's village at ease.
32833-a-woman-s-place:
Mark Clifton strands three survivors in a lifeboat falling back to Earth, in a story from Galaxy Science Fiction of May 1955. Miss Kitty, a schoolteacher with academic degrees she wears like a tiara, half wakes to hear Sam Eade and Lt. Harper discussing what they must tell her. The two men have escaped the wrecked spaceship with her, and they are holding something back.

On a new Earth that proves a paradise, the question becomes who will people it. Miss Kitty, whose full name is Katheryn Kittredge, thinks through Mendelian law while stripping rice: line breeding fixes traits, but recessives in both parents can turn dominant. A nurse later tells her plainly that her plain sense, not madness, guided her proposal to the two men. The story asks where a brilliant woman's place lies when civilization must start again.
32922-a-veldt-official-a-novel-of-circum:
Bertram Mitford sends Roden Musgrave to a post he cannot find on any map, in a novel of colonial circumstance. Aboard ship off Port Elizabeth, Musgrave reads his appointment as provisional clerk to Doppersdorp's Resident Magistrate, and distributer of stamps. The pay is not profuse, and he asks aloud where the very mischief Doppersdorp is.

A bronzed skipper in quasi-naval uniform bets a bottle of Heidsieck that Musgrave cannot answer a first question about the country, then proves unable to answer it himself. At Doppersdorp, Musgrave soon gains a reputation for favouring native servants against white employers in cases before him. That reputation is a death knell to popularity among Boers and English stock-raisers alike. Lambert, the district surgeon, and Sonnenberg, who traps a servant with a planted theft, circle the new magistrate as a weapon against their enemies.
33049-the-origin-of-the-world-according-:
J. W. Dawson, principal and vice-chancellor of McGill University in Montreal, wrote The Origin of the World, According to Revelation and Science in 1877 to bring scripture and geology into one conversation. Dawson takes as his text Job's line, speak to the earth and it shall teach thee, and dedicates the work to the Earl of Dufferin, governor-general of Canada.

The book argues that the earth's record and the biblical account can be read together without forcing either, a position many Victorian scientists and churchmen tried to hold. Dawson writes for educated general readers, not only for specialists, and his chapters move between rocks, fossils, and verses. As history, it captures a moment when geology was reshaping how people thought about creation, and when a leading Canadian scientist tried to keep faith and science in the same room.
33081-sir-jasper-carew-his-life-and-expe:
Charles James Lever's Sir Jasper Carew: His Life and Experience presents itself as the memoirs of a man whose life was crowded with strange incidents. It was illustrated by E. Van Muyden and Phiz and published in Boston in 1904. Lever's notice warns readers that writers of travels often omit their most eventful passages to gain credence. Gentlemen and ladies who live at home at ease take little account of adventures that are the daily lot of more precarious lives.

Sir Jasper answers the charge that no man could meet so many adventures simply: by change of place and fortune, and by being thrown on the highways of the world. The memoirs that follow mix travel, duels, love, and reversals in the high-spirited manner of Lever's Irish novels. They read as a picaresque life.
33145-come-out-of-the-kitchen-a-romance:
Alice Duer Miller's Come Out of the Kitchen, a romance published in 1916 with illustrations by Paul Meylan and scenes from the play, opens in the office of Randolph Reed. Reed is a real estate dealer whose window bears magnificent gold block lettering. Reed deals in real estate, and from behind his gold pattern he peers eagerly one autumn afternoon, chewing a frayed cigar.

Miller's romance turns on a household where servants and masters exchange roles, and where a young woman must come out of the kitchen to claim her place. The story, also successful as a play, mixes comedy, class, and love with a light, modern touch. It remains a charming period romance for readers who enjoy a heroine who refuses to stay where society put her, and a plot that lets wit win over rank.
33152-tales-of-romance:
Andrew Lang's Tales of Romance gathers heroic stories for young readers. It is based on tales in his Book of Romance and issued in a new impression in 1919. It has four colored plates and fifteen other illustrations by H. J. Ford and Lancelot Speed. Its contents include the story of Robin Hood, Wayland the Smith, adventures of William Short Nose, and the sword Excalibur. The list goes on to how Grettir the Strong became an outlaw, with his death to follow.

Colored plates show Slagfid pursuing the wraith over the mountain, the chariot of Freya, Alix kissing Rainouart, and Arthur meeting the Lady of the Lake to receive Excalibur. Text pictures catch Robin Hood meeting Little John and shooting his last arrow. Lang retells old tales , keeping their wonder without softening their danger. The book remains a fine first meeting with the heroes of northern and Arthurian story.
33195-was-it-right-to-forgive-a-domestic:
Amelia E. Barr's Was It Right to Forgive?, a domestic romance published in Chicago in 1899, opens with Peter Van Hoosen. Peter Van Hoosen grew out of Dutch Calvinism, Dutch hard work and thrift, and a firm belief in Judgment Day. His early drives were inherited leanings, carefully schooled; the last was a deliberate principle drawing a sharp line between just and right, false and wrong. People whose religion was merely conventional stand in contrast to his stern conscience.

Barr builds a domestic story around that conscience, asking whether forgiveness is a duty, a weakness, or a gift, and what a family owes to a wrongdoer. Her heroine and hero must weigh judgment against mercy in a household shaped by Calvinist rigor. The novel remains a thoughtful period romance, earnest about faith and family, and it gives its title question a human answer rather than a slogan.
33209-the-dual-alliance:
Marjorie Benton Cooke's Dual Alliance opens with Barbara Garratry, thirty and Irish, to whom the world looks like a bright colored ball for tossing. It was published in Garden City in 1915 and illustrated by Mary Greene Blumenschein. As a tiny mite her father dubbed her Bob, Son of Battle, for obvious warlike traits. Bob Garratry she has been ever since, fighting her way to the top with spirit and humor. Illustrations show Paul calling her on the telephone every night at midnight.

Cooke, author of Bambi, David, and The Girl Who Lived in the Woods, writes a romance of two alliances, friendship and love. The alliances are tested by pride, misunderstanding, and the telephone's nightly ring. The novel is with Irish wit at its center. It remains a pleasant period romance for readers who enjoy a heroine who fights her own battles and wins her own terms.
33401-the-little-schoolmaster-mark-a-spi:
J. H. Shorthouse's Little Schoolmaster Mark, a spiritual romance published in 1894, follows a humble teacher whose inner life carries the tale. Shorthouse, author of John Inglesant, writes of Mark's faith, doubt, and growth, in a story first issued in parts in 1883 and 1884, then gathered in a complete edition in 1885. The book's reprints to 1894 show its steady readership.

The romance's appeal lies in its quiet, reflective tone, where a schoolmaster's soul matters more than outward action. Its prose is gentle and thoughtful, suited to readers who love spiritual fiction. For fans of Shorthouse, Little Schoolmaster Mark offers a tender, old-fashioned tale of a man seeking God in a small, daily life.
33482-the-furnace:
R. Macaulay follows a young artist and his companions through youth, travel, and changing ideas in an Italian coastal world. The novel opens with royalty arriving by steam yacht in a busy harbor, watched by a crowd, reporters, and a quick-eyed illustrator for a satirical paper. From that public scene it turns inward, to friendships, ambitions, and the search for a standpoint from which to judge life.

Thirteen chapters carry the characters from city youth through seaside places, retrospect, and broken barriers toward a parting of roads. Macaulay writes about art, idleness, work, and the pull of home, using the furnace of experience as a figure for how young people are tested and changed. The book is reflective and episodic rather than plot-driven.
33597-our-admirable-betty-a-romance:
Jeffery Farnol writes a lively period romance around Lady Betty and the men who circle her. The story opens with a major's cherries, a ravisher of those cherries, and a wall climbed in pursuit. It then widens to include a poacher, Sergeant Zebedee Tring, a viscount, and a household of fine gentlemen. Gossip, letters, ghosts, and a pewter pot used to quell scandal keep the comedy moving.

Betty herself proves the center of the book: spirited, generous, and determined to make her own resolutions about love and marriage. Farnol's dialogue sparkles, and his chapters balance farce with genuine feeling as the major recovers and loses his youth, treasonable matters surface, and a ghost is finally laid. Readers of Georgian romance will enjoy its high spirits and old-fashioned charm.
33610-pharos-the-egyptian-a-romance:
Guy Boothby frames an Egyptian romance as a letter from Sir William Betford of Dorset to George Trevelyan in London. Betford confesses himself puzzled by an extraordinary and sad case. Betford asks his friend to weigh the evidence for both of them. Either Forrester has gone mad and dreamed his whole account, or he is sane and has endured more than almost anyone. The preface sets up a mystery of accusation and self-blame.

From that framing, the novel unfolds a tale of ancient Egypt reaching into the present, with the figure of Pharos at its center. Boothby, already known for Doctor Nikola and similar romances of mystery, mixes archaeology, occult suggestion, and adventure. Readers of late Victorian fantastic romance will find a swift, eerie story built on a single haunting question of sanity and guilt.
3364-dr-breen-s-practice:
William D Howells published this novel in 1881 around a woman doctor at a seaside resort. A hotel perches at the edge of a bold headland, facing southeast across open sea to the horizon. Behind the hotel spreads a great woodland that, two centuries on, has reclaimed the barren shore the first Pilgrims seized from it.

The forest has begun to efface the inroads made in recent years by bold speculation, Howells adds, and the hotel stands between wild nature and new money. Dr Breen's practice, professional and personal, unfolds in that border country. A doctor claiming a man's profession, in a place still deciding what to allow: Howells's new woman at work.
33681-poems-of-the-great-war-published-o:
Published in London in 1914 on behalf of the Prince of Wales's National Relief Fund, this fourth-edition collection gathers English poets' free offerings to the cause of national relief. Most poems had appeared recently in the press in the days just after the declaration of war. Robert Bridges opens the collection, with contributions from Henry Newbolt, Maurice Hewlett, R. E. Vernède, Laurence Binyon, and William Watson.

Further poems came from Punch, the Daily Telegraph, the Daily Mail, the Sphere, the Westminster Gazette, the New Witness, the New Weekly, and the Daily Chronicle. William Watson's Duty urges the rich to give gladly from wealth's overflow, while the poor poet gives brain and heart. The volume is a vivid record of Britain's first wartime poetry.
33823-the-gay-adventure-a-romance:
Richard Bird published this light romance in Indianapolis in 1914, with a frontispiece by F. Vaux Wilson. Its hero, Lionel Mortimer, is a young gentleman of few means and no firm plans, and its heroine outshines him at every turn. A plot, a change of lodgings, a rise in the world, and a telegram keep the pair in motion.

Bird plays the tale for comedy: stagey scenes, crossed orbits, and thrills that arrive one after another. Tony Wild and other side figures add mischief and aid. The novel is a bright, old-fashioned entertainment, meant to amuse rather than to instruct, and it moves at a brisk, cheerful pace.
33837-architecture-gothic-and-renaissanc:
T. Roger Smith wrote this textbook on European building, published in New York and London in 1880 and edited by Edward J. Poynter. It covers the rise of Gothic, or pointed, building in the twelfth century through the close of the Renaissance style in the eighteenth. A front picture shows the Certosa near Pavia, begun in 1393.

Smith explains the history, features, and famous examples of each style in short, clear chapters. Students learn to read a church, a tomb panel, or a roof crest for its age and manner. The book still works as a plain guide to two great ages of building in Europe.
3390-my-mark-twain-from-literary-friends:
William Dean Howells remembers his friend Mark Twain in this memoir from Literary Friends and Acquaintance. It was in the little office of James T Fields that Howells first met his friend of now forty-four years. The office stood over the bookstore of Ticknor and Fields at 124 Tremont Street, Boston. There Howells met Samuel L Clemens, and a lifetime's friendship began.

Fields was then editor of the Atlantic Monthly, and Howells his proud and glad assistant. Howells held a pretty free hand as to manuscripts, and an unmanacled command of the magazine's slush, as he recalls it. The memoir that follows traces a friendship across a lifetime: two humorists, one from the West and one from the East, meeting in Boston and never parting in print. It is the warmest portrait Twain ever received from a fellow writer.
3391-a-belated-guest-from-literary-frien:
William Dean Howells recalls Bret Harte in this memoir essay from Literary Friends and Acquaintance.
