Harte's journey east from California in 1871 drew wide attention, almost like the progress of a prince. Howells met him on the Atlantic shore at the start of that fame. The essay looks back from a later time, when both men are older and the excitement has cooled.

Howells writes about memory itself as much as about Harte. He notes how pleasant it is to sit by the fire and call back names, looks, and tones from the past. Famous friends lend a glow to the person remembering them, and he basks in it for a time. The piece suits readers interested in American literary circles and in how writers remember each other.
3392-cambridge-neighbors-from-literary-f:
William Dean Howells remembers Cambridge neighbors in this memoir from Literary Friends and Acquaintance. He went to make his home in Cambridge as a wholly literary spirit. In that mood, he writes, he could hardly have been more content if he had found himself in the Elysian Fields, with an agreeable eternity before him. At twenty-nine, indeed, one is practically immortal.

At that age, time had for him the effect of an eternity in which he had no pressing business. The memoir that follows peoples that eternity: Lowell, Longfellow, and the Cambridge circle, seen by a young man who had come to live among his heroes. Readers get literary Cambridge as a young writer saw it: golden, leisurely, and already passing even as he enjoyed it.
3393-studies-of-lowell-from-literary-fri:
William Dean Howells paints a personal portrait of James Russell Lowell in this memoir from Literary Friends and Acquaintance. He first met Lowell at Cambridge in 1860, when he came east from the West on a literary pilgrimage, and he knew him better after moving to Cambridge in 1866. The essay covers the years up to Lowell's death, with long evenings of talk in Lowell's study.

Howells warns that his Lowell may look different from other people's Lowell. He records suppers at two o'clock dinners, walks, and conversation rather than a formal life history. The value lies in the close view of a leading American poet, critic, and diplomat as a friend saw him, warm, talkative, and deeply rooted in New England.
3395-oliver-wendell-holmes-from-literary:
William Dean Howells remembers Oliver Wendell Holmes as a Boston figure of a special kind in this memoir from Literary Friends and Acquaintance. Where writers elsewhere might rise from obscure corners, Boston writers, Howells says, often came from known families and dropped, as he puts it, from the skies. Holmes belonged to that settled world of law, science, and letters.

The essay sketches Holmes in conversation and in society rather than listing his books. Readers meet a witty doctor and poet who could hold a table with talk and verse. Howells also notes how Boston itself was changing, so the piece doubles as a farewell to an older city where a few families set the tone for its culture.
3397-roundabout-to-boston-from-literary-:
William Dean Howells traces his own road to Boston in this memoir from Literary Friends and Acquaintance. As a young man he lived in Venice with literary hopes always present, sending poems to magazines across the English speaking world. Nearly all came back, except three pieces that editors kept, one for the Atlantic Monthly, one for Harper's, and one for the New York Ledger.

Defeat in verse pushed him toward prose, since he had to earn a living by some sort of writing. The essay follows that slow turn from rejected poet to working editor and novelist. It gives an honest view of a writing life: repeated failure, small breaks, and the steady work that finally builds a career.
34130-the-princess-galva-a-romance:
David Whitelaw's 1911 romance The Princess Galva follows Edward Povey, a clerk worn down by twenty-two years of service to one firm. A letter from New York, a taste of borrowed rank, and a meeting with Galva pull him from his counting-house into a plot of love and deceit.

Chapters run from London lodgings to Penzance, a cathedral, a seaside house, and Bloomsbury, through imposture, flight, a shot in the grounds, and revenge. Whitelaw keeps the pace brisk, and Edward's own final note closes a tale of a plain man caught in a royal game.
34202-the-girl-from-tim-s-place:
Charles Clark Munn's 1906 novel follows Chip McGuire, a girl raised in harsh hands at a place called Tim's Place. After a long day of toil with no kind word, she flees barefoot into the woods at night, with only the forest tales of Old Tomah in her head.

Her flight runs through fir and spruce, swamp and briar, while fear gives shape to the wild things around her. The tale then turns to her search for safety, work, and people who will treat her as kin. It keeps the rough speech and hard life of a forest home close at hand.
34277-a-mysterious-disappearance:
A Mysterious Disappearance is a detective novel by Gordon Holmes, published in New York by Edward J Clode in 1905. Its first chapter is headed Last Seen at Victoria, and its sleuth is Inspector White. The contents promise thirty-one chapters of inquiry.

Alice, Lady Dyke, opens the book in her boudoir on a foggy November night, dressed to go out and checking an address in a long, closely written letter. She rings for her man James, her face hardened, resolved on a course she has mapped out. From there the chapters fan out: the lady's maid, two addresses in Raleigh Mansions, the Jollity Theatre, and a Miss Marie le Marchant. Breaking the bank, the Riviera, a disputed handwriting, and Lady Helen Montgomery's son all feed the puzzle. How Lady Dyke left, and how she disappeared, are held for the final chapters.
34440-a-jewish-chaplain-in-france:
A Jewish Chaplain in France is a memoir by Rabbi Lee J Levinger, published by Macmillan in New York and London. Levinger served as a chaplain with American forces in France in the Great War. A group photograph of Jewish welfare workers at Le Mans in March nineteen nineteen fronts the book. Levinger stands at the centre of that group.

The book records ministry to Jewish soldiers far from home, in camps, hospitals, and burial grounds. Services, festivals, food needs, and letters home all fell to the chaplain and welfare staff. The photograph names his fellow workers one by one. As a first hand record of faith work in a modern army, it holds a rare place.
34576-by-violence:
John Trevena, author of Bracken and Sleeping Waters, published his novel By Violence with the Four Seasons Company at Boston in 1918. Edward O'Brien wrote the opening note, dated February 26, 1918. The tale opens on a short, odd message about wooden enemies.

Simon Searell reads the note as he tramps foggy streets in Stonehouse. Oliver Vorse, an uneducated man, meant the spring wood-anemones by his harsh phrase. Searell passes a cheap iron church he has given up, with its brass sticks and false flowers. He seeks a deeper faith through solitude and mystic thought. Faith, doubt, and plain folk in a poor town form the ground of Trevena's tale.
3461-essays-on-life-art-and-science:
Samuel Butler, author of Erewhon and The Way of All Flesh, gathers essays on life, art, and science in this volume, edited by R A Streatfeild and published in 1908. Contents include Ramblings in Cheapside, How to Make the Best of Life, Art in the Valley of Saas, Thought and Language, and The Deadlock in Darwinism. One essay defends a Holbein drawing in Basle against those who call it a copy.

Butler writes as an independent thinker, willing to quarrel with experts on art and on evolution alike. His essays mix travel notes, family sketches, and sharp argument, all in a clear, personal voice. The book suits readers who like Victorian essayists who think aloud and who refuse to follow fashion in science or art.
34614-the-little-girl-who-was-taught-by-:
The Little Girl Who Was Taught by Experience was printed at Boston in 1827. No author is named on the title page. A copyright entry dated June 19, 1827 stands at the front. The heroine is little Lucy, whose mother died when she was very small. Her mother would have taught her to check her faults, the narrator says. Bad passions are likened to weeds in a garden bed. Left alone, they choke the mild virtues just budding into beauty.

Lucy passed to a most indulgent father. Word reached her aunt in Boston that the child was growing disagreeable. The kind, sensible aunt feared worse faults ahead. The tale follows Lucy's lessons learned the hard way. It is a plain moral story for children of its day, told in a grave, tender tone.
34654-character-and-opinion-in-the-unite:
George Santayana, late professor of philosophy at Harvard, wrote Character and Opinion in the United States, first published in 1920. Its second title promises memories of William James and Josiah Royce, and of academic life in America. Seven chapters carry the survey.

Santayana opens on New England's Indian summer of the mind in the mid 1800s. Its poets and preachers, he says, kept a pure but barren view of life. Later chapters treat James and Royce as men, then turn to materialism and idealism in American life. English liberty in America closes the book.
34772-stained-glass-tours-in-france:
Charles Hitchcock Sherrill wrote Stained Glass Tours in France, published in New York and London in 1908. He dedicates the book to his remorseless critic, his wife. A frontispiece shows the interior of the Sainte Chapelle in Paris, built by Saint Louis in 1248, its walls almost entirely sheets of richly toned glass.

Contents proceed by century: thirteenth century and earlier, then the tours; fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, then their tours; the sixteenth century likewise. Itineraries and an index close the book. Illustrations include a medallion panel from the Louvre and a lancet at Tours. Readers get a traveller's guide that turns French cathedrals into a glass itinerary.
3487-augustus-does-his-bit-a-true-to-lif:
George Bernard Shaw writes a wartime farce about Lord Augustus Highcastle, a well meaning aristocrat who believes he is serving his country. The play was first performed by the Stage Society at the Court Theatre in London on January 21, 1917. Shaw's preface recalls his own trip toward the Flanders front, where passports and official favors made him think about how war work really gets done.

Augustus blunders through offices and interviews, convinced that his rank and good intentions count as duty. Shaw turns the comedy on patriotic cant and on the gap between talk and action. The piece is short, brisk, and very much of its moment, suiting readers who like Shaw's satire at its most direct.
34884-tales-of-the-trains-being-some-cha:
Charles James Lever writes railroad tales under the name Tilbury Tramp, Queen's Messenger, in a Little, Brown volume from Boston dated 1907. Phiz drew the plates for the tales. A short song of pistons and valves heads the front matter in place of a motto.

Lever argues in his opening that rail travel has changed minds as much as manners across the land. A man who has gone a hundred miles from home is no wonder now, he notes with jest. Soon the wonder will be the man who has not been everywhere, he adds. To cling to old stage-coach plots while all life shifts, he holds, is like trying to stand firm in an earthquake. Boz and the workhouse tale now rival the old murder school, he claims.
3489-fabre-poet-of-science:
Georges Victor Legros writes a life of Jean Henri Fabre, the French naturalist famous for his studies of insects. The book draws on Fabre's letters and on long conversations with the author, and Fabre himself allowed his friend to speak for him in many passages. Legros calls the early chapters a biography of a solitary student, tracing how a poor boy became a scientist.

The life follows Fabre from school teaching to his field in Provence, where he watched wasps, beetles, and spiders for decades. Legros shows both the man and the method: patient watching, simple tools, and writing that made insects vivid to ordinary readers. The book suits nature lovers and anyone who wants to know the person behind the Souvenirs entomologiques.
34892-castle-hohenwald-a-romance:
Castle Hohenwald is a romance after the German of Adolph Streckfuss, Englished by Wister and issued at Philadelphia in an edition of 1906. The copyright of the translation reaches back to 1879. Wister had Englished many German novels, and their titles fill the page: The Old Mamselle's Secret, The Second Wife, Too Rich, and Margarethe among them.

The tale opens at a ball, as the music ceases. Gentlemen lead their partners to their chaperones, then crowd out on the balcony for the cool spring air. Their host, a president, warns in vain against such rashness in the night air. He turns to his friend the colonel and gives up on the heedless young folk of the day. Behind that light opening stands the castle of the title and its family's tangled loves.
34957-the-children-of-alsace:
René Bazin wrote a novel of a house torn twixt France and Germany. Its French name is Les Oberlés, and it deals with Alsace. Angelo Rappoport wrote the front note for this form. The book came out in New York in 1912. Bazin also wrote The Nun and Redemption.

A February night in Alsace starts the house tale. A test, a first kin meet, and the hearth's guards come next. The frontier line cuts through hearts as well as fields. An Easter watch and a stay at Carolis fill the mid parts. The Oberlé kin must choose which land owns their souls. Grave prose suits a grave, split land.
34995-too-rich-a-romance:
Adolph Streckfuss tells a German tale in Too Rich, a romance in English by Wister, printed at Philadelphia in 1878. Lippincott made the book, with copyright the same year. Wister had Englished a shelf of German novels, among them The Second Wife and Only a Girl.

Chapter one opens on a very warm day in summer. Lindens on a broad promenade droop their dusty leaves over slow walkers. The heat drives many into cool side streets. Others take refuge at a famed restaurant for its sherbet, a favourite haunt of young sprigs of fashion. Officers of the garrison regiments lounge there with townsmen of rank. The choice of evening amusements is weighed in the shade, in spite of the heat.
35116-saint-michael-a-romance:
Werner wrote this German romance, and Wister turned it into English; the copyright dates to 1886, and this printing came from Philadelphia in 1901. The scene opens at Easter, with spring storms over snowy mountains and an old castle of the Counts von Steinrück. The castle's lord is dead, and his body is brought home to the family vault.

With him, the younger branch of his house ends in the male line, leaving a widow and a little daughter. The book sets its tale of love and duty in that stern mountain world of rank, grief, and old family pride. Werner's romances were widely read in English through Wister's smooth translations.
35212-the-cathedrals-of-southern-france:
Francis Miltoun wrote on the cathedrals of southern France with ninety plates and plans. L C Page and Company issued the work at Boston in the Roman year MDCCCCV. Rights rest from 1904, with a third impression noted. Blanche McManus drew the pictures, plans, and diagrams throughout.

Parts treat the south in general, lands south of the Loire, and the Rhone valley. St Front at Perigueux, Notre Dame at Le Puy, and St Trophime at Arles lead the stops. Miltoun had written the northern France volume in the same series before. Travelers gain a warm, learned tour of great churches town by town.
35229-the-alpine-fay-a-romance:
The Alpine Fay is a romance from the German of Werner, translated by Wister. Lippincott published the translation at Philadelphia, with rights dated 1889. The contents run to twenty seven chapters. A mountain home, an alm pasture, and an avalanche mark the tale's high points.

The story opens after a storm in a high Alpine valley. Rainbows hang over the peaks while clouds camp on the slopes. The lonely valley road, once near empty, swarms with engineers and labourers. A railway is to stretch its iron arms into the seclusion within two years. Against that invasion the novel sets its mountain folk and their loves. Chapters promise the last of an old family, a bale fire, and a betrothal. Werner was among the most read German novelists of her day.
35311-the-eichhofs-a-romance:
Moritz von Reichenbach wrote The Eichhofs, a romance from the German, printed at Philadelphia in 1896. Wister translated it; her versions of German novels were prized as pure and elevating home favorites. The pen name hides Valeska Bethusy-Huc, as a note explains.

Chapter heads trace the family at Eichhof: two discontented fathers, hidden springs, gossip, and a marriage. A farewell glass and a death bed follow, then cloudy weather at Eichhof. A heroine named Thea rounds her first promontory. Found and lost, at the tomb, and shadows of coming events mark the tale's turns of fortune.
35349-freedom-through-disobedience:
Freedom Through Disobedience is a speech by C R Das, printed at Madras in 1922. Das was president of the Indian National Congress at Gaya that year. The speech takes up the trial of Mahatma Gandhi for sedition. Das sets the scene beside an older one: Christ before Pilate, charged as one who perverted the people. Gandhi, he notes, took an other course from that silence. He owned his guilt and pressed the prosecutor to own his.

The speech is a defence of civil disobedience as a path to freedom. It speaks from inside the non-cooperation movement of its hour. Das was a great Bengali lawyer who gave his wealth to the cause. The pamphlet is a short, hot piece of the Indian freedom fight in print. It shows how the movement read its own acts in world history.
35489-famous-men-of-science:
Sarah Bolton wrote these lives of famous men of science, copyrighted in 1889 and here in a seventh thousand. Her preface quotes Garfield: no page of history is so instructive as the early influences that shape eminent men.

The contents give fourteen lives, from Galileo and Newton through Linnæus, Cuvier, the Herschels, Humboldt, Davy, Audubon, Morse, Lyell, and Agassiz, ending with Darwin and Buckland. The sketches stress hard beginnings: poverty, illness, and failures before the true calling. Bolton notes that Franklin appears in her Famous American Statesmen instead. Young readers get science told as biography, with energy and patience as the moral.
35513-the-ledge-on-bald-face:
Charles Roberts wrote The Ledge on Bald Face, a nature story collection printed in London in 1918. A frontispiece shows a great dog shaking his victim as a terrier shakes a rat. Roberts's popular nature stories list The House in the Water, Kings in Exile, and The Secret Trails as companion volumes.

Contents give the ledge story first, then The Eagle, Cock-Crow, and The Morning of the Silver Frost. Jim the backwoods police dog fills a five-part tale of Brine's Rip. A book agent, a hole in the tree, a bear's trail, fire at the mills, and a dancing bear man follow. That stark naked mountainside faced full south, scorched by sun. Animal story readers get Roberts.
35542-house-rats-and-mice:
David E Lantz wrote House Rats and Mice, issued in October nineteen seventeen as Farmers' Bulletin eight hundred and ninety-six. Lantz was an assistant biologist with the Bureau of Biological Survey. The bulletin was free from the Department of Agriculture at Washington.

The rat, Lantz states, is the worst animal pest in the world. From filth it enters homes and stores, spoiling food and spreading plague. Rats and mice, he says, destroy over two hundred million dollars of goods each year in the United States. A pair of brown rats breeds six to ten times a year. Lantz urges war on rats by denying them food and hiding places, in an organised way.
35573-vermont-a-study-of-independence:
Rowland E Robinson wrote Vermont, a Study of Independence, for the American Commonwealths set. Houghton, Mifflin and Company issued the book in Boston in eighteen hundred ninety two. Horace E Scudder edited the state history series it stands in. A map of the Green Mountain state goes with the tale.

The lake road of war opens Vermont’s long fight for self rule. French and Indian wars scour the wild woods in chapter two. New Hampshire grants then sow the seed of the great row. The Green Mountain Boys rise to guard their claimed farms. Westminster’s blood shed and Ticonderoga’s fall crowd the war years. Bennington’s win marks the high tide of their fame at arms. Secret Haldimand talks show Vermont toyed with a British tie. War of eighteen twelve and the great Civil War close the set.
35616-home-fires-in-france:
Dorothy Canfield wrote Home Fires in France, printed at New York in 1918 and given to General Pershing. Contents hold notes from a French village in the war zone, a permissionaire sketch, and vignettes from life at the rear. A fair exchange, the refugee, a little Kansas leaven, eyes for the blind, and a honeymoon piece follow.

American boys halted first at the age of the place, Canfield reports: a village of a thousand souls that has kept its identity a thousand years. Great events mark Paris, Rome, or Stratford, but nothing in particular ever happened here beyond birth, life, and death. That fact gave the boys a queer feeling in the quiet grey street. War relief readers get Canfield's France.
35672-gloria-victis-a-romance:
Gloria Victis is a romance by Ossip Schubin, translated from the German by Mary Maxwell and published in New York by Gottsberger in 1886. Schubin had earlier written Our Own Set. A motto from Chesterfield sighs over poor human nature.

The first chapter opens in a baroness's dressing room. The Baroness Melkweyser sighs into her toilet glass while her maid dresses her hair. A week has passed since a man named Capriani entrusted an affair to her, and she has found no favourable moment. The match she must promote would make Gabrielle a sister-in-law to a duke. Society intrigue drives the plot from its first page. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
35678-france:
Gordon Home surveys the French for English readers in France, published at London in 1914 with thirty-two full-page illustrations in colour. A frontispiece shows the western facade of Amiens Cathedral, and plates range over Paris streets, Breton calvaries, Loire chateaux and Mont Blanc. Chapters treat the genesis and character of the French, family life, marriage and the birth-rate, and self-government.

Further chapters cover education and religion, Paris and town life, rural life, the rivers of France and the watering-places. Architecture from Roman to Gothic and the national defences close the survey, with a sketch map and index.
35688-alice-in-wonderland-a-dramatizatio:
Alice in Wonderland is a dramatization of Lewis Carroll's two Alice books by Alice Gerstenberg of Chicago. A C McClurg and Company published the play in December nineteen fifteen. Gerstenberg reserved the production rights in all countries. The play was first staged at the Fine Arts Theater, Chicago, on February eleventh, nineteen fifteen.

After a successful run it opened at the Booth Theater in New York that March. William Penhallow Henderson designed scenery and costumes, and Eric De Lamarter wrote the music. The cast list makes Lewis Carroll himself a character, discovered playing chess. Vivian Tobin played Alice, with Florence LeClercq as the Red Queen. The scenes run from Alice's home through the looking-glass room to the court of hearts. Gerstenberg's script kept Carroll stageable for school and community theatres.
35715-the-early-history-of-the-colonial-:
The Early History of the Colonial Post-Office, by Mary Woolley, was reprinted at Providence in 1894 from the Rhode Island Historical Society. The paper belongs to a Brown University historical seminary set edited by Franklin Jameson. Woolley opens with a letter of 1652 from Samuel Symonds of Ipswich to John Winthrop the younger at Pequot.

Symonds pleads that he writes seldom only because he never knows when or how to send a letter. Woolley notes that all writers of the day shared that bind. With no home postal service, colonists pressed neighbors, kin, merchants, and sea captains into service as carriers. The paper traces how that patchwork grew into an ordered colonial post, in a short scholarly study.
35855-studies-in-the-out-lying-fields-of:
Studies in the Out-lying Fields of Psychic Science is a book by Hudson Tuttle, printed at New York by Holbrook and Company with copyright of 1889. Tuttle had already written Arcana of Nature and Origin and Development of Man. He dedicated this volume to Alfred Giles of Hyde Park, Massachusetts. The dedication calls Giles an erudite scholar, a fearless investigator and an unshrinking advocate of his convictions.

The book opens with an analysis of its own argument. There is a psychic ether, related to thought as the luminiferous ether is to light. It may be regarded as the thought atmosphere of the universe. That state may be normal or abnormal. From these grounds Tuttle builds his case for the phenomena of spiritualism and mind reading.
35899-the-philippines-a-century-hence:
The Philippines a Century Hence is a forecast essay by Jose Rizal. The essay stands in a set that marks his famed novel at its quarter mark. A past voice of a great chief lends praise at its front. This book came out at Manila in the year nineteen twelve.

Rizal asks what his isles will be one full age from his own day. A German roamer guess on the isles fate first set his mind to work. He holds that the old shut rule of the isles can no more stand. Trade with the world must crack the old walls, blow by blow. The plea is for ground work now to fit the isles for self rule.
35902-final-proof-or-the-value-of-eviden:
Ottolengui published 'Final Proof; or, The Value of Evidence' with Putnam's Sons in 1898. A prefatory note sets the scene. Barnes the detective and Robert Leroy Mitchel, the gentleman who imagines he can outdo detectives at their own work, first met in 'An Artist in Crime' some years before. A murder mystery in 'The Crime of the Century' followed, and this volume gives cases from the interval.

Twelve cases fill the contents, mixing jewels and frauds: the Phoenix of Crime, the Missing Link, the Nameless Man, and the Montezuma Emerald. A singular abduction, the Aztec Opal, the Duplicate Harlequin, and the Pearls of Isis follow, with a promissory note, a novel forgery, and a frosty morning behind them. The first case opens at Mitchel's breakfast table, where Barnes's card is brought in early and the detective is drawn up to share the good coffee.
35912-the-finger-of-fate-a-romance:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote this romance, issued by Chapman and Hall in an edition dated 1872, opening in a pheasant cover within ten miles of Windsor. Two young sportsmen hunt there with thoroughbred setters and a keeper, and they are Nigel and Henry, the only sons of General Harding, an old Indian officer. The General bought his Bucks estate with a hundred thousand pounds garnered during twenty years of service in the East.

The brothers look so unlike in face, hair, and coloring that a stranger would scarce believe them brothers, and in the exact sense they are only half-brothers. Both call the General father, but their thoughts of a mother go to two different graves, one near Hyderabad and one in an English churchyard. Reid builds his tale of fate and family on that contrast, set around an Elizabethan red-brick mansion and its park.
36092-north-devon-pottery-and-its-export:
Malcolm Watkins, a keeper of past culture at the national museum, wrote a study dated 1960 on North Devon pottery. Digs at Jamestown and Plymouth had turned up shards of two wares that no one could name. One was a bold yellow ware with lines cut through slip, and the other a coarse red kitchen ware full of grit.

Watkins shows that both wares share one tale of make, trade, and sale to the shore towns of America. Shards help date a site and show how well its folk lived and what they prized. The piece is the first in his long plan to trace all the pots used by English settlers in the New World.
36224-notes-on-the-kiowa-sun-dance:
Notes on the Kiowa Sun Dance, by Leslie Spier, is part six of volume sixteen of the Anthropological Papers of the American Museum of Natural History. The museum published the paper in New York in 1921. A figure gives the groundplan of the dance lodge. Spier states his source at the start: the notes were obtained from Andres Martinez, called Andele, a Mexican captive of the Kiowa, in August 1919.

The last Kiowa sun dance, a note records, was held in 1887. The dance, Spier explains, is the prerogative of the man who owns the sacred image, the tai'me. He deputes the lesser offices where he sees fit, though they tend to run hereditary. The image is above all a war medicine, which makes the Kiowa rite kin to the Crow's. The notes measure Andele's account against the earlier record by Scott.
36247-the-red-mouse-a-mystery-romance:
William Hamilton Osborne mixes mystery and romance in a novel issued in New York in 1909, with pictures by the Kinneys. The tale opens on Miriam Challoner, who has spent the best years of her life excusing her husband. Word reaches her that even their fast set calls him mad Challoner and says he is going to the dogs.

Miriam will not discuss her shame with anyone, and silence turns her blame inward. She fears the shrugs of her set and the easy verdict that a wife is at fault for a husband's fall. Osborne builds his plot on that proud, unhappy marriage and the money that feeds its ruin. Readers get a society mystery of the Edwardian years, sharp on wealth, talk, and blame.
3641-who-cares-a-story-of-adolescence:
Cosmo Hamilton writes a story of adolescence about a boy and a girl, as his own playful preface puts it. When asked what the novel is about, Hamilton answers only that it is about a boy and a girl. When asked if they marry or are happy, he replies that all love stories are happy if it is love. The book itself follows a girl who writes that she is miserable, with nothing to live for, since her mother married again.

Hamilton treats the pains of growing up with sympathy and humor: first love, family change, and the feeling that adults do not understand. The novel suits young readers and adults who remember adolescence, in a light, early twentieth century romance that takes young feeling seriously.
36451-richard-iii-his-life-character-rev:
Richard the Third, His Life and Character, by Clements Markham, was published in London in 1906. Markham says he reviews the king in the light of recent research. The book opens at Fotheringhay, with the lands of the Duke of York, his marriage, and the birth of Richard.

Early chapters follow Richard as a child, even as a prisoner of war at the age of seven. They then turn to the death of his father and brother at Wakefield. Sandal Castle, the march, and the battle are all set out in turn. Readers get a life that tries to judge a much blamed king afresh, starting from his youth and the wars that shaped him.
36476-riches-of-grace:
Riches of Grace compiles experiences in the Christian life by E E Byrum. The Gospel Trumpet Company of Anderson, Indiana, published it in 1918. It belongs to the Christian Life Series and sold in cloth at $1.00. The subtitle promises trials and victories along the way. Two texts from Ephesians and Hebrews head the title page. Twenty-seven chapters, plus a closing poem, fill the volume.

The experiences range across the world. A minister, a prisoner, and a little Chinese girl testify early. Persecutions of an evangelist and the secret of a perfect life follow. A young Jewish rabbi's conversion takes a chapter. Mohammedans in Egypt and missionaries in the British West Indies extend the map. The confession of a murderer stands at chapter twenty-four. Byrum's preface states the pastoral aim. Many honest hearts long for a righteous life but meet obstacles.
36626-the-childhood-of-king-erik-menved-:
Ingemann writes a royal romance in The Childhood of King Erik Menved, an historical romance, printed in London in 1846. Bruce and Wyld made the book, rendered from the Danish by Kesson. It stands as volume seven of a library of foreign romance. The translator writes the preface, since the author gave none.

The author has given no preface to this romance, Kesson opens, and the translator would be content to follow his example on one ground. Had the author already enjoyed a name in England, his book would need no herald. But the names of Danish writers are little known in England, he argues. The literature and language of Denmark have not here received the degree of attention which they so justly merit. While the poets and novelists of France and Germany are familiar to many readers, the public has yet to learn Denmark's names.
3676-the-firefly-of-france:
Marion Polk Angellotti writes a wartime melodrama set in France during the First World War. The story begins, as the author puts it, in the restaurant of the Hotel St Ives, an odd spot to serve as stage wings for a melodrama pure and simple. The narrator has survived shell fragments taken by a French surgeon from his head, and a British officer at Gibraltar who held up his papers.

The tale follows spies, soldiers, and a heroine called the Firefly through dangers in wartime France. Angellotti writes with speed and color, in the style of 1918 adventure fiction. The book suits readers who enjoy old fashioned war melodrama, with narrow escapes and a brave woman at its center.
36768-triumphs-of-invention-and-discover:
Triumphs of Invention and Discovery in Art and Science is a popular survey by J Hamilton Fyfe. It was published in London in eighteen seventy one, with a motto from Milton on peace and her victories. A picture of George Stephenson's home fronts the book. The preface argues that peaceful wins deserve the fame given to war.

Inside, short accounts celebrate makers and finders in art and science. Railways, engines, and other new machines of the age sit beside finds in study and craft. The tone is proud and plain, aimed at general readers rather than experts. The book shows how Victorian readers were taught to admire invention as a moral force.
36852-the-story-of-antony-grace:
The Story of Antony Grace, by George Manville Fenn, is a boy tale. Appleton issued the New York edition in 1888, with plates by Gordon Browne. Antony narrates, a boy in a house fresh from his father funeral. The day after, a stranger walks in and makes himself at home there.

Rowle hangs up his hat, draws a long clay pipe from his sleeve. Cook snubs him; the boy must fetch the visitor a light instead. Rowle punches the leather chair, smokes, and bids Antony show him round. A calm, at home air marks the man as somehow in possession. Loss, guardians, and a boy path through change drive the story.
3708-an-introduction-to-chemical-science:
Williams wrote this school textbook to lead beginners into chemistry through plain facts and homely tests rather than through theory alone. It works through the common elements and their compounds, with gases, acids, salts, and metals each getting clear notes on how they act and how they can be shown at a bench. Short trials let a pupil see a result with his own eyes before the book states the rule behind it.

The middle chapters give plain safety sense as well, such as testing well air with a lowered candle before going down, since heavy gases can pool unseen and kill. Mine damp, volcanic fumes, and the gases of breath all serve as live cases. The book still reads as a window on how science was taught a century ago, when care, sight, and smell stood beside the balance and the flask.
37140-a-proposal-under-difficulties-a-fa:
John Kendrick Bangs wrote a one-act farce, first issued in 1896 and here in a 1905 printing with plates. The scene is a smart New York drawing room on a Wednesday afternoon in late October. Robert Yardsley enters alone, glad to have got so far, and scared of what comes next.

Yardsley has come to ask Dorothy Andrews to wed him, and he scolds his own fear in the mirror. He is brave among men, he says, but this task shakes him. A second suitor, Jack Barlow, waits in the cast list, with a maid named Jennie. Bangs, a famed comic writer, milks a lover's nerves for laughs.
37190-the-main-chance:
Meredith Nicholson's The Main Chance was published by Bobbs-Merrill of Indianapolis in 1903, illustrated by Harrison Fisher. Forty-two chapters of business and society follow its men: A New Man in Town, Warrick Raridan, At Poindexter's, the Knights of Midas ball, and a morning at St Paul's. Late in the book come John Saxton, Receiver, shots in the dark, and home through the snow.

Chapter one puts the charge on the table at once. William Porter, president of the Clarkson National Bank, tips back his swivel chair, placidly puffs a cigar, and opens: well, sir, they say I am crooked. He watches the effect on the young man across from him, John Saxton. Saxton answers that this is said of every successful man nowadays. Porter ignores him and rolls the cigar to the other side of his mouth. The title is the gambler's phrase for the one good opening.
372-prince-otto-a-romance:
Robert Louis Stevenson sets this romance in the small German state of Grunewald, ruled by the dreamy Prince Otto. Otto, more poet than king, drifts from his clever wife Seraphina and falls into plots hatched by courtiers and rebels. A count, a farmer's daughter, and a band of schemers push the small court toward crisis.

Stevenson mixes court jest with real peril, as Otto must at last act like a prince or lose all. The prose is light and often comic, yet the stakes grow grave. The book shows an early Stevenson trying a new form, with wit, grace, and a keen eye for weak rulers and strong wills.
37350-the-ancestry-of-modern-amphibia-a-:
The Ancestry of Modern Amphibia: A Review of the Evidence is a scientific paper by Theodore Eaton of the University of Kansas. It appeared in the University of Kansas Publications of the Museum of Natural History in July 1959. The paper runs from page 155 to 180 with ten figures. Its first section compares the modern orders of amphibians with two extinct groups, the labyrinthodonts and the lepospondyls.

Figures show the skulls of fossil forms such as Saurerpeton, Amphibamus, and Protobatrachus, drawn from earlier authors. The comparison works bone by bone through the skull. A passage preserved in the copy notes that the exoccipital bones form the two condyles. It adds that there are no separate openings for the eleventh and twelfth nerves, since those nerves are not separate in modern amphibians. The opisthotic bone is missing in all but one family.
37422-the-life-and-death-of-doctor-faust: William Mountfort's Life and Death of Doctor Faustus Made into a Farce, dated 1697, appears here as an Augustan Reprint Society volume. The Clark Memorial Library at Los Angeles issued it in 1973, with an introduction by Anthony Kaufman. The pages shown are front matter and the notes to that introduction. They cite Mountfort's Six Plays of 1720 and Borgman's 1935 Harvard life of the playwright. The farce text itself lies beyond the pages shown.
3745-the-road-to-providence:
Maria Thompson Daviess gathers a set of linked village tales around the doctors Mayberry, mother and son, of a Tennessee country town. Mother Mayberry rules the kitchen with a light hand for risen biscuits. Her son Tom runs the barn and the practice, and together they answer every call on the road to Providence. A singer lady, a peony girl, a little raven with a covered dish, and a tag gang of small helpers fill the chapters.

The stories run warm and funny, with deacons, sick neighbors, and weddings crowding the lanes. Daviess writes in local speech that stays readable, and her people help one another without fuss. Readers who like gentle community tales will find Providence a pleasant place to linger, with kindness treated as a daily habit rather than a sermon.
37520-surnames-as-a-science:
Surnames as a Science is a philological work by Robert Ferguson, member of Parliament and fellow of the Society of Antiquaries, printed at London in 1883. Ferguson had already published The Teutonic Name-System, and this volume is of the nature of a supplement to it. He inscribes it to Mrs R H Dana, nee Longfellow, of Boston.

That portion of our surnames which dates back to Anglo-Saxon times, the preface argues, forms part of the general system by which Teutonic names are governed. It is distinctly a branch of a science, and has been so treated by the Germans, on whose lines Ferguson generally follows. One object is to show that this portion is very much larger than has been generally supposed. Many names hitherto otherwise accounted for fall under it.
3758-the-gates-of-chance:
Van Tassel Sutphen links a dozen New York tales of chance, crime, and detection through a single curious thread. The book opens with a visiting card thrust into the narrator's hand, penciled with an evening call at a Madison Avenue address for a Mr Esper Indiman. From there the stories turn on a red duchess, a queen of spades, and an opal button. A brass baggage check and an upset apple cart join them, each a small object with a large secret.

One later tale finds a woman's rooms ransacked by detectives and a letter hidden beyond their reach, while her captors rage at their failure. Sutphen writes with a light, urbane touch, and New York's streets, clubs, and crossings frame every puzzle. Readers who like short mysteries with wit will find a book best taken one gate at a time.
3759-fridthjof-s-saga-a-norse-romance:
Esaias Tegner retells an old Norse saga as a verse romance, and this translation by Thomas and Martha Holcomb keeps its ringing dialogue. Fridthjof, a hero of the north, loves Ingeborg, the sister of kings, but her brothers Helge and Halfdan bar the match. Honor binds him to a quest for gold owed to King Angantyr, and the lovers must part while Fridthjof sails to claim it.

The middle scenes stage the parting as a debate, with Ingeborg pleading and Fridthjof vowing to return, sword at his side. Sea voyages, kings' halls, and pagan rites fill the later cantos. Readers who enjoy epic love stories will find a tale of loyalty tested by pride, exile, and the hard code of the Viking age.
37614-jungle-peace:
William Beebe published Jungle Peace under copyright of 1920, shown here in the Modern Library line at New York. He offers the volume to Colonel and Mrs Theodore Roosevelt with deep friendship. A note says most chapters first ran in The Atlantic Monthly. The jungle chapters treat the Bartica District of British Guiana, with one set at Para in Brazil.

Contents move from sea wrack and islands to the Pomeroon Trail and a hunt for hoatzins. A wilderness laboratory, army ants, and jungle night follow in turn. Beebe writes as a flyer fresh from war who craves green peace. Photographs by the author and by Paul Howes picture the work. Science softens into wonder without losing its facts.
37750-guy-fawkes-or-the-gunpowder-treaso:
William Harrison Ainsworth wrote Guy Fawkes, or The Gunpowder Treason, a historical romance with steel plates by George Cruikshank. Ainsworth finished the tale at Kingston Lisle in July 1841. His dedication thanks a friend whose kindness was near maternal.

A preface quotes Doctor Lingard on the harsh laws revived against Roman Catholics under James the First. Those penal laws, Ainsworth holds, drove men to the famous plot. The romance then tells of Fawkes and his fellows, their grievances, and their design against king and Parliament. History and fancy are woven close together.
37793-the-story-of-florence:
Edmund Gardner's The Story of Florence, illustrated by Nelly Erichsen, was published by Dent of London in 1900 and reached a second edition the same year. Gardner gives the book to his sister, Monica Mary Gardner. A Botticelli frontispiece, Pallas taming a Centaur, faces the title.

Thirteen chapters walk the city's history and streets together. The commune and people of Florence come first, then the times of Dante and Boccaccio, the Medici and the quattrocento, and the road from Fra Girolamo to Duke Cosimo. After that the book turns guide: the Palazzo Vecchio and the Uffizi, Or San Michele, the Bargello and Santa Croce. Then the Baptistery, campanile, and Duomo, San Lorenzo and San Marco, and across the Arno. A genealogical table of the Medici and a chronological index of architects, sculptors, and painters close the volume.
37919-in-accordance-with-the-evidence:
Oliver Onions wrote In Accordance with the Evidence, copyrighted in 1913 and published in New York by Doran. Onions had earlier written The Exception. The novel is told in three parts named for places: Holborn, Woburn Place, and the Garret. Its narrator writes his jottings in Pitman's shorthand.

He took up shorthand again after a gap of a dozen years. His old partner in the practice was Archie Merridew, whose clear, high-pitched voice was the last that ever dictated to him for speed. Archie died, and the narrator dropped the skill suddenly. Now, in a third-floor bedroom near King's Cross, opposite an electric sign that changed from green to red, he sets down his account. The title promises testimony, and the book delivers a confession in evidence form.
380-weir-of-hermiston-an-unfinished-roma:
Robert Louis Stevenson left this Scots romance unfinished at his death, and it stands as his most praised late work. Archie Weir, son of a harsh hanging judge, is cast out to a lonely farm after defying his father. There he meets Kirstie, and love, pride, and family doom tangle in the moorland parish.

An opening note sets the scene at a cairn where a Covenanter once died, a place of old blood and silence. Stevenson's Scots prose is stern and musical, full of moor, mist, and law. Though cut short, the book grips as a tragedy of father and son, and of a young man caught between duty and heart.
38142-the-seven-cardinal-sins-envy-and-i:
The Seven Cardinal Sins: Envy and Indolence is one volume of a five-volume set of novels by the French writer Eugene Sue, in the Dagobert Edition of 1899. The volume holds two tales, called simply Envy and Indolence, with pictures throughout.

Envy begins in 1828 on the road from Blois to Pont Brillant, near the famed castle of the Marquises of that name. A lonely farmhouse by the road draws the eye for its ugliness. By June 1845 a young mother has lived there seventeen years, and the yard has grown over with trees and flowering vines. Sue builds his study of envy on that household. Frederick Bastien, a character in the tale, is named at the head of the volume. Sue's set gives each of the seven sins its own story of French life.
38160-a-hero-of-romance:
Richard Marsh wrote a boys adventure printed at London with pictures by Harold Copping. Marsh had written The Datchel Diamonds and The Crime and the Criminal. Perhaps you don't know who I am, the frontispiece cries from page one hundred fifty five. Punishment at Mecklemburg House opens the tale on about as miserable an afternoon as one could wish.

It was half holiday, but no half holiday for the lad shut in the schoolroom, a tall boy of some fourteen years. Tutor baiting, at Mother Huffham's, a little drive, and an evening at Washington Villa follow. Preparing for flight, the start, a doss house, Petersham Park, and out of the frying pan into the fire fill the road. To Jersey with a thief and the land of golden dreams close a runaway's wild ride.
38171-imprudence:
Mills Young wrote this novel, Imprudence, in an edition printed in London in 1920. Chapter one opens in still evening light in May. The last rays of the sun lie warm on fields and leafing trees. Blackthorn blooms in the hedges. Below lies a township in a hollow, and over it rise the tall red-brick chimneys that rule the place, Wortheton.

Those chimneys stand for wealth, industry, and set order, and for the drab need to labour. Against them walks a girl alone on the dusty road. Her face is young, but her look is world-weary and her brown eyes sullen. She has, the narrator says, the springtime of life in years, and a hard schooling in life already behind her.
38176-the-stronger-influence:
F E Mills Young set her novel The Stronger Influence in South Africa, in an edition from George H Doran at New York dated 1922. Book one opens at Coerney station, where visitors for the Zuurberg leave the train for a cart up the steep mountain road. Four travellers get down together.

An elderly couple and a middle-aged man of their acquaintance go in search of refreshment. A young girl, a stranger to them all, walks alone to the cart in the tree shade. She has been ill and takes a holiday to speed her recovery. Heat, golden light, and silence brood over the platform. Mills Young wrote many tales of South African life, and place shapes this one from the start.
38196-eunice:
Eunice is a novel by Margaret Murray Robertson, in an edition dated eighteen ninety from a London house. Its first chapter, Going Home, opens on a fair morning by the Connecticut River. A group of schoolgirls waits at a small wayside station on its banks. They have crossed the river by ferry boat and wait for more of their number.

The girls stand at the foot of Mount Tom, bright in morning sunshine. Across the river, shadows still cling to the face of Mount Holyoke. Spring is promised but not yet come to that valley scene. The elms show no green, though their buds are ready to burst. Meadows are greening and catkins swell on the willows by the brooks. A girl called Nellie Austin is told that her Faithful is coming by boat.
38250-the-honour-of-savelli-a-romance:
Levett Yeats published The Honour of Savelli with Appleton in 1895, calling it a romance and meaning the word as a program. His preface renounces the moral. He has made no effort to point one; all that has been done is an attempt to catch the spirit of the true romance, and to amuse.

The book was partly written in the intervals of work in India. It was completed during furlough on a medical certificate. For Italian history of the story's period, the author takes Dumas for his model, while hoping his scheme is worked out on original lines. He uses, as far as possible, the language an Italian of the early sixteenth century would speak. A district officer writing cloak-and-sword romance between tours of duty: the empire produced the amateur, and this is his holiday work.
38288-our-national-defense-the-patriotis:
George Maxwell wrote Our National Defense, subtitled The Patriotism of Peace, as the fourth book of the Homecrofters Rural Settlements Association. The association issued it in 1915, with copyright of 1916, from Washington and New Orleans. Maxwell gave the book to all homecrofters, under Milton's line that peace hath her victories no less renowned than war. His prefatory note holds that a battle for peace needs facts for ammunition.

He argues that Congress is not at fault for the country's unreadiness, since the stream cannot rise higher than the fountain and the people's will is law. The people, he says, are set against a big standing army, yet can demand safety without the cost or menace of militarism once they know the facts. The book pleads for a defense built on settled farmers rather than on an army.
384-the-lost-prince:
Frances Hodgson Burnett tells of Marco Loristan, a boy in dingy London who plays at a secret game with his father. Marco and his friend, known as the Rat, drill a squad of boys, guard a lamp signal, and dream of Samavia, a far land torn by strife. What starts as play turns grave when Marco must carry a real message across Europe.

Burnett mixes adventure with a warm tale of loyalty, as two boys brave cities, frontiers, and spies. The lost prince of the title proves closer than Marco dreams. The book charms young readers with its blend of game and peril, and its faith in honor kept in secret.
38474-loaded-dice:
Ellery Clark wrote Loaded Dice, a novel in three parts issued at Indianapolis in 1909 with art by Graham Cootes. The tale opens at the Federal Club, set on a tall hill above a fast growing city by a broad bay. A game of bridge there starts a chain of deals, dinners, and traps in high life.

Part one, The Foothold, builds a snare and springs it, with a scandal stopped just in time. Part two, The Game, moves to a mining claim, a ship launch, and hard fights over cash and votes. Part three, The Reckoning, sorts the throw of the dice into the hand of man and the hand of God. Clark mixes sport, wealth, and public life.
38657-love-among-the-lions-a-matrimonial:
Love Among the Lions, subtitled A Matrimonial Experience, is a comic novel by Anstey, author of Vice Versa. Dent published it in London, and the tale is told by its hero himself. Theodore Blenkinsop claims his pages give the only true account of the affair. That affair gave London nine days of talk and guesswork, he says.

Blenkinsop, twenty eight and single, tastes tea for a city firm at a good wage. He lodges over a dairy in Highbury and feels no wish to wed at all. Then a stroll round Canonbury Square changes his whole world in one afternoon. The picture list tells where the tale runs: a lady met, a proposal scene. Let us be married in the lion's cage, one plate caption boldly reads. His wedding dress and a small procession into the arena follow in turn.
38665-the-courtship-of-morrice-buckler-a:
A E W Mason edited The Courtship of Morrice Buckler, a romance issued at London and New York in 1896. The tale claims to be the record of an English gentleman's growth in the years 1685 to 1687. Buckler wrote it in his own hand some while after. Mason had writ A Romance of Wastdale.

Three editions came out in five months of 1896. Chapters trace a cut off note, a trip to London, and a strange guise at Bristol. Sir Julian Harnwood and Count Lukstein enter the plot. Swords take up the talk in one chapter. The Countess Lukstein draws Buckler back and forth in doubt. A game of hide and seek and a half way house mark the late turns. The tale mixes love with risk in a past age.
38691-down-under-with-the-prince:
Down Under with the Prince, by Everard Cotes, was first printed in London by Methuen in 1921, with twenty three plates. Cotes had written Signs and Portents in the Far East. A plate shows the Prince on deck of the battle cruiser Renown.

Cotes says the book tries to be a gangway to the Renown for the reader. The reader would travel by battle cruiser, by train, on horseback, and by motor with the Prince of Wales. Chapters treat Barbados, Panama, southern California, and Honolulu first. Neptune boards the Renown, then Fiji, Auckland, and the North and South Islands of New Zealand. Victoria and the rest of Australia close the tour. Royal tour fans get a press man warm record of the 1920 voyage.
38985-my-lady-rotha-a-romance:
Stanley Weyman, famed for A Gentleman of France and Under the Red Robe, wrote this romance of war in old Germany. Longmans, Green printed My Lady Rotha in New York in 1894. A plate near the end shows the death of Tzerclas.

Heritzburg and the Countess Rotha open the tale, and a burgomaster's demand sets the fire alight. Marie Wort, Rupert the Great, and a camp in the forest crowd the early chapters. A theft, a duel in two parts, and a general's banquet raise the stakes. Stalhanske's Finns charge in one chapter. Wounds, flight, and haste fill the list shown here, in a tale of love and arms.
39074-curiosities-of-medical-experience:
J G Millingen wrote Curiosities of Medical Experience, issued in London by Richard Bentley in eighteen thirty nine in a second, much larger form. Millingen was a surgeon to the forces and house doctor at the Middlesex pauper lunatic asylum at Hanwell. He gave the book to Sir James McGrigor, head of the Army Medical Department. Greek and Hebrew notes appear in the text.

Millingen gathers odd cases, old cures, and strange facts from long practice. His posts gave him sight of war wounds, madness, and poor folk ills alike. The book mixes tales of patients with notes on drugs, diet, and the mind. Victorian readers prized such storehouses of curious fact. Doctors and general readers alike can see how medicine was thought of and done in that age.
39137-shrewsbury-a-romance:
Stanley Weyman wrote a tale named for the town of Shrewsbury, printed in 1898 with twenty four pictures by Claude Shepperson and given to the author's brother Henry. Weyman's earlier tales, listed at the front, deal with the massacre of St Bartholomew, the days of Henry of Navarre, and the French rising, all tales of old wars.

Picture heads promise tense scenes: a duke lifting his hat in scorn, a pistol jerked up from behind, a hidden cupboard, and a ring of cold steel pressed home. There are curses on King William too. The tale belongs to Weyman's line of swift romances of plot and sword play in the great crises of past ages.
39168-sophia-a-romance:
Stanley J Weyman writes a romance of old London in a Longmans, Green volume with rights held from 1899. Ads at the front list his past tales, among them A Gentleman of France and Under the Red Robe, each with its price. Sophia carries twelve full-page plates and a price of one dollar and fifty cents in that list.

Weyman gives the book to the memory of James Payn on the dedication page. Twenty-six chapters run from A Little Toad and At Vauxhall to King Smallpox and A Dragon Disarmed. Chapter heads name a clock-maker, a chair and a coach, strolling players, and two portraits. The mix points to love, masks, and risk in a past age of coaches and playhouses.
39286-colour-as-a-means-of-art-being-an-:
Frank Howard wrote this art manual, Colour as a Means of Art, printed at London in 1849. Howard also wrote a sketcher's manual and a book on the spirit of Shakespeare. His subtitle states the method: an adaptation of the experience of professors to the practice of amateurs. A dedication letter to a royal academician explains the aim at length.

The endeavour, Howard writes, is to fix and develop the accepted general principles of colouring as a means of art, for amateur and student. It leaves aside the poetical expression and close copying of nature that great works need. Contents bear this out. A first chapter treats harmony and tone. A second gives rules for making pictures in colour, drawn master by master. The principles of Cuyp, of Both, of Hobbema and Ruysdael, of Teniers and Ostade, of Titian, of Rubens, and of Turner are taken in turn.
393-the-blue-lagoon-a-romance:
H. de Vere Stacpoole follows two castaway children, Dick and Emmeline, in this island romance. A shipwreck strands them on a lush Pacific isle, where they grow from children to young lovers with no guide but nature. A kind old sailor dies early, leaving them to learn food, shelter, and love on their own.

Later books bring a schooner, a child, a cyclone, and a strange visitor who seeks the isle's secret. Stacpoole writes the lagoon in rich, bright detail, from reefs to palms. The novel charms as a tale of innocence and first love, set far from all laws but those of sea and sky.
39834-after-the-divorce-a-romance:
Grazia Deledda wrote a novel of a man freed by divorce and the wife he left. Maria Hornor Lansdale turned the book into English. It came out in New York in 1905. A verse from Saint Luke heads the book. The tale is set in the year 1907, as its first page says.

In the strangers' room of the Porru house, a woman weeps. She sits on the floor with her head on her arms. All hope seems gone from her life as the book starts. Law, faith, and kin ties press on both wife and man. Deledda writes with grave force on love that law has cut.
39933-the-amazing-inheritance:
Frances R Sterrett turns a department-store salesgirl into a queen in a comic novel issued by D Appleton and Company in 1922. Her name also fronts a shelf of earlier tales, The Jam Girl among them.

Tessie Gilfooly works in the hardware department of the Evergreen store at Waloo. Mr Walker, her long, thin chief, has just scolded her. A customer asked for a frying-pan, and Tessie handed over a saucepan. Tessie insists the woman asked for a saucepan. Tears gather in her blue eyes at the injustice. Then a man brings amazing news. She is a queen. The tale plays the fairy-story wish against the hard grind of shop work. Sterrett writes with warmth for the girls behind the counters.
39978-the-royal-mail-its-curiosities-and:
James Wilson Hyde, a superintendent in the Edinburgh post office, recounts the oddities and romance of the Royal Mail. The hosted text is the third edition, issued in London in 1889, with new matter and fresh pictures. Hyde gives the book to Henry Fawcett, the late postmaster-general.

In his introduction Hyde calls the post office the people's own institution, open to rich and poor alike. By his day it carried letters and parcels, sent telegrams, banked savings, insured lives, and sold government licenses. Chapters treat mail packets, lost letters, odd coincidences, and postmasters, among much else. Readers get an insider's store of postal lore from the age of the mail coach and the early train.
40014-john-burnet-of-barns-a-romance:
John Buchan writes an old Scots tale in John Burnet of Barns, a romance printed at Toronto in 1899. The Copp Clark Company made the book, with copyright in 1898. Buchan gives it to the memory of his sister. Four books carry the life, from Tweeddale to the Westlands.

The tale is told in the first person, as a history of a life lived in stirring times. An adventure in the wood of Dawyck leads, then the house of Barns and a spate in Tweed. The teller goes to college at Glasgow and rides out on his travels. The Low Countries hold a voyage, a supper party, and a fight on the Alphen Road. Hillmen, the cave of the Cor Water, and a fight in the moss of Biggar fill the close.
4005-herb-of-grace:
Rosa Nouchette Carey's novel opens its eighth chapter on a studio door left ajar, where a sweet voice sings a lullaby and a young man named Malcolm peeps in rather than knock. A line from Maeterlinck sets the theme: wherever you travel, you meet only yourself on the road of fate.

The story follows Malcolm and the household around him through love, work, and the search for a worthy life. Carey writes in the plain, kindly manner of late Victorian family fiction, with studios, gardens, and sickrooms as its stages. Readers who like gentle domestic novels with a moral thread will find the book easy company and quietly moving.
40154-sing-a-song-of-sixpence:
Mary Holdsworth wrote a tale for children, issued at Edinburgh and London in 1892. Nellie, a small girl, holds a brand new sixpence fresh from the Mint. The coin burns a hole in her pocket all day and drives her school work out at one ear.

Nellie must learn her poetry or Miss Primmer will keep her in and she will miss a trip out with her nurse and Reggie. As she tries, her mind runs to all she might buy: a lamb with a blue sash, sweets, and wool for stockings for her pa and ma. Plain wants and bright dreams fill a short, warm tale.
40155-akbar-an-eastern-romance:
Akbar, an Eastern Romance, was written in Dutch by Van Limburg Brouwer and first printed at the Hague in 1872. Allen published this English version in London in 1879, as publishers to the India Office. Clements Markham added notes and an introductory life of the Emperor Akbar.

Markham calls Akbar the greatest and best native ruler who ever held sway over Hindustan. The author, an oriental scholar, worked from contemporary writers to show the thoughts and habits of the emperor and the manners of his court. Markham argues that English readers, above all, should know this period, when native administration was at its best and fullest accounts survive.
40273-the-bolsheviki-and-world-peace:
The Bolsheviki and World Peace, by Leon Trotzky, was printed by Boni and Liveright in New York in 1918. Its author's preface is dated from New York on January 4 of that year. Eleven chapters run from the Balkan question and Austria Hungary to the war against Czarism, the collapse of the International, and the revolutionary epoch.

The preface states the argument whole. The forces of production that capitalism evolved have outgrown the limits of nation and state, and the whole globe has become one economic workshop. The present war, Trotzky writes, is at bottom a revolt of those forces against the political form of nation and state. It proclaims the downfall of the national state, and with it the downfall of the capitalist system of economy that built it.
40295-lord-montagu-s-page-an-historical-:
James's Lord Montagu's Page, an historical romance of the seventeenth century, was published at Philadelphia by Childs and Peterson in 1858. A biographical sketch from Allibone's dictionary of authors precedes the novel. It gives its subject's full name as George Payne Rainsford James, born in London about the year 1800.

The sketch says Washington Irving encouraged the young writer, whose first work was a life of Edward the Black Prince in 1822. James then turned to historical romance with Richelieu, which won the favor of Sir Walter Scott and of Christopher North in Blackwood's. Darnley and De L'Orme followed, and the sketch lists the novels that made him one of the most prolific romancers of his day.
40342-the-freedom-of-science:
The Freedom of Science, by Joseph Donat of the Society of Jesus, professor at Innsbruck University, was published by Joseph F Wagner at New York in 1914. The imprimatur is Cardinal Farley's. Five sections treat the freedom of science and its philosophical basis. Freedom of research and faith, and the liberal freedom of research, follow in turn.

Freedom of teaching and theology as science close the argument. Donat's preface to the English edition says the work already had many friends in German Europe. It issued, he writes, from the throes of dissension and strife, and now seeks readers among English speakers.
40390-cathedral-cities-of-france:
Herbert Marshall and Hester Marshall wrote Cathedral Cities of France for Dodd, Mead in 1907, with sixty colour pictures by Herbert Marshall. A view of Laon from the plain faces the title page. The chapters rest on notes from five summers spent in France.

The authors warn that the chapters mark no fixed scheme and skip some cathedral cities. They thank Viollet-le-Duc on architecture, Henry James for A Little Tour in France, and Cecil Headlam for The Story of Chartres. Freeman's Norman Conquest and war letters from The Times of 1870 and 1871 also helped. Each city gets its church, streets, and history in a traveller's voice, meant as suggestions for those who follow.
40394-sketches-from-the-subject-and-neig:
Sketches from the Subject and Neighbour Lands of Venice is a book of travel essays by Freeman, printed at London. Freeman also wrote Historical and Architectural Sketches, chiefly Italian, as a companion volume. Reviewers quoted at the front praise the pairing of historian and antiquary in one writer.

The Times holds that the two sides of his mind save each other. History escapes shallowness, and dry learning escapes pedantry. The Examiner counts twenty-two pictures from the author's own pencil. It calls him a guide and instructor in the towns of Italy, in their buildings and their past alike. The sketches lead readers through Venetian lands with a scholar who draws what he describes.
40398-the-turn-of-the-balance:
Brand Whitlock opens his 1907 novel with Elizabeth Ward at a wide hearth, glad of the first snow. The night past held rain, fog, and wet streets on Claybourne Avenue; the morning turns the town white and still. An excerpt from Howells on boyhood justice stands at the front, a hint of the book's moral bent.

Whitlock, a reform mayor of Toledo, wrote fiction steeped in city life and law. He gave the book to the memory of Samuel Jones, the Toledo mayor famed for fair rule. Jay Hambidge drew the plates. What starts as a quiet home scene widens into a tale of conscience and public life.
4041-conscience:
A short story about conscience follows George, a man who keeps brushing aside small warnings that a duty is not a trifle. Weeks pass with no acknowledgment of money owed, until a letter asks Mr. Pratt to pay two hundred dollars promised some weeks before to Mr. Reid.

Reid is a poor man, to whom two hundred dollars is an important sum, and the delay weighs on him. The tale turns on how a small evasion grows into a moral debt, and on what it costs to set it right. Readers who like plain moral fiction will find a brief, pointed story about promises, money, and the voice that will not stay quiet.
40475-the-indian-in-his-wigwam-or-charac:
Henry Schoolcraft wrote a study of the Indian in his wigwam, drawn from his own original notes and manuscripts, and issued at Buffalo. Its subtitle promises the characteristics of the red race of America. The title page carries his long list of learned societies, from London to Copenhagen and Montreal.

Schoolcraft had spent years among the tribes as an agent and explorer, and presided over a society formed in 1831 to better the native race's condition. The book sets down what his notes held on Indian life, language, and custom at first hand. His spellings of Indian words follow his own system, kept as printed. General readers of his day met the wigwam through his eyes.
40476-children-of-the-dawn-old-tales-of-:
Elsie Finnimore Buckley retold old Greek tales in Children of the Dawn, a book for young readers with art by Frank Pape. A long preface maps the vast store these tales come from. They live in Homer and Hesiod, bloom in Greek drama, and pass to Rome in Virgil, Ovid, and the tales of the Metamorphoses.

Eleven tales make the set, drawn from a trove the preface calls near endless. Love, daring, skill, and grief thread them, with gods at odds, men and women as heroes or prey, and Fate dark at the back of all. Hero and Leander front the book, her torch lit each night as he swims the strait. Plain, terse prose keeps the old fire while it trims the tales for youth.
40522-yorkshire-family-romance:
Yorkshire Family Romance is a book of county tales by Frederick Ross, printed at Hull in 1891. Ross also wrote Celebrities of Yorkshire Wolds. A plate shows Sir John Hotham. The contents read as a roll of Yorkshire's storied houses and their fates across a thousand years.

The Synod of Streoneshalh opens the set, in a Northumbria at peace after anarchy and bloodshed. The doomed heir of Osmotherley, Eadwine the royal martyr, and Siward the viceroy follow. Later tales treat a murderer's bride, the black-faced Clifford, the shepherd lord, and the felons of Ilkley. The Ingleby boar's head, the Eland tragedy, the Plumpton marriage, and the burning of Cottingham Castle fill out the list. Ross writes local history as family romance, half record and half legend.
40527-in-league-with-israel-a-tale-of-th:
Annie Fellows Johnston wrote In League with Israel, a tale of the Chattanooga Conference, in 1896. Curts and Jennings of Cincinnati and Eaton and Mains of New York sold the book. Johnston gives it to the Epworth League, with a charge drawn from an old parable. What Paul was to the Gentiles, she urges, the League may become to the Jews. The world, re-reading the parable, asks who the neighbor is, and names Israel in their midst.

Music sheets stand in the book, with a song set down for the reader. It opens in a library at dark, where an old rabbi bends near his book as June twilight deepens. The first chapter is named for the rabbi's protege, the young charge at the heart of the tale.
4062-gaston-de-latour-an-unfinished-roma:
Walter Pater left Gaston de Latour unfinished, a romance of French youth in the age before revolution. A general of 1789 judged French young men of quality behindhand, urging king and nobles to care better for their education.

Enlightened and moral, Pater's young clerics and nobles might know their duties and abuse their privileges less. The fragment follows Gaston through courts, churches, and salons, with Pater's fine prose lending grace to every scene. Readers who love Pater will value this beautiful torso, even where the story breaks off. Its grace survives in every scene.
40640-the-following-of-the-star-a-romanc:
The Following of the Star is a romance by Florence Barclay, author of The Rosary. It was copyrighted in 1911 and often reprinted; this copy is the seventeenth printing. The frontispiece shows its hero David in Africa. The book is dedicated to the author's son in the ministry.

The contents divide the tale under the heading Gold. Chapters open at the still waters of Brambledene, where David stirs the quiet. Diana Rivers of Riverscourt stands high-fenced against him. An uncle's will, a voice in the night, and the eve of Epiphany move the plot. The later part takes David to Africa, as the picture promises. Barclay's romances mixed love with faith for a wide circle of readers.
40706-an-introduction-to-the-history-of-:
Walter Libby wrote An Introduction to the History of Science, issued by Houghton Mifflin in Boston, New York, and Chicago in nineteen seventeen. Libby taught the history of science at the Carnegie Institute of Technology. He gave the book to his students of the last twelve years in the Chicago and Pittsburgh districts. His aim, he says, is to foster a democratic culture that minds the daily task. Plates and an index aid the text.

Libby traces how science grew, from old world lore to modern labs, in clear chapters for general readers. Dalton symbols for the elements are set out in a transcriber note, with circles for hydrogen, oxygen, and carbon. The book treats great makers, their tools, and their times as one human tale. Students get a humane door into science, stressing work, doubt, and slow gain. The tone is warm and plain, not dry or remote.
40722-dan-carter-and-the-great-carved-fa:
Mildred Wirt wrote Dan Carter and the Great Carved Face, a Cub Scout mystery printed at New York in 1952. Six Cub Scouts squat Indian fashion around a glowing log behind a Den Dad's home in Webster City. Sam Hatfield, cubmaster of Den Two, promises an important announcement for the special night meeting.

A missing Cub, a grotesque carved face on a cliff wall, strange visitors, and another loss start the hunt. Dan makes a sand painting, loses a paddle, finds an underground stream, and explores a cave with the den. A man in the cave, a pow-wow, and a turquoise toad close the clues. Boys got camping, Native lore themes, and teamwork.
40744-psychology-and-social-practice:
Psychology and Social Practice is an address by John Dewey, published at Chicago in 1901. The University of Chicago Press issued it as number two of its Contributions to Education. Dewey headed the departments of philosophy and education there. He had delivered the piece as his presidential address. The American Psychological Association heard it at New Haven in 1899. He had hoped, he says, to treat psychology's whole relation to social science.

That larger treatment was not ready, so he narrows the ground. Education, a social affair first of all, becomes his test case. Educational science is first of all a social science, he argues. Through that one field he approaches the wider question. Experience, he hopes, will check the flights of abstract reflection. Large words must translate into specific images before they guide practice.
40791-life-of-edward-the-black-prince: Life of Edward the Black Prince is a school biography by Mullins of Marlborough College. The series offered classic texts with introductions and notes for classroom use, priced in shillings. Mullins also prepared the series volume on Southey's Life of Nelson. The life itself, a short account of Edward, Prince of Wales, must be met in the body of the book.
40806-little-jeanne-of-france:
Madeline Brandeis wrote Little Jeanne of France. Grosset and Dunlap issued the tale at New York in 1929. Brandeis made motion pictures of child life abroad. Her photos from France fill the book. The tale is given to children of every land. Eighteen chapters carry Jeanne's story.

Madame Villard and Paul open the action. A call To the Front moves men off to war. Paris scenes follow, with Suzanne and Jeanne. A puppet show, the Guignol, gets its own chapter. An outing in the Bois and a spoiled Margot build the middle. Auntie Sue's shop and a drive through Paris close in. A call for help and Margot's own story end it. Gentle war-era fiction, the book shows French life to American children through a small girl's eyes.
40825-fictitious-symbolic-creatures-in-a:
John Vinycomb wrote Fictitious and Symbolic Creatures in Art, published by Chapman and Hall in London in 1906. Vinycomb, a member of the Royal Irish Academy, gives special attention to the use of such creatures in British heraldry. Saint George and the dragon opens the illustrated text.

Early chapters treat angels, cherubim and seraphim, and the emblems of the four evangelists. The dragon gets a long study, from Christian art to the royal heraldry of Britain. Hydra, wyvern, chimera, and cockatrice follow. Later chapters take up the unicorn, the pegasus, the centaur, the griffin, the sphinx, the phoenix, and the harpy. Vinycomb explains what each beast meant and how artists drew it. The book serves heraldry students and anyone curious about the monsters on shields and church walls.
40829-devil-s-dice:
Devil's Dice is a sensation novel by William Le Queux. Rand, McNally published this edition at Chicago and New York in 1897. Its first chapter is called Queen of the Unknown. The narrator gazes down the vista of a tristful past. There are things that cannot be uttered, he begins. Scenes still entrance him, and incidents make him hold his breath. The prologue of this drama of London life was enacted three years ago. Its astounding denouement occurred quite recently, he says.

During those three weary years he trod a Via Dolorosa, he writes. The tragedy of his life presses on him perpetually. Yet brief moments of peace came with the angel of his solitude. That sweet childlike companion brought supreme happiness at times. Le Queux opens with a confessional flourish of sorrow. Mystery and romance are promised in his lushest manner.
4090-from-ritual-to-romance:
Jessie L. Weston's From Ritual to Romance argues that the Grail legends grew from old vegetation rites. A chapter on Tammuz and Adonis looks at how Aryan forefathers faced nature's ordered sequence of birth, growth, and decay.

By prayer and supplication, they threw themselves on the mercy of the god who granted or withheld rain and river water. Weston links dying gods, seasonal rites, and the Grail quest into one bold thesis, famous for shaping T. S. Eliot's Waste Land. Readers interested in myth, folklore, and the roots of romance will find a short, provocative classic.
40911-the-ether-of-space:
The Ether of Space is a physics book by Sir Oliver Lodge. Harper published it in London and New York in 1909. It belongs to a library of living thought. Lodge was a fellow of the Royal Society. He had lately been a professor of physics at Liverpool. He inscribed the book to the founders of that college.

The contents move from history to experiment. Early chapters treat the ether as the carrier of light. The interstellar ether is cast as a connecting medium. Motion's influence on phenomena follows. Lodge then describes his own ether machine. A frontispiece shows it whirling in action. Later chapters weigh the ether's density and strength. Three appendices treat gravity and Fresnel's law.
41043-the-old-first-massachusetts-coast-:
The Old First Massachusetts Coast Artillery in War and Peace, by Frederick Morse Cutler, was copyright 1917 and published at Boston and Chicago.
