Cutler was a first lieutenant and the regiment chaplain. A frontispiece shows the first state camp, at Neponset in 1849. Two editions appeared in spring 1917.

Contents open with the coast artillery itself, then dated chapters: 1784 to 1840, and 1840 to 1861. Responding to the President call, and the Fighting First, cover the Civil War. Chapters for 1866 to 1878, the old Tiger First, the Cape, and since 1878 follow. Appendices give a genealogy of the coast artillery, the present companies and their captains, and a bibliography. Pictures show the South Armory at Boston, and Fort Monroe in 1861. Readers get a regimental history written from inside, by its chaplain.
41068-syndicalism-in-france:
Louis Levine wrote Syndicalism in France, with an introduction by Professor Franklin H Giddings, in a second revised edition reprinted at New York in 1970 by AMS Press. The book first formed part of Columbia University studies in history, economics, and public law. It was first issued as The Labor Movement in France in 1912 and revised in 1914.

Levine notes that the term syndicalism sounds strange to an English reader. Its equivalent would be unionism, he says. A syndicat is a union of workingmen on a trade or industrial basis for defence of economic interests. Revolutionary syndicalism has a broader sense than the word alone suggests, he holds. A critical analysis of existing institutions and a socialist ideal sit within it, he sets out. The book then traces French unions, strikes, and doctrine for American students.
41071-a-son-of-perdition-an-occult-roman:
A Son of Perdition is an occult romance by Fergus Hume, printed in London by William Rider and Son in a new, cheaper edition. Hume had won fame with The Mystery of a Hansom Cab. He gives the book to Annie Besant of the Theosophical Society.

Hume thanks C W Leadbeater in a note for the account of star worship in chapter fifteen, drawn from papers on ancient Chaldea. Chapters move from Love in Idleness and a prophecy to its fulfilment and plotting. Later heads name a warning, a stay in Cornwall, and the spider and the fly. A trance and a disciple of love stand near the close. Readers get love, fate, and hidden lore in Hume lush manner.
41370-stained-glass-of-the-middle-ages-i:
Stained Glass of the Middle Ages in England and France is an art book printed in 1913. Lawrence Saint painted the plates and Hugh Arnold wrote the text that describes them. Plate one shows the Ascension window at Le Mans, perhaps of the eleventh century. Contents open with the making of a window and the beginnings of stained glass.

Style chapters then trace the craft across the medieval centuries in both lands. Church windows serve as the chief record of faith, colour, and skill in glass. Painted plates let readers see detail that dim church light often hides on site. Students of Gothic art gain a guided tour of two great glass schools.
41440-poppea-of-the-post-office:
Mabel Osgood Wright, writing as Barbara, told a small town tale printed at New York in 1909. A front plate by the Kinneys shows Poppea slipping out a long window. Twenty chapters carry the book. It opens on the tenth of March, with the mail late.

The six thirty New York mail has not come by eight, the closing hour. Postmaster Oliver Gilbert paces his narrow office, head bent like a hunting dog's. A dozen men wait about the stove for the last social event of their day. Heads bring the Feltons, a naming, and a mystery of the name. Incognita, a proposal, and night and morning fill the middle. The scar on the hand and John Angus close the tale.
41822-phroso-a-romance:
Anthony Hope wrote this romance, published by Methuen in 1897, the shelf of his books already holding The Prisoner of Zenda. The narrator, newly rich by a cousin's death, wants one thing money can buy: retirement on an island of his own.

The contents name the place Neopalia and promise a fever, a raid, a cottage on the hill, and the secret of the Stefanopouloi. Later chapters bring a strange escape, the jaws of a trap, and an unknown friend. His fiancée Beatrice calls it a horrid little island and swears she will never set foot in it. Readers get a Ruritanian adventure on a Greek-flavored isle, told with Hope's light hand.
41849-the-human-race:
The Human Race, by Louis Figuier, was published in New York in 1872, with two hundred and forty-three wood engravings and eight color plates. Chapter one asks what man is, how he differs from other animals, where he first appeared, and whether mankind is one species. Figuier argues for the unity of mankind, with kinds or varieties within one species.

The book then surveys the peoples of the world in the order of its day, starting with European branches such as Teutonic, Latin, Slavonian, and Greek families. Height, skull, skin color, language, and industry are weighed for each group. Its schemes of race are those of 1872 science, now long superseded, but the plates and scope show how Victorians sought to order human variety.
41990-the-cid-campeador-a-historical-rom:
Antonio de Trueba y la Quintana wrote 'The Cid Campeador' as a historical romance, and Henry Gill translated it from the Spanish for Longmans in 1895. Chapter headings in the old manner tell the story in advance: love affairs begin almost when others end, and festivities close with a blow on a face. Rodrigo and his squire ride between Leon and Vivar, and Diego Lainez hopes his honour will be avenged.

Rodrigo fights the Count of Gormaz, and Ximena demands justice from the king against Rodrigo Diaz himself. Later chapters marry Rodrigo and Ximena, give Rodrigo his horse Babieca, and send him against the Moors in the mountains of Oca. Bandits who think as cavaliers, a converted Moorish princess, and plots of treason widen the cast around the hero.
42029-the-girl-scout-s-triumph-or-rosann:
Katherine Keene Galt wrote this girls' novel, the third volume in a Girl Scouts series published by the Saalfield Publishing Company. Its copyright dates to 1921. The story follows Rosanna, a red-haired girl with sea-green eyes and a long thick braid, as she faces a room of scouts she has never met.

Rosanna arrives early on purpose, hoping to meet the strangers one by one rather than walk in under many watching eyes. The opening sets up her shyness, her pride in her hair, and the social test ahead of her. Readers get a period story about troop life, friendship, and a young heroine learning to hold her own among new companions.
42106-how-to-fence:
How to Fence is a complete instruction book printed by Frank Tousey in New York, entered for copyright in 1884. Its title page promises full instruction for fencing and the use of the broadsword, plus instruction in archery, described with twenty one practical illustrations. The contents add broadsword exercise, hurdle racing, pole leaping, throwing the hammer, and putting the shot.

Fencing, the text says, is the art of using the small sword or rapier, a straight blade of about thirty two inches made for thrusting only. French masters lead the art, and every French regiment keeps its master of arms. Physicians are quoted praising fencing as exercise: it sets more muscles working at once than most sports and expands the chest.
42266-antiquities-of-the-mesa-verde-nati:
Antiquities of the Mesa Verde National Park: Cliff Palace, by Jesse Walter Fewkes, came out in Washington in 1911. It is Bulletin 51 of the Bureau of American Ethnology. Fewkes led dig and repair work at the site in the summer of 1909. The work ran from May to August that year. His report treats Cliff Palace as a type of early culture in the region.

Pages cover the site, old trails, walls, towers, and plazas. Room by room notes list living rooms, milling rooms, granaries, and kivas. Plates show the ruin before and after repair. Later parts deal with pottery, tools, textiles, and burials. The book is a full record of a major cliff dwelling and the work done to save it.
42276-in-greek-waters-a-story-of-the-gre:
In Greek Waters is a boys' adventure novel by Henty, set in the Grecian war of independence. Henty's hero is drawn into the Greek cause from an English village. The contents promise a yacht, a wreck, fire-ships, Chios and the rescuing of the garrison of Athens.

The opening chapter presents Mr Beveridge of Seaport, a scholar so learned that visiting professors seek him out and the universities respect his treatises. The villagers wish him less learned and more practical. From that sheltered study the tale launches its young hero toward brigands, pashas and Turkish defeats, in Henty's usual compound of schoolroom and gunpowder.
42431-lawrence:
Lawrence, covering the artist's life from 1769 to 1830, belongs to the Masterpieces in Colour series edited by T Leman Hare. The series list pairs each painter with a writer: Botticelli, Chardin, Constable, Corot, Dürer, Gainsborough, Hogarth, Holbein, and many more. The Lawrence volume is credited to S L Bensusan, who also wrote the Reynolds, Romney-era companions Murillo, Rubens, and Titian entries in the same list.

Such volumes joined a short life and criticism to colour plates of the painter's best-known work. Thomas Lawrence was the leading portrait painter of his age in England. Readers get an Edwardian art primer in colour, made for the general reader's shelf.
42459-bernard-treves-s-boots-a-novel-of-:
Bernard Treves's Boots is a secret service novel by Laurence Clarke, published in 1920. Hodder and Stoughton issued it at London. Clarke dedicates it to Emsley Carr, a newspaper editor. Carr had suggested the book, the dedication says. Valuable first hand incidents from him figure in its pages. The date beneath the dedication is January 1920.

Chapter one opens at the Ryde Recruiting Office in wartime. Captain Gilbert questions a tall recruit of twenty six. The man gives his name as John Manton, firmly and twice. Gilbert studies his pale, vigorous face with bewilderment. He asks Manton to wait outside until eight that evening. Something in the recruit's face plainly troubles the captain. An assumed name and a hidden past stand behind that interview.
4251-the-life-everlasting-a-reality-of-r:
Marie Corelli subtitled this romance A Reality of Romance. Its contents trace a heroine's spiritual story from a fairy ship and an angel of a dream. They pass through memories, visions, and doubtful destiny. Later chapters bring a love-letter and the house of Aselzion. A magic book, dreams within a dream, and a passage into the light follow.

Corelli opens with a prologue on voices in the wilderness. Such voices, she warns, are usually ignored. Her heroine then learns by vision and love rather than by argument. Readers who enjoy Corelli's blend of romance and mysticism will find her mix here: a love story used for ideas about the soul and life after death.
42599-the-duke-s-sweetheart-a-romance:
The Duke's Sweetheart is a romance by Richard Dowling, in a new edition printed at London in 1885. Ward and Downey issued it. Dowling also wrote The Mystery of Killard and Under Saint Paul's. The contents divide into two parts, the Duke of Long Acre and the Duke of Shropshire.

Charles Augustus Cheyne, Duke of Long Acre, had no land. In the United Kingdom or any other state he owned not a perch of ground. He held no mines, railways, or stock of any kind. All his money came from his own industrious fingers and brain. Neither the Heralds' College nor the Lord Chancellor had ever heard of his dukedom. Dowling builds his tale on a title without an acre.
42600-under-st-paul-s-a-romance:
Under Saint Paul's, a romance by Richard Dowling, was issued in a new edition in London in 1885. Dowling also wrote The Duke's Sweetheart and The Sport of Fate. Ads list his popular novels from the same house. He dedicates the book to Byron Webber, the literary friend who first lent him a helping hand. Three parts structure the tale.

Part one, Saturn Shall Be King, moves from a lesson in flirtation to the Criterion and Stratford. Part two, Deposing Saturn, brings a betrothal, derelict women, and a pilgrimage to Saint Paul's. Part three, Miserere Nobis, turns to anxiety, despair, and a nervous suitor. London streets, churches, and theatres frame a tale of love and fate in Dowling's rich Victorian prose.
42671-pride-and-prejudice:
Pride and Prejudice is Jane Austen's novel of manners, here printed from the first edition of 1813. That edition, published in London by Egerton in three volumes, named no author. The title page credits only the author of Sense and Sensibility, and this file reproduces the opening volume.

The novel begins with its famous sentence: it is a truth universally acknowledged that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife. The mother of the Bennet girls then brings the news that Netherfield Park is let at last. Bingley has taken the place on the spot and will move in before Michaelmas, with servants in the house before him. From that small neighbourhood fact Austen builds the comedy of the Bennet sisters, their mother, and the proud Darcy, in the most read of all her novels.
42714-the-luminous-face:
Carolyn Wells wrote The Luminous Face, a detective novel printed at New York in 1921. Wells also wrote The Come Back, In the Onyx Lobby, and The Curved Blades. Contents promise Doctor Fell, a telephone call, the Lindsays, a threat, a fur collar, confessions, statements, and at last the luminous face itself.

Pollard calls it a bit thick that Mellen has been dead six weeks and the mystery of his taking-off still unsolved among friends. Doctor Davenport nods that few murders are ever brought home to their villains in real life. Phil Barry, an artist drawing caricatures on his evening paper, drawls faulty statistics on discovered murderers. The talk sets a country-house style inquiry in motion.
42721-a-german-deserter-s-war-experience:
An unnamed German soldier tells his war story here, in a translation by Koettgen printed in New York in 1917. The tale first appeared in German in a New York German-language socialist paper. Its author was a young miner who escaped from Germany after fourteen months of fighting in France, and who hid his name to shield his family.

The translator praises him as a keen observer who never stopped questioning the war. Trained at a mining school, he understood trench warfare better than most common soldiers. He hated militarism, the preface says, and found no romance in war, only butchery, grime, vermin, hard toil, and disgrace.
42801-the-young-lovell-a-romance:
The Young Lovell is a tale of old days by Ford Madox Hueffer. It was put out at London in nineteen thirteen. A line from a march song of the north stands at its head. His past tales of the old world are list at the front. The Fifth Queen tales stand first in that list. More tales of queens, moons, and bright eyed maids stand past them.

The tale opens in the dark of a stone church. Young Lovell of the castle rose from his knees. So he broke his vow. He had knelt from the mid of night, and it was now the sixth hour of the day. He stag gered as he rose. A mint of echos brushed through the black. The blood made flames in his eyes and roared in his ears.
42816-unveiling-a-parallel-a-romance:
Unveiling a Parallel is a utopian romance by Two Women of the West. The Arena Publishing Company issued it in 1893. Its contents list eleven chapters of another world. A Remarkable Acquaintance and A Woman open the tale. The Auroras' Annual and Elodia follow in the list. The Vaporizer and Cupid's Gardens give Martian wonders. New Friends and A Talk with Elodia fill the middle. Journeying Upward and The Master raise the theme. A Comparison closes the chapter list.

The first chapter opens with an Emerson motto on new persons. The narrator compares music and love to a delirium of joy. So it was with me when I set my feet on Mars, he says. The romance unveils a parallel society on the red planet. Its women and customs mirror Earth by contrast. The book is a feminist utopia in romance dress.
42926-the-last-of-their-race:
Annie Swan wrote The Last of Their Race, a novel printed at London in nineteen eleven. Isla Mackinnon steps out of the Castle of Achree in Scotland on a cool, clear March day. She wears shabby gloves with long cuffs and a tweed hat with a pheasant wing. In her hands, though she does not know it, lies the fate of Achree itself.

For half of her twenty-six years Isla has been the chief hope of her house. That day will test her strength, for the home faces a threat no one else can meet. Heads of later parts name the Indian mail, bridge builders, and a house of woe. Swan tells a tale of an old Scots family, its pride, its losses, and the girl who holds it up.
4296-friarswood-post-office:
Charlotte M. Yonge, author of The Heir of Redclyffe, wrote this children's story around a village post office at Friarswood. It opens with Ellen King scolding a tramp who has come in to buy a loaf, calling him a pig and wishing the police would keep such folk out of decent shops. The scene sets the village tone at once.

Later chapters bring hay-making, a new friend, and the strange lad of the first chapter into the children's circle. Yonge writes for young readers with a moral eye, showing kindness tested by prejudice. The 1909 edition carries colored pictures by A. G. Walker, and the tale suits family reading aloud.
42983-the-history-of-the-british-post-of:
Hemmeon published The History of the British Post Office with Harvard University in January 1912. A Baldwin fund paid for the printing of the scholarly volume. Four chapters sort the post into eras by its use to the state. State support before 1635 gives way to revenue farming in the next age.

Taxation rules from 1711 to 1840, with mail coaches, franking, and dead letters in turn. Dockwra's London penny post, Allen's cross posts, and Palmer's coaches mark the reforms in line. Rowland Hill's plan and inland penny postage crown the third era in triumph. Popular service forms the fourth age, as contents promise at the cut. Tables in an appendix track Scotland and Ireland in hard figures.
42998-venice:
Venice, with text by Dorothy Menpes and pictures by Mortimer Menpes, was published in London in May 1904, and reprinted in 1906 and 1912. A front picture shows crossing the Piazza. The book belongs to a colour illustrated series that also covered Japan and Brittany.

Contents open with arrival and first impressions, then history. A glimpse into Bohemia, architecture, and St Mark follow. Painters of the Renaissance get a chapter, then streets, shops, and courtyards. The islands of the lagoon and social ups and downs come next, and gondolas and gondoliers close the book. Pictures list the Grand Canal, a pink palace, Palazzo Pisani, the Salute at sunset, San Giorgio Maggiore, and the Bridge of Sighs. Readers get a painter Venice, seen in colour and on foot.
43069-the-hundredth-chance:
Ethel Dell wrote The Hundredth Chance, a novel copyrighted in 1917 and reissued by Grosset and Dunlap in New York. Dell had written The Way of an Eagle and The Knave of Diamonds, among the most popular romances of the war years. A frontispiece shows a man laying his hand gently over a woman's and asking if she is afraid to say it.

The contents divide the story into parts. The Start gives beggars, an idol, an accepted suitor, and a magician. Chapters move through a declaration of war, a reckoning, and the only port of escape. A wedding morning, a wedding night, and the day after stand at the centre. Dell's romances turned on proud, damaged men and the women who redeem them. Her title promises the arithmetic of that redemption: even a hundredth chance is enough.
43081-on-the-road-to-bagdad-a-story-of-t:
Captain Brereton wrote On the Road to Bagdad, a story of Townshend's gallant advance on the Tigris, published by Blackie of London in 1917. Wal Paget drew the pictures. Brereton's other war tales, With Joffre at Verdun and With Our Russian Allies, are named on the title page.

Twenty chapters march up the river in Mesopotamia. A frontier station opens the tale, where Geoffrey Keith appears. The Persian Gulf and a first encounter set the campaign moving. A motor-boat goes into action, and a cutting-out party raids by night. Esbul the Armenian joins the heroes, and capture follows. A breakout succeeds, and the road to Bagdad opens. British boys got the eastern war as a river campaign of boats and rescues.
43130-lettice:
Lettice is a novel by Mrs Molesworth, published by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge in an edition dated 1884. Illustrations are by F Dadd. The first chapter is called It Has Come, and it opens on a girl fighting tears.

Lettice stands at a window in a Spanish town and will not let herself cry. Below, a cart laden with wood sticks against the stones of the hilly street. Two bullocks blink while their driver tries to light his pipe. Spanish labourers in green and scarlet sashes climb past like princes in disguise. A youth looks up with pity, and Lettice starts indignantly. Her mother is an invalid, nervous and fanciful, she tells herself. But the voice from the other room is calm and even cheerful. Molesworth wrote many such tales of girls under quiet sorrow, where duty is learned at home.
43150-the-constant-prince: Christobel Coleridge wrote this tale of old times, in an edition of 1879. The first leaf of the book is a short word from the author on the craft of such tales. It is oft thought, she says, that the writer of a tale of old times makes the men and women of the past seem more fine than they were. Her word is cut off at that point in the text shown. The title names the hero by his one great trait: the prince who stands firm.
43162-hugh-crichton-s-romance:
Hugh Crichtons Romance is a novel by Coleridge, in a form put out at London in the late eighteen hundreds. It is told in two parts, and the first part is cast as Hughs own tale. A short line on a light that never was on sea or land heads the first part.

The second part turns to a woman of the tale, named in its head. A French verse at its start calls her pale yet rose, small, with great hair. She oft says she dares not, and never says she will. The text then opens on a town in Italy in the glow of a summer dusk, where sun makes even plain cloth and roof stone seem rich with hue.
43209-in-the-track-of-r-l-stevenson-and-:
In the Track of Stevenson and Elsewhere in Old France, first published in 1907, is Hammerton's book of travel sketches. He had already written a volume of Stevensoniana. Ninety-two illustrations crowd the pages. Most of the sketches appear in print here for the first time.

The first half walks Stevenson's own roads. One part crosses the Cevennes, as Stevenson did with his donkey. Another follows the route of An Inland Voyage by canoe and canal. The country of the Camisards, the wonderland of France and the town of Tartarin fill later chapters. A French fair and a palace of angels close the set. The book serves readers who like their travel seasoned with a favorite author.
43351-a-chain-of-evidence:
Carolyn Wells, who wrote The Gold Bag, stands behind this detective tale. Lippincott printed A Chain of Evidence at Philadelphia in 1912, with plates in colour by Gayle Hoskins. The Girl across the Hall opens the cast, and tragedy strikes in chapter two.

Janet Pembroke, Doctor Post's discovery, and several clues fill the early list. The inquest begins, and the teller gives evidence in the first person. An awful implication, George Lawrence, and persons unknown keep the hunt hot. A chained door, an initialled handkerchief, and the famed Fleming Stone crowd the late chapters. The chain of evidence itself, chapter by chapter, closes the case in Wells's neat style.
43507-an-account-of-valle-crucis-abbey-l:
A two penny guide to Valle Crucis Abbey was printed at Llangollen in 1891 by Hugh Jones. It promises an account of the abbey and all the fresh finds. The ruin stands in a lovely, shut in valley two miles from the town. Routes by road, canal and rail are all laid out.

Walkers may cross the Dee bridge, stroll the canal side, or ride from Berwyn station. The abbey was built in the year 1200 by Madog, lord of Dinas Bràn. It took its name, Vale of the Cross, from an old carved pillar in a near field. Cistercian monks lived there, of an order founded in France in 1098, and the house was given to the Virgin Mary.
43527-the-quest-a-romance:
Justus Miles Forman wrote this romance, published by Ward, Lock in 1909 with illustrations by W Hatherell. The contents follow its hero through thirty chapters, from hearing of a mystery and meeting a dark lady to journey's end.

Ste Marie hears of a mystery, makes a vow, and is haunted by a pair of eyes. He meets old David Stewart, sets forth on the great adventure, and takes a hurt volunteering in a good cause. A golden lady enters; evidence heaps up swiftly; a black cat and an overheard conversation thicken the plot. The frontispiece shows a man fallen on his knees at a lady's feet. Forman, author of The Garden of Lies, writes society romance with a mystery spine.
4365-supplementary-copyright-statutes-us:
The United States Copyright Office put these extra notes on the law in one text. The items include paper 3 on notice, paper 15 on renewal, and paper 15t on longer terms. Paper 22 covers high points of changes in the law from the Uruguay Round trade deal. The WIPO treaty on the rights of authors is in the set as well.

The opening note explains that a notice is no longer needed under the law of the United States, though it is often of use. Each paper is set off by a page break and a row of stars. The set serves as a shelf of notes for readers who need the office's own words on notice, renewal, and treaty changes.
43693-summary-narrative-of-an-explorator:
Henry Schoolcraft tells here of his expeditions to the sources of the Mississippi River. An expedition in 1820 began the work, his title states in full. A second journey in 1832 found the river's origin in Itasca Lake, the title goes on to say.

The book appears by authority of the United States, with appendixes attached. The original report on the copper mines of Lake Superior stands among them. Observations on the geology of the lake basins and the summit of the Mississippi join it, with all the official reports and scientific papers of both expeditions bound in for the record.
43811-merkland-or-self-sacrifice:
Merkland, or Self-Sacrifice, by the author of Margaret Maitland, came from Stringer and Townsend of New York in 1854. A front plate shows the Prodigal's solemn pledge in Mrs Catherine's little room, and the title page carries a cry of offering brought back seven-fold. The tale is Scottish, grave, and steeped in old family wrongs.

It opens in talk: Anne Ross fears that Mrs Catherine's expected visitor is an Aytoun girl, kin to a terrible story Anne's stepmother wants kept from Lewis. A brother's crime, a changed name, and a feud that should not descend fill the first scene.
43819-every-day-science-volume-7-the-con:
The Conquest of Time and Space is the seventh volume of Every-Day Science, a popular science series by Henry Smith Williams, assisted by Edward Williams. The Goodhue Company published it in New York and London in 1910. Illustrations include the Wright aeroplane in France in 1908, with Wilbur Wright and a pupil aboard.

The first chapter treats the conquest of the zones. It moves from the geographical knowledge of the ancient Egyptians through the mariner's compass, its deviation, and the non-magnetic ship Carnegie. The log, the sextant, the astrolabe, and the chronometer receive their histories. Harrison's timepieces and his prize close the list in the contents shown. The volume measures how instruments shrank the world. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
43942-plague-its-cause-and-the-manner-of:
Plague is a medical monograph by Thomas Wright Jackson, published by Lippincott in 1916, with bacteriologic observations by Otto Schöbl of the Bureau of Science at Manila. Jackson had served on the American Red Cross sanitary commission to Serbia in 1915 and directed plague suppression at Manila. The book treats the disease's cause, spread, menace, control, diagnosis and treatment.

The second chapter sums up the new science of plague: the bacillus, its conveyance by fleas, chronic plague and immunity in rats, and the stability of the bacilli's virulence. The third chapter turns to practice, above all the Manila epidemic of 1912 to 1914. Jackson dedicates the book to Aldo Castellani, his comrade of the Serbian campaign.
44091-green-fire-a-romance:
Green Fire, a romance by Fiona Macleod, was issued by Harper and Brothers in New York in eighteen ninety six. The book is in three parts. The first part is called The Birds of Angus Ogue. The second part is called The Herdsman. A short third part ends with a chapter on the beauty of the world.

The tale opens in spring, when green growth runs from tree to tree and field to field. Birds nest in ash and beech, and eggs shine blue green in the light. Eucharis speaks first, in a dim wood full of new leaves. Love, youth, and dreams of the wild past shape the mood. Readers who like lush prose and old lore will find much of both here.
44122-silver-chimes-in-syria-glimpses-of:
Silver Chimes in Syria gives glimpses of a missionary's experiences, written by W S Nelson. The Westminster Press published the book in Philadelphia in 1914. Nelson had served in Syria for twenty-five years. He dated his dedication from Homs on July 17, 1913. The dedication honours his wife, his helper in all his work.

The chapters begin with arrival in Syria in 1888 and the study of Arabic. Travel, evangelistic trips, and a visit to Aleppo follow. Nelson describes new stations, camping life, persecution, and emigration. Syrian enterprises and the supporters at home get chapters of their own. The Tripoli Boys' School fills a long chapter near the end. The book closes on a question of sound: the muezzin or the bell. Photographs show the schools at Latakia, Homs, and Tripoli.
44192-the-crystal-palace:
Peter Berlyn and Charles Fowler wrote The Crystal Palace, a history of its building and craft wonders. James Gilbert put it out at London in 1851, the year of the great show. The book is given, by leave, to Prince Albert, whose name stood with the show. It calls the palace the storehouse of world wonders in art, science, and craft. A sister work on the sights inside was to follow, with hundreds of prints.

Inside, the pair trace the building committee, the rival plans, and the fight over the first design. They then tell how Paxton won the day and how his glass house was raised. Parts treat gutters, sash bars, glass, roof beams, and iron drills and punches. Builders and show-goers alike get a plain tale of a feat of glass and iron.
44292-the-bruce:
John Barbour, Archdeacon of Aberdeen, wrote The Bruce, a long Scots verse tale. W M Mackenzie edited the best texts for Adam and Charles Black in London in 1909. Twenty books of verse fill pages 1 to 377 of the hosted form. Notes, added parts on Bannockburn, and a word list aid the reader.

Mackenzie weighs how far the poem can serve as true history. He finds Barbour loose in dates yet strong in sharp detail. Judges from Green to the Cambridge History clash in his survey. Students gain a famed poem of Robert Bruce with full tools for close study.
44327-the-beggar-s-purse-a-fairy-tale-of:
The Beggar's Purse, subtitled A Fairy Tale of Familiar Finance, is a story booklet by Samuel Hopkins Adams, written in 1918 to sell War Savings Stamps. A notice by the Smith and Porter Press of Boston explains the plan. The publishers first meant to print a few copies and give them away, in hope the story would aid the sale of stamps.

Before the booklet was finished, large firms asked to buy it in quantity for their own people. Adams agreed to take no pay, and the press agreed to print and deliver any size edition at actual cost. They would count themselves repaid, the notice says, if every book sold one stamp. The tale opens on Van Tenner of Philadelphia, a man who pursued life by fixed habits. He lived, ate, slept, rose, worked and went to his club with perfect regularity, on an income he never overstrained.
44399-stoneheart-a-romance:
Gustave Aimard wrote Stoneheart, a romance issued at London in 1874. Aimard had writ Bee Hunters and Smuggler Chief. Nineteen chapters carry the tale. Heads name a virgin forest, an ambush, an attack on a presidio, and a camp of Redskins, in the terms of the day.

Chapter One is named Sympathy and opens with a long thought on that feeling. Aimard holds that liking masters us whether we will or no. Folk draw or repel us at first sight for no clear cause. That first sense seldom misleads, he says. Don Torribio Quiroga, disgrace, a prisoner, and a chase fill the plot. A fall and the hand of God close the late chapters.
44481-the-home-its-work-and-influence:
Charlotte Perkins Gilman wrote The Home, Its Work and Influence, copyrighted in 1903 and republished at New York in 1910. Gilman gives the book to every man who maintains a home, every woman who keeps house, and every baby reared at home.

A poem opens the argument, with a deep voice singing of home as safety, comfort, duty, love, and mother. Chapters then treat the evolution of the home, domestic mythology, and present conditions. The home as a workshop gets two chapters, on the housewife and the housemaid. Home cooking, domestic art, and domestic ethics follow, toward lines of advance.
44658-history-of-orrin-pierce:
History of Orrin Pierce is a short moral tale for the young. A Sunday school union in Philadelphia put the book out for its list. Its rights line dates the work to the year eighteen forty seven. The tale opens in a neat cottage by a clear stream near the sea.

Little Orrin learns of God and the world at his mother knee from birth. She reads him tales of the making of the world before he can read. Walks to the shore serve as lessons in the works of God around him. Flower beds and a bird house mark the good order of the home. The book aims to shape a pious mind by soft daily habit and talk.
44695-king-robert-the-bruce:
King Robert the Bruce, by Murison, is a short life in the Famous Scots series. Oliphant Anderson and Ferrier printed it at Edinburgh and London, dated July 1899. The series had lives of Carlyle, Burns, Knox, and Scott already out.

Murison gives the book to his university, Aberdeen, in a Latin tag. A verse motto sings the patriot king: in the name of De Bruce, Scotland still rejoices. It thrills Scottish heart-strings, as when the Bannock ran red from the fray. His ashes may lie in darkness and silence, the verse runs. But while the day-star rises and the ocean rolls, his deed cannot decay. Joseph Brown designed the ornaments of the volume. The printing came from an Edinburgh press, Turnbull and Spears. The life follows the patriot king of the verse.
44912-private-papers-of-william-wilberfo:
Private Papers of William Wilberforce collects the letters and sketches of the great abolitionist. A kinsman, Wilberforce, collected and edited them, with a preface. The volume appeared in London in 1897, with portraits. Its frontispiece shows Wilberforce as member of Parliament for the county of York.

The contents fall into four clear parts for the reader. Letters from Pitt, the prime minister and friend, come first. A sketch of Pitt by Wilberforce himself follows those letters. Letters from friends, and then home letters, complete the private record. One illustration shows the Wilberforce Oak at Hollwood, in Kent. Beneath that tree, after talk with Pitt, Wilberforce resolved on his course. He would give notice in the Commons of his plan against the slave trade. The papers let readers watch public resolve grow from private friendship.
45035-sir-william-wallace:
Sir William Wallace, by Murison, belongs to the Famous Scots series of short lives. A list at the front names the volumes then ready in that series. Thomas Carlyle by Macpherson and Allan Ramsay by Smeaton stand in that roll. Hugh Miller, John Knox, and Robert Burns fill out the early list of Scots.

The Balladists, Richard Cameron, and James Simpson share the shelf in the advertisement. Thomas Chalmers, James Boswell, and Tobias Smollett follow in the same list. Sir Walter Scott by Saintsbury and David Hume by Calderwood stand further down. Wallace by Professor Murison closes the roll of famous lives in the front. Scotland guardian gets a brief scholarly life in this shilling series volume.
45132-studies-of-travel-greece:
Studies of Travel: Greece is a travel and history book by Edward Freeman, copyrighted at New York in 1893. A drawing of the Parthenon, made in 1829, stands at the front. A sentence from the book itself serves as its motto on the title page. In the life of cities, it says, nothing preserves like early overthrow, and nothing destroys like unbroken life.

Freeman dedicates the volume to the memory of Margaret Evans. She had been the companion in Greek travel of her father, the writer of these papers, the dedication says. Freeman was a historian of the old school, who read a landscape as a document. Ruined Greek cities, preserved by their early fall, were his ground. Athens and her sisters here speak through stones he walked among.
45175-vacation-days-in-greece:
Rufus Richardson, formerly director of the American School of Archaeology at Athens, wrote Vacation Days in Greece. Scribner's published it at New York in 1903, dedicated to his son, the companion of his travels. The chapters wander widely: Corfu, a day in Ithaca, Delphi the sanctuary of Greece, Dodona, the bicycle in Greece, Acarnania, Aetolia, Thermopylae, and Thessaly. An ascent of the highest mountain in Greece, Taygetos and Kithaeron, the Styx, Epidaurus, and Messene follow, ending with a tour in Sicily and Dalmatia.

The frontispiece is the bronze charioteer found at Delphi. Corfu opens the book: a week wandering its olive forests and vineyards brings an intoxication without wine, though the poor and blind begging alms keep it from heaven. Richardson writes as a scholar on holiday, exact about sites and roads, with photographs of temples, monasteries, and the theatre at Epidauros.
45236-the-camp-fire-girls-in-glorious-fr:
Margaret Vandercook takes her girls abroad in The Camp Fire Girls in Glorious France, printed at Philadelphia with copyright in 1919. The Winston Company made the book, with plates. Vandercook had writ the Ranch Girls and the Red Cross Girls runs.

Nineteen chapters run from a March day to a farewell to France. The Chateau Yvonne, the retreat, and the road to Paris open the war's end. Armistice Day in Paris and Versailles follow. A home in Versailles, a dinner party, and plans and purposes fill the peace. A day in Paris, a pilgrimage, and foundation stones deepen the tour. Chapter one opens at an old French farmhouse. Its windows stood open, curtains blowing like white flags of truce, and girls' voices, gay and speaking English, came from indoors.
45245-the-long-patrol-a-tale-of-the-moun:
Cody rides the northland in The Long Patrol, a tale of the Mounted Police, printed in New York in 1912. Hodder and Stoughton and Doran made the book, with copyright the same year. Cody had writ The Frontiersman and The Fourth Watch. He gives the book to that noble body of men, the Royal North West Mounted Police. He had lived several years among them, he says, and shared their hospitality in the far flung Canadian northland.

Thirty one chapters run the patrol. Unleashed, the terror of the mountains, and a child in the midst open the tale. The shadowing horseman, the fur trader's store, and the den of plotters build the plot. The capture, links of steel, and the trailing serpent fill the mid run. A cry across the water and the signal fire raise the chase. Upholding the law and old trails and new close the book.
45264-the-tale-of-two-bad-mice:
Beatrix Potter wrote and drew The Tale of Two Bad Mice, printed at London and New York in 1904. A fine doll house stands in a nursery, red brick with white sashes, real cloth drapes, a front door, and a chimney. It belongs to two dolls, Lucinda and Jane, though its grand meals come bought in a box.

One still dawn, when the dolls are out for a ride, two mice creep from a hole by the hearth. Tom Thumb and his wife Hunca Munca push in, climb the stairs, and find a feast laid out. The ham will not cut, the knives bend, and their joy turns to rage. Small size, neat plates, and sly fun make the tale a sharp gem for young readers.
45291-the-missing-prince:
The Missing Prince, by Farrow, is dated 1886 on its title page. Harry Furniss drew the page illustrations. His daughter Dorothy drew the vignettes. Farrow had written The Wallypug of Why before. A letter to his little friends fronts the story. Thousands of children's faces, he says, now turn toward him for a tale. He values their criticism above the papers' praise, and asks them to write. Letters may go to his publishers in Paternoster Row. He wants notes on their dogs, cats, and rabbits too. A school story, Schooldays at St Vedast's, is promised next.

The prince of the title is missing, and the tale must find him. Farrow gives the book to a small friend known as Boy. The preface itself shows his method: direct talk to child readers.
45432-monica-s-choice:
Flora Berry wrote Monica's Choice, a girls novel printed in London in 1904 with six illustrations. Monica Beauchamp is left in another woman's care when Conrad goes away, to that woman's regret. Chapters track Monica through school, friendships, scrapes, and small acts of courage at home and abroad.

Friends Lois, Olive, and Roger share her trials, and a young clergyman climbs down to aid a party in danger. Talk of a medal for bravery crowns her deeds near the close of the tale. The final verdict is that the child has chosen well in life. Young readers get a warm story of duty, kindness, and growing up.
45451-the-man-who-did-the-right-thing-a-:
Sir Harry Johnston wrote The Man Who Did the Right Thing, a romance issued at New York by the Macmillan Company in 1921. The Gay-Dombeys and Mrs Warren's Daughter are named as his other novels. Johnston owns in his preface that the central idea came to him years before, out in Africa. It rests in part on what happened at Unguja and elsewhere, though he has shifted his truths so no living person should be wounded.

He tells how the tale was planned the year before, at a friend's Swiss home. There he and his wife, in hammocks under pine-trees, argued what his imagined people would say and do. He gives the book to his hostess of the Châlet Soleil. The romance is of East Africa, told by a man who knew it.
45481-what-is-christian-science:
Mangasarian wrote What Is Christian Science, a brochure from Watts at London in 1922. His stated aim is to understand the creed and define its mission. He verifies all his citations with care, the note says. He appeals to readers willing to hear both sides of the question. Sharp sayings from the founder's works stand quoted at the front.

Blood, heart, lungs, and brain have nothing to do with life, one saying runs. The food, stomach, and clothing of a child are of no serious import, says another. Followers meet critics with one reply, Mangasarian holds: you do not understand it. To demand belief before understanding, he answers, is to ask a man to see before he opens his eyes. The brochure presses the creed's claims against plain reason and daily fact.
45564-patience:
Patience, by James Alexander, was entered at Philadelphia in 1852 and issued by the Presbyterian Board of Publication at 265 Chestnut Street. Its text is the apostle's word: let patience have her perfect work. An advertisement explains that the meditations, once delivered in substance to a Christian assembly, were written as a pastoral gift.

The gift was for an esteemed friend who had been more than two years confined to her dwelling by a dangerous, lingering, and sometimes exceedingly painful malady. Alexander opens by observing that some words often in our mouths are little understood, and some praised virtues hardly ever practiced. Patience is true of all others: every man needs it, knows he would be the better for it, and falls short of it. The meditations carry the apostle's comfort into other chambers of trial.
45691-the-mystery-of-space:
Robert Browne wrote a study of the hyperspace movement, issued in New York in 1919, and dedicated it to the memory of his wife. His subtitle promises an inquiry into the birth and true nature of space. A line from Tyndall fronts the book, on how thought ranges far beyond the senses.

Part one opens with the claim that finding a fourth dimension marks a stage in the growth of the mind. Browne sketches the movement's past, from Egypt, birthplace of geometry, through Kant and Riemann. He then sets out the new geometry that grew from doubts about the parallel postulate. Mind and space are his twin themes throughout.
45790-winged-wheels-in-france:
Michael Myers Shoemaker wrote Winged Wheels in France, a motoring travel book issued by Putnam's Sons at New York and London in 1906. Shoemaker had written of the southern seas, the great Siberian railway, and the heart of the Orient before it. Winged wheels are the wheels of a motor car, and the book rides them from Monte Carlo and Nice across the south of France.

The road runs through Aix and Arles, past the castle of King René at Tarascon, to Nîmes, Montpellier, and the old walls of Carcassonne. Lourdes, Pau, and Biarritz follow, then the mountain road to Saint Jean Pied de Port and over into Spain. Pictures fill the book, among them the tomb of Agnes Sorel at Loches. It is early motor touring told by a practiced travel writer.
45828-ways-of-war-and-peace:
Delia Austrian's Ways of War and Peace was published at Larchmont, New York, in 1914, the year the European war began. She dedicates the book to her mother, with whom she had seen both the beauty of Europe and the horrors of war. The opening chapters describe the Students' Hostel in Paris, a home for American and English girls studying art and music.

War chapters follow: How Would You Like to Be a Refugee, What Mobilization Means, and The Price of War and the Price of Peace. She asks what the world war will mean to womankind. The Queen of Holland's work for peace and the doings of royal women get chapters of their own. William the Second at close range and King George the Fifth, head of the Allies, are sketched. Christmas Without a Santa Claus closes the contents.
45860-the-116th-battalion-in-france:
The 116th Battalion in France is a unit history written by the battalion's adjutant and printed in Canada in 1921. The cover shows the colours of some Canadian battalions on Wolfe's monument in Westminster Abbey. The 116th colours, worked and presented by the ladies of Ontario County, stand in the centre. The battalion's headquarters were at Whitby, with companies across the county.

When war broke out in August 1914, recruiting centres opened through Ontario County. The 34th Regiment was asked at once to supply a draft of one hundred and twenty-five men for the First Contingent. The chapters take the battalion through Vimy Ridge, a raid, Hill Seventy, and Passchendaele. Later chapters cover rest billets, the August 8th attack, Cambrai, and Mons. An honour roll closes the book. The history joins county pride in Ontario to the record of a battalion in the Great War.
45908-peggy-raymond-s-way-or-blossom-tim:
Peggy Raymond's Way, or Blossom Time at Friendly Terrace, is a girls' novel by Harriet Lummis Smith. The Page Company of Boston published it in 1922, in the Friendly Terrace series. It opens in spring vacation, with Amy Lassell sewing and restless. Her friend Peggy Raymond, never happy unless busy, sets the pace for the household and its circle. Frank Merrill drew the illustrations.

The chapters follow telephone parties, a rummage sale, and a secret of Priscilla's. They take in the Friendly Terrace orphanage, a dinner party, a football game, and the end of school life. A missing bride and a July wedding close the book. Peggy's way is steady good sense applied to other people's tangles. The book is a warm specimen of the wholesome American series fiction girls read between the wars.
4598-the-story-of-creation-as-told-by-th:
T. S. Ackland, once a fellow of Clare College, Cambridge, and vicar of Wold Newton, wrote this short book to set the Bible's creation story beside modern science. He argues that the creation history is not a side piece of revelation. It is its foundation, since it states how man stands to God as maker, and to the world made for his home. Many readers, he notes, claim that this history cannot be squared with facts science has found.

Five chapters state the case, then face difficulties in geology, astronomy, and physiology, before closing with science as a help to interpretation. Ackland writes for readers troubled by the clash, and he tries to show a way through it without giving up either faith or fact. The book suits anyone curious about Victorian attempts to read Genesis and science together, in plain, earnest argument.
46035-a-spring-walk-in-provence:
Archibald Marshall wrote A Spring Walk in Provence, issued at New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1920 with pictures from photographs. Marshall had written Exton Manor and Sir Harry among his novels. The walk begins among hills and olives and moves through flowers and scents into old Provence, town by town and church by church.

Draguignan and Saint Maximin, the great battle of Caius Marius, Aix, and Salon lead on to Les Baux and Mistral. Saint Remy, Avignon, and the palace of the popes fill the middle chapters. Vaucluse, Nîmes and the Pont du Gard, Aigues Mortes and the Camargue close the road at Arles. Marshall writes the walking tour as a gentle art, in a land of sun and old stone.
46069-vanished-halls-and-cathedrals-of-f:
Vanished Halls and Cathedrals of France is a travel book by George Warton Edwards. The work appeared in 1917 with thirty two plates in colour and monotone. Edwards writes and pictures the old towns of northern France before the reader's eye. Many of the halls and churches named were soon to suffer in the Great War.

The opening chapter stands in Arras on a summer market morning. A deep cathedral bell sounds over the gabled Flemish town. Peasants crowd the square with booths, flowers, butter, and cheese. Carts painted green unload while boys fit the stalls together. Edwards shares a bowl of coffee with the market folk for a thank you. His eye rests on roof tops old in Shakespeare's day. The book preserves such scenes as records of a world passing away.
46233-with-the-black-prince:
William O Stoddard wrote With the Black Prince, a boys’ tale of old wars. His uniform set of tales sold at a dollar fifty the volume then. The front pages praise his books in the words of the press. Stoddard’s name stood high with young readers of his day.

The Red Patriot told of a boy in the Revolution’s hard years. Little Smoke taught Sioux life through tale and chief’s portraits alike. Crowded Out of Crofield cheered a farm boy’s fight in New York. The Battle of New York kept the Civil War’s dread days in view. On the Old Frontier sang the last raids of the Iroquois host. Chris found its hero. In this tale a lad rides with Edward, the Black Prince of Wales. Knightly wars in France give the boy his tests of nerve and faith.
46261-friends-of-france:
Friends of France is a war record by members of an ambulance service. Its subtitle names the field service of the American Ambulance in France. Houghton Mifflin published it in Boston and New York in 1916. Piatt Andrew, who organized the service, writes the introduction to it. The members dedicate it to Mr and Mrs Robert Bacon.

Their effort in America accomplished much for the service, that page says. A letter from section leaders follows the introduction in the contents. Galatti describes the organization of the service in chapter one. At the back of the front, Dunkirk and Ypres, comes second. American volunteers drove ambulances under shellfire for France in 1915.
46316-verdi-man-and-musician-his-biograp:
Frederick Crowest wrote a biography of Verdi, man and musician, with especial reference to his English experiences, published at London in 1897. A signed photograph of the composer, inscribed at Genoa in February 1897, fronts the volume. The book is dedicated, by permission, to Adelina Patti, empress of song, whose powers had taught England the genius of Verdi.

The first chapter settles birth, parentage, and child-life: the dispute over his township, the baptismal certificate, the inn kept by his parents, and a boy who was no musical wonder or show-child. Enchanted with a street organ, he became acolyte at Roncole church and was bought a spinet. Clerk, student, and professor follow. A life told for English opera-goers is the volume.
4633-philip-steele-of-the-royal-northwes:
James Oliver Curwood published Philip Steele of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police in 1911. It opens with a chapter called The Hyacinth Letter, in which Steele writes a letter he may never mail, to lessen his loneliness in a log cabin. Outside, wind drives sleet off the lake like shot, surf beats driftwood on the rocks, and tall pines whistle and wail as they straighten after each blast. Tomorrow, he expects, will be a desolation of snow.

Later chapters bring a face out of the night, a skull and a flirtation, and a silken scarf. They go on to a beauty-proof hero, a pretty face followed, a tragedy in the cabin, another letter, a trail taken up, and Isobel's disappearance. Readers get a brisk northern romance of police work, love, and pursuit, with Curwood's snow, storm, and lonely cabins, and a hero who must choose between duty and desire.
46363-her-dark-inheritance:
Mrs E Burke Collins wrote this dime novel, issued as number 66 of the Hart Series with an 1892 copyright by George Munro. The Arthur Westbrook Company of Cleveland published the form held here. Chapter names promise a dark night's secret, a fairy prince, a thief in the night, and a mad passion.

Serena drives the plot: her first love letter, her game, her new scheme, and at last her failure. Beatrix hears the secret and sees the game. An old man's secret, a midnight interview, and a death bed fill the middle. Keith hears the news late in the tale. Threats, deadly peril, and a martyr's turn raise the stakes before the close, where all is well.
4638-california-1849-1913-or-the-ramblin:
L. H. Woolley, member of the Society of California Pioneers and of the Vigilance Committee of 1856, wrote California 1849 to 1913. Its subtitle is The Rambling Sketches and Experiences of Sixty-four Years' Residence in that State. He says the year 1849 holds a thrilling sensation for a California pioneer, not felt by those who came later. His purpose is not publication or praise, but to deposit his recollections in his descendants' archives.

He left the Green Mountains of Vermont to cross the plains to California, the El Dorado, the Land of Gold. By way of Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Cincinnati, St. Louis, and Independence, Missouri, he joined the first mule train of Turner, Allen and Company's Pioneer Line. Forty wagons, a hundred and fifty mules, and about a hundred and fifty passengers left the frontier on May 14, 1849. Readers get a pioneer's plain, first-hand California memoir.
46581-the-mystery-of-choice:
The Mystery of Choice is a set of tales and verse by Robert Chambers. Chambers was known for a book of a king in a bright hue. This book came out in New York in the year 1897. A long verse at the front gives the book to a grave young dame.

The verse says he can sing of maids, men, and grass, and no more. Arms and the man are past his song, he tells the dame with rue. Sea, fields, and woods are the stock of his muse in her eyes. Choice is the theme: which road a man takes when the ways split. East or west, to go or to stay, the verse asks at the end. The tales work the same theme in prose of love and chance.
46586-alice-wilde-the-raftsman-s-daughte:
Alice Wilde: The Raftsman's Daughter, a forest romance by Mrs Metta V Victor, was printed at New York by Irwin P Beadle and Company in 1860. A front plate shows Alice set on a thing in the garret she must fetch. The tale opens at David Wilde's saw mill, where young Ben Perkins bobs for stray logs in the creek. Quick and deft as he is, he slips from a log and takes a ducking, to his hot shame.

For Alice rows up in her skiff at that hour, come to meet her father's boat, and her laugh rings out. Heads ahead name suit refused, an awful guest, and a cold house-warming. A meeting in the woods, a tornado, and Ben and Alice close the run. Dime fans get mill, raft, and courtship in the green woods.
46708-the-dead-letter-an-american-romanc:
Seeley Regester wrote an American romance printed in New York in 1867 by Beadle and Company. A portrait fronts the tale. Part one opens with the letter, then events of a night and a figure beneath the trees. Moreland Villa, Burton the detective, and two links in the chain follow. The haunted grave, the spider and the fly, and the anniversary deepen the plot.

The letter returns to open part two, with visits, a confession, and an embarking. A narrator in the dead letter office sorts bundles of lost mail with quick hands, the text shows. Love, a hidden crime, and a detective's patient chain make an early American mystery. Beadle's cheap romances reached rail cars and farm kitchens across the young country.
46763-michael-faraday-man-of-science:
Walter Jerrold wrote a life of Michael Faraday for a publisher of evangelical literature. His preface takes its keynote from Faraday's own words to Professor Tyndall, who had urged him to accept the presidency of the Royal Society. Tyndall, I must remain plain Michael Faraday to the last, ran the reply. Modesty, the biographer argues, is the key to the man.

Faraday's life was simple and unadventurous in outward event, yet its work is the story of natural science advancing through the century's first half. Jerrold aims less at the laboratory detail than at the testimony of those who knew him. Unselfishness and perseverance against adverse birth and fortune are the lesson he draws for readers.
46782-the-vintage-a-romance-of-the-greek:
Benson set his romance in the Greek War of Independence and built it in three parts: The Vineyard, The Eve of the Gathering, and The Treading of the Grapes. Harper and Brothers published the novel in New York and London in 1898. Benson dedicated it, by permission, to Olga, Queen of the Hellenes.

The story opens at a house on the road to Nauplia, huddled silent under midsummer noon like a city of the dead. Mitsos, Yanni, and Nicholas Vidalis carry the action through brigand tales, a midnight ordeal, and the port dues of Corinth. The third part reaches the fire-ship adventure, the training of the troops, and the fall of Tripoli. Nicholas goes home at the close, back to the house on the Nauplia road.
46883-goethe-and-schiller-an-historical-:
Mühlbach's Goethe and Schiller, an historical romance, was translated from the German by Chapman Coleman. Appleton published it in New York in 1899, from a copyright of 1867, and the author is credited with Joseph the Second and His Court and Frederick the Great and His Court. An illustration shows Schiller in his attic.

The first book follows Schiller's trials, with Henrietta von Wolzogen and Charlotte von Kalb, and ends with an adieu to Mannheim. Later books bring the death of a king, Schiller in Dresden and his Song to Joy. Goethe enters with Moritz, and the Italian journey ends in an adieu to Italy, before a fourth book of return and reconciliation.
4703-flower-of-the-north-a-modern-romanc:
James Oliver Curwood published Flower of the North in January 1912. He dedicates it to his comrades of the great northern wilderness, and especially to the Jeanne d'Arcambal who will find herself the heroine. The book opens with Gregson praising a girl's hair, eyes, and colour to Whittemore, swearing she was the handsomest girl he ever saw. She would not give him a look, yet he plans a full-page cover of her for Burke's magazine.

From that artist's admiration grows a modern northern romance of love, pursuit, and wilderness adventure. Curwood writes the long silent trail, its joys and hardships, with his usual vigour. Readers get a popular Canadian romance, with a strong heroine at its centre, for readers who like love stories set against snow, rivers, and rough frontier life.
47088-german-atrocities-from-german-evid:
Joseph Bédier, professor at the Collège de France, sets out to prove German atrocities from German evidence alone. Bernhard Harrison translated the pamphlet for Armand Colin of Paris in 1915, in the series Studies and Documents on the War. Bédier refuses all French and Belgian testimony, true though he holds it.

His documents, he says, are criticized as minutely as a peacetime scholar would question an old chronicle or chart. Accusations are easy and proof is hard, and any evidence an adversary cannot dispute will long be dismissed as lies. German documents, by contrast, no living man, not even in Germany, can attempt to refute. The charge is that the German armies sometimes violated the law of nations.
47216-the-building-of-castello-de-san-ma:
Albert C Manucy, historian at Castillo de San Marcos National Monument, wrote The Building of Castillo de San Marcos. The National Park Service issued the booklet at Washington for twenty cents. It stands as Interpretive Series History Number One. A caption calls the fort the oldest existing masonry fort in the United States. It overlooks the entrance to St Augustine Harbor in Florida.

A pirate raid, Manucy says, forced the Queen of Spain to build the fort. On May twenty eighth, sixteen sixty eight, a raid struck that led to the work. Chapters treat beginning the Castillo, the years of construction, and defending San Marcos. A glossary closes the guide. Sentries in the watchtower looked over the Atlantic toward treasure fleets bound for Spain. Visitors get a short, clear tale of stone, guns, and empire.
47587-anatole-france:
Anatole France is a life and study of the French author by Brandes, in a set of books on men of letters of the day. It came out at London in the year cut in Roman marks on its title page. A front print shows a bust of its man by a named hand.

Its first lines lay down a test of a true author. On each page of his works, it holds, stands at least one line or phrase that no man else could have writ. Two such lines are then set as proof and weighed word by word. One, on a famed kind priest of souls, jokes that all men will reach bliss, unless there be no bliss at all. The wit marks its man as the heir of a great doubter of France.
47627-the-quest-for-a-lost-race:
Thomas Pickett read The Quest for a Lost Race before the Filson Club of Louisville on October 1, 1906, and the club printed it in 1907 as its twenty-second publication. Pickett, a physician and club member, presents the theory of Paul Du Chaillu, the explorer and ethnologist.

The theory is stated on the title page: the English-speaking people of today are descended from the Scandinavians rather than the Teutons, from the Normans rather than the Germans. Pickett supports it with an alphabetical series of Norse, Norman, and Anglo-Norman surnames. The lost race of the title is the Northman in the English blood, hidden under Saxon labels. Filson Club papers were Kentucky gentlemen's scholarship, read aloud before printing. This one shows the era's racial philology in full dress: history argued from name lists, with the Vikings claimed as America's ancestors.
47685-lancaster-s-choice:
A dime novel by Mrs Alex McVeigh Miller, copyrighted in 1884. George Munro held the original copyright. The Arthur Westbrook Company reprinted it at Cleveland in the Hart Series. Forty chapters fill the tale. Old Lady Lancaster opens the story in possession of a problem. She owns twenty thousand pounds a year outright.

Her dower came with her marriage to the late Lord Lancaster. The title and estates passed to his nephew Clive. Spendthrift lords before him dissipated everything unentailed. Clive keeps only an army captain's pay. His aunt still reigns at the ancestral home. She will leave him her fortune if he marries to please her. The shake of her grey head threatens otherwise. Miller wrote scores of such romances for Munro's lists.
4770-work-a-story-of-experience:
Louisa May Alcott, author of Little Women and Little Men, published Work, A Story of Experience, at Boston in 1901. A Carlyle epigraph stands at its head: endless significance lies in work, and in idleness alone lies perpetual despair. Alcott dedicates the book to her mother, whose life has been a long labour of love, inscribed gratefully by her daughter.

Contents follow Christie through servant, actress, governess, companion, and seamstress, then through the mist and a cure for despair. Mrs. Wilkins's minister, beginning again, a strawberry bed, and Christie's gala lead to waking up, which, midsummer, and mustered in. The colonel, sunrise, little heart's-ease, and at forty close the tale. Illustrations by Sol Eytinge show Christie, Aunt Betsey, Mrs. Stuart, Hepsey, and others. Readers get Alcott's novel of a woman earning her living, with work as dignity and hope.
47702-through-the-gates-of-old-romance:
Jay Mills wrote these true tales through the gates of old romance. Lippincott printed the book at Philadelphia in 1903, John Rae drew plates. A front plate shows the Park Theatre, New York, in 1807. Contents open with an unrecorded Philadelphia romance of the Franklins.

Nathaniel Moore love story and Aaron Burr last days follow in turn. Philip Freneau poetic courtship and the Chevalier de Silly appear next. Susanna Rowson of Charlotte Temple fame meets her grenadier here. Ghosts of a Staten Island manor and André last love close it. Mills gathered the tales of old New York romance.
47776-the-dreadnought-boys-on-battle-pra:
Captain Wilbur Lawton wrote a boys naval tale printed in New York in 1911. Its heroes are Ned Strong and his red haired friend, both near eighteen. They stand in a village store and post office and gaze at a bright poster. The poster fires them with one wish, to join the navy.

Uncle Sam takes the two raw recruits, and ship life starts at once. The boys face a coward's blow, a bully who needs a lesson, and a spell in the brig. A cold bath, a plot, and hard drill test them in turn. Battle practice gives the book its title and its climax, as the boys prove they have the right ring for sea service.
47826-a-tender-attachment-a-farce:
A Tender Attachment is a farce printed in Spencer's Universal Stage, a London series of comedies, dramas, and farces. Each play in the series sold for fifteen cents and carried a full description of the necessary stage business. The series suited both public and private performance.

The opening pages list the catalogue. Lost in London, a drama in three acts, heads the list, with comedies by Buckstone and others behind it. Cast sizes are given for every piece, so a manager could shop by company strength. A tender attachment, as a title, promises the love intrigue standard to the one-act farce. Cheap acting editions spread the popular stage across two countries. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
4792-in-freedom-s-cause-a-story-of-walla:
G. A. Henty wrote In Freedom's Cause, A Story of Wallace and Bruce, addressing his readers as dear lads. He says few figures in history have exercised such influence on events as William Wallace and Robert Bruce. He argues Scotland owed her freedom from English domination to their courage, perseverance, and energy.

Contents follow the story from Glen Cairn and Leaving Home, through Sir William Wallace, the capture of Lanark, and a treacherous plot. The Barns of Ayr and a cave in the Pentlands follow. The council at Stirling, the battle of Stirling Bridge, and the battle of Falkirk lead to Robert the Bruce, the battle of Methven, and the castle of Dunstaffnage. Colonsay, a mission to Ireland, and an Irish rising carry the war on, through the siege of Aberfilly, a prisoner, and an escape from Berwick, to Edinburgh and Bannockburn. Readers get a stirring boys' adventure.
48039-from-the-north-foreland-to-penzanc:
Clive Holland wrote a book of the south coast of England, illustrated by Maurice Randall and published at London in 1908. It is inscribed to the Marquess of Ormonde, commodore of the Royal Yacht Squadron. Ten chapters walk the coast from the North Foreland to Penzance, port by port.

The first treats Ramsgate, Deal, Dover, and Hythe among the Cinque Ports. Portsmouth, the Isle of Wight ports, and Southampton follow, then Poole, Weymouth, and Lyme Regis. Torquay, Dartmouth, Plymouth, Fowey, and Falmouth close the road west. The North Foreland itself, the first chapter says, stands dazzling white on a bright summer's day, its turf by turns the greenest in England.
48184-mary-tudor-queen-of-france:
Mary Croom Brown's biography of Mary Tudor, published by Methuen in London in nineteen eleven, tells the short, crowded life of Henry the Seventh's younger daughter. Twelve illustrations face the text. The book appears in a Romantic History series beside lives of Margaret of Austria and the Nine Days' Queen. Brown draws on the calendars of state papers for England, Venice, and Spain.

The chapters follow the princess through a childhood betrothal to Charles of Castile. That match collapsed amid European complications, and she married instead the aging Louis the Twelfth of France. Widowed within months, she risked everything on a secret marriage to Charles Brandon, Duke of Suffolk. She then had to confess and do penance before her brother Henry the Eighth forgave the match. Portraits of her parents, her husbands, and Wolsey illustrate the story.
48276-the-hand-of-providence:
The Hand of Providence is a history book by Elder Ward, published at Salt Lake City in 1883 at the Juvenile Instructor office. Its subtitle states its scope: the hand of providence as shown in the history of nations and individuals, from the great apostasy to the restoration of the gospel. Mount Calvary forms the frontispiece.

Ward's preface argues with the reader directly. Do not throw this book down carelessly, he begins. Other histories, he grants, are plentiful, but most are too large for the sons and daughters of toil. Many flatter party or sect, and tell of legalised slaughter and tyrants. The real benefactors of the race, and the overruling hand of God, go unnoticed in them. Does God rule the world? Yes, answers the book, and it sets out to prove it from the record. It is Mormon history teaching for the young, written against the secular textbooks.
48296-linnet-a-romance:
Grant Allen wrote this romance, published at New York by the New Amsterdam Book Company in 1900. Allen notes that the story was written amid the scenery it describes, the Tyrol, and that he borrowed touches of local color from a well known book on Tyrol and the Tyrolese. A poem by William Watson is quoted near the end.

The opening chapter introduces Florian Wood at Zell in the Zillerthal, the valley Allen calls the most Tyrolese corner of the Tyrol. From it come the wandering zither-players and singers who carry their voices through every capital and spa in Europe, leaving with a few copper coins and coming home rich. Fifty-two chapters follow Linnet, Florian, and their circle through first nights, wagers, Schloss Tyrol, and questions of God's law against man's.
48486-duality-of-voice:
Duality of Voice is an outline of original research by Emil Sutro. Putnam's Sons of New York and London brought it out in 1899. Sutro had writ The Basic Law of Vocal Utterance before this study. There is nothing in our composition purely material or spiritual, Montaigne heads it. Six chapters run from an introduction to the physiology of voice.

Comments of a distant reviewer and fragments fill the first chapter. The voice of the oesophagus and its vocal cords stand treated there. The human voice chapter weighs introspection, extirpation, and tongue movements next. Impression and expression bring in the phonograph and stuttering in turn. Our mother tongue treats national traits and the American nation. Nationality and race distinctions fill the fifth chapter of the study. Anglo-Saxon and German idioms stand compared for breath and rhythm. Sutro claims disclosures far in advance of his time and generation.
48513-his-master-s-voice:
His Master's Voice, by Randall Garrett, ran in Analog in March 1962, with drawings by Krenkel. The frame of the tale praises Spaceship McGuire, who had lots of knowledge but no wisdom. McGuire asked questions too deep for any thinker, such as who a man is.

The narrator, Oak, calls on Shalimar Ravenhurst at Raven's Rest, a mountain-sized rock in the Belt. Ravenhurst is one of the sharpest operators out there, but he makes folk dislike him without trying. He pours Madeira with great care, since wine falls in slow motion where the pull of gravity is faint. A splash can send it gushing all over the room. The talk that follows turns on identity and the strange ship.
48537-billy-bounce:
Denslow and Dudley Bragdon wrote 'Billy Bounce,' published by Dillingham at New York in 1906, with pictures by Denslow himself. The frontispiece shows Billy excitedly finding a large fried egg, and the chapter list promises pure nonsense from the start. Billy faces the dark plot of Nickel Plate, the polished villain, jumps to Shamville, and is captured by Tomato.

Later chapters play with words as much as places: adventures in Eggs-aggeration, pease porridge hot, a wishing bottle, and time in Silly Land. Billy meets a sea urchin and a ne'er do eel, visits Spookville and the volcano of Vociferous, and ends in the Queen Bee Palace. The illustrations list bogies, dream food sprites, and a black cat-o-nine tails, all in Denslow's playful manner.
48552-the-blissylvania-post-office:
The Blissylvania Post-Office is a story for young readers by Marion Ames Taggart. It came out in 1897. The title names a play post office run by a group of girls.

The tale opens on a wet, foggy day when a bright idea strikes. Chapters follow the club through a narrow escape and a mystery tenant. A picnic, a wedding and the end of the year round out the plot. Margery, one of the girls, has a plan of her own. The story is light in tone and built on friendship, games and small scrapes. The club's rules and ranks give the game a charm of its own.
48707-gentlemen-of-the-jury-a-farce: Gentlemen of the Jury is a farce issued in Boston by George Baker in 1873, in the Amateur Drama line that took its motto from Shakespeare: all the world's a stage. Baker's catalogue in the copy lists the companion volumes of Spencer's Universal Stage, comedies and farces at 15 cents each, adapted to public or private performance. A courtroom turned into farce, printed cheap for amateur companies, is the whole design.
48723-a-parody-on-patience:
A comic sketch, printed under the heading A Trip to Niagara Falls, follows a Chicago family on a day's outing. Trevellyan, a hard-worked stock broker, takes his wife and the girls May and Nellie to the Falls for a holiday. Deacon Fitney, who knows how to do the Falls properly, is put in charge of the whole plan.

The Deacon's one fault is an unreasonable love of buttons, which cover his dress beyond what the law requires, with a gold-headed one on his scarf. The party leaves at four-thirty by the Michigan Central Limited Express, in palace cars behind five sleepers and a dining car. May and Nellie glue their noses to the window as the train runs out past Lake Michigan.
48758-france-and-england-in-north-americ:
Francis Parkman wrote A Half-Century of Conflict as part six of his France and England in North America series. This second volume appeared in Boston in the new library edition of his works, with a frontispiece portrait of Sir William Pepperrell after a painting by John Smibert.

Chapter sixteen follows the search for the Pacific, from schemes for a western sea to the journeys of La Vérendrye and his sons among the Mandans and toward the Rocky Mountains. Chapter seventeen turns to the chain of posts and the rival claims of France and England. Readers get Parkman's narrative history of the struggle for a continent, built on explorers, missions, and forts.
48822-three-years-in-the-service:
McCall, a private of Company B, wrote a record of the doings of the Eleventh Regiment of Missouri Volunteers. The book was printed at Springfield in 1864, while the Civil War still raged. McCall tells the tale from the ranks, as a common soldier who walked twenty-five miles to enlist.

He joined a company forming at Springfield, Illinois, in July 1861, under a recruiting officer named Weber. The men rode by rail amid cheers and waving handkerchiefs, crossed the river below St Louis, and drew rations at the arsenal. Weeks at the Marine Hospital taught them drill, eight hours a day, on straw and plank. Readers get an unpolished, firsthand account of how a western regiment was raised, fed, and drilled in the war's first summer.
48824-countess-vera-or-the-oath-of-venge: Mrs Alex McVeigh Miller wrote Countess Vera, or The Oath of Vengeance, a novel issued in Lovell's Library at twenty-five cents. Miller had written A Dreadful Temptation and Queenie's Terrible Secret. The tale runs past twenty-six chapters. The opening pages of this copy carry only the title, the author's other works, and advertisements, so the story itself cannot be told from them.
48994-the-old-humanities-and-the-new-sci:
Sir William Osler wrote The Old Humanities and the New Science. Houghton Mifflin Company issued it at Boston in 1920. Harvey Cushing wrote the intro for it. Osler gave the talk to the Classical Association. The date was May 16, 1919 for that address. A roll of past presidents fronts the book.

The Earl of Halsbury led the line in 1905. Lord Curzon and S H Butcher follow him. H H Asquith stands in the list for 1908. The Earl of Cromer and Sir Archibald Geikie join. Frederic Kenyon of the British Museum stands at 1913. Gilbert Murray closes the shown roll at 1917. A great doctor's plea for Greek and Latin in a science age argues the two cultures need each other's leaven.
49115-eight-sermons-on-the-priesthood-al:
Mayow Wynell Mayow wrote Eight Sermons on the Priesthood, Altar, and Sacrifice, issued in Oxford and London by James Parker and Company in eighteen sixty seven. Mayow was perpetual curate of St Mary, West Brompton, and late student of Christ Church, Oxford. He inscribed the volume to Walter Kerr, Lord Bishop of Salisbury. The dedication remembers a connection with the diocese of nearly a quarter of a century.

A Bishop Pearson epigraph heads the book. In Christianity there can be no concerning truth which is not ancient, Pearson wrote. Whatsoever is truly new is certainly false, the epigraph holds. The principles of Christianity are now as freely questioned as the most doubtful points, it laments. The sermons were preached at St Mary, the advertisement begins. Theology readers get high church sermons on priesthood and the altar from the Oxford Movement years.
49166-indian-currency-and-finance:
Indian Currency and Finance is a study of money in British India by John Maynard Keynes. Keynes was a fellow of King's College, Cambridge when he wrote the work. Macmillan published the book in London in 1913. The contents move from the state of the rupee to banking and the rate of discount in India.
