The first chapter recalls that India minted silver freely until 1893. When silver fell in gold value, trade suffered and state finance was badly strained. The mints then closed to free silver coinage, and the rupee was cut loose from its metal worth. By holding back new issues, the government raised the rupee to a fixed gold value by 1899. Later chapters treat the gold exchange standard, paper currency, council bills, and the reserves held in London.
49191-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-30:
Chambers Edinburgh Journal was a weekly sheet run by William and Robert Chambers in that town. The copy here is Number 310 of the new series, dated Saturday, December 8, 1849. A lone copy cost a penny and a half in that age. The lead piece in this issue bears the plain title Knowledge.

That piece faults the old way of praise for the hunt of lore. For long, it says, lore was sold to the crowd by the shine of wealth and rank it could bring. Lives of men who rose by smarts were raked from all past time as bait. The point was to spur the bold with the hope of rich rewards. Such bait, the piece holds, makes lore seem grand for the wrong cause.
49212-the-warfare-of-science:
The Warfare of Science, by Andrew Dickson White, president of Cornell University, was published in New York in 1888. White gives the little book to Henry Sage, a Christian man who, he says, welcomes all truth and fears none. A prefatory note traces the work growth.

In shorter form it was a Phi Beta Kappa oration at Brown, and a lecture in New York, Boston, New Haven, and Ann Arbor. It then came out in a science monthly. White has now revised it with care, fixed some errors, and greatly enlarged it. New matter treats Galileo in astronomy, Aquinas in chemistry and physics, and church distrust in anatomy and medicine. Readers get a famous case that science and theology had long been at war.
4923-king-midas-a-romance:
Upton Sinclair's King Midas opens in the two joyful months of spring when poets have the woods and waters to themselves, from the first bloodroot to the fading wild rose. In that season the romance follows a young poet and the wealthy world that tempts him, recasting the Midas legend for a modern age.

Gold, art, and love contend in the story, as the hero learns what his gift is worth when money enters the bargain. Sinclair, better known for social protest, here works in a lyrical register. Readers get an early Sinclair romance about the price of turning everything one touches into wealth, and what remains when the glitter fades.
49282-the-chronicles-of-the-imp-a-romanc:
Jeffery Farnol wrote The Chronicles of the Imp, a romance, in a new cheaper edition. Sampson Low at London put out this form in 1915. Farnol had written The Broad Highway and The Amateur Gentleman. Clement Shorter adds an appreciation of the author and his work. Shorter calls Farnol an Englishman whose best book smells of his own country.

Yet The Broad Highway was written in America, Shorter notes. Three American publishers refused that book before it found its home. A loyal friend brought the manuscript to a publisher with happy results. Shorter owns that he recalls that bringing with more warmth than his own first reading. The friend in the story is Rymer, who stood by his judgment. A plate shows a man edging along a branch, kicking out to reach a boat. Farnol gives a romance of the road and the heart.
49284-a-maid-of-brittany-a-romance:
A Maid of Brittany, a romance by May Wynne, came out from Greening in London in 1909, in a popular edition with a frontispiece by Brock. Wynne also wrote Henry of Navarre and When Terror Ruled. A transcriber's note warns that chapters twenty two to twenty four disagree about an injury, and no second edition was at hand to settle it.

Chapter one opens after a hawking party. Guillaume de Coray stands over an unconscious stranger and swears he is a French spy. His cousin Gwennola pleads the man's case before her father: the golden spurs on his heels proclaim his knighthood. Guillaume points to the stranger's horse, its docked ears and mane marking it, in the fashion of the time, as a French knight's mount.
49285-the-romance-of-the-commonplace:
Gelett Burgess wrote The Romance of the Commonplace, a set of essays dated nineteen hundred and two at San Francisco. Burgess gave the book to his sisters Ella and Ann, with whom, he says, this philosophy was proven. A line from Stevenson heads the title page.

In a personal opening, Burgess owns that the essay bares a writer more than any other form. Fiction lets a teller escape, and verse can hide a man in figures of speech. Here, he says, his character and mind lie open, and he shivers with shame. He has reworked his pieces so none begins with a big letter I. The essays treat life itself, on which each reader feels a critic.
493-falk-a-reminiscence:
Joseph Conrad tells of Falk, a taciturn tug captain with a dark past, in this sea story framed as a dinner tale. Seamen dining near the Thames recall a voyage where Falk's ship, food, and love for a captain's niece tangle in strange ways. Hunger, pride, and a long-kept secret drive the plot.

Conrad writes in his slow, probing style, letting the tale unfold through talk and memory. Falk proves both brutal and tender, a man shaped by the sea's harsh law. The story stands as a compact study of desire, guilt, and the bonds that hold seamen together.
49400-experience:
Catherine Cotton tells a life in Experience, issued by W Collins Sons in London, first impressed in June 1922 and reprinted many times since. A publisher's note owns the charm at once: this chronicle has no plot. It presents a happy, witty, simple-minded woman who drew love because she gave it out.

Cotton's preface asks why realism must mean gloom, when humor, happiness, and love are just as real. The book is dedicated to five gallant gentlemen who gave their lives for England. It opens at a birthday lunch with Uncle Jasper, where Meg, the narrator, is teased over his glasses.
49478-a-mysterious-disappearance-a-farce:
Baker and Company published this farce for the amateur drama in 1876. Its author was a house name, credited on the title with pieces from Sylvia's Soldier to A Drop Too Much and We Are All Teetotalers. The Amateur Drama series put farces into the hands of parlor actors.

Captain Boliver Bobstay has mysteriously disappeared, as the cast list says. Charles Cleverly, an amateur farmer, his wife, and his sister Nelly furnish the household. Dixon Dolby is out for a day's sport, and Carlos Carrots is the farm hand. Persis Grievous appears as the Widow Bobstay, in a red wig with long curls, light blue spectacles, and girlish dress. The costumes are specified to the wig: the captain needs a bald wig and a black wig with whiskers for disguise. A farm-house sitting room, a girl discovered dusting, and the machinery of mistaken identity does the rest.
49480-poison-a-farce: Poison is a farce in the cheap play lists of George Baker of Boston, with rights held from 1876. Its front pages are trade lists, not scenes. They price new plays at fifteen to twenty-five cents. They also name farces in the Spencer Universal Stage set. Each entry gives a count of men and women in the cast. No scene text shows in the head of this copy. The lists still fix its trade: short, cheap stage fare for home and hall use.
4956-the-duke-s-prize-a-story-of-art-and:
A story of art and heart in Florence, this romance invites the reader on a fancy voyage across the Mediterranean to the Tyrrhenian Sea. The narrator touches at Gibraltar, Corsica, Sardinia, and Sicily, praising storied shores that have been the poet's theme for ages, before reaching the city of art itself.

In Florence, love and ambition contend around a duke's prize, as artists and lovers weigh beauty against reward. The catalog entry is anonymous. Readers get a romantic tale of Italy, lush with scenery and sentiment, in the tradition of novels that treat Florence as a school for the heart.
496-the-little-lame-prince:
Dinah Maria Craik, writing as Miss Mulock, tells fairy tales for children in this volume, opening with the title story. A beautiful prince of Nomansland, lame from a cruel trick, learns courage and kindness in a lonely tower. His godmother's gifts, a magic cloak, and a traveling cloak help him see his kingdom truly.

Shorter tales follow: an invisible prince, Prince Cherry, the prince with the nose, the frog prince, and Clever Alice. Craik writes with warmth and plain moral sense, never scolding. The book endures as a gentle classic, where a lame child's heart proves stronger than his legs.
49686-little-prudy-s-cousin-grace:
Little Prudy's Cousin Grace, by Sophie May, is a volume of the Little Prudy series. Lee and Shepard entered it in 1864; this edition comes from Lothrop, Lee and Shepard of Boston, with copyright renewed in 1892. Eleven chapters carry the story, from The Cup and Saucer to The Children's Fair.

Grace Clifford and Katharine Hallock are the cup and saucer of chapter one: dear friends, linked in everyone's speech as Grace and Cassy. Grace is eager and vivid, with bright blue eyes and auburn curls; she laughs in ecstasy and weeps in showers. Cassy is gentle and brown eyed, and never storms. The two Hoosier girls, nearly twelve, have sworn never to marry. They will live together in a cottage with chickens, pigeons, and a cat. They have exchanged rings as pledges. Cassy's regard ring is set with gems whose initials spell the word Regard.
49728-how-to-settle-accounts-with-your-l:
Stirling Coyne wrote this one-act farce, first played at the Theatre Royal, Adelphi, on Monday, July 26, 1847. The running time is given as fifty minutes. Whittington Widgetts, a West-end tailor, heads the cast, with Barney Twill as his page and light porter.

Jacob Brown, a hairdresser at the Opera, a postman and a waiter complete the men. Cheri Bounce, an opera dancer, and Mary White, a young laundress, bring the bill at the title into play. Costume notes give Widgetts three changes of coat, from blue to green to black, for a short, brisk stage piece.
49818-animal-life-and-intelligence:
Animal Life and Intelligence, by C Lloyd Morgan, professor at University College, Bristol, was published by Ginn and Company at Boston in 1891, and dedicated to his father. A Kentish plover with eggs and young, from the British Natural History Museum exhibit, fronts the book.

Morgan's preface sets his aim against the many anecdotal books on animal intelligence. Romanes and Mivart, he grants, brought real training to the subject, and he offers his own years of study. Organic evolution fills the first part, since heredity and natural selection intertwine with habit and instinct throughout.
49925-in-defense-of-the-flag-a-true-war-:
In Defense of the Flag is a true war story by David W Stafford, published in nineteen hundred four. Stafford served in Company D of the Eighty Third Pennsylvania Volunteers, as his title page states. A captain of a sister company vouches in verse that every word is true. A portrait of Stafford fronts the illustrated book.

Scenes and incidents of the Great Rebellion, the Civil War, are pictured from a private soldier's view. Thrilling escapes from southern prisons are promised in the subtitle itself. Stafford writes as witness, not historian, forty years after the guns. Such veteran memoirs, sold by the men themselves, kept regimental memory alive in small towns.
4995-true-to-himself-or-roger-strong-s-s:
Roger Strong, a boy paid by Widow Canby to watch her orchard, catches Duncan Woodward stealing pears in this boys' story of standing one's ground. Duncan, only son of Darbyville's wealthiest merchant, sneers at Roger and tells him to mind his own business, but Roger answers that minding the orchard is exactly his business.

The trouble in the orchard opens a tale of Roger's struggle for place, as a poor boy defends honest work against rich-boy bullying. Authorship is left unnamed in the record. Readers get a straightforward moral adventure, where courage means doing a small job well even when the thief outranks you.
50002-the-hand-made-gentleman-a-tale-of-:
The Hand-Made Gentleman is a tale of the battles of peace by Irving Bacheller, printed at New York in 1909. Bacheller also wrote Eben Holden and Silas Strong. Harper issued the book, dedicated to his friend Bailey. The narrator tells his own life from the start.

He was born in 1843, and his first peril was being named Solomon. He escaped with the lighter penalty of Jacob, printing Jacob Ezra Heron on his slate at five years old. His assets were his name, his mother, a friend named Lizzie McCormick, and a little green book from his grandmother. His liabilities were a number of unpunished sins. Bacheller opens a long life of self-making.
50109-the-mysterious-stranger-a-romance:
The Mysterious Stranger: A Romance is a tale by Mark Twain, printed at New York and London in 1916 with illustrations by N C Wyeth. The first chapter opens in 1590, in winter. Austria was far away from the world, and asleep; it was still the Middle Ages there, and promised to remain so forever.

The village of Eseldorf drowsed in peace in a hilly and woodsy solitude in the middle of that sleep. It was a paradise for the boys who tell the story. They were not overmuch pestered with schooling. Mainly they were trained to be good Christians, to revere the Virgin, the Church, and the saints above everything. Beyond these matters they were not required to know much, and in fact not allowed to. Knowledge, they were taught, was not good for the common people. Into this sleeping village the mysterious stranger comes.
50125-the-court-of-philip-iv-spain-in-de:
Martin Hume wrote a past of Spain at the court of Philip the Fourth. The book came out in London in 1907. Hume kept the state's Spanish files at the Public Record Office. He taught Spanish past and letters at Pembroke College, Cambridge. A front plate shows Philip at age fifty-five, from Velazquez's hand.

Philip's christening in 1605 and an English embassy lead in. Lerma's rule, the land's want, and the Moriscos' cast-out fill it. The boy king's youth, his match, and Olivares's rise come next. Court pomp on a poor land is the book's grave theme. Hume paints pomp and rot in one frame.
50193-the-messenger-of-the-black-prince:
The Messenger of the Black Prince, by Thomas A H Mawhinney, was printed in Philadelphia by the Penn Publishing Company under a 1928 copyright. Manning de V Lee drew the plates. Mawhinney had written The Sword of the House de Marillac and English Oak and Spanish Gold.

A plate shows a lance almost torn from the hero grasp. Chapters open with the King fool, an attack in the woods, and a visitor in the night. The Black Prince, the silver hafted dagger, and a solitary house in the woods pace the mid tale. The highwayman of Tours, the Three Crows Inn, pursuit, and a scrivener turned traitor raise the stakes. The defense of the cave, a fight in the inn, and the Abbot of Chalonnes close the run. Boys of the day got France in the Hundred Years War.
50247-a-temporary-gentleman-in-france:
A Temporary Gentleman in France is a set of home letters from an officer at the front in the Great War, published in nineteen eighteen. Introductory chapters are by Captain A J Dawson of the Border Regiment. The British War Office gave leave to publish the letters, a note states. Names in the letters were deleted or changed for safety.

A temporary gentleman was slang for a wartime officer promoted from civilian life for the war only. His letters home give a junior officer's view of France, the trenches, and his men. No other change was made to fit them for print, the publisher stresses. The plain letter form keeps the voice close and unpolished.
50380-annals-anecdotes-and-legends-a-chr:
Annals, Anecdotes, and Legends, by John Francis, came out in London in 1853 as a chronicle of life assurance. Francis had earlier written a history of the Bank of England. His book is given, by leave, to the Marquess of Lansdowne, heir of Sir William Petty.

Early parts trace Petty and his work on vital statistics, then Roman and Saxon roots of the trade. Sea risk, pilgrims to the Holy Land, and early offices all come under review. Later parts tell of Halley's life tables, the first court trial on a life policy, and firms like the Amicable and the Sun. Bubble-era schemes, frauds, and odd firms fill the rest, told with tales of the men behind them.
50431-dick-kent-with-the-mounted-police:
Milton Richards sends Dick Kent and his chum Sandy McClaren back north in this 1927 volume from the Saalfield Publishing Company. The boys have spent a year of adventure two hundred miles north of Hay River Landing in Canada. Fort du Lac, where the factor Martin MacLean barters for furs, has proved too quiet for them. They plan to return to Fort Good Faith, where Sandy's uncle Walter still has trouble with the outlaw Bear Henderson.

An exhausted Indian runner staggers in with word of trouble, and the tale is off. The contents promise rapids shot, a fire, a grizzly, a rifled cache, a blizzard, and stolen huskies. A hungry wolf pack, a ghost, and an attack on the fort follow in the twenty-six chapters. Richards had already written four earlier Dick Kent books, from the Far North to the malemute mail.
5062-the-winds-of-chance:
Rex Beach's Winds of Chance opens with a shell game on a folding table, as Mr. Lucky Broad places a crisp ten-dollar bill in an eager palm and proclaims that the gentleman wins and the gambler loses. The eye is quicker than the hand, he announces, while he rearranges three worn walnut shells and conceals a pellet the size of a small pill beneath one.

The pellet's erratic comings and goings summon and hold his audience, and the novel follows fortune's winds from such small cons to larger gambles in the North. Beach writes the gambling frontier with gusto. Readers get an adventure of chance and character, where luck itself becomes a player in the story.
50622-the-silver-menace:
The Silver Menace is a serial story by Murray Leinster, from The Thrill Book of 1919. It ran in the magazine's September first and fifteenth issues. The tale opens at night aboard a great white yacht. Her engines throb steadily through calm water. For once no merry party of guests crowds the decks. Alexander Morrison, a millionaire steamship magnate, has the ship nearly to himself.

His daughter Nita sits with him in wicker chairs on the after deck. They talk of the Riviera season just ended. Suitors had run after her there, she teases, only as a road to her father. Then the yacht's way through the water begins to change. A velvety checking of speed hints at the menace of the title. Leinster mixes society talk with sea mystery.
50635-dave-dawson-with-the-eighth-air-fo:
R Sidney Bowen wrote Dave Dawson with the Eighth Air Force, a war tale for boys published in nineteen forty-four. The book forms part of the War Adventure Series from Crown Publishers. Bowen gave the book to Joel Stivers.

Dave Dawson flies a Lockheed Lightning over cloud-filled skies in England. The fighter climbs till it stalls, and one engine sputters and throws black smoke. Dave calls the plane a cranky crate of junk, then tries the move again. Chapters with names like No Man's Sky and Winged Fury promise hard fights ahead. Spies, secret rooms, and a gift for Hitler drive the plot.
50820-mrs-dot-a-farce:
Mrs Dot is a farce in three acts by the playwright Maugham. It was first played at a London house in April 1908. The print here came out in London in the year 1912. Its first name on the stage was a man's name and the word entire.

The cast is headed by a rich dame whose pet name gives the play its own. Her nephew serves as her aid and stands in the cast list. An aunt, a young gent, and a grave friend fill out the house. A lady and her girl, a tailor, and a law man come and go. The first act sits in the gent's rooms on a fine street. The last two acts move to the dame's house by the river. The fun turns on aims crossed in love and in coin.
50964-leonora-d-orco-a-historical-romanc:
Leonora d'Orco is a historical romance by G P R James. Alphons Durr published this copyright edition at Leipzig in 1860. The book stands as volume 50 of Durr's Collection of Standard American and British Authors. James had written Lord Montagu's Page, The Old Dominion, and Agnes Sorel. The first chapter opens in a mountain pass near Lago Maggiore.

The pass, in later years, was famous for robbery rather than festivals. Travellers lost their wealth there, and sometimes their lives. James sets his story at the end of the fifteenth century and the start of the sixteenth. Art, letters, and science were being reborn, he writes. Yet society festered beneath the golden embroidery. Brilliant festivals stood between acts of violence and rapine. Into that Italy of pageants and highwaymen steps Leonora, the heroine of the title.
51024-the-diggers-the-australians-in-fra:
Patrick MacGill wrote of the Australians in France in a book printed at London in 1919, with an introduction by Hughes. MacGill had written Children of the Dead End, The Rat Pit, The Great Push, and Soldier Songs. From the day Children of the Dead End came into my hands, I have been amongst the most devoted of your worshippers, Hughes writes to him.

No words of mine are needed to commend this story of the achievements of the Australian soldiers in France, he adds. The imperishable deeds of Australia's glorious soldiers have carved a deep niche in the topmost towers of the temple of the immortals. The war has made of Australia, a young community without traditions, a nation proudly conscious of itself. MacGill served in the ranks and writes the diggers from inside their trenches and jokes.
51321-prime-difference:
Prime Difference is a science fiction story by Alan Nourse, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in June 1957. George Faircloth is one hundred and forty per cent fed up with his wife Marge. Divorce, in his future, is ruin by law. The Family Solidarity Amendment of 1968 and the Aggrieved Spouse Compensation Act would leave him a pauper for life.

So Faircloth looks for another way out. A desperate man, he reasons, might buy himself an Ego Prime, a second self. Being two men rolled out of one would solve his problems, though which one he would be stays an open question. Nourse plays the notion for rueful comedy. The story is a neat specimen of the 1950s science fiction domestic satire, where the future's gadgets meet the present's marriages.
51600-the-border-boys-along-the-st-lawre:
Border Boys Along the Saint Lawrence is a boys adventure novel by Fremont Deering, copyrighted in 1914. The tale belongs to a series that took the Border Boys across many frontiers. Prior books sent them to Mexico, Texas, and the Canadian Rockies with Rangers. A frontispiece shows a boat of living flame outlined in green glare at night.

Contents promise rapids, a close shave, and a mysterious gray night craft on the river. The boys trail the ghost craft down to Montreal and run into peril adrift. A misleading light, an island camp, and an explosion fill the middle chapters. River smuggling and chase give this Saint Lawrence outing its drive.
5170-poems-of-experience:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox's Poems of Experience gathers lyrics on faith, endurance, womanhood, and the life of feeling. The collection was published in London in 1917 after several reprintings. Its contents run from The Empty Bowl and Keep Going to a Battle Hymn of the Women, a tribute to the actress Clara Morris. Poems on science, the city, and the voice of the voiceless appear among them.

Wilcox writes in plain, musical verse meant to comfort and encourage, and her popularity rested on that direct appeal. Readers will find here the optimistic, moral voice that made her one of the most widely read poets of her day, in poems short enough to read aloud and remember.
51714-the-great-experience:
Julia Farr wrote a novel printed at Salt Lake City in 1920 by the Deseret News. Farr had written Venna Hastings. I have but one lamp by which my feet are guided, and that is the lamp of experience, Patrick Henry is quoted at the front. The book is lovingly given to her Ephraim friends, Mrs Catherine Thompson and family.

Chapter heads carry mottoes: even a child is known by his doings, and no great truth was ever born into the world without the throes of suffering. Society's nothingness and its sacrifice, Edith's choice, and the glamor gone fill the early chapters. Go, preach the gospel to all the world heads the missionary turn. Betty's new friends, the treachery of the world, and friendship's claim come next. A contrast of husband and lover, Edith's release, and the dream of the past close a Utah tale of faith and love.
51773-scent-makes-a-difference:
James Stamers wrote a tale of sleep, dreams, and a strange cure house. The tale ran in Galaxy Magazine in April 1961. Its hero wants one good night of sleep above all. What he gets is time with the worst pack of sleep walkers in past tales. Odd things start at dawn in his odd new world.

A fried egg floats up through stone steps and breaks on his shoe. Bacon comes next by the same strange road at meal time. The lift in the house reads his blood, weight, and brain waves aloud. It finds no fault in his body at all. Dream logic rules each scene that ensue.
51854-the-rat-race:
Jay Franklin wrote this complete novel of a man in another body. Galaxy Publishing issued it as its science fiction novel number ten. A bomb destroys the battleship Alaska as the tale opens here. Lieutenant Commander Frank Jacklin wakes in New York in shock.

He finds himself in the body of Winnie Tompkins, dissolute broker. Jacklin must fit into Tompkins life, wife, mistress, and secretary included. His foreknowledge of the Alaska sinking drags him into Washington intrigue. Where the real Tompkins is stays the mystery till the climax. The blurb calls the tale delightful, provocative, and a striking novel of the American scene.
51863-seven-centuries-of-lace:
Seven Centuries of Lace is a lace history by Mrs Pollen, published in 1908. Macmillan of New York and Heinemann of London issued the book in that year. Alan Cole wrote a preface, and 120 full page illustrations fill the volume. Contents run from an introduction and glossary to needlepoint and bobbin lace chapters.

Plates show the Assisi alb said to have been worn by Saint Francis himself. The alb of Pope Boniface of 1298 gets plates of the whole and of details. Needlework from Egypto Roman tombs of the second and third centuries follows. Textile history gains a pictured survey of the lace maker art.
51889-robert-emmet-a-survey-of-his-rebel:
Robert Emmet is a short past of the Irish chief by Louise Guiney, out in nineteen four. A David Nutt house of London brought the book out that year. A face plate shows Emmet at age twenty five in court sketch form. Guiney calls her work a loose chant on past, not a strict lore tract. It rests on all sound print of the theme and on state vault sheets.

She was first to use those Hardwicke sheets ere they were put in rank. Some bits of them broke her print claim by a sheet of last fall. Four of seventeen Emmet babes lived to grow in that Cork house. Dr Emmet was a man of clear brain and pure fame, she writes. Kirk, Norman blood, and Kerry wife lines met in that house stock.
51921-the-lay-anthony-a-romance:
The Lay Anthony is a romance by Hergesheimer, put out at New York and London in the years just past the great war scare of its day. A long quote from an old bard of Italy heads the book, on love not lost when we pass from this false world to true life. Its gift word calls it a fig thing of a bloom that never dies.

Its first lines set its hero in a drug shop crowd of his town. Not for the fame of a great car cup, it says, nor for the boast of a ball team crown, would he own to that gay, jeer crowd that he was pure. In the plain sense of the word, he means. In hush, and in a most sound way, he was shamed by his pure state.
51928-the-dark-fleece:
Joseph Hergesheimer wrote The Dark Fleece, a novel first published by Alfred Knopf of New York in 1918 inside a volume called Gold and Iron. The 1922 Knopf edition reprints it. The first chapter bears a single name: Olive.

Olive Stanes lives in old Cottarsport, in a low house of weathered boards midway up Orange Street. The town's buildings cling to the rocky soil like salt weed on the harbor rocks. Her half brother and sisters, Hester, Jem, and Rhoda, made a playground of the great boulder in the yard, a fort, a mansion, and a ship in turn. Olive, the only child of Ira Stanes's first marriage, took no such wild pleasure in it. She stood in the portico a careful child beside their gay ease, in a family where money was never plentiful. Readers get Hergesheimer's rich, slow prose on a seaport girlhood.
51980-the-royal-end-a-romance:
Henry Harland published his romance The Royal End with Hutchinson at London in 1909. His earlier books The Cardinal's Snuff-Box and My Friend Prospero head the title page. Part first opens at the Lido near Venice, where Ruth and Lucilla Dor dine outdoors. Balzatore strains to reach Lucilla, and Bertram orders him down with stern words.

Sunset dies over Venice and the moon rises from the Adriatic as the women walk home. Figs, veils, mosquitoes, and a missing gondola fill their slow, witty talk. Lucilla sighs for Byron, who used to ride on the Lido in his day. Harland writes light, languid dialogue over a Venetian night. Romance here starts as comedy of manners under moonlight.
52057-abandonment-or-absolute-surrender-:
Caussade's teaching fills this volume: Abandonment, or Absolute Surrender to Divine Providence, a work printed after his death, revised by Ramiere and rendered from the eighth French edition by Ella McMahon. Benziger Brothers printed it at New York, Cincinnati, and Saint Louis in 1887, with the blessing of the Archbishop of New York.

A long preface defends the doctrine and marks its limits. Truth, it warns, turns to error the moment it is shrunk or stretched too far. The virtue of giving oneself wholly to God's care had been twisted before, by the Quietists of the seventeenth century, into sorry disorders. The preface sets out rules, drawn from reason and faith together, to keep readers inside the safe bounds.
52096-plays-being-an-unhistorical-pastor:
John Davidson gathered five plays in one volume published in London and Chicago in 1894. The set holds An Unhistorical Pastoral, a romantic farce, Bruce as a chronicle play, Smith as a tragic farce, and Scaramouch in Naxos as a pantomime.

The pastoral opens the book, with a cast led by Alardo, King of Belmarie, his son Rupert, nobles, rustics, a shepherd, and fairies including Oberon, Puck, and Titania. Its first scene lands the king on his own coast after a disastrous cruise past icebergs and pirates. Readers get an odd, inventive mix of verse drama forms from a Scottish poet better known for his ballads and lyrics.
52209-the-silent-shore-a-romance:
Bloundelle-Burton wrote The Silent Shore, a romance sold by Maxwell at London. Its title page takes a verse on death as a landing on a silent shore, where no waves beat and no storms roar. A prologue tells a tale of thirty years past. Two young men of about twenty-five talk in a private room at an inn in Le Vocq, a dull fishing town west of Havre.

One man swears he knows the year a man was wed, in 1858, and his own birth in May of 1859. The facts clash, and talk turns to a hard choice. Was the first wife no true wife, or was the act bigamy? The man will not think ill of a cold, stern father. The tale starts, then, with a family secret and a stain to clear.
52250-a-nurse-s-life-in-war-and-peace:
Laurence wrote A Nurse Life in War and Peace, printed at London in 1912, with a preface by Frederick Treves. Laurence had writ a book on modern nursing in hospital and home, and held the Royal Red Cross. Contents start at school, where she sets her mind on nursing, and move through first training.

Early chapters give hospital food, first special cases, quarantine, and night duty. A year in South Africa follows: Kimberley diamond fields, a meet with Cecil Rhodes, and circuit work in Cape Colony. Back home come typhoid cases, tracheotomies, and ward sister posts. Egypt and the Nile, then war in the Sudan with night and day nursing, close the span shown. Full, brisk diaries show a nurse world before modern drugs.
52512-the-duchess-of-dublin-a-farce:
The Duchess of Dublin is a farce for amateur players, entered for copyright at Boston in 1873 and issued in the Amateur Drama series by George Baker. Baker's list on the opening pages names dozens of his short plays, from Sylvia's Soldier to We're All Teetotalers. The piece gives its cast, their costumes, and the setting in full.

The scene is the office of Dr Adam Aconite, a young physician whose sister Annie is in the cast. Around them gather Frank Friskey, rich and gouty Oliver Oldbuck, a speculator, Silas Sharpset, a widower, a fat man with a bad cough, and an autograph hunter, Miss Abigail Alllove. The title role belongs to Maggie Mullen, dressed as a kitchen girl with her sleeves rolled up. Readers and players get a compact farce built for laughs, with every wig and bandage spelled out in the costume notes.
52586-clash-of-arms-a-romance:
John Bloundelle-Burton's Clash of Arms, a romance, was first published by Methuen in London in October 1897. This copy is the new and cheaper issue of 1905. A motto from Brantome, in French, boasts of a sword so bloodthirsty that its owner is forever drawing it from the scabbard.

The first chapter, The Bravo, opens at a sick man's bedside. He frets that Andrew Vause, who has roamed and fought about the world for five years, will arrive only in time to see him in his coffin. Vause has delayed for an urgent interview with the King, but he always kept his word. The contents promise the Vicomte de Bois-Vallee, the little wood at Entzheim, Marion Wyatt and an escape.
52637-the-dreadnought-boys-on-aero-servi:
The Dreadnought Boys on Aero Service, by Captain Wilbur Lawton, was copyright in 1912. Lawton had sent his boys on battle drill, on a destroyer, and on a submarine. The tale opens on a June day at Hampton Roads, where the great ship Manhattan lies with a fleet.

A notice on the board stirs the whole crew. Enlisted men may apply for posts in a test aero squad, under Lieutenant De Frees. Old sailors scoff at risking their skins in the sky. Twenty-five chapters bring a rescue by plane, a plot, and a boy at bay. Ned thinks up a new device, and a drop from space follows. Boys get a brisk tale of the navy at the dawn of flight.
52649-traitor-and-true-a-romance:
John Bloundelle-Burton wrote a romance first published in 1906 at London. It opens at the Taverne Gabrielle, in the Rue des Franc Bourgeois in the Marais, at supper-time on a summer evening. Opposite stood the house Henri the Fourth had built for the fair Gabrielle d'Estrées, which gave the tavern its name.

The landlord's family takes its own supper in the lull. In one corner an ancient bourgeois sips Arbois wine with his cronies; in another, a young officer of the Perche regiment shares a savoury ragout with a masked lady. Near the door sit two men of a rougher kidney. Old Paris, full-blooded and perfumed with romance, is the author's element.
52733-denounced-a-romance:
John Bloundelle-Burton's Denounced: A Romance was published by Appleton at New York in 1896. It is number 200 of Appleton's Town and Country Library. A publisher's page praises his earlier In the Day of Adversity, quoting the Saint James's Gazette at length. The epigraph is from a Jacobite ballad: the adder lies in the corbie's nest. Thirty-two chapters and an appendix make the book. Its chapter titles set the politics at once: a home coming, a subject of King George, then the subjects of King James.

Kate makes an appointment; a woman's letter arrives; my lord goes out of town and returns. Denounced falls as chapter nine. Archibald escapes, the pair fly for France, and the Bastille looms at chapter twenty-one. The opening chapter brings a bluff-bowed galliot laboring through a storm toward the Suffolk coast.
52781-fortune-s-my-foe-a-romance:
Fortunes My Foe is a romance by J Bloundelle Burton in a cheap set line. Ads in the front praise a kin tale of arms clash by the same hand. Press lines call his work brisk, with held pace and strong deed scenes. No year is shown in the front pages of the hosted text.

A tale of Charles the First in his wild road years earns warm ad praise. That note claims the scenes feel as if the reader stood in those days. The set sold cloth books at one dollar and thin prints at half that. Old age courts, swords, and love form the stock of his mode in print. Keen craft at scene and pace won him a wide home crowd.
52802-the-later-renaissance:
David Hannay wrote The Later Renaissance as the sixth volume of Periods of European Literature, a 12-volume series edited by Professor Saintsbury. William Blackwood and Sons published it in Edinburgh and London in 1898, at five shillings net. A line from Matthew Arnold stands at the front of the series list, calling Europe one great confederation for the life of the mind.

The series plan maps the whole of European letters, from the Dark Ages and the flourishing of romance through the fourteenth century and the earlier Renaissance. Hannay's volume takes the story into the later Renaissance, the age after the first great revival had spread across the continent. His preface explains the rules of the series and defends the place he gave each literature. Students of the period get criticism written to a shared plan, volume fitting volume like stones in one arch.
52957-the-land-of-bondage-a-romance:
John Bloundelle-Burton wrote this romance, published by White in London in 1905. Part one is the narrative of Gerald, Viscount Amande, the contents announce. A funeral opens his story, with an unpeaceful passing and a beggar and outcast to follow in the chapters.

Into the land of bondage, the springe is set and the bird draws near, the list goes on. Trapped and caged, a mother, a noble kinsman and impressment close part one of the tale. Part two turns to the narrative of Joice Bampfylde of Virginia, in a story of the press gang and colonial seas.
52970-servants-of-sin-a-romance:
John Bloundelle-Burton writes a French romance in Servants of Sin, printed in London in 1900. Methuen made the book. It was dramatised and produced for copyright purposes in London that May, licensed as a drama in four acts. Its motto is a lament: how doth the city sit solitary that was full of people; now is she become as a widow. Burton had writ In the Day of Adversity, Across the Salt Seas, and The Clash of Arms.

Contents name the cast. Monsieur le Duc leads, then the Montjoie ladies at home. The romance of Monsieur Vandecque and a sister of mercy follow. The duke's desire and the duke's bride turn the tale. Man and wife, the street of the holy apostles, and alone deepen it. The prison of Saint Martin des Champs and the condemned bring the law in. Marseilles and the pest close the shown run.
530-driven-from-home-or-carl-crawford-s-:
Horatio Alger Jr. follows Carl Crawford, a boy of sixteen driven from home with thirty-seven cents, in this success tale. Carl, son of a doctor at Edgewood Center, trudges country roads with a gripsack, a good education, and strong arms. Resting under an oak, he plans how to conquer fortune alone.

Alger tracks Carl through jobs, rivals, and kind strangers, praising pluck and honesty at each turn. The boy's fine handkerchief hints at a better past he will not beg upon. Young readers will find a brisk, hopeful story where a cast-out lad earns his way by work.
53042-a-hitch-in-space:
Fritz Leiber writes a space tale told by a guard on beacon duty, with plates by Gray through the text. Joe Hansen serves with the Shaulan Space Guard out Scorpio way, he opens. His partner Jeff Bogart has grown an imaginary companion on their long rounds together.

The twist lands at once: that phantom companion turns out to be Joe Hansen himself. Joe sees the gain at first, since the phantom Joe can hear Jeff's endless talk while the real one rests. Their ionic jeep checks orbital beacons, relays, and rescue depots round five Shaulan planets on a dull, long job. Jeff's praise of Joe runs so warm and thick that it irks the real man ten times an orbit, Joe grants.
53157-wood-and-stone-a-romance:
John Cowper Powys wrote Wood and Stone, A Romance, issued at New York in 1915 and given to Thomas Hardy with deep praise. Powys calls Hardy the greatest poet and novelist of the age. Twenty nine chapters carry the long tale. Chapter One is named Leo's Hill.

The tale opens midway between Glastonbury and Bridport. A hill shaped like a crouching lion stands where Somerset plains meet Dorset valleys. Heads name Nevilton, Francis Taxater, the pariahs, and Mortimer Romer. Myth, power, art, and nature get chapters of their own. A lake, an orchard, a quarry, and a royal watering place set late scenes. The book is a long, dense romance of place and mind.
53278-lord-lawrence:
Lord Lawrence is a biography by Sir Richard Temple in the English Men of Action series, published by Macmillan in 1889. Its subject is John Lawrence, the Punjab administrator who became Viceroy of India. The contents run from his early life, 1811 to 1829, through the Delhi territory and the trans-Sutlej states to the Punjab board of administration.

Temple, himself an Indian administrator, presents Lawrence as the type of the Englishman hardened for empire abroad. The introduction argues that such men's stamina and courage were nursed at home, under grey skies and mist, in the dales and smoky cities of Britain and Ireland. The chapters that follow take Lawrence from chief commissioner of the Punjab into the war of the mutinies of 1857. The volume is the series' imperial hero at his most characteristic: the Punjab as the school of the men who held India.
53298-taking-the-census-a-farce:
Elizabeth F Guptill wrote Taking the Census, A Farce, held in 1914 and sold at ten cents for home staging. Three folk fill the cast. Mr Cole is the census taker. Mrs Almira Johnson and her young son Alexander fill the other parts. The scene is Mrs Johnson's home.

Mrs Johnson winds yarn while Alexander holds it for her stockings. The boy's arms tire and he begs to rest and play ball. His mother holds him to the task with sharp words and a switch. A loud rap at the door brings the census taker in. The humor rests on home talk in the dialect style of its day. The piece is short and built for one room and few props.
53306-little-prudy-s-captain-horace:
Sophie May wrote this children's book in the Little Prudy series, reissued by Saalfield in 1919. The series list names six books, from 'Little Prudy' itself to 'Little Prudy's Dotty Dimple' at the end. Making candy opens the contents, and camping out and a journey follow.

Grace and Horace Clifford live in Indiana, and so are called Hoosiers by their neighbours. Their home stands a little way out of town, with broad grounds around it. From the front windows the children can see the wide Ohio river. Horace becomes captain of a company, tries to get rich and meets a little Indian in later chapters.
53339-rodmoor-a-romance:
Rodmoor is a romance by John Cowper Powys, published in New York in 1916. The title page carries lines from an old ballad, of riders wading rivers above the knee and hearing the roaring of the sea. The book is dedicated to the spirit of Emily Bronte. Powys had two earlier romances and books of essays in print by then.

The chapter titles sketch a coastal world of houses and tides. They name a borough, a dyke house, sea-drift, vespers, sun and sea, priest and doctor, low tide, and the sisters. Two men are named in later chapters, Hamish Traherne and Brand Renshaw. The Bronte dedication and the sea-haunted chapter list together set the mood: a tale of a shore community, told under the shadow of the author of Wuthering Heights.
5338-mark-rutherford-s-deliverance:
Mark Rutherford's Deliverance, in the 1913 Hodder and Stoughton edition, follows a man's struggle toward intellectual and spiritual freedom. Its chapters run from newspapers and M'Kay, through Miss Leroy and a necessary development, to Drury Lane theology, holidays. The Latin-titled chapters come next, on the way through the sea and the scourge that shall not approach the tabernacle.

Rutherford, the pen name of William Hale White, writes a semi-autobiographical novel of doubt, work, and deliverance from narrow creeds. The book offers readers a quiet, thoughtful portrait of a Victorian mind finding its own faith, in prose that values honesty above display.
53388-answering-the-phone-a-farce: Answering the Phone is a short farce issued by the Tullar-Meredith Company of New York and Chicago, publishers of amateur entertainments. The surviving head of the text is chiefly the firm's own catalogue rather than the play itself. Around the title sit adverts for companion pieces: a Christmas minstrel show, a class play in four acts, a summer vacation comedy, and a boarding-school episode. The catalogue promises short, witty plays needing only a few players, easy to stage for home and school use.
53440-marjorie-dean-s-romance:
Pauline Lester wrote Marjorie Dean's Romance, published by the Burt Company in New York in 1925. The book belongs to the Marjorie Dean Post-Graduate Series, written for girls from twelve to eighteen. Lester had already carried her heroine through high school and college series before this post-graduate set.

The story opens in Brooke Hamilton's study on a pale spring afternoon. Sun breaks through gray clouds and floods the stately room, transfiguring the face of its single occupant. Marjorie Dean raises her brown eyes from a time-stained sheet of paper she has been studying. She greets the sunburst with a fond, friendly smile, and her bright brown curls catch its gold. The scene sets a romance in the genteel world of the series: friendship, family, and love among college-bred young people.
53466-motor-matt-s-mariner-or-filling-th:
Motor Matts Mariner is a weekly motor tale in the Motor Stories line. The Street and Smith house in New York put the five cent issue out. This number is dated September the twenty fifth, nineteen hundred and nine. Its full sub title adds the phrase of filling the bill for Bunce.

A hard jolt in a car throws Matt and his mate Bunce at the start. Heads in the list name a green patch, a home made speeder, and a trap. A steam yacht, a port shot, and a foe win mark the sea turns. Bunce hatches a plan and speaks well for himself in his own part. The tale mixes road speed and boat chase in pulp form for boys.
53482-the-russian-advance: The Russian Advance is one of the Daily Telegraph War Books, a cheap set of short war volumes at one shilling net each. Its shelf mates in the set tell how the war began, the fleets at war, the fight round Liege, and the Red Cross in war. The title names its ground: the Russian push in the Great War then raging. Form and mates are all the head shows, so this note stays at that level.
53934-the-sabbath-and-the-crystal-palace:
The Sabbath and the Crystal Palace is a tract transcribed from a Shaw edition of the 1860s. Its author argues that the question of Sabbath observance has been brought before the public again, and points thought settled beyond doubt are disputed. A change of circumstances, it is said, requires a change of views, and the present character of society is pled to justify revising the old principles.

The attack, the tract grants, comes this time from professed friends, not open enemies. Much formerly contended is now conceded: the divine institution of a day of rest is admitted, and its beneficent character owned. The only dispute is the form those influences should take, above all whether the Crystal Palace may open on the day. The tract holds the old line: the ordinance is the security of national religion.
53990-the-story-of-paul-jones-an-histori:
The Story of Paul Jones is a historical romance by Alfred Henry Lewis, published in nineteen hundred six. Illustrations by two artists appear in the book, as the title page states. Paul Jones was the Scots born sailor who became a hero of the American navy. Chapter one is called His Baptism of the Sea.

The tale opens in July seventeen fifty nine with a new brig in her home harbour of Whitehaven. Sail makers are fitting her first suit of sails as her owner comes aboard. Young Jones's sea start is thus staged in a working port scene. Romance and record mix as Lewis follows Jones from apprentice sailor to famed and feared sea captain.
54208-standard-measures-of-united-states:
Arthur Wurtele, a railroad engineer, compared the standard measures of three nations in this book. Spon printed Standard Measures at New York and London in 1882. An appendix on bringing in the metre closes the plan.

Wurtele read wide for the work, as his first pages own. Kelly's Universal Cambist, Maunder's Weights and Measures, both great encyclopaedias, and the Coast Survey reports stand in his list. The one clear sum he found was Hilgard's 1876 report to the Coast Survey, which matched his own findings. A standard of length looks simple, he says: a bar of metal of a set length. What rests on that bar — trade, science, and law — fills his book.
54265-luck-and-pluck-or-john-oakley-s-in:
Luck and Pluck, or John Oakley's Inheritance is a boys' novel by Horatio Alger the younger, first of his Luck and Pluck series. The publisher's lists at the front display Alger's empire of print. The Ragged Dick series runs to six volumes at a dollar and a quarter each. The Campaign series stands complete in three.

Ragged Dick himself heads the catalogue, with Fame and Fortune and Mark the Match Boy behind him. Ben the Luggage Boy and Rufus and Rose were announced for 1870. The Luck and Pluck series was to run to six volumes at a dollar and a half. John Oakley's inheritance gives this opener its engine: a poor boy, a legacy, and the pluck to deserve it. Alger's formula of honesty rewarded made him the best loved boys' author in America.
54346-queens-of-the-renaissance:
M Beresford Ryley wrote Queens of the Renaissance, first published in 1907 with twenty-four illustrations. A frontispiece shows Beatrice d'Este and Ludovico kneeling, from an altarpiece. Six lives fill the book. Catherine of Siena opens it.

Beatrice d'Este, Anne of Brittany, and Lucrezia Borgia follow. Margaret d'Angoulême and Renée, Duchess of Ferrara, close the set. Portraits and places are pictured throughout, from St Catherine's house at Siena to a bust of Beatrice in the Louvre. Readers get the women of the Italian and French Renaissance told as biography for general readers, courts, convents, and marriages of state included.
54547-young-stowaways-in-space:
Young Stowaways in Space, by Richard Elam, was copyrighted by Lantern Press in 1960, with illustrations by Gerald McCann. Elam also wrote Young Readers Science Fiction Stories. Chapter one is set aboard the space ship Orion, but it opens at night in an orphanage dormitory.

Twenty cots fill the room, and one stands empty. Garry Coleman dresses quietly beside his cot, anxious not to disturb the man in charge of quarters. His friend Patch, short and towheaded in the next bunk, wakes and demands to know where he is going. To the spaceport, Garry says, to watch the Orion blast off for the Von Braun Space Station, and Patch insists on coming too. Nineteen chapters promise stowaways in space, a crew adrift in the deeps, an order to abandon ship, and first hours on Luna.
54699-the-last-of-the-de-mullins-a-play-:
The Last of the De Mullins is a play by St. John Hankin, printed at London in 1909 and named a play without a preface. The cast lists Hugo De Mullin, his wife Jane, his sister, and his daughters Janet and Hester, with a local doctor, a curate, and a maid. The De Mullins live at the Manor House in Brendon Underwood, a village in Dorset.

Acts one and three play in the inner hall, with its stone window, great fireplace, and long line of family portraits. Act two moves to the edge of Brendon Forest, days later. The play opens at noon on a fine September day as Hester comes in with the curate, Brown, a stout man in seedy clerical dress.
547-baron-trigault-s-vengeance:
Émile Gaboriau continues the tale of Pascal Ferailleur in this sequel to The Count's Millions. Ruined by slander and a vile plot, Pascal hides under a false name, torn between despair and a hunger for vengeance. Baron Trigault, a schemer of wealth and wit, offers him a path to strike back at his foes.

Gaboriau writes with melodramatic sweep, from Paris salons to hidden lodgings. Love for Marguerite, lost by a fatal letter, drives Pascal's grief. The novel charms fans of French sensation fiction, where honor, fortune, and revenge tangle in a web of plots.
54827-leonardo-da-vinci-pathfinder-of-sc:
Henry S Gillette wrote a life of Leonardo da Vinci for young readers, issued in the Immortals of Science series. Gillette says plainly that he cares most about Leonardo the man of science. He also warns that some gaps in the life have been filled with his own guesswork. Chapters move from Florence and a studio of his own through Milan, Cesare Borgia, and late hopes that fell apart.

Readers get a painter who also studied flight, water, the body, and machines. The book treats his notes as the work of a man far ahead of his age. It suits readers who want a short, warm life story that keeps the science at its center.
55040-the-nursery-alice:
Lewis Carroll made a small Alice for the very young, and Macmillan published it in 1889 at two shillings. Twenty coloured enlargements of Tenniel's drawings fill the book. The text is Carroll's own, cut and shaped for nursery readers.

The preface is addressed to any mother. His ambition now is to be read by children from nought to five. Not read, he corrects himself: thumbed, cooed over, dog's eared, rumpled, and kissed. The chapters keep the famous order. The white rabbit leads, then the pool of tears and the caucus race. The pig baby, the Cheshire cat, and the mad tea party follow. Who stole the tarts closes the small book.
55078-the-birthplace:
Henry James wrote this tale of a couple offered a post at a birthplace shrine. The tale is dated 1922 in the heading of this printing. Grant-Jackson, a pushing friend, sounds out the Gedges by letter. The offer seems too good to be true to them at first.

The post fell vacant when one of two keeper ladies died there. Her daughter stayed on alone but now plans to wed and leave. A united couple is wanted, sisters or a married pair alike. Hopeful candidates already besiege all who hold a voice in choice.
55154-the-twins-and-how-they-entertained:
Elizabeth Guptill's The Twins and How They Entertained the New Minister is a short farce printed by the Tullar-Meredith Company in 1914, price ten cents, with amateur performance permitted. The cast is three: Bobby and Betty, the twins, and Jones, the new minister. One room, a reception room, holds the whole play.

Betty opens it, seating the minister with a grown-up air. Not the show chair, whose leg is broken and not yet fixed; the Morris chair, where sister's beaux always sit. Bobby storms in: it was his turn to answer the doorbell, and Betty camps in the hall to beat him to every caller. She leaves him to explain the Caller's game, her own invention, played on Thursday, the maid Christine's day out, when Mamma dislikes answering the bell herself.
55230-the-day-after-death-or-our-future-:
Louis Figuier, a French writer, set out his view of life after death and called it science. A new English edition came out in London and New York in 1904 with ten astronomical plates. Figuier says man is a triple alliance of body, soul, and life. Death, for him, is the breaking of that alliance.

Chapters ask where the soul goes, if all men rise to a higher state, and how the reborn being lives. Perverse souls and dead infants are reborn, he claims, while good souls dwell in ethereal space. Later parts place beings in the sun itself. The book mixes faith, space lore, and hope into a curious system of the next world.
55278-chess-generalship-vol-i-grand-reco:
Chess Generalship, Volume One, subtitled Grand Reconnaissance, is a chess treatise by Franklin Young, printed at Boston by the International Publishing Company in 1910. Young's whole system rests on one idea, stated in his epigraphs. He who first devised chess play made a model of the military art, representing all the workings of war. Emanuel Lasker is quoted to the same effect: chess is constructed to carry out the principle of a battle, and its whole theory lies in that form of action.

One Chicago paper ranked his system beside the masterpieces of Newton, Hamilton and Darwin. Young was an American chess writer who treated the board as a battlefield in earnest. Grand Reconnaissance opens his campaign: before tactics, the player must survey the whole position as a general surveys ground. The volume is the first step of a military science of chess.
55327-over-the-border-a-romance:
Robert Barr wrote Over the Border, a romance published by Frederick A Stokes at New York in 1903. Barr dedicated the book to his publisher, with whom his literary life had been pleasantly joined since he began to write. The first book is named The Girl. Its first chapter opens at Hampton Court, in the Home Park. The end of October has been fine, and the turf stands green and firm.

Down a forest aisle walks a distinguished party at a painful pace. The pace is set by a tall, thin, disease-stricken man, bent before his time. His piercing eye stays untamed by deadly malady. He is Thomas Wentworth, Earl of Strafford. Behind locked doors his enemies are already planning his ruin. Strafford, they know, will strike first and hard if a whisper reaches him.
55420-for-the-defence:
Fergus Hume, author of The Mystery of a Hansom Cab, wrote this crime novel, copyrighted in 1897. Its scene is Hurstleigh in Surrey, at a house called Ashantee. Retired Major Laurence Jen bought the place after his one campaign in West Africa.

Jen lives there with two boys he took in, Maurice Alymer and David Sarby. The chapter list promises a devil-stick, a cry in the night, cross-examination, and a trial. Hume builds the case piece by piece, with Major Jen himself turning detective. A final surprise closes the tale. Hume was a master of the late Victorian mystery, and the court scenes here show his craft.
55427-a-tour-through-old-provence:
A Tour Through Old Provence is a roam book by Forrest with his own drawn cuts. One hundred eight cuts in tone and line dress the book through. A London house of Stanley Paul brought the work out in its day. Avignon, town of the popes, opens the tour from the Rhone stream. Its walls, bell spires, and great papal hall draw praise from all who near.

Fields and vine lands of rich hue ring that stern guard town. Alps east and Cevennes west frame the wide Rhone vale in the view. Gauls, Greeks, and Romans left their marks on that vale in turn. Parts run through Villeneuve, Tarascon, and the rock town of Les Baux. Montmajour, Arles, Nimes, and Orange close the eight part scheme.
55798-false-evidence:
Phillips Oppenheim wrote False Evidence, a novel from Ward, Lock at London in 1911. The book was written some years before and here takes library form for the first time. A front plate shows men starting back from the muzzle of a father's revolver. Contents open with a prologue and a part called My Apology. The first cloud, a mysterious meeting, and a headland scene set the plot.

Devereux Court, Colonel Devereux, and his land agent take the middle stage. A fight for life, a convalescence, a moonlight ride, and a midnight visitor raise the pace. Marian surprises the hero, and Rupert Devereux faces him at last. Brigands in Palermo, a villa party, and a horrible mistake fill the late parts. Oppenheim gives a brisk tale of honor, lies, and a stain to clear.
55847-known-to-the-police:
Thomas Holmes wrote Known to the Police, issued at London in 1908 by Edward Arnold. Holmes was secretary to the Howard Association. He had writ Pictures and Problems from London Police Courts. The book is given to his wife with warm thanks for a shared life of joys and sorrows.

Fourteen chapters draw on twenty one years in London police courts. Burglars he has met and the black list of drunkards open the set. Police court marriages and odd sentences follow. Freed prisoners and the last dread penalty get chapters. Housing the poor and the rowdy acts of the poor fill the middle. Heroism in the slums and folk who have come down close the book. Holmes writes from close daily work with the poor.
56077-love-insurance:
Earl Derr Biggers wrote a novel printed at Indianapolis in 1914. Biggers had written Seven Keys to Baldpate. A sporting proposition opens the contents, then an evening in the river and journeys end in taxi bills. Mister Trimmer limbers up and Mister Trimmer throws his bomb follow. Ten minutes of agony and chain lightning's collar fill the early road.

Outside a gilt lettered door on the seventeenth floor of a New York office building, a tall young man in a fur lined coat stood shivering, the tale begins. Why did he shiver in that coat? He shivered because he was fussed, poor chap, rattled from the soles of his custom made boots to the apex of his Piccadilly hat. After the trained seals, wanted board and room, two birds of passage, and tears from the Gaiety lead on. A love policy, a lord, and a wager drive Biggers's bright farce.
56177-the-island-of-fantasy-a-romance:
The Island of Fantasy, a romance by Fergus Hume, author of The Mystery of a Hansom Cab, was printed by Fenno in New York in 1905, from a copyright of 1892. A motto promises the cure for sorrow and weariness at the fountain of the vale. Chapter one is titled A Mind Diseased, and its verses call on drugs and perfumes in vain to soothe a darkened brain.

The scene is the dining room of Roylands Grange at eight on a still summer evening, the ladies retired. Two men linger over their wine, but only the elder attends to his port. The young man at the head of the table stares at his empty glass and his empty plate, his thoughts miles away. Youth is moody and age cheerful: Rector Carriston cracks nuts and sips with appreciation, while woe is writ large on the face of Maurice Roylands.
56442-romantic-cities-of-provence:
Mona Caird travels in Romantic Cities of Provence, issued by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York and T Fisher Unwin in London. Sketches by Joseph Pennell and Edward M Synge illustrate the road, and a plate of the cloisters of St Trophime at Arles fronts the book. A first chapter casts the spell of Provence.

The chapters proceed through Avignon, Petrarch and Laura, the cities of the lagoons, and the birth of chivalry. Arles, Tarascon, the Pont du Gard, Carcassonne and the Albigenses, Les Baux, and the Camargue follow. The Song of the Rhone closes the journey. Lyrical travel fills it.
56480-hymns-in-human-experience:
Hymns in Human Experience is William J Hart's study of what hymns do in people's lives, published by Harper and Brothers of New York and London in 1931. A portrait of Ira D Sankey fronts the book. Hart opens with Frank L Stanton's verses on the good old hymns.

His first chapter argues that Christianity came to the world on the wings of song, and that a hymn is much more than poetry: it belongs with the things of the spirit. The chapters then follow hymns through experience: songs in the night, hymns mothers loved, and preachers who sing. Soldiers' songs, hymns heard within prison walls, and the music of submerged lives come next. One chapter is given to The Old Rugged Cross alone. Negro songs, Christmas and Easter melodies, funeral music, and patriotic occasions complete the survey, with an index of hymns.
56485-hyde-park-its-history-and-romance:
Hyde Park: Its History and Romance is a book on London's great park by Mrs Alec Tweedie. A frontispiece shows the Four-in-Hand Club driving in the park. The contents run from the park's first charter to its trees. One chapter lists the trees, shrubs, and plants of the park in an appendix. The plates mix old prints and portraits. Tyburn, where men were hanged, stood at the park's edge. Its grim past gets its share of the tale.

King Edgar's charter to Dunstan is shown in a map of Westminster. Henry the Eighth, who took the park for his hunting, has his portrait in the list. A cheesecake house, wells for drinking and bathing, and a prostitute drummed out of the park all appear. The book joins the park's royal past to its gay social present. It is a ramble through five hundred years of one green space.
56530-literary-landmarks-of-venice:
Literary Landmarks of Venice, by Laurence Hutton, was published in New York in 1896. Harper and Brothers issued the book, with many pictures. Hutton had written like guides to London, Edinburgh, and Jerusalem. He gives this one to William Dean Howells, whose Venetian life had gladdened his own. A picture list maps the tour. The Othello house and the council chamber of the doges come first. Petrarch and Laura, Byron's palace, and the Rialto as Shylock knew it follow. The house where Browning died closes the list.

Hutton opens with a rueful joke: Venice can be compared only with itself. Ruskin called it a golden city paved with emerald. Yet the living Venetians, Hutton charges, have lost their grip on beauty. Hotel wallpapers offend him. The old art, he says, stays superb.
56795-the-story-book-of-science:
Jean-Henri Fabre wrote The Story-Book of Science, a book for the young put into English by Florence Constable Bicknell. The form here came from the French form at count nine and ten, in New York in 1917. Fabre had won a name with a book on the life of bugs in groups. A first part, named The Six, opens the talks.

Talks bear names like The Fairy Tale and the True Story, side by side. The build of a town, cows, and a sheep fold give a farm start. An old pear tree, the age of trees, and the span of beast life turn to the woods. A pot, the metals, and the craft of plate work turn to the shop. Flax, hemp, cloth stuff, and paper trace the stuff of dress and books. Silk, the change of the worm, and spiders fill the last span of the list.
56849-camp-fire-girls-in-war-and-peace:
Isabel Hornibrook wrote Camp Fire Girls in War and Peace, published in Boston by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard in August 1919. John Goss drew the pictures. Hornibrook had already written Girls of the Morning-Glory Camp Fire and Camp Fire Girls and Mount Greylock, named at the front.

The contents mix camp life with the war just ended. Chapters carry titles like Gas Valley, The Minute-Girl, and Camouflage. The girls play submarine, meet aviators unawares, and honor knights of the wing. A wandering powder puff and a camp at twilight keep the lighter side in view. Later headings promise a launching and a search for the spark. The front picture shows a young man named Fenn bowing over the Guardian's hand. Girls who had lived through the war years got their own troop at work and play, in the shadow of real events.
56861-gambolling-with-galatea-a-bucolic-:
Curtis Dunham wrote Gambolling with Galatea, a bucolic romance printed at Boston in 1909. Oliver Herford drew the pictures. Dunham had written The Casino Girl in London and Two in a Zoo.

A mock grave preface warns readers not to laugh: light minds, Dunham says, would doubt the talk of Balaam and his ass and scoff at the gratitude of Aesop's lion. Six parts follow the farm animals: the initiation of the two-legged partners, fair warning to the horseless, and Pig-malion and Galatea. The obsequies of Bos Nemo, a horse detective, and Taurus Cupid fill the rest. The humour is dry and deadpan throughout.
56929-pictures-of-hellas-five-tales-of-a:
Pictures of Hellas: Five Tales of Ancient Greece, by Peder Mariager, was translated from the Danish by Mary Safford and published in New York in 1888. Safford says the author preface is so full that she has nothing to add, except thanks for help in the obscure recesses of Greek literature.

Mariager notes that most recent romances and dramas of classic times depict the great rupture between paganism and Christianity. Hypatia, Fabiola, and The Last Days of Pompeii are named as cases. The cause, he says, is plain: a period of strong contrasts invites fine treatment. His tales take their material from a different, no less interesting epoch. They give pictures of the flowering of Hellas, in its distant centuries of strength. Readers get Greek tales set in the pagan prime, not in its fall.
56975-thoth-a-romance:
Thoth, a romance issued without its author's name, reached a third edition at Edinburgh in 1889. Press notices pasted in front praise its strangeness. The Saturday Review said its glory is that the reader never knows what will happen next.

In a preface the author protests that the tale was not copied from She, having been planned more than twelve years before. The first plan, we are told, was philosophical. Reviewers dwelt on the veiled, awful picture of the women, mothers of the ruling race in a wonderful city. Mystery and high fancy drive the tale.
57009-history-of-lace:
History of Lace is a reference work by Mrs. Bury Palliser, entirely revised, rewritten, and enlarged under the editorship of Jourdain and Alice Dryden. Scribner published it in New York in 1902, with 266 illustrations. Its frontispiece shows a lady of about 1614 in Flemish lace, from a family portrait.

The contents begin with needlework, then cut-work, then lace itself. Italy follows: Venice, and Milan the great. Chapter by chapter the book follows the lace-making towns and schools of Europe, their patterns, stitches, and trade. Lace was once a fortune worn on a collar, and its history joins art, women's work, and commerce. Palliser's history, renewed by new editors for a new century, remained the standard account in English of how thread became treasure.
57037-the-prince:
Niccolo Machiavelli's The Prince, in Luigi Ricci's English translation, was published in 1909 by Humphrey Milford for the Oxford University Press, in London, New York, Bombay, and a dozen other cities. The work is addressed to Lorenzo the Magnificent, son of Piero di Medici, and the dedication letter stands before the chapters.

Gifts, Machiavelli writes there, are how men seek a prince's favour, offering what they hold most precious. The chapters then sort the kinds of government: hereditary and mixed monarchies, new dominions won by one's own arms, by fortune, or by villainy, the civic principality, and church states. Soldiers take the middle chapters, mercenary, auxiliary, and native. Liberality and stinginess, cruelty and clemency, and whether a prince is better loved or feared follow, closing with fortune and an exhortation to free Italy from the barbarians.
57132-caesar-borgia-a-study-of-the-renai:
John Leslie Garner wrote Caesar Borgia, a study of Renaissance Italy. T Fisher Unwin issued the book in London in nineteen hundred twelve. Seventeen plates dress the life of the Pope’s feared son. Garner reads the man through the hard school of his age.

Alexander, Julius Caesar, and Napoleon open his test of self love. Each won by fraud and force, and each lost his gains, he notes. Machiavelli praised Borgia for grasping feudal wealth’s true law. Spoil, squeeze, and crime held that old form up, Loria argues. No Washington, no free land still freed: such is Garner’s creed. The man is his age’s child, shaped by its soil and stress. Set him in ripe times and the same mold yields a genius. Borgia best read his hour and fought as its dark champion.
57243-thinking-as-a-science:
Henry Hazlitt wrote Thinking as a Science, issued in New York by E P Dutton and Company with copyright in nineteen sixteen. Eleven chapters fill the book. Chapter one is The Neglect of Thinking. Every man knows there are evils in the world which need setting right, Hazlitt opens. Every man has pretty definite ideas as to what these evils are, he adds. But to most men one evil in particular stands out vividly, he notes.

To the Socialist this evil is the capitalistic system, to the prohibitionist intemperance, to the feminist the subjection of women, he lists. To the clergyman it is the decline of religion, and to Andrew Carnegie it is war, he adds. Hazlitt own pet evil is the neglect of thinking itself. Later chapters treat thinking with method, concentration, prejudice and uncertainty, and debate. Self improvers get a clear, famed handbook on clear thought.
5726-the-fairy-land-of-science:
Arabella Buckley invites young readers into science through a series of lectures called The Fairy Land of Science. Lectures begin with how to enter, use, and enjoy this fairy land. They then turn to sunbeams and their work. Later lectures treat the aerial ocean in which we live, a drop of water on its travels, and water and ice as two great sculptors. Voices of nature and further wonders follow.

Buckley treats science as a story to be watched, not a list to be memorized, using fairy language to make physics and natural history vivid. Readers learn how sunlight, air, and water shape the world, through images a child can picture. The book suits families, teachers, and young readers who enjoy Victorian science writing that still feels fresh in its wonder.
57314-the-yellow-face:
Fred White wrote a mystery printed at New York and London in 1907. White had written The Crimson Blind, The Corner House, and The Midnight Guest. Nostalgo opens the chapters, then the Chopin nocturne and the mystery of the strings. The speaking likeness and a vanished clue follow. The flickering firelight fell upon the girl's pretty, thoughtful face, the tale begins.

Her violet eyes looked like deep lakes in it. She stood with one small foot tapping the polished brass rail of the fender. Claire Helmsley was accounted fair, the opening runs. Vanished, Number Four Montrose Place, and the Chopin fantasie fill the road. The man with the fair moustache, what did she know, and the shadow on the wall raise the stakes. Lady Barmouth, the bosom of her family, and a broken melody lead toward the mouse in the trap. White's sleek tales filled railway bookstalls for decades.
57347-a-motor-flight-through-france:
Edith Wharton records early motoring in A Motor-Flight Through France, published at New York by Charles Scribner's Sons in October 1908. Three parts carry the car from Boulogne to Amiens, Beauvais and Rouen, down the Loire and the Indre to Nohant and Clermont, and on through Auvergne to Bourges. A second flight runs from Paris to Poitiers, the Pyrenees and Provence.

Photographs face nearly every chapter, from Amiens Cathedral and the chateau of George Sand at Nohant to Carcassonne and Mont St Michel. A final flight to the north-east closes the tour, with cathedrals as its steady landmarks.
57408-captain-lucy-in-france:
Aline Havard wrote a girls' war novel in 1919, a sequel about Captain Lucy and Lieutenant Bob. It opens with Janet Leslie resting on shady grass after hard work. The summons takes the cast to the allied front in France. Chapters promise a glimpse of Bob, the fortune of war, and an English prisoner.

A German ally, a little French heroine, and a fight over Argenton follow. The plan of the defenses and a chance in a thousand raise the stakes. Later chapters cross the lines, and the final one is titled The Yanks Are Coming. Pictures by Ralph P Coleman show guns sounding close and a meadow landing place.
57441-the-underground-world-a-mirror-of-:
The Underground World, a mirror of life below the surface, by Thomas W Knox, was printed at Hartford by the J B Burr Publishing Company in 1877. Knox wrote Overland through Asia and Camp Fire and Cotton Field. Many plates fill the book.

The title promises vivid descriptions of the hidden works of nature and art. It takes in mines and mining in all parts of the world, caves and their mysteries, and famous tunnels. Down in the depths of the sea, volcanoes and their eruptions, and petroleum stand in the plan. The underground life of man and the lower animals, the works of the ancients, and buried treasures close the scope. Knox aims at a plain, entertaining account of all who delve and dare underground. Wonder fans get a fat Victorian marvel book.
57670-scenes-in-the-west-or-the-sunday-s:
Scenes in the West, or The Sunday-School and Temperance, was printed at Philadelphia in 1873. The Lutheran Board of Publication issued the book. Its author signs only as a missionary. The preface says the tales rest on real life incidents. They show, he writes, the power of godliness in a person. The blessings of the Sunday-school, the prayer-meeting, and the temperance cause fill the plan. Eighteen chapters make the volume. The missionary leads, then misfortunes and relief. A Sunday-school is organized by chapter ten.

The temperance cause takes chapter twelve by name. Families named Steele, Mason, Kerr, and Brown pass through the scenes. Chapter one opens in Indian summer, bees storing for winter and birds heading south. Death closes the set. The book is frontier church work told as improving story.
57857-antar-a-bedoueen-romance:
Terrick Hamilton, Oriental Secretary to the British Embassy at Constantinople, translated this Arabian romance from the Arabic. John Murray published it at London in 1819, the first attempt, the editor says, to transpose an Arabian story into a European language. Antar was no invention. He was the son of an Arab prince of the tribe of Abs by a black captive woman, born a slave in the sixth century. By heroism and by genius for poetry he rose to the confidence of his king.

Antar is the poet of one of the seven poems suspended in the temple at Mecca, the Moallakat. The romance was put together from traditional tales by a scholar of the court of Haroun-al-Raschid. Story-tellers in the coffee-houses of Egypt, Syria, and Arabia still draw their tales from it. The introduction promises the Bedouin as he was: hospitable, warlike, and free.
57944-burgo-s-romance:
Burgo's Romance, by Speight, author of Back to Life and Hoodwinked, was published at Philadelphia in 1894 by Lippincott in an authorized edition. Twenty-two chapters run from A Young Man About Town through Cut Adrift, A Clue, In Durance Vile, and Dacia Explains, to A Mystery Solved. Burgo and Dacia Roylance carry the plot.

Chapter one opens in the conservatory at the back of a London house. A dark handsome face bends close to a fair and glowing one. A trembling white hand is clasped in a sinewy brown one. Black eyes flame with love; blue eyes drop in sweet confusion under long brown lashes. Shaded lamps glow through ferns and tropical flowers. Speight sets a sensation romance of love, loss, and a mystery patiently unraveled.
57985-letters-to-persons-who-are-engaged:
Letters to Persons Who Are Engaged in Domestic Service is a book of counsel by Catherine Beecher. Leavitt and Trow published it at New York in 1842 from Broadway. The letters are addressed to the servants of American households in that young republic. Beecher would become the leading American writer on the household in her generation.

Her letters treat service as a calling to be raised, not a place to be scorned, in its argument. She writes on the duties, the wages, the manners, and the self respect of the domestic in her pages. The book belongs to the moment when American housekeeping was passing from family labour to hired help in the cities.
