Together her works built the doctrine of scientific housekeeping in America, and this early volume shows its moral foundation: service dignified by skill, honesty, and a clear contract between the parties.
58039-the-foundling-or-the-child-of-prov:
A foundling tells his own life in this two part account of 1823. The Foundling, or the Child of Providence, was printed for the author. Copies sold at the Surrey Tabernacle in London that year. A verse from Deuteronomy stands as the motto on the title.

An opening dialogue sets an Investigator questioning a man called Friendly. Friendly owns weak nerves yet a mind wonderfully upheld by grace. Conflicts of body and mind exercise him beneath the sun daily. He tells how the plague breaks out and is healed again. Weston printed the sheets at Crosby Row in the Borough for the Surrey Tabernacle sale.
58201-the-westminster-alice:
Hector H Munro, called Saki, wrote The Westminster Alice. The Westminster Gazette issued it at London in 1902. F Carruthers Gould drew its pictures. The book begs pardon of Sir John Tenniel up front. Macmillan's leave let them borrow Alice, it says. Carroll's girl walks into politics here.

Alice in Downing Street opens the fun. Alice in Pall Mall and Alice at Lambeth follow. Alice and the Liberal Party fills a chapter. Alice at Saint Stephen's takes her to Parliament. Tea at the Hotel Cecil and a fog come later. The Aged Man and Spades in Wonderland close it. Verse at the start calls her a dreaming child. Figures flit turvey-wise through her dream there. Topical satire in nonsense dress let Saki prick the great with a child's plain questions.
5825-the-courage-of-the-commonplace:
Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews explores everyday courage in The Courage of the Commonplace, opening at Durfee with a girl and her chaperon in a desirable second-story window looking down on a tree. Brant, a senior and a Bones man, holds a leading place in college life, and the story that follows tests what courage means outside battlefields and grand crises. Ordinary choices, loyalties, and losses carry the weight.

You get a quiet, earnest tale of young people learning to face disappointment, duty, and love without applause. Andrews writes with warmth and moral clarity, favoring character over sensation. The book suits readers who enjoy early twentieth-century stories of college and home life, and anyone who believes the hardest bravery is often the least noticed.
58305-miss-nume-of-japan-a-japanese-amer:
Onoto Watanna wrote this Japanese-American romance, printed at Chicago and New York under copyright in 1899. An introduction praises her quaint, free style, sweet as a bird's chirrup and wild as a hawk's scream. She wrote, it says, for the imaginative, and not for the wise whose judgement would freeze her warm current.

The chapters run from parental ambitions through Cleo, a dance on deck, and a study of the coquette. Jealousy without love, the man she did love, and merely a woman mark the turns of the tale. Watanna, who wrote of Japan for American readers, builds a light romance across two worlds, full of mood and impulse rather than plot machinery.
58567-plutarch-on-the-delay-of-the-divin:
Plutarch on the Delay of the Divine Justice is Andrew Peabody's English translation of a Plutarch dialogue, published in Boston by Little, Brown in 1885. Peabody supplied an introduction and notes. The hosted edition adds a synopsis of the argument.

The dialogue takes up an old complaint against Providence. The guilty seem encouraged because punishment comes late, while their victims lose heart at the delay. The late-arriving punishment, the objectors say, is not even recognized as punishment when it comes. Plutarch answers these objections in turn. The synopsis maps the discussion section by section, and an index follows the text. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
58635-cavalry-a-popular-edition-of-caval:
Cavalry, by General von Bernhardi, was published at New York in 1914. Doran issued this popular edition that year. Its full form is Cavalry in War and Peace. Bernhardi had written How Germany Makes War before. Field-Marshal Sir John French adds a preface. Atteridge edited the edition from Bridges's translation. Bridges served in the 4th Royal Irish Dragoon Guards. His note urges young officers to learn French and German. Foreign military writing, he says, is rarely Englished in time. Contents open on how war use shapes training. Reconnaissance fills the first great part. Army cavalry, patrols, and the screen are set out in order.

Raids close that part; the action of cavalry fills the next. Attack, defence, and fights against every arm are treated. The battle of encounter gets its own long section.
58730-miracle-by-price:
Irving Cox wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Worlds of If in October 1954. Its head note says old Doctor Price was called an inventive genius but no miracle worker, and asks what he was doing for a small fellow named Cupid. The tale opens as a memo between lawyers' men.

Walter Gordon reports on the late doctor's laboratory, a place of senile clutter, he says, fit for a psychiatrist rather than a physicist. Among a score of unfinished gadgets, two stand complete. One is a small box with two knobs and a speaker grid, which hums when turned. Price's card names it a Semantic-Translator, and prices it to wholesale for about three-fifty per unit.
58735-peace:
Peace is a science fiction story by Norman Arkawy and Stanley Henig. It appeared in Worlds of If magazine in October 1954. The story opens with a welcome addressed to Earthmen. Alien voices bid them take a rightful place in peace. By endless struggles, the voices say, they have earned it. The tale then turns to documents from a future war. A peace communique dated April 2049 leads those documents.

The communique declares the war over between Rios and Nwad. The aggressor leader Iverson is safely exiled on an asteroid. Other leaders are confined on their respective space islands. Peace is restored on both planets of the system. A report to the people of Rios follows the communique. It explains the war, its causes, and the victors' proposed policy. The story is told through official papers and their tones.
58792-anatole-france:
George wrote this monograph on Anatole France for the Writers of the Day series, edited by Bertram Christian. Henry Holt and Company published it in New York, first issued in 1915. A portrait of France stands at the front, and George's own novels are listed on the series page.

Five chapters divide the man. After an introduction, George treats France as satirist and critic, then as philosopher and theologian. Historian and politician follows, and the craftsman and the man closes the study. Bibliographies of the French titles and their English and American forms end the book. In the introduction George tells how he set himself to read every one of France's works while a European war raged around him. The subject, the great pacifist and ironist, would have smiled at the sentence, he thinks. English readers got the master of French prose weighed in wartime.
58807-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Ambrose Bierce is a finding list compiled by David Widger. It gathers, in one place, the titles of Bierce's books held in that free library. Fantastic Fables and a famous war tale of Owl Creek stand near the head. The Devil's Dictionary, the Parenticide Club, and The Fiend's Delight follow in the list.

A son of the gods paired with a horseman in the sky, a style manual, and cobwebs from an empty skull come next. The collected works in volumes, the letters, and poetry sets close the roll. Tables of contents for the single volumes are then printed in full. The dictionary's contents run simply from A to Z. The Parenticide Club shows its four grim tales by name. Widger's index serves readers hunting one Bierce piece among many.
58877-washington-and-the-riddle-of-peace:
Washington and the Riddle of Peace is a set of pieces on a great meet. Wells wrote them as the meet sat in the chief town in 1921. The meet was called to curb the arms of the great sea powers. The pieces first stood in the press of two lands that year.

Wells calls the stakes vast and the men at the meet small. Curbs on arms that stop at counts alone are vain, he holds. The peace made at Versailles left two great powers out in the cold. The tomb of the lone dead man and the chief's trip there are weighed. Japan, its past and its fate, takes a run of three parts. France in the glare and the catch word of the hour come next. The book ends on the tie of lands and the risk of a fall of all.
58947-doctor-dolittle-s-post-office:
Hugh Lofting wrote and illustrated Doctor Dolittle's Post Office, published by Stokes at New York in 1923. A prologue and four parts structure the tale. On the voyage home from West Africa the Doctor sets up the Royal Mails of Fantippo and the animals' paradise of No-Man's-Land, with the swiftest mail in the world carried by birds. Part two shows the most unusual post office, Cheapside the London sparrow, and the birds that helped Columbus.

Part three is storytelling: the animals' magazine, with tales by Gub-Gub, Dab-Dab, Jip, Too-Too, the white mouse, and the pushmi-pullyu. Part four brings parcel post, the great mail robbery, pearl divers, Obombo's rebellion, and the Doctor's release. Lofting's own drawings fill the illustration list, from the houseboat post office to the double letter boxes of Fantippo. The book is the third Dolittle volume.
59000-memoirs-of-an-american-lady-with-s:
Memoirs of an American Lady, with sketches of manners and scenery in America as they existed previous to the Revolution, is by the author of Letters from the Mountains. This edition was published in New York in 1836. A notice celebrates the authoress, Mrs Grant of Laggan.

Among the scenes an American traveller is bound to visit abroad, the notice says, is her Edinburgh abode. In acknowledgment of what all owe to her, the present work, being out of print, is republished. It identifies Mrs Grant with America, warmly. The memoirs themselves look back to colonial Albany and the old Dutch and English society of New York before the war. Her memories of Schuyler hospitality and frontier manners became a classic source. Readers get a Scottish woman recollections of pre Revolutionary America, treasured on both sides of the Atlantic.
59104-the-dance:
A reference volume fills this item: The Dance, volume ten of The Art of Music, copyrighted at New York in 1916. The set is a library of information for music lovers and musicians, in fourteen volumes. Mason of Columbia is editor-in-chief of the set, and the dance volume has its own department editor, Narodny, named on its title page as a ballerina of the Imperial Russian Ballet.

Contents promise a world tour of the art. A first chapter treats the mind of dancing: its beauty, national character in dances, religion and the dance, and the history of folk-dancing and ballet. Chapters follow on dancing in ancient Egypt, with temple rites and the festival of the Sacred Bull. Dancing in India and its sacred dancers come next. The dances of the Chinese, the Japanese, and the American Indians close the tour.
59228-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled this index of the Project Gutenberg works of Anatole France, listing each work with its table of contents. The shelf is long: Penguin Island, Thaïs, The Crime of Sylvestre Bonnard, The Red Lily, and The Aspirations of Jean Servien stand near the head of the contents list.

Other works include the life of Joan of Arc in two volumes, The Gods Are Athirst, Honey-Bee, The Revolt of the Angels, and The White Stone. Penguin Island's own contents open with the life of Saint Mael and the baptism of the penguins. Readers get a finding list for a Nobel laureate's fiction in English, useful for choosing where to begin.
59460-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger gathers the tables of contents of D H Lawrence books held by Project Gutenberg into one index file. Sons and Lovers leads the list, followed by Touch and Go and Women in Love. Each entry gives chapter heads in full so readers can find a part fast.

Contents for Sons and Lovers trace the Morels from early married life to Paul's launch into work and love. Women in Love heads run from Sisters and Shortlands to Breadalby and Coal-dust in the part shown. Plays, poems, and travel books fill the rest of the list, among them Tortoises, Sea and Sardinia, and Twilight in Italy. The file serves as a map to the set, not as a work by Lawrence himself.
59503-home-manufacture-and-use-of-unferm:
Home Manufacture and Use of Unfermented Grape Juice is Farmers Bulletin Number 175 of the United States Department of Agriculture, printed at Washington in 1903. Its author, George C Husmann, led the grape work of the Bureau of Plant Industry. The note that sends it out says farm homes asked how to keep juice sweet at home scale. Heads treat the grape's make-up, the causes of ferment, and ways to block it.

Then come home making, work in larger lots, and the tools: a cloth hand press, a drip bag, and a small heat rig for filled bottles. Last heads give the juice's food worth and a few good recipes. Farm readers get plain steps to save fruit now lost each fall, and turn it into a sound drink for the house.
59505-sales-resistance:
Henry Still wrote Sales Resistance, a science fiction tale in Worlds of If in August nineteen hundred fifty six. Its world makes buying a duty and a mark of worth. Perry Mansfield, a plain non buyer, stands at its center. A note on his door shakes his calm at the tale’s start.

A Master Salesman has picked Perry for his next call, the card says. Such a call ranks with a mayor or a bishop in that world. It means his credit stands at the top of all marks. Pride should flood him, but dread fills him instead. He wants no big costly thing and needs none at all. His shrink, Doctor Stone, would scold his wrong tastes as sick. Walking two blocks home marks him a misfit in that age of flying stools.
59530-wine-dark-seas-and-tropic-skies-re:
Wine Dark Seas and Tropic Skies, by A. Safroni-Middleton, mixes memoir and romance from the South Seas, and it was issued at New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1918. The subtitle calls the book reminiscences and a romance of the South Seas. A front view shows a lagoon scene at Apia. The volume was printed in Great Britain by the Riverside Press.

Safroni-Middleton writes as a traveller who knew the islands at first hand. The title joins the wine dark sea of old poetry with the bright skies of the tropics. Readers get both a personal record of Pacific life and a woven love tale. Books of this kind sold the South Seas to readers at home in the war years. The charm of the book rests on place, mood, and memory.
59565-me-a-book-of-remembrance:
An unnamed woman tells her own life in this book of remembrance, printed by the Century Company at New York in 1915. She calls it simply Me. Her gift page names Lolly, her friend who was, and Jean, her friend who is.

A cold, blizzardy day in March opens the tale at Quebec. The girl of seventeen leaves home by train, her kin weeping and shivering on the platform. She cries a bit at the window, but her heart is light, for home was not glad. Her father was an artist, and they were very poor. Her mother had danced on the tight-rope in her youth, and bore sixteen children in a hard life.
59729-an-account-of-the-destruction-of-t:
Jean le Rond d'Alembert, the French philosopher and co editor of the great Encyclopédie, wrote this account of the destruction of the Jesuits in France. It was printed in London in seventeen sixty six. The Society of Jesus had been dissolved in France only a few years before. A storm of pamphlets for and against it had filled the press.

D'Alembert promises to be the rare writer on the affair with no party to serve. His advertisement notes that nearly everything else published breathed animosity or fanaticism, from defenders and attackers alike. He waited until minds had cooled before offering his own version of the causes and circumstances. The dedication praises a magistrate who turned the court's attention to fanatics of every party. The work is a cool, ironic piece of Enlightenment polemic.
59785-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
The Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of James Joyce, compiled by David Widger, is a finding guide to the Joyce texts then held by Project Gutenberg. It lists five works: Dubliners, Chamber Music, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, Ulysses, and the play Exiles. For each it prints the full table of contents.

Readers can scan the stories of Dubliners from The Sisters to The Dead, or the poems of Chamber Music by their first lines. Such indexes were Widger's specialty, made so that readers of the free library could navigate whole authors at a glance. The volume is a small piece of digital-library history, from the years when Joyce in plain text was itself a novelty worth cataloguing.
59809-the-case-for-spirit-photography-wi:
The Case for Spirit Photography, by Arthur Conan Doyle, was copyrighted in 1923 and published in New York by Doran. The title page promises corroborative evidence by experienced researchers and photographers. Nine chapters open with the Crewe circle and Doyle's own experiences, then turn to evidential tests and their results. Attacks on sitters and mediums are answered in turn.

Doyle lists his other works of the cause on the title leaf: The New Revelation, The Vital Message, and The Coming of the Fairies among them. Plates show sitters with psychic pictures of the dead: a mother with her father, a woman with her uncle. The creator of Sherlock Holmes here argues, in earnest, that cameras can record spirits. The book is a key text of the post-war spiritualist campaign.
59936-peter-jameson-a-modern-romance:
Peter Jameson, a modern romance by Gilbert Frankau, was published by Alfred A Knopf of New York in 1920. It ran to four printings in its first year. Frankau dedicates it to the average man and woman of the English speaking peoples. The contents mix business and war: the home and the office, a firm called Nirvana Limited, playing at soldier, and the crest of the wave.

The foreword walks the reader into the city of London. Take the Central London tube to Bank station, it says, fight for a place in the lift, and climb the stairs to Lombard Street. There the counting houses stand where Jameson's world begins. Later chapters bring a crisis, a decision, and guns: attack, forward, action left. A suicide club, a city of fear, and broken men follow, and the last chapter asks whether it is an end or a beginning.
59977-canning-freezing-storing-garden-pr:
Canning, Freezing, Storing Garden Produce is Agriculture Information Bulletin Four Hundred Ten of the United States Department of Agriculture. The bulletin reprints part four of the nineteen seventy seven Yearbook of Agriculture, Gardening for Food and Fun. It was issued in December nineteen seventy seven. A contents list opens the guide. Part four treats home food preservation under many heads.

The Whys of Food Preservation, by Edmund A Zottola and Isabel D Wolf, stands first. How to Minimize Quality Losses and the economics of home preservation follow. A beginner guide to home canning and a primer on home freezing come next. Pressure canners, vital for low acid foods, get a chapter. Canning fruits and vegetables, freezing the harvest, and jellies and jams follow. Pickles, wine making, and home drying close the craft. Home gardeners get a full federal preservation manual.
5998-waverley-or-tis-sixty-years-since:
Walter Scott's Waverley, or 'Tis Sixty Years Since, appears in an 1893 edition with an introductory essay and notes by Andrew Lang. Scott dedicates the collection to the king, hoping his fiction may amuse hours of relaxation or relieve languor, pain, and anxiety, and so add in small measure to his people's happiness.

The chapter list points to Rose Bradwardine and her father, repentance and reconciliation, a more rational day, Waverley domesticated at Tully-Veolan, and a creagh, or cattle raid. The tale sets a young visitor among Scottish lairds and their households. Its subtitle marks the distance of sixty years from the events.
60096-mr-fortune-s-practice:
Bailey wrote a second book of cases for his detective, Reginald Fortune, first published at London on May 17, 1923, and reprinted in cheap forms for a decade after. Seven cases fill the contents, from the Ascot tragedy to the unknown murderer, by way of a president of San Jacinto, a magic stone, and a snowball burglary.

The first case opens at Ascot on Cup Day, in heat haze and flounces, where Sidney Lomas, chief of the Criminal Investigation Department, finds Fortune sprawling pensive on a seat. Fortune is the adviser of all official people when surgery or medicine can elucidate what is or is not crime. Plump, pink, and amiable as a nice boy, he thinks while others bustle.
601-the-monk-a-romance:
Matthew Gregory Lewis tells a gothic tale of lust, sorcery, and damnation in this notorious romance. Ambrosio, a famed Madrid monk, falls from pride to sin through Matilda, a demon in disguise, while Agnes and Raymond suffer in dungeons and convents. Ghosts, magic, and a bleeding nun haunt the plot.

Lewis writes with lurid, fevered prose, mixing horror with moral warning. A preface in Horatian verse jokes about the book's fate in shops. The novel shocked readers of its day and endures as a landmark of gothic fiction, where a holy man learns that pride opens every door to hell.
6011-the-little-lady-of-lagunitas-a-fran:
Richard Henry Savage sets a Franco-Californian romance against gold-rush California, forty-two years after its golden star first glittered in the American flag. The state's checkered history begins with the rush of 1848 and 1849, when cosmopolitan free lances swept away defenceless Indians and robbed the great native families, the old Dons.

Mad riot and wild excess marked those early days, while society slowly made headway against motley adventurers. Savage places his little lady of Lagunitas amid French and Californian claims, treasure, and old family pride. The introduction frames a romance of a land still settling its fortunes.
60275-bobbins-of-belgium-a-book-of-belgi:
Bobbins of Belgium is a book of Belgian lace, lace-workers, lace-schools, and lace-villages by Charlotte Kellogg. She was a member of the Commission for Relief in Belgium. A portrait of Queen Elisabeth of Belgium stands at its front. A note by the transcriber sets out the rules of the text: old spellings of dialect words have been kept, and print slips set right in silence.

The note states one point of spelling in full. The front portrait calls the queen Elisabeth, as shown in the photo with her signature. Through the body of the book her name is spelled Queen Elizabeth. Both forms have been left as printed. The book is a record of the lace craft and of the women and schools that kept it up in Belgium.
60316-the-bakhtya-r-na-ma-a-persian-roma:
The Bakhtyār Nāma is a Persian romance in English dress. Sir William Ouseley translated it from a manuscript text. Clouston edited the volume, adding an introduction and notes. It was privately printed in 1883 in an edition of three hundred and thirty copies.

Thirty of those copies were printed on hand-made paper and numbered. The book is dedicated to General James Abbott of the Royal Asiatic Society. A verse from the Anvār-i Suhailī stands at its head, warning that a king's command should come only after long reflection. Clouston notes that the romance is generally reckoned a staple of Persian tale telling. He also laments how little Oriental literature was cultivated in Britain for all its Asian empire. The volume is a scholar's gift book, small and choice.
60337-birds-beasts-and-flowers-poems-by-:
D H Lawrence gathered poems in a book printed in London in 1923, with some pieces first seen in papers and reviews. Groups sort the poems as fruits, trees, flowers, beasts of the gospels, small creatures, reptiles, birds, and animals. A last group, ghosts, and a poem on the American eagle close the set.

Pomegranate opens the fruits, with Lawrences voice telling the reader flatly that he is not wrong. Snake, the most famed piece here, sits among the reptiles with a set of tortoise poems. Fish, bat, mosquito, turkey cock, humming bird, kangaroo, and mountain lion all get poems of their own in turn.
60451-the-mystery-of-suicide-place:
The Mystery of Suicide Place is a novel by Alex McVeigh Miller, printed at Cleveland in the Hart Series. Maybelle Maury of Mount Vernon returns from a tour of Europe in October 1894. Her chaperon, a New York society leader, presents her to young Beresford, the only son of a New York millionaire. The meeting sets the whole machinery of the tale in motion.

Fifty-two chapters pile up plots, midnight hours and haunted spots. Floy, proud and pretty as a princess, is thrown on the world and persecuted. Letters stab hearts, pride is brought low, and the house itself is said to be haunted. A startling revelation and a last victim bring the long sensation novel to its close.
60492-the-seventy-s-course-in-theology-f:
B H Roberts, of the First Council of Seventy, wrote this fifth-year manual of the Seventy's Course in Theology, published at Salt Lake City in 1912. Its subject is divine immanence and the Holy Ghost, headed by a passage from the Doctrine and Covenants.

The introduction doubles as a farewell to the course itself. Roberts explains that one united manual will now serve the Seventies, High Priests, and Elders quorums alike, since the gospel is one and the duty of knowing it equal. He hopes the larger plan will draw the best scholarship the church can offer. Students of Mormon theology get a valedictory volume on one of its loftiest themes.
60576-americans-by-choice:
John P Gavit wrote Americans by Choice, issued in nineteen twenty-two as one of the Americanization Studies. Gavit was a vice-president of the New York Evening Post. The series also held works on schooling, health, and the immigrant press.

Tables in the book use court numbers from one to twenty-nine, with number eleven always missing, as in the source. Wide tables are split into parts for the page. The study treats how newcomers become citizens by choice and law. It stands beside mate volumes on land, neighbourhood, and work. Allen T Burns directed the whole set of studies. Facts and figures, set out in tables, carry much of the case.
60649-in-the-jag-whiffing-service:
In the Jag Whiffing Service is a science fiction story by David R Bunch, taken from Worlds of If for February 1959. A blurb asks why the jag stuff in those black rings was so wonderful, yet had to come with so many extra accessories. The narrator serves on the cargo saucers.

He says he always held there was an easier way, and that the invasion, when it comes, will prove him right. But tradition is strong, and old line thinking keeps even a whole planet in a rut. The big cargo saucers grew bigger each year as the jag whiff places spread. More and more folk went on the jag, in part for troubles in the sky, strange balls whirling and objects going beep and wuff. Space tale fans get a sly alien trade tale.
60669-around-the-wicket-gate-or-a-friend:
Around the Wicket Gate, or a friendly talk with seekers concerning faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, by Spurgeon, was copyrighted in New York in 1890. A text from Matthew heads the book: enter ye in at the strait gate. The American Tract Society issued this edition by special arrangement with the author and his publisher.

Spurgeon says millions live far off from God and peace. His present care is a smaller company. These are folk not far from the kingdom, who have come right up to the wicket gate and yet hang back. A free welcome waits over the door and the porter stands ready, yet men linger for foolish reasons. Spurgeon, the great London preacher, answers those reasons one by one in warm, plain talk.
6078-louis-agassiz-his-life-and-correspo:
Elizabeth Cary Agassiz edits the life and correspondence of Louis Agassiz, warning that the book lacks both full personal narrative and close scientific analysis. She began by weaving facts, letters, and journals into narrative to prevent the loss of scattered papers of unquestionable family value.

As the work grew, she felt the story of an intellectual life marked by rare coherence and unity of aim might serve a wider use, as stimulus and encouragement to others. The European part of Agassiz's life is little known in America, she notes, while its American period is unfamiliar in his native land. The volume bridges both.
60872-the-magical-chance:
The Magical Chance, by Dallas Lore Sharp, came out in 1923 with Houghton Mifflin. Sharp had written The Lay of the Land and The Hills of Hingham. Seven essays make up the book. The first grows from a talk with his niece, who is about to leave college with no work in sight.

Sharp asks why youth feels the world is old and its great deeds all done. He answers that new tales, songs, and deeds still wait for the young. Later essays treat the lure of romance, the hunt for copy, and the duty to dig. Two turn to fields and woods after loggers pass. Readers get warm counsel on work, books, and hope, drawn from a long life of teaching.
60922-murder-beneath-the-polar-ice:
Murder Beneath the Polar Ice is a science fiction story by Hayden Howard, printed in Worlds of If in July 1960. The blurb warns that the Arctic Sea was deadly in every way, in its icy water, crushing ice, and hungry beasts, yet something there was deadlier still. The tale opens inside a fleet missile submarine, in an air-conditioned compartment full of lounging sailors.

The men watch Barney, a diver in a black rubber suit, sweating as he tightens the control cables of a torpedo-like craft with two open seats. The narrator, his diving buddy, calls Barney a legend, famed from the Korean coast landings. A murderer among the crew grins, careful not to sweat through his woolen layers.
60951-the-service:
The Service, an essay by Henry David Thoreau, takes the soldier as its figure for the true servant of a cause. A line of Virgil stands as motto. The contents divide the piece into three parts: the qualities of the recruit, what music we shall have, and a question not of numbers but of where the enemy are. Thoreau writes in his early, combative manner.

The brave man, the essay opens, is the elder son of creation, to whom his fellows are as strangers. If a man stands on truly elevated ground, his truth will be heard even by the dwellers in the valley, though the words may only reach them as echoes. Thoreau praises the recruit who serves with his whole soul rather than with his hands alone. The piece turns the drill field into a school of character.
6115-the-long-chance:
Peter B. Kyne opens The Long Chance at sunrise on the Colorado desert, as dawn's advance guard pauses on snow-encrusted peaks before charging down to rout night's lingering shadows. A coyote leaves his den in the tumbled malpais, points his nose skyward, and voices his morning salute to the Hosts of Light.

Far in the waste, seven dark objects detach from shadows and crawl toward the mountains. Like motes in a beam of light, they come out of the Land of Nowhere where greasewood meets horizon blue. A desert call for help, three fires by night and three smoke columns by day, signals the tale. Kyne writes desert adventure with a wide eye.
61378-joyce:
Joyce is a novel by Mrs Oliphant, issued at London in 1891, reprinted from editions of 1888 and 1889. Oliphant's other novels are named on the title page. The first chapter opens on a coming of age that is, and yet is not, a coming of age. The hero of the feast is a bearded man, not a youth.

He had been absent in all sorts of dangerous places since the age when he should have left wardship behind. His uncle's will had set that age late, at twenty five. He was nearer thirty when he came home, bronzed, with decorations on his breast. His character was quite unlike that of the young hero to whom such honours are usually paid, the narrator says. The family estates, not entailed, hang on his return.
6139-marvels-of-modern-science:
Paul Severing, with Theodore Waters as editor, looks at wonders of new science in 1910. He starts with flying craft: early tries, the airship, Langley's tests, the Wright brothers, Count Zeppelin, and new flight records. Wireless follows, with the Marconi set and waves through the air.

Radium, moving pictures, tall towers, ocean liners, and strange new plants fill out the book. Parts deal with Becquerel and the Curies, Edison's film viewer, Lumiere's camera, New York's tall blocks, and huge ships. Severing writes for plain readers keen to grasp new powers. He keeps each marvel short, clear, and full of zest.
61422-stories-of-romance:
Stories of Romance, in the Little Classics series edited by Rossiter Johnson, gathers five tales. Houghton Mifflin issued the Boston and New York volume in 1914. Copyright of the series dates to 1875 under Osgood in the front matter. Iris, by Oliver Wendell Holmes, opens the contents at page seven.

The Rosicrucian by Craik and The South Breaker by Spofford follow in the list. The Snow-Storm by John Wilson and The King of the Peak by Cunningham close the set. Iris comes from The Professor at the Breakfast-Table, as its head note states. The narrator foretells a girlish shape to fill the blank at their table, it begins. Pocket classics put famed short tales in one neat volume for train reading.
61423-cesare-lombroso-a-modern-man-of-sc:
Hans Kurella wrote Cesare Lombroso, A Modern Man of Science, translated from the German by M Eden Paul and published at New York. Havelock Ellis read the translation in manuscript and advised on terms, the translator notes at Christmas 1910. Contents open with Lombroso's predecessors in research.

His science of the criminal follows, then the attacks on his views. Woman as criminal, the political criminal, and the criminal mind get chapters of their own. Later chapters weigh his life work as a reformer, his methods, and his thought. Pellagra and farm reform appear, and an appendix covers his work on spirits and sittings. Readers get the founder of the field assessed by a German admirer just after his death, science and quarrels together.
61449-persephone-of-eleusis-a-romance-of:
Clare Winger Harris published Persephone of Eleusis, a romance of ancient Greece, in Boston in 1923. Its contents sweep across the Persian Wars, from chapters at the Hot Gates and the defence on the Acropolis to the miracle of Salamis and a hero of Plataea.

Later chapters bring in the prophet at Delphi, the theatre of Dionysus, and the celebration of the Mysteries at Eleusis. Names such as Themistocles, Ephialtes, and Ladice thread through the plot. Readers get a historical novel that ties a love story to famous battles and sacred rites. Harris later became known for science fiction, and this early novel shows her working in historical romance first.
61484-nicolette-a-tale-of-old-provence:
Nicolette, a tale of old Provence by Baroness Orczy, was copyrighted in New York in 1922. Orczy was famed for The Scarlet Pimpernel and a shelf of romances from El Dorado to The Laughing Cavalier. Sixteen chapters follow the house of Ventadour, from faded splendor to a turning point and a grey dawn.

The tale opens midway between Apt and the Durance, on the south slope of the Luberon, at an old castle. Once the stronghold of the proud lords of Ventadour, kin to the counts of Provence, the place had fallen low by the time Bertrand de Ventadour was a boy. Honor of the name, a family record book, orange blossom, and Christmas Eve set the romantic stakes.
61505-sappho-and-her-influence:
David Robinson wrote Sappho and Her Influence, a volume in the Our Debt to Greece and Rome series. Marshall Jones put it out at Boston in 1924. Robinson taught Greek lore and the study of old stones at Johns Hopkins. The book is given to the memory of Basil Lanneau Gildersleeve, his master and friend. A plate of Alma-Tadema's Sappho, held at the Walters Gallery in Baltimore, fronts the work.

The series was made by gifts from patrons who sought a larger size for this book. Its aim is to show what modern life owes to old Greece and Rome. Robinson turns that aim on Sappho, the famed Greek singer of Lesbos. The book traces her life, her songs, and the mark she left on later verse. Students of Greek letters get a clear guide to a famed, fragmentary voice.
61682-frank-brown-sea-apprentice:
Frank Brown, Sea Apprentice, is a sea story by Frank Bullen, author of The Cruise of the Cachalot. Dutton printed it in New York in 1907, with illustrations by Arthur Twidle. Chapter one, The Call of the Sea, opens in a counting house family in the north of England, where a father argues against the sea with all his force.

The elder Brown rose by steady service to a post at five hundred pounds a year, and impoverished himself to fit his son for the great firm. Sailors are necessary, he allows, but plenty of boys with unhappy homes and neglected schooling will take up seafaring; his Frank is not one of those. Sixteen chapters carry the boy anyway: outward bound, his first gale, a great fight, and at last a chapter headed Captain Brown.
61918-adventures-in-silence:
Adventures in Silence is a book by Herbert W. Collingwood on life as a deaf man. It was put out in New York by The Rural New Yorker, with a copyright date of 1923. The book is given to E. W. C., whose rare sympathy and sisterly grasp, the page says, helped one deaf man through the silence. The contents set out the course of the work.

An opening essay stands first, then Terrors That Are Imaginary and On the Road to Silence. Head Noises and Subjective Audition, Facing the Hard Situation, and A Heart for Any Fate stand in the list. Memories of Early Life and Experimenting with the Deaf Man stand there too. Companions in Trouble, The Approach to Silence, and Mixing Word Meanings carry the list on. The book is a first-hand account of deafness and of how a man meets it.
62028-the-soul-of-ann-rutledge-abraham-l:
The Soul of Ann Rutledge, subtitled Abraham Lincoln's Romance, is a novel by Bernie Babcock, published by Lippincott in 1919. Babcock opens with a note on the flood of Lincoln literature. No one, she argues, had yet given a full story to one of the greatest loves in history. Her book sets out to repair that lack.

Chapters follow Lincoln from One April Day and Clary's Grove through The Railsplitter and into his courtship of Ann Rutledge at New Salem. A color frontispiece by Gayle Hoskins shows Ann telling Abraham that the place seems holy, with him as its prophet. Babcock treats the romance as the mold of Lincoln's later faith and character. The novel helped fix the Ann Rutledge legend in American popular memory.
62075-gods-of-space:
Ray Cummings flies to a dark world in Gods of Space, from the Spring 1942 issue of Planet Stories. The head blurb calls Planetoid 150 a world of horror. A star of death, ruled by a weird and beautiful Earthian goddess, it warns.

The tale opens on the approach. The weird purple glow of the planetoid was apparent now, even to the naked eye. The end of Roy Atwood's long, lonely journey was at hand. In the narrow control turret of his small spaceship he sat gazing. The world, far beyond Mars, was a great leaden disc occupying nearly a quarter of the sky. On Earth, his father had located a treasured substance there with a giant spectroscope, seen as a faint band in the light. Atwood came seeking that substance, the Xarite, and its glow was puzzlingly strong.
62164-the-migrations-of-early-culture-a-:
Grafton Elliot Smith, professor of anatomy at Manchester, argued that early culture spread by migration, in a university memoir printed in 1915. His study turns on the practice of mummification. Where that custom is found round the world, he holds, it proves peoples moved and carried customs and beliefs with them. The preface owns the pages were crudely flung together.

They were meant, he says, as an appeal to ethnologists to recognise the error of their ways and repent. Only a very small fraction of his evidence is set forth here. Much of the most illuminating information reached him only since the memoir went to press, he adds. The bold diffusion theory made Smith a famed and fought over name.
62314-stranger-from-space:
Hannes Bok placed his tale Stranger from Space in Planet Stories for March 1943. On Venus, under dust clouds that roof the sky, the girl Koroby faces marriage to Yasak. Her bridesmaids laugh while she admits she wants romance instead. She longs for a man to drop from the skies and carry her away.

The head note gives the twist in advance and calls it odd. When a godlike visitor lands in a metal globe, awe turns to letdown, since his godliness proves strangely off key. Bok sets lush Venusian twilight, clay huts, and jungle against that wish. Readers get pulp longing with a sting, told from the bride's side of the bargain.
62322-eye-service-and-love-service:
Eye service means working only while someone watches, while love service means working gladly and from the heart. A short Dean and Son farthing book from London puts that contrast into a tale for young readers. Two sisters, Bessie and Meggie, are left in charge of a cottage and their baby brother Dick while their mother goes out to glean at harvest time.

Bessie cleans and carries butter to neighbours, and both girls resist the urge to quiet the baby with treats he should not have. Next door, Jenny Bryant does the opposite once her mother leaves. She lets friends in, talks with a gipsy fortune teller, and puts fine lace work at risk. The contrast makes the lesson plain without a long sermon.
62416-juggernaut-of-space:
Juggernaut of Space is a science fiction tale by Ray Cummings. It ran in Planet Stories in the fall of 1945. A doom no mind had dreamed of reaches for Earth in the tale.

Robert Rance tells the story in his own voice. Rance reports science news for a New York broadcast station. Fame came to him through the weird affair of the Crimson Comet. Now a worse peril calls for Earth's champions. Yet the only folk who can fight it are five captives on another world. Cummings builds a brisk tale of peril, brains and escape. The tale first ran in a pulp magazine of the war years.
6242-parables-of-a-province:
Bronzed pipes hang on the side of Margath Mountain, tall and perfect, said to be the organ played by some son of God when the world was young. Hepnon the cripple says golden music still comes from them at sunrise and sunset, and no one laughs, for his dark, dreaming eyes make belief easy. Nine parables follow, among them a guardian of the fire, the singing of bees, a white omen, sojourners, and a forge in the valley.

Parker writes these as short fables of a province, each built on a single image and a moral felt rather than preached. A tent of purple mat, a little city, and a place called Peradventure give the set its range, from wonder to warning. The prose is simple and pictorial, inviting the reader to hear, as Hepnon does, music in ordinary hills and work.
62431-etruscan-tomb-paintings-their-subj:
Frederik Poulsen wrote on the tomb art of the old Etruscans. His book came out through Oxford University Press. Its theme is what those tomb walls show and what they mean. Notes sit at the foot of each part in the book. Fine plates in the full book show the walls in hue.

Feasts, hunts, games, and dance crowd the tomb walls' world. Gods and the dead share scenes with horse and lyre. Poulsen reads each scene for what it says of that folk. Their life, faith, and death hopes stand in his claims. Art and past fans share the worth of his work. A lost folk speaks here in paint.
62485-edgings-crocheted-tatted-hair-pin-:
Star Book Number 81, issued by the American Thread Company in 1951, gives lace edging patterns for hand work. It covers crochet, tatting, and hair pin lace in one cheap booklet. The first item is a tatted motif and edging numbered 810, shown on the cover. Its list calls for two balls of Star tatting crochet thread and one shuttle.

The steps are given in short code, with rings, chains, picots, and joins spelled out step by step. A handkerchief is the base for the first design. Later pages give more edgings in the same terse style. Makers who can read old pattern shorthand can still work these designs today.
62631-three-bright-girls-a-story-of-chan:
Annie E Armstrong wrote Three Bright Girls, a story of chance and mischance, issued by Blackie and Son in London, Glasgow, and Dublin. W Parkinson drew six page plates. Armstrong had earlier written Madge Mistake, A Very Odd Girl, and Violet Yereker Vanity. Thirty six chapters fill the tale. A front plate shows Molly reading a letter from Hugh. Doris, Molly, Daisy, and Honor are the bright girls.

Early chapters bring hot chestnuts, Doris first dinner party, and shopping and a rehearsal. Startling news, a house of mourning, and a facing of the future darken the middle. The brothers Talboys, the Horton boys, and Dr John Sinclair add young men to the mix. Doris makes a pudding, Daisy falls ill, and Dick brings good news. A ball, a fairy tale, and Doris wedding close the tale. Girls got home pluck, love, and loss in warm mix.
62680-the-superstition-of-divorce:
The Superstition of Divorce, by Chesterton, was published by the John Lane Company in New York in 1920. The book grew out of five articles in the New Witness, written during a press controversy over loosening the marriage laws. Its chapters treat the superstition itself, the tragedy of the modern family, the vow, the tragedies of marriage, and the vista of divorce.

Chesterton argues that reformers who treat marriage as a mere contract mistake its nature. Like his beloved window, a thing gains beauty from its frame, and freedom without walls ends with neither walls nor windows. His defense of the vow is witty, paradoxical, and deeply felt. The book remains a classic statement of the case against easy divorce.
62718-discover-the-excitement-of-hairpin:
Discover the Excitement of Hairpin Lace is a pattern book, number 1760, offering designs for beginners and advanced workers, with knitting and crochet besides. Its promise is that hairpin lace is easy: all the worker needs is a branded hairpin lace loom, by Susan Bates or Marcia Lynn, and a crochet hook.

Basic directions open the teaching in steps. Remove the cross bar, form a slip loop half the width of the loom, and work the first strip with the hook passing through loops as the loom turns. Side lessons cover keeping the twist in loops, working loops straight, and preventing slant when strips are joined, alternating the starting ends so the work does not ride uphill. Counting loops gets its own note: mark the fiftieth or hundredth loop on each side, keep both sides equal, and mind the gauge at the center of the loom.
62740-walker-of-the-secret-service:
Walker of the Secret Service, by Melville Davisson Post, is a book of thirteen detective tales. Appleton printed it in New York and London in 1924. The tales had run in magazines from 1920 on, under earlier copyrights.

Post had written of Uncle Abner and of a Paris prefect of police before this set. The titles map the beat: The Outlaw, The Holdup, The Bloodhounds, and The Secret Agent. The Big Haul, The Passing of Mooney, and The Diamond follow. The Expert Detective and the mysterious stranger defence come later. The Girl in the Picture, The Menace, and The Symbol close the set. The first tale opens at a circus, outside the tent. A boy with no money for the wonders studies the painted alley. Near the entrance sits a little man in a canvas chair, watching.
62760-the-mysteries-of-florence:
George Lippard wrote this sensation novel, published by Peterson at Philadelphia and entered for copyright in 1864. Lippard had written 'The Quaker City,' 'The Empire City' and many other feverish tales before this one. Book the first, called the Red Chamber, opens the contents of the volume.

The signet ring of Albarone starts the plot in chapter one of the list. White dust in a goblet of gold, the embrace of a brother and a death trap follow in order. Florence, its palaces and its secrets give Lippard a rich ground for the gothic manner that made his name.
62834-adventures-in-elegance:
Adventures in Elegance is a recipe booklet built around canned fruit pie fillings. Its pages urge home cooks to try new uses for the cans. Fillings can top cheese cakes or glaze ham slices. They can also fill pies, breads, and party sweets in short order.

One bread, Bonny Berry Bread, layers blueberry filling in sweet dough. A crumb top of sugar, flour, and spice crowns the loaf. Cherry kolaches fold crescent roll dough round cherry filling. An orange glaze drips over the hot rolls. A Dutch apple coffee cake starts from a boxed mix. Each dish lists clear amounts and oven heat. Home bakers get fast treats with a store bought core.
62940-mrs-spring-fragrance:
Sui Sin Far's Mrs Spring Fragrance was published by McClurg of Chicago in May 1912. The title page also names the author as Edith Eaton. Two companies of stories fill the book: tales of Chinese Americans, opening with the title story, and a second part of tales of Chinese children. The Silver Leaves and The Peacock Lantern stand among them.

The first part moves through the lives of Seattle's and San Francisco's Chinese in the new land. The Inferior Woman, The Wisdom of the New, and The Story of One White Woman Who Married a Chinese stand early. In the Land of the Free, The Smuggling of Tie Co, The Prize China Baby, and Lin John follow. The acknowledgment thanks the magazines that first printed the stories, the Independent, the Century, Hampton's, and the Ladies' Home Journal among them.
62964-the-peacock-feather-a-romance:
Putnam published this romance in 1914, dedicated to Herbert Thring's wife. The prologue is a prisoner. In a building on the cliffs, a man clings to the bars of his window and watches the sea change from blue to grey. Night after night for three years he has looked from that slit.

Tonight he looks for the last time; tomorrow he will be free as the sea-gulls. The chapters turn to a piper: the first-born, a deserted cottage, and Peter in residence. The Lady Anne, a concert and after, and a moonlight piping follow. Letters, a thunderstorm, and the everlasting why follow, until Democritus arrives to stay and the return closes it, as the Latin has it. A peacock feather is a slight thing to hang a romance on, and Moore hangs a prison, a piper, and a love story from it.
62997-saboteur-of-space:
Abernathy's novelette ran in Planet Stories in the spring of 1944. Fresh power is coming to Earth, the headnote says, energy to bring life to a dying planet. Two men stand in its way, a cowardly rat and a murderous martyr, pawns in a game. Ryd Randl watches the sky over Dynamopolis light with searchlights as a ship comes down to Pi Mesa.

Dynamopolis sprawls at fourteen thousand feet, built to be the power center of North America and freezing in a power shortage. The few dives open keep men from freezing in the streets. Burshis surprises Ryd with a drink on the house: the ship is the escort from Mars, and relief is in sight in the year 819. Ryd's pinched, old-young face is known at the bar, and nobody looks at him. Pulp science fiction wrote the future as a town, and the saboteur as its shadow.
6304-without-prejudice:
Israel Zangwill gathers miscellaneous work from four or five years, mostly first printed month by month in the Pall Mall Magazine, under the title Without Prejudice. He has left out pieces that hang on other people's books, plays, or pictures, seeking unity in a set that can stand alone. The result is a book of essays and fancies, witty, digressive, and fond of turning a familiar saying on its head.

Topsy turveydom is not so easy as it looks, he warns, for the trouble lies not in inverting but in finding what to invert. Language holds ancient saws, but only a real humourist knows which can stand on its head without falling. Zangwill writes on travel, morals, and modern life with the same trick, asking readers to feel their surroundings again rather than rush past them. The essays reward a slow, amused attention.
63053-lead-kindly-light-its-origin-and-i:
Allan Sutherland wrote Lead Kindly Light: Its Origin and Its Romance for a series on famous hymns of the world. Frederick A Stokes issued the volume at New York, from a copyright of 1905. Henry C McCook wrote the opening essay, on how faith and song have been wed from the earliest ages.

McCook traces sacred song from savage chants to the Levitical choir of the Hebrew temple. He quotes Miriam's song at the Red Sea, on Israel's deliverance from Egypt. Sutherland then tells how the hymn itself came to be written and what its words have meant to singers since. Plates and a warm, plain style suit the book to general readers.
63062-terror-out-of-space:
Leigh Brackett's Terror Out of Space ran in Planet Stories in the summer of 1944. Lundy flies an aero-space convertible alone through the pearly Venusian sky. His co-pilot, Jackie Smith, lies knocked out beside him. Behind the cabin door Farrell screams and fights his straps, mad since he was taken. In a strongbox in the safe sits It, the thing they captured. The headnote states the rule: to see the terror is to become its slave.

Lundy, of the Tri-World Police Special Branch, must carry It back to headquarters at Vhia. The cold knot in his belly tells him he is afraid, and fear can make a man weak when he needs strength. Brackett sets the whole tale inside that flight. The horror has no name or form, only the wish it plants: to see behind its shadowed eyelids.
6308-hypatia-or-new-foes-with-an-old-fac:
Charles Kingsley warns that a picture of fifth century life must hold much that will pain readers. The age was hideous and great at once, with virtues and vices side by side in the same persons. In the year 413, some three hundred miles above Alexandria, the young monk Philammon sits on inland cliffs above a desert waste. Tombs, quarries, and half cut pillars sink in sand around him.

Alexandria itself is the novel's stage. Hypatia, philosopher and counsellor to Orestes, faces Cyril and his followers. Goths move through a dying world, and Miriam, a day in the city, and a new Diogenes fill the chapters. Philammon, watching monks curse Hypatia and Orestes to torment, asks whether these are ministers of a gospel. Kingsley writes a fierce, learned romance of faith, philosophy, and power in a city losing its old gods.
6333-public-speaking-principles-and-prac:
Irvah Lester Winter designs this book for students of public speaking, to set out the main principles of effective platform delivery and to supply ample material for practice. It can form a separate course or a training thread inside another course, and it honours Charles William Eliot, who taught by example the power and beauty of perfected speech. Principles come first, then practice in many forms.

Part one discusses tone, vocal flexibility, word formation, emphasis, feeling, picture, and action, then platform practice: formal address, public lecture, informal discussion, argument, after dinner speech, and occasional poem. Part two gives practice pieces, from Burns and Byron to Shakespeare, Kipling, and Patrick Henry's Virginia speech of March 1775. Winter writes a working textbook, not a theory alone.
6351-red-fleece:
Will Levington Comfort, writing in 1915 and dedicating his book to the hour when troops turn home, opens with a woman and an exile. Peter Mowbray first sees her at the corner of Palace Square nearest the river, not a starer by nature, his mind on work and the trickery of events. Their eyes meet full and leisurely, in a stirring silence before self and convention rush in, and he hopes at first for some flaw to break the pull.

The chapters that follow are stark in title: a court of execution, a house of amputations, a bomb proof pit, a skylight prison, a field of helmets, and the green of cedars. Russian soldiers lie unticketed, faces bandaged beyond recognition. Mowbray searches cots until midnight, asking what they do with the dead. Comfort writes war as exile and witness, where a glance in a square leads to a field hospital.
63579-a-narrative-of-the-life-and-travel:
Nancy Prince published her own narrative of her life and travels at Boston in 1850. She was born at Newburyport in 1799, granddaughter of Tobias Wornton, stolen from Africa as a lad.

Her grandfather, though a slave, fought at Bunker Hill in the Revolutionary army. Prince tells of her marriages, a voyage to Russia, and nine years' residence in St Petersburg, with its manners and customs. Later chapters take her to the West Indies, cast away at Key West, and through scenes witnessed at New Orleans. She writes, she says, because providence has wonderfully preserved her unprofitable life. She entered the copyright in her own name at Boston.
6364-warlock-o-glenwarlock-a-homely-roma:
George MacDonald opens in a rough, wild glen on the debatable land between highlands and lowlands, where the family took its name and gave back much of its character. Most folk speak both Scotch and Gaelic, mingling Celt and Teuton traits. The country grows more barley than wheat, more oats than barley, more heather than oats, more boulders than trees, and more snow than anything, thinly peopled, with bare hills and small streams.

Castle Warlock, the kitchen, the drawing room, an afternoon sleep, and the school lead the chapters, with Grannie's cottage, dreams, home, and a student to follow. Cosmo conducts a lady to the stable in the frontispiece, and a laird, Lady Joan, and Lord Mergwain, fond of his bottle after luncheon and dinner, fill the house. MacDonald writes a homely Scottish romance of glen, kin, and quiet wonder.
63745-beyond-rope-and-fence:
Beyond Rope and Fence is a horse story by David Grew, told with love. Boni and Liveright of New York issued the book in nineteen twenty two. Grew gives it to Dora, the old horse who inspired the tale. She may never know his sympathy, despite caresses and full oat measures, he writes.

Dora stood motionless, dreaming of free happy years on the plains long gone. Her strange sad eye light told him of those lost days of liberty. Chapters open For the Love of Her Foal, then To the North follows. Death in the Howl of Coyotes and A Seeking That Found come next. The book gives a horse life from inside her own longing heart.
63862-stalemate-in-space:
Charles Harness wrote this space story, first printed in Planet Stories in the summer of 1949. Two mighty battle globes have crunched together and hang locked in a death-struggle beyond the Lesser Magellanic Cloud.

Nine years on, Evelyn Kane wakes in her sealed cubicle inside the Defender. The votron's code murmurs die now in her ears: her countrymen have lost. Sealed in dormant by the mentors, she has one duty left, to find the relay and set the great prime movers going, so conquerors join the conquered in the grave of space. But life, doled out by the second, is too delicious to abandon at once. Her memories of building the globe with her father hold her. Readers get a somber tale of revenge delayed.
63869-ordeal-in-space:
Ordeal in Space, by Ralph Sloan, was produced from Planet Stories for Fall 1949. A head note sets the trap. This was Lieutenant Mike Logan chance: alone in space with the man he ached to kill. That man was bound, and taunted him, knowing Mike had to bring him in alive.

A needle gun points through cell bars at Edward Snyder, a hulking form with a blue furred Moon mimic squirming on his lap. Behind the gun are Logan cold hands, cropped black hair, and bloodless face. It took him three hours to slide past the guards of the transient prison. Snyder looks up and asks if it is something personal, or official. Logan answers: ask your questions in hell. He tells Snyder: you killed Johnny, this is for him. Readers get a revenge tale in space.
64110-at-the-sign-of-the-fox-a-romance:
Barbara's romance opens in the hill country of the Moosatuk, where Robert Stead and Doctor Russell tramp down a pent road from hunting. The Hurst edition carries a 1905 Macmillan copyright and a motto ballade by Richard Burton. The dedication gives the book to the brave.

A cast list called The People introduces Brooke Lawton, a young woman who sees things as they might be. Her father Adam, a country-bred New Yorker of affairs, heads the household with Pamela of Virginia. Lucy Dean sees things as they are, and Silent Stead is sportsman and misanthrope. Tatters, a person disguised as an old collie dog, completes the company.
64118-ariel-a-shelley-romance:
André Maurois wrote a life of the poet Shelley as a romance, translated by Ella D'Arcy and first published in 1924. It opens in 1809 at Eton, where George the Third had appointed Dr Keate as headmaster. Keate was a terrible little man who thought the flogging-block a necessary station on the road to perfection.

He ended a sermon on the sixth beatitude, the book says, by threatening to flog the boys until they were pure in heart. Chapters follow Shelley through Hogg and Harriet, Godwin, and Byron's silence, toward Ariel set free. Blake's lines on the garden of love, filled with graves, head the first part. Maurois tells the life at a novel's pace.
64121-the-theosophical-path-illustrated-:
The Theosophical Path is an illustrated monthly magazine edited by Katherine Tingley, bound here as volume one, July to December 1911. The New Century Corporation published it at Point Loma, California, the seat of the theosophical community there. A long index opens the volume, sorting six months of articles, poems, and reviews by title.

The entries show the magazine's range: the astral body, ancient astronomy, ancient calendars, and the scope of art. Several pieces treat Helena Blavatsky and her teachings, and one asks whether she was a plagiarist. Ancient America appears in studies of Copan and a Maya codex, while Athens, Paris bridges, and Welsh legend poems fill out the mix.
64236-under-foch-s-command-a-tale-of-the:
Captain Brereton wrote Under Foch's Command, a tale of the Americans in France, in his Stories of War line. Front ads list his tales of the Caucasus, Baghdad, Cossacks, Waterloo, Lucknow, the Zulu War, and the Dardanelles. The Westminster Gazette is quoted: when Brereton has a war subject he always does it well.

Under Haig in Flanders and With Joffre at Verdun form sister volumes on the Western Front for boy readers. This tale puts American soldiers under the French commander Foch in the Great War's final campaigns. Brereton's method mixes real battles, named places, and boy heroes at the front in harm's way. Young readers of the war years got Allied adventure with a documentary flavour throughout.
64270-asteroid-justice:
V E Thiessen sets a man-hunter loose in the asteroid belt in a tale from Planet Stories, Fall 1947. Sam Knox drifts in the Wanderer at the belt's edge.

The headnote asks what Knox is up to, drifting helplessly in a tiny eggshell with two weeks' grub. The mining fleet hangs before him like stars, lights twinkling in the black. The miners spread their nets for errant meteors, hunting sudden wealth. They are a clannish tribe, bound by danger and known to one another season by season. Knox has sat a week among them without a sign shown. His job is not wealth in an asteroid's heart. His job is to find Pell. What Sam Knox hunted, he found. Thiessen builds the tale on patience worn as bait.
64326-black-silence:
Emmett McDowell wrote Black Silence, a science fiction tale printed in the Fall 1947 issue of Planet Stories. Matthew Magoffin and the men and women of the first expedition to Mars sit in the messroom of the Argus, two and a half years out, and talk of home. Lynn, the expedition's photographer and reporter, wants first a real bath, not one out of a tea cup.

The music stops mid-bar. A news flash from the Union of South America tells of a plague spreading fast in the Andean region. Black spots cover the body, with high fever and death in two to three hours. No germ has been found, and all tries to curb the spread have failed. The league at Lima meets to seal the whole area. The tale sets a joyful homecoming against a horror rising on Earth.
64331-the-martian-circe:
The Martian Circe is a science fiction story by Raymond Jones, printed in the magazine Planet Stories in the summer of 1947. Its billing asks the question outright. Who is the sweet-voiced singer weaving a spell of dreams and drugs that drives men mad and threatens to smash the System?

The singer is Alayna, called the Queen of the Silver Stars. When she sings in the Starhouse, the brawling, laughter, and loud curses of the Martian tavern stop, as they stop for no other singer. Captain Roal Hartford steps into the smoke and stale smell of the place and stands motionless in the doorway, listening. He has dared the death of the Thousand Minds to learn her dreadful secret. Jones sets a myth of enchantment, the Circe of the Greeks, among the taverns of a conquered Mars.
64368-water-color-renderings-of-venice:
Water Color Renderings of Venice is a portfolio of plates by Pierre Vignal. Jansen of Cleveland issued it in 1925. William Powell wrote the introduction. Fifteen plates of Venice make up the set. The Rialto and Saint Mark's Square stand among them. The clock tower and the ducal palace follow. Canals, churches, and quiet streets fill the rest.

Powell's essay praises Vignal's pure technique. No white paint touches his palette, it says. Each wash is laid once and never reworked. Drawing is done in a fine, light pencil line. The subject is kept simple and broad. Prints are near the size of the originals. Vignal ranked high among French water colourists. The plates catch Venice in clear, bright air.
64510-a-daughter-of-witches-a-romance:
A Daughter of Witches, a romance by Joanna E Wood, author of The Untempered Wind and Judith Moore, was published by W J Gage and Company at Toronto in 1900. The opening finds Miss Temperance Tribbey at the back door of the old Lansing house. A great wooden spoon drips red syrup in her hand, while Grip the mastiff barks at the gate.

Sidney Martin walks up the lane and knocks at the front door instead, a choice that harms his standing with Temperance, who is busy preserving fruit and in no mood for callers.
64536-english-folk-song-and-dance:
Frank Kidson and Mary Neal wrote English Folk-Song and Dance, issued by the Cambridge press in nineteen fifteen. Kidson's part treats song, and Neal's part treats dance. Two hundred pages or so cover both arts.

Kidson defines folk-song, traces its source, and shows how tunes change as they travel. Classes of song run from narrative ballads to love songs, sea songs, and carols. Children's singing games and the printed ballad sheet close his part. Neal treats the morris dance of today, the tools of the trade, and extra figures. The sword dance and the furry dance follow. A book list ends the song part.
64681-jessica-trent-s-inheritance:
Evelyn Raymond's Jessica Trent's Inheritance was published by David McKay of Philadelphia in 1907, in the Girls Own Library. Raymond had written Jessica Trent and Jessica the Heiress before it, and this volume continues the girl's story. Nineteen chapters carry her from a parting at a railway station to school, a telling valedictory, and the dream made real.

The first chapter is the farewell. Jessica clings to her mother on the platform, crying that she cannot bear to go. Gabriella Trent answers as befits the daughter of Cassius Trent: bravely and hopefully, eagerly, as one who goes to finish his life work. The mother is almost heartbroken; the joy of her life leaves on the outgoing eastern train. Jessica pleads to come home next year, and is told only, if it seems best. The ancient mansion, a first girl friend, and Ephraim with a bundle wait at the journey's end.
64840-healing-rays-in-space:
Healing Rays in Space is a science fiction story by Harvey Haggard, printed in Comet in March 1941. Chapter One, Strange Bargain, opens in a big library of platinum and teakwood. A monstrous man in expensive dress thrusts scarlet pins into a chart of the solar system. Below the chart runs a label: Marshall Space Lines, 1990 to 2055.

Beside him sits a wisp of a girl in a wheel chair, her hair like starclouds on a summer night. Her father gloats that it took fifty years to scalp the Thallin Starways. Yet crushing an enemy, he admits, has a bitter edge. He would give everything he ever owned, every red copper, for the one thing his empire cannot buy. Haggard sets a space magnate's triumph against a father's helpless love.
65035-inheritance:
Edward Ludwig wrote a science fiction tale printed in the October 1950 issue of a pulp magazine. Martin crawls out of a dark cave with his pup after two days lost in stale air. A dog named Sandy waits and barks at his feet as he fights his way to the light.

At the cave mouth the day feels like a sea wave of light, and hunger and thirst hit at once. The first lines warn that the world Martin knew is gone, though the tale holds back what has changed. Fear, love for the dogs, and plain need to live drive the opening scenes.
6523-the-post-office:
Tagore sets his play in the house of Madhav, who has taken in a sick child named Amal and now dreads the day the boy must leave. A doctor speaks in old medical terms of bile and palsy, while Madhav begs for plain help, not book lore. Around them gather a flower girl, a dairyman, a watchman, and a gaffer, each with a small part in Amal's narrow world.

Amal waits for the king's letter, and the post office itself becomes his hope of a wider life beyond his room. The play is short and tender, with speech that feels both simple and full of meaning. The Post Office asks what a child can dream when illness keeps him indoors, and how grown folk answer that dream.
65246-master-race:
Richard Ashby wrote this science fiction tale, first printed in Imagination in September 1951. A headnote sets the turn of it: the invaders sent a scout to Earth to learn what kind of life lived there. But what sort of finding, the note asks, could they draw from comic book heroes? One moment Eddie is piloting a fast plane over green jungles. The next he is wide awake in his room.

Across the room his dog Rags whines softly, sniffing the damp night air at the open window. The Scotty is stirred by something out of the ordinary, and the dog is no coward. Eddie slips from bed and listens: roosters at the next farm, stock shifting in the barn, birds in the cottonwoods. Then he catches a low sound, like organ notes heard from outside a church. Looking up, he gasps at sharp white lights above the oak tree.
65269-the-ice-crop-how-to-harvest-store-:
The Ice Crop is a practical treatise on ice by Theron Hiles, printed by Orange Judd in eighteen ninety three. Its long title promises how to harvest, store, ship, and use ice well. Farmers, dairymen, dealers, shippers, and packers are all named as its readers. Ten chapters and a set of recipes for iced dishes fill the book.

The preface notes the ice trade's huge growth in the last forty years past. Yet few records exist by which that growth can be truly measured. Chapter one sketches the trade's start, with Boston ice sent to the West Indies. That first cargo sailed in the winter of eighteen o five to six. Cutting and storing take the longest chapter, then ice house building follows. Use in cooling, made ice machines, and shipping by rail close the course.
65320-kibun-daizin-or-from-shark-boy-to-:
Kibun Daizin, or From Shark-Boy to Merchant Prince, by Gensai Murai, translated by Masao Yoshida, with illustrations by George Varian, was published by the Century Company in New York in 1904. The publishers' note presents it as a story from the Japanese for young readers. The story was translated especially for Saint Nicholas.

The tale is founded on the life of Bunzayemon Kinokuniya, a Japanese merchant of the eighteenth century. His pluck, wisdom, and enterprise made him one of the most prosperous and respected men of his time. Kibun was his nickname: the syllables stand for his names, and Daizin means the wealthiest man. Murai had been a student at the Waseda School and a story writer for a Tokio daily. The chapters follow young Bunkichi: an ambitious boy, a plan to kill the shark, a capsized boat, a battle of stone missiles, and a great conflagration.
65581-jean-craig-finds-romance:
Jean Craig Finds Romance, by Kay Lyttleton, is a girls’ story in the Falcon Books line. Jean Craig had always wanted to be an artist, the blurb begins. When her family moved to Woodhow in Connecticut, she gave up her art lessons. Later she was able to take them up again, with new hope.

A career matters deeply to Jean, once her lessons resume. Then Ralph McRae comes along, and her mind wavers. She cannot decide what she wants most, art or love. Her sister Kit has a fine adventure of her own out west meanwhile. The blurb promises gaiety and humour in the Craig family tale. Jean Craig Grows Up stands as a companion book in the same series.
65725-centauri-vengeance:
Darius John Granger wrote this science fiction tale, Centauri Vengeance, printed in the October 1956 number of Imagination. A blurb at the head frames its hero. George Haven was the most powerful man in the galaxy. Now he had returned to Centauri and was afraid, for his past was staring at him.

Haven knows the trip is a mistake before he reaches his hotel. The Centaurian porters take his baggage with cold, distant correctness, and his wife Louise asks why they do not like him, when he had told her he would be a hero here. Haven, big and rich in his late thirties, says nothing. He sums up his own rise in one word: ruthless. The others, the manager tells him, are already waiting.
65831-iron-hand-chief-of-the-tory-league:
Iron Hand, Chief of the Tory League, or The Double Face, is a dime novel by Frederick Forest, published by Beadle and Adams of New York. This number is dated February 3, 1877, in volume six. The story was entered for copyright in 1871. Its thirteen chapters open with The Quarrel and The Murdered Man, then The Strange Face and The Night Ride.

The Red Witness, The Hot Trail, The Secret Mission, and The Hunted Life pace the middle. A Savage Friend, The Mask Removed, and The Unnatural Brother bring the unmasking. The first chapter sets the Revolution's grievances: colonists who had mastered the wilderness and helped break French power felt their manhood stirring. They would no longer submit to the narrow and oppressive policy of Great Britain.
65898-billy-whiskers-in-france:
Frances Trego Montgomery wrote this tale of a goat at the war, printed in 1919. Florence White Williams drew its cuts. Billy Whiskers is the goat of a set of books by the same hand: his kids, his trip to the South, and his days in camp are past parts of the set. The cut at the front shows Billy in the thick of the war: he ran straight on, he says, with bombs that fell all round him.

The list of parts gives the run of his war. Billy grows sick for home, meets a friend by chance, and makes an ill-timed sneeze. A chief takes him back, and he near kills the cook. He tells his own deeds, and his mate Button scares two maids of care and finds spies in a hay loft.
65981-travels-through-the-states-of-nort:
Travels Through the States of North America, volume two, by Isaac Weld, came out in a second edition in London in 1799. Sixteen plates enrich the set. The travels cover the years 1795, 1796, and 1797. Volume two is told in letters. Letter twenty eight leaves Quebec for Montreal. Post houses, calashes, and Canadian horses fill the road notes. Weld praises the views from the banks of the St Lawrence. He contrasts Canadian farming and character with those of the States.

Letter twenty nine takes the party up the river by bateau. Rapids above Montreal test the boatmen hard. Buffalo skins serve as bedding on the way. Weld notes how Canadians measure distance by smoking breaks. Trois Rivieres, La Chine, and Lake St Louis pass in turn.
66026-a-speech-on-the-principles-of-fina:
A Speech on the Principles of Finance was given by Victoria Woodhull at Cooper Institute in New York City. The date was Thursday, August 3, 1871, and the speech was printed the same year. Woodhull opens with a blunt question: money, is it a principle or a property?

She warns the student of history not to stop at kings, wars, and the rise and fall of states. Those facts, she says, are mere results that dress the page. Behind them lie the true motor powers of history, deeper and broader than the deeds they drive. She traces Assyria, Egypt, Persia, Greece, and Rome in quick strokes. Her point is that a new age of analysis has begun, one that asks what moves nations from within.
66056-the-great-harry-thaw-case-or-a-wom:
Benj H Atwell wrote The Great Harry Thaw Case. Its subtitle calls it A Woman's Sacrifice. A jury table fronts the book in cold print. Thaw's jury sat 47 hours 8 minutes, it says. Their verdict stands listed as disagreement there. Madison Square Garden fills one grim plate.

That hall was the scene of the Thaw-White tragedy. The Tombs prison fills a second plate. A circled window marks Thaw's cell there. Other trials stand compared in the table. Nan Patterson's juries disagreed three times in all. Molineux's second jury freed him in 25 minutes. A graphic, truthful narrative, the title boasts. A young girl's fight for fame fills its pages. Her lover baffled the world's great alienists, it claims. Trial pulp of the century's first great murder case fed the crowds the newspapers had already whipped up.
66073-death-in-venice:
Thomas Mann's novella appears here in English in The Dial for March 1924, in a translation from the German by Kenneth Burke. Gustav von Aschenbach, a famous writer past fifty, leaves his Munich apartment on a spring afternoon after a morning of strained work. The drive of composition will not stop, and the healing sleep he needs at midday has failed him. He walks out past the English Gardens toward the North Cemetery, hoping air and movement will restore him.

At the cemetery he studies the gold inscriptions on the Funeral Hall and loses himself in their mystic phrases. Five chapters carry the story from this restless walk to Venice, the city of the title. The Dial printing, in volume seventy-six of the magazine, brought Mann's tale of the aging artist to American readers in Burke's rendering, complete in a single issue.
66096-travels-through-the-states-of-nort:
Volume 1 of Travels Through the States of North America and the Provinces of Upper and Lower Canada, by Isaac Weld the younger, reached a second edition in London in 1799. Weld traveled in the years 1795, 1796, and 1797. Sixteen plates adorn the two volumes. A preface tells why an Irishman crossed the Atlantic in wartime.

Weld says war was laying waste fair parts of Europe and storms loomed over Ireland, so he wished to test tales of American ease with his own eyes. He asks whether the United States might serve as a fit refuge in a future crisis. His route ran through Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, New Jersey, and New York, then into Canada.
66210-repeat-performance:
