Repeat Performance is a science fiction story by Rog Phillips, taken from Imagination magazine for January 1954. A blurb says the little man knew Ben had been murdered, yet Ben was still alive. It asks if the future was wrong, or merely a dress rehearsal.

Pounding at the door wakes Benny at three thirty in the afternoon. He knows the gruff voice of Calahan, a cop, at once. Benny counts his night work in his head, two wallets on the subway for seventeen dollars and one in an elevator for forty five. An all night crap game near the Wilson El nearly cleaned him. An hour later he stands in a line up of a dozen men before a dark screen and floodlights. Readers get a crime tale where a foreseen murder hangs over a petty thief.
66295-venice:
Venice is a travel book by Beryl de Selincourt and May Sturge Henderson, pictured by Reginald Barratt. The New York edition was published in October nineteen oh seven. A view of the campanile serves as frontispiece. Contents run to eleven chapters, from an introduction and phantoms of the lagoons onward.

The nuptials of Venice and Venice in festival follow. A merchant of Venice and Venice of crusade and pilgrimage take their turns. Two Venetian statues earn a chapter. Venetian waterways fill two long chapters of their own. Artists of the Venetian renaissance come near the end, and a closing chapter treats the soul that endures. Venice herself is poetry, a poet quoted at the start declares. She creates a poet out of the dullest clay, the line goes on.
66360-john-s-other-practice:
John's Other Practice is a science fiction story by Winston Marks, first printed in the magazine Imagination in July 1954. A headnote jokes about its hero's invention. Slot machines usually pain the wallet, but Cunningham's Symptometer also diagnoses the pain.

The narrator tells how John Cunningham ruined a fine medical start. Warned that no romantic should take up his specialty, the handsome intern was married, divorced, disgraced, and broke within three years. He then set himself three goals. He would practice medicine without meeting patients, and win back the family fortune he had squandered. The narrator, now an investigator for a medical association, reports the strange practice that followed. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
66395-the-queen-of-space:
The Queen of Space is a science fiction story by Joseph Slotkin, taken from Imagination magazine for August 1954. Its heroine is Helen LaTour, who had the best hip wriggle in galactic burlesque. In fact it was so good that she hipped herself smack into another dimension. The tale is told in a hardboiled first-person voice by a man drinking on Venus.

He is relaxing with his second Plutonian Stinger in Charley's Venusian Retreat when hot jets sound outside. A scared little character bursts in, wiping his forehead with a huge handkerchief, and asks to join the table. Talk in the copy turns on a smuggler named Luigi. The space control, the little man doubts, will ever catch Luigi here on Venus. It is still a wild, mostly unsettled planet, he says, and besides, Luigi is too smart, speaking as if he knew Luigi personally.
66456-stellar-vengeance:
Frank Freeman wrote the tale Stellar Vengeance. Imagination magazine ran it in February 1955. Walt Granger finds aliens landed by accident, the blurb says. Scientific curiosity makes him capture one of them. Earth becomes the scene of vengeance for that act. A squat, ugly creature talks from a wooden cage.

You invite certain destruction by holding me, it squeals. Your time is short, the creature warns him. Granger kicks the cage's two-by-fours in answer. That's my worry, he grunts at the thing. He was on a geologic survey two hours before. The Millsport Range of rocks and gullies hosted it. He saw the ship rise and caught the creature strayed. Its comrades will return for it, it boasts. Their finding him will be easy, it adds. A surveyor's prisoner makes first contact a feud in Freeman's lean pulp tale of pride and payback.
66539-the-terror-out-of-space:
Dwight Swain wrote this science fiction story for Imagination in July 1954. It opens with a promise: somewhere in the void lies a planet with a new element that can transform men into supermen. It is Boone's job to find that world. Boone is a survey man weighing a rich offer in a drink shop in Gandor City.

Terral, a lean grey man from Associated Independents, ticks the points off on his fingers. Ten thousand credits an Earth year, win or lose. Full command of the field force, and a cut of profits for putting a mekronal unit into production ahead of the Cartel. He raises the bid to fifteen thousand and ten per cent, then accuses Boone of throwing away his future for a woman, Krobis's favorite. Boone clicks his glass down like a period and walks out into the alien night.
66558-the-prince-of-the-captivity-the-ep:
Sydney Grier published The Prince of the Captivity with Blackwood in 1902 at Edinburgh and London. The subtitle calls it the epilogue to a romance, fourth in the Balkan series. Her Uncrowned King and Warden of the Marches head the title page in full. Twenty-four chapters run from both sides of the question to a risorgimento at last.

Lord Usk rides the South Wales Express alone and glad of the empty carriage. A month back he had never seen Felicia Steinherz, and life seemed full enough then. Now her face fills his mind past harvest fields and late roses alike. Glimpses of an ideal in other women had fooled him before in his youth. Love at first sight launches a Balkan tangle of secrets.
66584-the-world-of-chance:
W D Howells sends a young newspaper man out into the world in a novel issued by Harper and Brothers at New York in 1893. The title page lists his other tales, A Hazard of New Fortunes among them.

Ray has lost his place on the Midland Echo. A business change threw him out. His town gives him a farewell dinner at the club. A friend walks the platform with him till two in the morning. They talk of their lives and their loves, as young men do. Ray boards the sleeper and lies wakeful. The champagne sends blood thumping in his ears. He smiles at the honour and affection shown him. Howells built his realism on such small, true moments of American town life.
66727-the-velocipede-its-history-varieti:
A guide to the velocipede fills this book, printed at New York in 1869. Its full head sets out its three fields: the past of the machine, its kinds, and its use. Cuts fill the book. The list of parts opens with the past and the birth of the velocipede. The bicycle is then set out on its own. Laws on the rights of the men who make the machines come next, a sign of a trade in strife.

Hints for men who would buy, and words of help for the new hand, fill the mid pages. The build of the bicycle is then told in full. Kind by kind, the makes of the day are named: those of Wood Brothers, Monod, Witty, and Pickering. Four-wheeled kinds, the three-wheeled kind, and a one-wheeled kind named the Flying Yankee have their parts.
66749-the-fortunes-of-perkin-warbeck-a-r:
The Fortunes of Perkin Warbeck is a historical romance by the author of Frankenstein, in an edition issued at London in 1857. A motto from an old French chronicle heads the book. It tells of a son of England, named Richard of York, who was said to be dead. He lived in good hope of being king of the English.

The flight from Bosworth Field opens the tale in chapter one. Elizabeth of York and Lady Brampton enter in the early chapters. Lambert Simnel, the earlier pretender, gets a chapter of his own. The battle of Newark and a discovery turn the plot toward its hero. Warbeck claimed to be a lost prince of the house of York. The romance follows his hopes, his backers, and his fall across Europe.
66753-traitor-s-choice:
Traitor's Choice is Paul Fairman's science fiction story from Imagination magazine of August 1956. Reed Kendall works at the Canadian Flats Ordnance Research Project, where the defense of the world is planned. The phonovision bell rings, and a man in a silver mask fills the screen. He orders Kendall, in a brutal tone, to lock his office door.

The stranger is a Centaurian agent, or serves them. His people ran a telepathic survey of every married scientist on the project. Only Kendall's love for his wife Clare fits their purpose. The mask lays out the choice in the story's own terms. If Kendall defies the aliens, Clare faces a horrible death. If he complies, a whole planet must die.
67090-the-worm-ouroboros-a-romance:
The Worm Ouroboros, a romance by E R Eddison, was first printed by Jonathan Cape at London in 1922, with art by Keith Henderson; a cheaper form came in 1924. Eddison warns at the start: it is no fable or code tale, but a story to be read for its own sake. Its war is of Demonland against Witchland. Lord Juss and his kin hold the Demon cause, and King Gorice rules his foes from Carcë.

The heads run rich and strange: a wrestling bout for Demonland, conjuring in the Iron Tower, and two armed trips to Impland. Koshtra's heights, Queen Prezmyra, and the fleet at Muelva mark the mid run. The battle of Krothering Side and the latter end of the lords of Witchland close the war. Tale fans get a vast, high, barbaric romance.
67139-shepherds-for-science:
W C Tuttle wrote a Western tale told in the loose speech of cow country. The teller, Ike, rides with Dirty Shirt Jones and three burros toward Piperock town. Gold hunting has failed, and both men long for home and good food. On a hill they meet Magpie Simpkins, sheriff of Yaller Rock County.

Magpie swears both men in as deputies on the spot, to their shock. His cause is sheep, a thing both cow men claim to scorn. Three thousand sheep owned by two partners sit at the heart of the case. Tuttle mixes dry fun with a neat plot of fraud and pride.
67294-what-price-peace:
Frederick Libby wrote a one cent tract on the price of peace, issued in January 1925 from Washington by a council for stopping war. A short form of his case fills the first page, since the tract was sold by the hundred for wide sharing. War causes, he says, meet us on every hand, and peace has not come.

Army men say readiness for war is the way to peace, Libby notes, yet he holds that path will hasten a new world war. He calls for a world court, a world town meeting in the League, and the outlawing of war. Goodwill must be grown from the schools up, he adds, on a long uphill road.
67437-dr-paull-s-theory-a-romance:
Diehl wrote this romance, Dr Paull's Theory, printed at New York in 1893 and dedicated to Henry Irving. Diehl also wrote The Garden of Eden. Sixteen chapters carry it, and several are pages from diaries and notebooks: extracts from the diary of Hugh Paull, and matter found in an old notebook of Lilia Pym.

Chapter one is named Fate. Hugh Paull, house-surgeon to a great city hospital, sits at his desk in a quiet room, working in his spare hours on a treatise about nervous disease. A public event has blocked the streets and stilled the usual noise. A knock comes: an accident has been brought in, an old gentleman thrown from a carriage when his horse bolted. In the ward the old man lies still as death, with a grand face fit for a painter.
67501-adolescence:
Stephen Paget read this lecture to Oxford University Extension students in the Sheldonian Theatre in August 1917. Constable printed it in London that year. The lecture series treated the near future, with problems of construction and reconstruction after the war as its general subject.

Paget notes two gaps pointed out or felt after the reading. The head of University College noted that he had said nothing of how sisters help young men stay straight. Paget also shrinks from exact words for a boy's sex education, holding that a parent or teacher must be able to speak plainly when duty calls.
67511-alice-and-beatrice:
Alice and Beatrice, by Grandmamma, was published in New York and London, with illustrations by John Absolom. Contents open with a visit to Grandmamma, walks to the sea shore, and bathing in the sea.

An evening walk, a steamer, and lacemaking follow. A rainy day brings a story of Pretty and the bear. Russia and the frozen sea come next, then a cellar, a walk to the shore, and a rainbow. Bees swarming, and the fable of the ant and grasshopper, fill chapter six. A sail to Branscombe, with horses carrying coals, and a walk on the hillside with tame and wild rabbits follow. Later chapters treat a shipwreck, a parrot, a kitten, squirrels, and cider making. The length of day in Russia and Finland is explained. Readers get a Victorian childrens book of seaside visits, animal lore, and talk.
67543-the-god-of-civilization-a-romance:
God of Civilization is a romance by Mrs Pittock in a monthly library. Eureka Publishing of Chicago issued it in the Mid Ocean Library, November eighteen ninety. The library cost three dollars a year by subscription, issued monthly in parts. Pittock next novel, Was He a Leper, is announced as in press here.

That tale is laid in Honolulu and deals with the scourge of leprosy. This romance opens with Mabel Miller tired of parties, calls, and theatre going. She wishes something would happen to break the monotony of her life. Her friend marvels, for no girl has more delightful changes of amusement. Winters of gaiety and summers at Santa Cruz or Monterey fill her year.
67546-in-the-name-of-a-woman-a-romance:
A W Marchmont wrote In the Name of a Woman, a romance of plot in Bulgaria. Frederick A Stokes issued the third edition in New York with a nineteen hundred copyright. D Murray Smith drew the pictures. Marchmont had won note for By Right of Sword.

A woman’s cry for help splits a hot night in Sofia. The teller had seen spies trail her past the great church square. He bursts through a gate with his sword cane half drawn. Princess Christina stands at the heart of the web that follows. A duel, a ball, and a palace scene raise the stakes. Spies, a countess with a ruse, and a jail cell fill the midst. A push for the frontier ends the chase in a ruined hut.
67646-all-for-love-or-her-heart-s-sacrif:
All for Love is a dime novel by Mrs. Alex McVeigh Miller, issued as number 1172 of the New Eagle Series of popular copyrights. The series sold carefully selected love stories at fifteen cents a volume. Its list names the reigning writers of the trade: Georgie Sheldon, Charles Garvice, Harriet Lewis, and May Agnes Fleming among them.

The publisher's notice makes the pitch. With such a profusion of good books, no single title can be urged. Any line holding the complete works of those authors is worthy of attention, especially at fifteen cents. The volumes run from 256 to 320 pages, in good type, readable from start to finish. All titles are always in print. Miller's tale, her heart's sacrifice, belongs to the great flood of story papers that carried romance to factory girls and farm wives across America.
67688-some-problems-of-the-peace-confere:
Charles Homer Haskins and Robert Howard Lord wrote on some problems of the peace conference in a book printed at Cambridge in 1920 by the Harvard University Press. The book is given to Archibald Cary Coolidge. Tasks and methods of the conference open the study: the tasks, the problem of frontiers, and the organization of the conference. Great peace conferences are proverbially slow bodies, they begin.

The negotiators of Munster and Osnabruck spent five years on the treaty of Westphalia, and the conferences of Paris and Vienna labored a year, they note. Belgium and Denmark, with Schleswig, the Kiel Canal, and Heligoland, take the second study. Alsace Lorraine, the Rhine and the Saar, a resurrected Poland with Danzig and Galicia, and a collapsed Austria follow. Two Harvard men who served at Paris explain the settlement's hardest knots.
67839-stoles-knitted-crocheted-hairpin-l:
Stoles: Knitted, Crocheted, Hairpin Lace is a pattern book, Star Book 133. The American Thread Company issued it from Broadway, New York, for home makers. Dawn wools, nylon, or orlons are the yarns it is built around here. Adagio, the collar stole on the cover, leads the patterns in full.

Adagio runs twenty one by sixty eight inches, in violet worsted wool. Row by row directions spell out its knit and purl pattern repeats. A matching collar is knitted apart and sewn to the stole ends. Allegro follows in bulky yarn, twenty by sixty six inches without fringe. Gauge notes and stitch keys guide each project in the book.
67905-count-zarka-a-romance:
Sir William Magnay wrote Count Zarka, a romance of plot and sword play in a small state. Ward, Lock and Company issued the book in London in nineteen hundred three. Maurice Greiffenhagen drew its front plate of crossed rapiers. Minister Gersdorff opens the tale with a plan too hot to hold.

Prince Roel of Rapsberg has vanished, and the loss deepens daily. Gersdorff trusts one man in his bureau with the dark task. Young Galabin takes the charge with a bow and a smile. Rozsnyo town holds the core of the strange affair in its walls. Zarka plays terrorist, keeps watch, and finds a secret room. Eyes in a rock cleft and a tell tale light raise the dread. A marriage of the dead gives the tale its grim heart. Prince Roel’s strange road to freedom closes the long game.
68101-yermah-the-dorado-the-story-of-a-l:
Frona Eunice Wait Colburn wrote a lost-race novel set near San Francisco. The book was first filed in 1897 and reworked in 1913. Its hero, Yermah, is called the Dorado in the title. A Swiss saw at the front says truth takes much earth to buy. Colburn gave the book to white knights of all ages.

Verse at the front sets the tale in Golden Gate Park. There, she says, the wise city of Tlamco once rose. A lost race left a spell on that ground, the verse claims. The novel builds a past of shrines and gold on the bay. Fans of lost-world tales get a West Coast turn.
68222-his-fortunate-grace:
His Fortunate Grace, a novel by Gertrude Atherton, was published in 1897. It opens in the house of a rich American father, Mr Forbes. His daughter presses him to share his fortune while he still lives. At the breakfast table the talk turns on wealth and its duties. The young heiress has been reading Marx and Henry George. She argues for a fairer spread of money.

Atherton sets the debate inside a family rather than a pamphlet. The father's caution meets his daughter's new ideas. Questions of votes for women and social reform enter the talk over coffee. The novel belongs to the 1890s wave of fiction about great American fortunes. It asks what the heirs of new money owed to society. It also asks whether a fortune handed over early is a blessing or a burden.
68236-the-colour-out-of-space:
H P Lovecraft wrote this story, printed in Amazing Stories in September 1927, where the editors praised it as one of the finest pieces of literature to come their way. It opens west of Arkham, among wild hills and farms now vacant.

The narrator, surveying for a new reservoir, hears the place called evil and its waste ground the blasted heath. Old Ammi Pierce, a little queer for years, is the only one who still talks of the strange days. French-Canadians, Italians, and Poles have all tried the farms and departed, put off by something imagined rather than seen. When the reservoir floods, the secrets will sink with the deep's. Readers get Lovecraft's most famous tale of a color that fell from the sky.
68256-rat-race:
George Smith wrote a science fiction story that ran in Astounding in August 1947. It opens on a telephone row: Peter Manton wants a dozen mousetraps on a Four-A-One priority, and supply man Brannon laughs at him. There is not a mousetrap in the country, since the makers now make bombsights and tanks.

Manton's laboratory building is rat-proof as a sealed gasoline can and holds no food, yet the mice bring their own. Brannon jeers that a lab which can spot a plane at fifty miles and split atoms should build the better mousetrap itself. Manton hurls a book at an impertinent mouse, watches it disappear, and the word disappear strikes home. The title is the hint.
68496-dwala-a-romance:
George Calderon wrote this romance, Dwala, printed in London in 1904 and dedicated to Kittie. Calderon also wrote The Adventures of Downy Green. Chapter one opens at sunset toward the Borneo mountains, where forest and sea give up their secrets in the softer light.

One sign of men marks the shore: a worn patch like a tiny wilderness in a vast oasis. Meat tins, empty bottles, and old newspapers litter the waterline. A tumble-down hut and shed stand under a rock, a pony looks out of a stable, and something rustles in a big cage. In a hammock sleeps a grizzled, battered man, one brown foot hanging over the edge. A strange figure called the Colonel watches him with a palm leaf, a being more akin to the forest than to men.
68552-the-flying-chance:
The Flying Chance, a tale by Gordon McCreagh, opens at the Philadelphia navy yard. The commandant looks up from a sheaf of papers from the Bureau of Naval Affairs. Ensign Rankin stands at attention before his desk in that first scene. A flat refusal meets the young officer as the talk begins.

Rankin shows no surprise on his brown and alert face at the news. His plea bursts out at once in a rush of protest. He passed in everything else, he insists to his chief. His balance was perfect, his nerve reactions top grade, his blood pressure and hearing sound. Only two paltry points in one test fell short of the mark. Early flight was so dangerous that the service would not waive the smallest flaw, the commandant replies.
68678-the-sporting-chance:
Alice and Claude Askew wrote this sporting novel, published by Ward, Lock in 1910. Every chapter title follows its hero: Mostyn makes his debut, Mostyn sees the Derby, Mostyn accepts a challenge, and so on to Mostyn completing his task.

The first chapter rides to the Derby by coach behind Sir Roderick Macphane, Old Rory. He is a famous whip and master of hounds who swears he will be in his coffin before traveling any other way. His colt Hipponous is the crowd's fancy, and winning the Derby is the ambition of his life. Mostyn Clithero rides at the back with his future brother-in-law. The Askews, who wrote The Shulamite together, blend racing, money, and love.
68686-critical-difference:
Murray Leinster wrote this science fiction tale for Astounding Science Fiction in July 1956. Massy waked one morning as his sleeping cabin's port closed of itself, the tale opens. The room-warmer began to whir while the bright room stayed bitterly cold around him on that morning.

His breath made a fog as he burrowed out from under his covering there. It is colder than yesterday, he thought uneasily in the first pages of the tale. A Colonial Survey officer on his first independent survey must not seem disturbed, in public or even in private, while a colony world turns colder than its charts allow.
68688-the-mill-of-silence:
The Mill of Silence, a mystery novel by B E J Capes, was copyrighted in 1896 and issued by Rand, McNally and Company in Chicago and New York. The book won second prize among eight hundred sixteen entries in the Chicago Record series of mystery stories. That prize series drew wide notice at the time.

Sixty short chapters carry the tale, from the inmates of the mill to a final chapter that asks who killed Modred. A pool of death, a specter hound, and the secret of the wheel mark its Gothic turns. The narrator pieces the case together through meetings, letters, and night pursuits. Its last pages promise one mystery explained and a shadow from the past faced at last.
68726-the-crystal-circe:
Henry Kuttner wrote the tale The Crystal Circe. Astonishing Stories ran it in June 1942. A stratoship from Cairo opens it, late. The teller waits in Manhattan's Port Room at dusk. A curved wall-window shows the landing field. A silvery ship rolls over the tarmac there.

Skyscrapers of New York rise beyond the field. Then the teller spots Arnsen in the room. Steve Arnsen's great shoulders mark him at once. Ten years back they were classmates at Midwestern. Rakehell, laughing Steve dragged Doug O'Brien along. Doug was his room-mate and the dreamer's foil. A shadow of a dream lurked in Doug's eyes. Arnsen stares up with a queer tensity there. A small box snaps open in his hands. A pulp tale of an old friend and a crystal secret launches from an airport's dusk into Kuttner's weird worlds.
68853-pastiche-and-prejudice:
Walkley, the drama critic, gathered essays reprinted from The Times in a volume issued at New York in 1921. The title piece takes up pastiche, the deliberate writing in another's manner. Renan is quoted on Lamennais, who built a style from reminiscences of the Bible into what Renan called a pastiche of genius.

Pastiches of genius are rare, Walkley answers, because genius is rare, and because a writer may mimic another's form but cannot reproduce his spirit. Parody is the pitfall of the kind. Max Beerbohm did not escape it, he says, but Proust did, in a volume of imitations of Balzac, Saint-Simon, and others. Criticism of books and the stage fills the rest.
68858-lady-barbarity-a-romance:
J C Snaith wrote Lady Barbarity, a romance. D Appleton and Company issued it at New York in 1899. Snaith had written Mistress Dorothy Marvin before. Fierceheart the Soldier bears his name too. Twenty-one chapters and an epilogue fill it. Deplores the Scarcity of Men heads the first.

The Rebel Appears and Disappears in turn. An Odd Passage in the Meadow follows at four. I Mix in the High Political heads the fifth. Miss Prue's monstrous behavior fills the ninth. I Play Catherine to Mr Dare's Petruchio stands tenth. An ordeal and playing with fire come next. I Defy Dear Lady Grimstone heads the twelfth. I Come to Tyburn Tree darkens the end. To deny I am handsome would be affectation, she opens. Her face and shape reprove such denial, she says. A witty Jacobite romance lets its heroine narrate her own rebellions.
68860-from-outer-space:
Robert Zacks wrote this tale of old space men and their listeners. The story ran in Startling Stories in May 1952. A grizzled veteran leans back under a transparent dome at start. Young men sit in a half circle, eyes glistening, for his tales.

They have never seen Earth, home of their species, at all. A silvery fungus scar marks the old man chin and brow. Fireflies on one planet seared with heat, not cold, he tells. Each day the group waits hungry for his talk of old Earth. Earth insects fed not on alcohol, he adds, unlike the cold fighting kinds abroad.
68895-a-soldier-s-mother-in-france:
A Soldier's Mother in France is Rheta Childe Dorr's wartime report from the American Expeditionary Force. The Bobbs-Merrill Company published it in Indianapolis in 1918. Dorr had written Inside the Russian Revolution. She dedicates the book to the other mothers, in September 1918. Her own credential is a service pin. It carries a single red star for her only son.

Dorr went to France as a correspondent, sent in spite of being a woman. More than a million American women, she writes, wear pins like hers. Before France she wore hers for one soldier. Afterward she wore it for the whole American army. Thirty-one chapters record what she saw. She adopts the army, visits the trenches, and studies wound shock. Trench fever's defeat gets a chapter. Clemenceau the Tiger and a Lafayette, we're here finale close the book. Writing, she hopes, will lessen other mothers' anxiety.
68922-the-adventure-of-the-broad-arrow-a:
The Adventure of the Broad Arrow is a tale of gold in the dry west. Morley Roberts wrote it, and it came out in London in 1897. The first scene is a bar in a mining town in the heat. A man drinks and says a man can be damned yet live.

Miners know that hell well, he tells the men at the bar. The tale then runs out into sand with no water in sight. A creek bed, the ash of a fire, and a lone white man mark the trail. A gold outcrop and a fight on a stream raise the stakes of the hunt. Sand storms, a road with pits, and a tribe's chief crowd the plot. The mark of the broad arrow ties the threads of the tale.
69104-cadets-of-gascony-two-stories-of-o:
Burton Stevenson wrote two tales of old France that Lippincott published in 1904. Anna Whelen Betts drew the pictures. The first tale, Marsan, calls itself a romance of the Midi. It opens at the corner of a street in Montauban, where a great, stained house blocks the way.

The teller chances on an adventure there, and walks into a hornet's nest. A ride to Cadillac, a vision in the night, and the den of the wolf follow. A Roquefort sets his price and exacts a promise. The tale turns on a vengeance of ten years. The second tale, A Child of the Night, moves to Paris. Its teller finds himself brother to a charming girl and bears torture. Stevenson writes in the cloak and sword vein.
69299-men-into-space:
Murray Leinster wrote Men into Space, a tale in a Berkley form put out in October 1960. Rights rest with Ziv Television Productions, from the year 1960. The tale opens in deep space, where naught has weight at all. A cent piece and a great ship weigh the same there, which is naught.

Ed McCauley strikes a match in the still air of his small room in space. The flame flares as a ball, not as the leaf form it takes on Earth. It then dies, and leaves a ball of white smoke in its place. A note tells that McCauley was a new first rank man when space trips were for bots alone. No man had yet gone up in a rocket and come back safe.
69344-poine-a-study-in-ancient-greek-blo:
Poine, a study in ancient Greek blood-vengeance by Hubert Treston, professor of ancient classics at University College, Cork, was published in London in 1923 by Longmans, Green. A French motto holds that nothing the Hellenes thought is a matter of indifference to the history of civilization. Book one treats poine in Homer across five chapters.

Treston first sets out the general rules of blood-vengeance. He compares cases from the modern Balkans, the Mediterranean, South America, and the old Germanic and Welsh laws. Then he splits the Homeric world in two: a Pelasgian system and an Achaean system, each with its own rules on murder, manslaughter, and kin duty. A trial scene on the shield of Achilles anchors his account of how courts for homicide began.
69362-mendel-s-principles-of-heredity-a-:
A defence of Mendel's principles of heredity was published at Cambridge by the university press warehouse, answering attacks on the new genetics. Gregor Mendel's pea experiments claimed that traits pass in discrete units. The biometric school answered with statistics of continuous variation. The defence takes the particulate view against the statisticians.

Mendel's own paper stands at the book's core, with the argument built around it. The volume reached London, Glasgow, Leipzig, New York, and Bombay through its publishers. It is a founding document of genetics, written mid controversy. The quarrel over unit characters versus averages shaped how heredity is still taught. Plain statement, not school history, fills its pages.
69409-straight-america-a-call-to-nationa:
Straight America is a book on Americanisation by Frances Kellor, published in New York by Macmillan in 1916 in a series called Our National Problems. Its subtitle is a call to national service. Kellor dedicates the book to the president-elect of 1916.

The first chapter asks what is the matter with America. For the first time in its history, Kellor writes, America is consciously ashamed. However divided the country is on preparedness, neutrality in thought has brought no peace of mind. In the midst of great prosperity the nation is restless and dissatisfied, making explanations and apologies. Later chapters treat Americanism, the native American, America-made citizens, the popular vote, and national unity. Kellor ran organisations for the assimilation of immigrants, and her book argues that a nation at war's edge must first make itself one people.
6948-the-secrets-of-the-german-war-offic:
Armgaard Karl Graves, with Edward Lyell Fox, claims to open the secrets of the German war office on the eve of general war. The publishers note the manuscript had lain in their hands since June 1, 1914, before Europe was plunged into war, and they date their foreword August 7, 1914. Graves needs no further praise of his sources, they say, since the chapters speak for themselves.

The first chapter tells how he became a secret agent. It opens on June 12, 1913, when a Liberal member rose in the Commons to demand the secrets of the strange case of Armgaard Graves. From Parliament to the hidden world of spies, the book mixes memoir with exposure. It reads as a wartime warning from a man who says he saw the machine from inside.
69550-mercia-the-astronomer-royal-a-roma:
A Garland Mears, author of Idylls, Legends, and Lyrics, wrote Mercia, the Astronomer Royal as a romance of the future. Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton, Kent and Company issued the novel at London in 1895. A three-part prologue opens in the year of grace 2002, when the world has seen many changes. Nations have risen and fallen, and small states have merged into greater.

Yet peace holds, Mears writes, since science has made war so deadly that a battle would wipe out both sides at once. Through all the years since the close of the nineteenth century, the question of woman's place has stayed at the front. Against that ground the tale sets Mercia, a woman raised to the post of Astronomer Royal. The novel is an early try at picturing a future world ruled by science and by women of learning.
69556-golden-rules-of-medical-evidence:
Stanley Atkinson wrote a small book of golden rules for cure proof in court. Atkinson was a barrister of the Inner Temple in London. He was a peace judge for the County of London as well. He kept the books of the Medico-Legal Society as its clerk. The book is number sixteen in a Golden Rules line.

Atkinson hopes to aid the plain cure man in the box. Old quest juries must grasp his facts, he stresses in front. Men who pose as pros should know both fact and form, he says. Short rules tell how to speak, what to show, and what to shun. Court and cure men share the worth of this brief.
69651-where-england-sets-her-feet-a-roma:
Bernard Capes wrote Where England Sets Her Feet, a romance first printed in March 1918. He gave the book to his son Gareth Wilfrid Capes, then serving in Palestine. Its first scene falls in the second year of Queen Elizabeth's reign.

Robert Angell, vicar of a Surrey village, loses his post over doubts about his faith and sets up a small school. A baby named Brion Middleton comes to board with the family. The chapter list promises an apparition, a voyage, and the taking of a carack. Old enmities and hidden truths drive the tale. The dedication was written in October 1917, while the war still held his son overseas.
69671-greener-than-spruce:
Greener Than Spruce, by Herbert Farris, is an Alaska tale of a green newcomer. Farris also wrote Plenty Grub and Plenty Gold before this book. The tale opens with an old trail veteran mocking young Harris Benton. Maybe greener men have hit Alaska, the old man says, but he doubts it.

The veteran has shown Benton a dozen times how to tie snowshoes. Camp craft lessons on tents and gear have left the teacher hoarse. Snow blindness has worn the old man eyes, so spruce green rests them. He must twist his head from bank to bank to keep that green in view. A plan forms to sled out after the young chechahco soon.
69711-the-star-dreamer-a-romance:
Agnes and Egerton Castle wrote this romance, The Star Dreamer, copyrighted and published at New York in 1903. Lists at the front name the pair's other tales, among them The Pride of Jennico, The Bath Comedy, and The Secret Orchard. A picture of a herb-garden behind an ancient barred gateway fronts the book. The story, a tale of a woman's influence, is dedicated to a lady praised as herself a gracious picture of gifted and generous womanhood.

Contents promise an argument and an introduction before the tale. The first book's chapters carry bright heads: fair, young capable hands; a mass of selfishness; rustling leaves of memory. Back at a new door of life follows. Then come quenchless stars eloquent, eyes blue as his star, healing herbs and warning texts, compact and acceptance, and laying the ghosts.
69879-newer-ideals-of-peace:
Jane Addams of Hull House, Chicago, wrote Newer Ideals of Peace, printed at New York in 1906 in the Citizen Library of economics, politics, and sociology. Addams gives the book to Hull House and its neighbours. Studies in the book trace the slow growth of moral substitutes for war, as a prefatory note states.

Addams had won fame with Democracy and Social Ethics, and the same set lists works by Ely, Ross, and Hobson. Her Hull House work put her daily among immigrants, workers, and the city poor. From that ground she asks how peace can grow as a positive good, not a mere lack of war: through city care, labour fairness, and wider human ties. Earnest and plain, the essays mark an early crest of her thought.
70009-the-plurality-of-the-human-race:
Georges Pouchet, doctor of medicine and aide-naturalist in the museum of Rouen, wrote The Plurality of the Human Race, here Englished from the second edition by Hugh Beavan. The book was published in London in 1864 for the Anthropological Society. Beavan gives his translation to Bulwer-Lytton, with respect due to a great writer and learned man. An editor's preface owns that author and editor differ much in opinion.

The society's committee had committed the translation to Beavan's care, and he took it up with some diffidence. It is likely the first work of its kind, he says, given to English readers in a handy and popular form. He chose a literal rendering where the two tongues parted, to keep Pouchet's real meaning. Of the work's clever nature and terse expression there can be little doubt, he allows, while frankly parting from some of its claims.
70073-caprice:
Ronald Firbank wrote Caprice, a novel printed in London in nineteen seventeen with a front picture by Augustus John. Firbank had earlier written Vainglory and Inclinations. He gave the book to Stephen Hammerton.

The novel opens on a Sunday, with church bells in loud dispute. Saint Mary peals in glee while Saint Ann complains in a cracked voice. Townsfolk toil up the winding ways to church. Gossip runs ahead of the tale: Canon Sinquier's daughter has gone over to Rome, or taken the veil. Firbank's light, sharp prose suits the smart, gossipy world he shows.
70277-med-service:
Murray Leinster wrote Med Service, a tale in a magazine of 1957. Van Dongen illustrated it for the August number. A quotation from a book on probability heads the tale. Unfavourable consequences can never have zero probability, it states. Their chance grows by a high power as actions lengthen, it adds.

Calhoun lay in his bunk and read that book in space. The little med ship floated in overdrive as he read. In overdrive travel there is nothing to do but pass time. A small creature slept curled in the cabin. Its tail was meticulously curled about its nose as it slept. Random noises were provided to keep him sane. Calhoun turned a page and yawned in the tale's progress. A click and a taped voice sounded when the tone came. Leinster gives the space lanes a doctor of their own.
70290-the-adventures-of-hatim-tai-a-roma:
The Adventures of Hatim Taï, a romance translated from the Persian by Duncan Forbes, was revised and edited with an introduction by William Rounseville Alger for a Boston edition of 1896. Alger notes the English version first appeared sixty-five years earlier under the Oriental Translation Fund as a costly folio.

That folio was buried in great libraries and scarcely reached the general public, so the publishers resolved to bring the work out in a handier shape. Forbes's philological preface matter was cut, condensed, and rearranged. Seven books of adventures follow, with notes. Readers get the tales of Hatim, the byword for generosity in Persian story, made readable for a wide audience.
70356-heroes-of-science:
Heroes of Science: Botanists, Zoologists, and Geologists is a collective biography by Martin Duncan, a fellow of the Royal Society, published at London in 1882 by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge. Its subjects are the naturalists to whom natural history owes its shape, from field botanists to the geologists who mapped deep time.

The preface warns that correct life-histories of most naturalists are hard to obtain, since many lived retired, uneventful lives, while the reformers and epoch-makers have had their lives well written. Abstracts of those biographies form a large part of the book. An introduction turns to school-leavers anxious about careers and argues, against the rush to get rich, that knowledge is more valuable than money.
70373-our-arctic-province:
Henry W Elliott wrote Our Arctic Province, a book on Alaska and the Seal Islands put out in New York. Rights run from 1886, and this form came out in 1906. Many drawn views from life and maps fill the book. It sits in a set of books on trips and bold deeds of its age.

Elliott notes that print on Alaska fills shelves and files past count. Scores of thick books and a thousand press notes treat its life and worth. He vows to set self aside and show the land as it is. Brush, pen, and word will work as one, so the reader can judge as if on the ground. A first part tells of the trip of Bering and the find of the land in July 1741. The wreck of the ship, the flight of the crew, and the rush of fur men from Russia follow.
70398-a-bibliography-of-the-writings-of-:
Edward McDonald compiled this bibliography of the writings of Lawrence, printed at Philadelphia by the Centaur Book Shop in 1925, with a foreword by Lawrence himself. An opening list groups the books by kind, the novels running from The White Peacock and Sons and Lovers to Kangaroo. Story volumes, poetry, plays, and travel books follow in the same list, ending with the Verga translations.

The main part gives first editions title by title, then lists Lawrence's pieces in other books and in periodicals, split into poetry and prose. A last section gathers studies and reviews of his work in books and journals. Lawrence's foreword, The Bad Side of Books, opens the volume, musing on books as voices in the air. He wrote it under a cedar tree at the foot of the Rockies, with the desert fading westward before him.
70403-the-miniature-menace:
The Miniature Menace, a novelet by Frank Belknap Long, was printed in Future combined with Science Fiction Stories in 1950. Captain Ralph Langford refused to open fire on an alien space craft, and was condemned without trial for it. Set free, he must probe the strange menace from beyond the stars. If the alien proves an enemy, it will be the most terrible men have ever met.

Langford steps from his deep space cruiser onto the Mars City landing field under harsh rocket glare. A lone girl at the field's far end makes him think of Joan, whom he is to see at hospital. Before he can cross, a Patrol officer strides up and puts him under arrest. Commander Gurney has had him certified as irresponsible before the Commission. Long spins a tale of disgrace, hidden enemies, and a captain fighting to clear his name.
70410-a-history-of-commerce:
Clive Day, Knox Professor of Political Economy at Yale, wrote A History of Commerce, first printed in 1907 and revised and enlarged through many reprints to 1925. Contents divide into ancient, medieval, and modern parts. General conditions, the oriental period, the Greek period, and the Roman period open the long survey of trade.

Medieval chapters treat town trade, land trade, fairs, sea trade, the Levant, and commerce in southern and northern Europe around the year 1000. Modern chapters follow exploration and discovery, credit and crises, the mercantile system, Spain and Portugal, and the Netherlands. England's exports, imports, shipping, and policy take three chapters near the close. Students got a standard textbook.
70456-tomato-products-pulp-ketchup-and-c:
Tomato Products: Pulp, Ketchup and Chili Sauce, Bulletin 21L of the National Canners Association research laboratory, was issued at Washington in August 1923. Bigelow, the laboratory's director, wrote it with Stevenson.

The pulp section insists on care from field to factory: growers should discard rotting tomatoes in the field, the fruit must be washed and sorted on belts. Sorters must give the passing tomatoes their full attention and not trim. Analysis follows, from microscopic examination to solids, sugar, acidity and salt, with long stress on getting specific gravity right. Tables give corrections for hot pulp and the make-up of ketchup, and a short closing part covers chili sauce manufacture.
7054-world-s-best-histories-volume-7-fra:
Guizot and Madame Guizot de Witt carry their history of France into volume seven, covering the Consulate through the Russian campaign. Chapter seven treats the Consulate of 1799 to 1804, chapter eight glory and success, chapter nine glory and conquest, and chapter ten the home government. Glory and illusions in Spain and Austria, the divorce of 1809 to 1810, and glory and madness in Russia close the volume.

The narrative opens with France, after ten years of shocks and sufferings, seeking a free and regular government to secure rights gained through tribulation. Monarchy overthrown, republic tried, and three constitutions accepted and rejected, France still struggled single handed with Europe. Only this seventh volume's span is described here.
70582-her-fairy-prince:
Her Fairy Prince is a novel by Gertrude Warden, printed at Philadelphia by Lippincott in 1895. Warden also wrote The Haunted House at Kew. The tale opens in Boulogne market-place on a hot August forenoon. Two Englishmen meet there after five years apart.

Hallo, Armstrong, cries the first, I thought you were in Australia. Hallo, Garth, answers the second, I thought you were in gaol. Captain Garth is stout, florid, and swaggering, with prematurely white hair and a heavy cavalry moustache. His clothes are carefully brushed and darned, his boots beautifully polished. Wallace Armstrong, the text notes, had already done his best to injure the fine heritage of vigour and beauty he was born with. Warden sets her romance among such worn, charming rogues of the Channel towns.
70615-the-ritual-and-significance-of-the:
Paul Radin's The Ritual and Significance of the Winnebago Medicine Dance was his Columbia dissertation, reprinted from the Journal of American Folk-Lore for April to June 1911. Radin lays out the rite in four parts: the Winnebago ceremony itself, the Ojibwa Mide'wiwin, the Menominee Mide'wiwin, and a reading of what the shared parts mean. A dedication keeps the memory of Evelyn Bresler.

The Medicine Dance is a society, entered by purchase. The Winnebago hold it to repeat a ceremony first set up by the Rabbit, when he initiated the first man into its secrets. Five bands take part, the Ancestor-Host's and the East, North, West, and South bands, each named for its leader. Any band may host, so every band must know the whole ceremony. The contents then sort its speeches, songs, and acts.
70768-the-fields-of-france:
Madame Mary Duclaux wrote The Fields of France, printed in London in 1905. Twenty plates in colour by MacDougall go with the book. She gives it to her mother, like her a lover of the fields of France. Contents open with a farm in the Cantal. A manor in Touraine follows.

The forests of the Oise and a little tour in Provence come next. How the poor lived in the fourteenth century, and the country house of the middle ages, close the set. The first piece is dated 1902. To grasp the Cantal, it says, stand on the pointed crest of the Puy Mary. Where a crater once yawned, a grey cone of clinkstone rises, the Puy de Griou, a perfect sugarloaf. Some twelve or fifteen deep valleys spread from it like the beams of a star.
71012-at-the-sign-of-the-golden-fleece:
Emma Leslie wrote At the Sign of the Golden Fleece, a story of Reformation days printed at London and Edinburgh. A plate shows Wolsey warning that Master Clark has chosen an over-bold messenger. Miles Paton carries the tale.

The preface states the aim: the beginnings of the English Testament. Only the Latin Vulgate was known in Europe before the fifteen hundreds. Greek scholars fleeing Constantinople brought the tongue to Italy, and Erasmus carried the new learning to Oxford. Chapters move from Oxford Fair to Paton Hall, a meeting with Tyndale, and the palace of Placentia. A secret marriage and a precious cargo come before the close.
71127-the-lands-of-silence:
Clements Markham published The Lands of Silence with Cambridge University Press in 1921. His portrait fronts a history of Arctic and Antarctic exploration in two parts. Part one alone runs to forty-four chapters. It starts with the Arctic regions, ice, and tribes around the pole, then turns to Norsemen in Greenland and early English voyages.

Frobisher, Davis, Baffin, and the Hudson's Bay men march through in order. Franklin, his lost expedition, and the long search fill the heart of the tale. Nansen's drift in the Fram, the North West Passage, and bids for the pole close the north. Markham writes as a geographer who knew many actors. Polar hunger, ice craft, and loss fill a grand survey.
71138-pioneers-of-space:
Professor George Adamski presents Pioneers of Space as a trip to the Moon, Mars, and Venus, in a first edition dated August 1949. Leonard-Freefield Company of Los Angeles printed the book, which Adamski dedicates to the goodwill of man. A foreword deals with facts about Mount Palomar before the voyage starts.

Adamski argues in that foreword that Earth cannot be the only world with human life, given the vast number of planets. The chapters then travel from Earth to the Moon, through surprise visits and honoured receptions, to a big city and a terminal city. Mars and Venus follow in turn, and a final chapter brings the party home.
71153-the-sacred-dance:
The Sacred Dance is a study in comparative folklore by Oesterley, a London vicar and scholar. Cambridge University Press published it in nineteen twenty three. The book asks why dance belonged to worship among early peoples of the earth. It takes the Old Testament as its starting point for the inquiry.

Chapters trace the dance among the Israelites in its many set forms. Processional dances, dances round a sacred object, and wild ecstatic dances are sorted. Vintage and harvest feasts, victory songs, weddings, and burials each had their dance. Oesterley then follows each kind through Syrians, Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans in turn. Inscriptions, pottery, old writings, and modern reports supply his facts for the survey. Hebrew words for dancing and their music get a chapter of their own.
7119-the-dolliver-romance:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Dolliver Romance survives in only three chapters the author lived to complete, with scenes and fragments beside them. An introductory note explains the romance would have given final form to his elixir of life theme, for which Septimius Felton was the preliminary study. Having abandoned that study and seemingly forsaken the scheme in 1862, Hawthorne renewed his meditation the following year.

The plan having developed to his satisfaction, he accepted a publisher's proposal. The story would begin as a serial in the Atlantic Monthly for January 1864, his first attempt at such a mode of publication. The fragments that remain hint at an old man, a draught of life, and a house haunted by time. The volume preserves a great romance cut short by death.
71268-skull-face:
Skull-Face, a weird tale by Robert Howard, was printed in Weird Tales across three issues in late 1929. It opens inside a hashish dream, where the narrator floats through strange lands far from earth. Something reaches across the void and tears at the curtains of his vision. A face pushes into sight, yellow like a skull yet alive, with eyes deep in the sockets and jaws that move as if in speech.

The thing's body stays vague, save for high, thin shoulders. For one instant another face peers over that shoulder and is seen with startling clarity. The mists then close again and the vision fades. The tale builds its horror on that unseen master and the dreamer it has marked. Howard wrote it in the pulp style of the day, mixing drug dreams, occult menace, into a story of a hidden power moving against the world.
71297-jurisprudence:
John Salmond, solicitor-general for New Zealand, wrote the treatise on jurisprudence that English-speaking law students used for a generation. This fourth edition of 1913 came from Stevens and Haynes of Temple Bar, alongside his law of torts, and it sets out law as a science with definitions that can bear weight.

The opening chapters ask what jurisprudence studies, how civil law differs from law at large, and how law relates to the administration of justice. Salmond proceeds by analysis: law and fact, the justification of law, its defects, general and special law. The New Zealand judge wrote with a clarity that kept the book in print for decades, and its distinctions still turn up wherever common lawyers define their terms.
71343-the-answering-voice:
Sara Teasdale chose the poems of The Answering Voice, one hundred love lyrics by women, printed in Boston in 1917. Teasdale had written Rivers to the Sea and Helen of Troy, and she gives the happy labor of choosing to her sister. A note at the front states her aim. She has tried to bring together the finest love lyrics written in English by women since the middle of the last century.

In that period, she writes, the work of women first stood level with that of men, and in no field have women done finer work than in poetry. True love poems by women were scarce before, she finds, with two old names excepted. She has taken no long poems and no translations. She has also passed over poems in which a woman writes in a man's voice rather than her own.
71732-norman-prince:
Norman Prince was an American volunteer who died for France, and Houghton Mifflin published this memorial volume in December 1917, with a memoir by George Babbitt. The dedication goes to the Lafayette Flying Squadron, the gallant young Americans who led the way their country was later to follow.

Prince helped found the American escadrille that flew for France before the United States entered the Great War, and he died of his wounds after a crash in 1916. The book builds his record in parts: memoir, his own story, his letters, words from his father, a comrade's tribute, and an account of his brother's service. Such volumes fixed the volunteer airmen in American memory as knights of a new element.
7183-doctor-grimshawe-s-secret-a-romance:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Doctor Grimshawe's Secret reaches print through his son Julian, who edited it with a preface and notes and dedicated it to George Parsons Lathrop and his wife. Julian admits the risk plainly. Friends of great writers often drag raw work from a closed desk with more zeal than judgment. A man in life tends to publish only what readers have time to read.

That honest preface frames a posthumous romance, offered not as a finished masterpiece but as a tale worth seeing in the light. Hawthorne's name promises his usual mix of mystery and moral shadow, and the editor's care lets readers judge the fragment for themselves. The book stands as a glimpse of work left behind at his death.
71884-the-great-masters-of-russian-liter:
Ernest Dupuy wrote The Great Masters of Russian Literature in the Nineteenth Century, and Nathan Haskell Dole translated it into English. Crowell and Company published the book in New York in 1886. Dupuy argues that Russian writing came into its own only in the last fifty years, after a long age of imitation.

Three prose writers get full studies. The book gives Gogol the first and longest section, then moves to Turgenev, and then to Count Tolstoy. An appendix and an index close the volume. Dupuy shows how Pushkin pointed the way toward a truly Russian literature before Gogol took it up. For English readers of the time, the book offered a clear first map of a foreign literature then little known.
71915-venice:
Clara Erskine Clement wrote Venice, the Queen of the Adriatic, with illustrations, issued at Boston by Dana Estes and Company with copyright in eighteen ninety three. Clement had earlier written Naples and Constantinople in the same manner. A front plate shows the Bridge of Sighs. Nineteen chapters and an index fill the book. Chapter one is To Day and Long Ago. A Summer Day stands second.

The Doges, their power and achievements, fill chapter three. The Venetians at Constantinople and modern processions and festivals follow. Gradenigo, Tiepolo, and the Council of Ten bring the secret state. Murano and the glass makers, Marino Faliero, and Burano and Torcello fill the middle. The Two Foscari, Venetian women, and the archives follow. The treasures of the Piazza, palaces and pictures, and the Accademia close the tour. Travellers get a full, loving city history.
72003-ending-the-depression-through-plan:
Bernard London wrote Ending the Depression Through Planned Obsolescence, a bold plan printed at New York in 1932. London starts from a paradox of plenty. Banks and stores stand full, mills and fields stand ready, yet millions lack a fair standard of life while stocks rot and prices fall.

Old thought held that nature is stingy and want is the rule, as Malthus warned in 1798. New tools and science, London says, have flipped the lack: the hard task now is to plan buyers, not spur makers. Fear makes folk use goods too long and kills jobs, he holds. His cure gives goods a set life span, so trade flows and work returns by design.
72104-interference:
Interference is a novel by Croker, author of Proper Pride and Pretty Miss Neville, printed at London in 1891 in three volumes. This is volume one, and its ten chapters open at Ballingoole, a town in the south of Ireland. Croker says the town startles strangers, being so amazingly unlike its name: it recalls, they say, a fine old English village.

Fifty years before the tale, Ballingoole was the stronghold of one of the most rigidly exclusive circles in the south. Retired officers, wealthy widows, and well born spinsters filled its noble houses, and a baronet graced the roll. Chapter heads promise gossip without tea, the Malones of Bridgetstown, Foxy Joe, and Betty making two conquests.
72105-interference:
Volume two of Interference, a three volume novel by Croker, appeared in London in eighteen ninety one. It continues an Irish country house story of cousins, chaperones, and coming out. Croker, the author of Pretty Miss Neville and Diana Barrington, sets the action among Anglo Irish families. In that world a girl's first season could settle her future.

The volume opens with Betty, now eighteen, invited to make her debut at Lord Enniscorthy's ball. She will go under the wing of the Moores of Roskeen, powers in the county. Her older friend Miss Dopping arranges the dress and the plan. The chapter titles promise quarrels and secrets: tales from Foxy Joe, a major's last telegram, and an unexpected bride elect. Croker keeps several courtships in play at once and lets gossip do much of the plot's work.
72191-second-chance:
Robert Hoskins wrote a science fiction tale printed in the April 1962 issue of a pulp magazine. A boy of twelve runs for his life from six boys on hot blacktop in summer. Trapped in a dead end lane, he is dug out of a pile of trash and beaten for tales told to the school head.

A man named Johnson views the scene on a screen, and his old wounds of nerve throb in shared pain. He brags that he got back at each boy, and that he was the last child they beat. Talk with Cavendish turns on if sweet revenge can heal a past that still hurts.
72210-interference:
Croker, author of Proper Pride and Diana Barrington, wrote this novel in three volumes, and White and Company published the third volume at London in 1891. Its contents run from a chapter called Miserrime through The Honeymoon, A New Life, and a confession and a surprise for George, to a chapter where Belle's wish is fulfilled.

Volume three opens at the Indian station of Mangobad. George Holroyd, on the strength of an increase of income, has bought two ponies and a cart and taken a bungalow with a rose-screened verandah. The station guesses the truth: he is to marry a bride of nineteen, Irish and pretty, from a quiet country life. The ladies besiege Captain La Touche for particulars and load the groom with advice. Then Holroyd electrifies the community by changing to a gloomy house, the very bungalow where the last tenant, Major Bagshawe, cut his throat.
7227-mornings-in-florence:
John Ruskin begins his mornings in Florence at Santa Croce with a firm guide's claim: if a visitor cares for old art at all, Giotto is the artist to examine first. Florence, Giotto's birthplace, shows his pictures of every date and kind, from small panels to vast walls, painted from age twelve to sixty. Assisi and Padua hold fine work too, but neither gives the full range.

Ruskin urges the reader to start with Giotto at his best time and in his best kind, then to learn the city through his eyes. The book walks church by church, turning looking into a discipline of attention. Ruskin's prose mixes art history with direct address, as if a learned friend stood beside the reader in the chapel.
72277-thunder-in-space:
Lester del Rey wrote this science fiction story for Amazing Stories in June 1962. Finlay illustrated the tale of a space station in a cold war sky. The men on the station had a word for trouble, the blurb says at the front: thunder.

Always it had been thunder on earth, the blurb goes on in its warning. Now warheads decayed and the Soviets played a mysterious game above the earth. In a formal garden in Geneva, two men sit on a marble bench as the tale opens, the old President trembling as he lights a cigarette and speaks of stalemate.
72517-little-men-of-space:
Frank Belknap Long wrote a tale printed in a magazine dated June and July 1953. A head note says the children in it were very young, yet faced a crunch that would have driven most grown folk mad. Long, the note adds, learned horror from H P Lovecraft and knew that the very small can scare more than the very large.

John Elwood watches his children come home across a lawn in bright October sun, lunch baskets in hand. Mary Anne leads, squealing at the sight of her father, while Melvin, aged eleven, hangs back with more care. Elwood for a glad moment forgets bills, scuffed shoes, and the mad side of being a parent.
72546-thomas-nast-s-christmas-drawings-f:
Thomas Nast's Christmas drawings were bound in one book for the first time. Harper and Brothers put it out in New York in 1890. The rights date to 1889, and Nast marks a card for 1892. Its sub-title calls the plates drawings for the human race. The house note says they speak to all, of each faith or none.

Santa, stockings, and feast fun fill plate after plate. One joke card wins a prize for straying most from its theme. That card shows summer heat, flies, and the Fourth of July. Nast's bold hand made the feast's look for his age. Young and old get his warm, sly cheer in full.
7259-shock-and-awe-achieving-rapid-domin:
Harlan K. Ullman and James P. Wade wrote Shock and Awe: Achieving Rapid Dominance for the National Defense University Press in December 1996, with L. A. Bud Edney, Fred M. Franks, Charles A. Horner, Jonathan T. Howe, and Keith Brendley. The text came from the Command and Control Research Program of the Office of the Assistant Secretary of Defense, where its pages counted as public information.

Its title names a doctrine of swift, overwhelming effect, meant to shape an enemy's will as much as his forces. The book lays out that idea in the sober prose of military study, with a foreword and prologue framing the argument. Readers meet a 1990s attempt to rethink dominance for a new age of war.
72640-the-pearl-of-patience:
The Pearl of Patience is a tale for boys by Mrs Madeline Leslie, out at Boston in the rights year of eighteen sixty-eight. It is the sixth part of a set of faith tales for boys, each named for a pearl of a grace. A twin set for girls runs in the same form. A verse on the prize past long grace in well work heads the book.

Parts treat a boys spell drill, a tooth pain, a girls tale, and a boys sin. The tale opens at the morn bell, with a small boy on the floor at war with a knot in his shoe. His mother will not let the nurse undo it for him, since he has not in truth tried. She bids him learn grace in small fights. That shoe knot is the first drill of the book.
72647-renaissance-literary-theory-and-pr:
Renaissance Literary Theory and Practice by Charles Sears Baldwin, edited by Donald Lemen Clark, surveys classicism in the rhetoric and poetic of Italy, France, and England from 1400 to 1600. First issued by Columbia University Press in 1939 and reprinted in 1959. It opens with the Renaissance as a literary period, then takes up humanistic Latin, Greek, and the rise of the vernaculars.

Later chapters treat imitation in prose and lyric, the romance cycles of Pulci, Boiardo, Ariosto, and Tasso, drama, and the poetics of Vida, Scaliger, Ronsard, and Sidney. A final chapter on prose narrative reaches Bandello and Marguerite de Navarre. The book is dedicated to the memory of Thomas More.
72716-hell-on-ice:
Edward Ellsberg, a commander known for books on salvage and submarines such as On the Bottom and Pigboats, published Hell on Ice in New York in 1938. Its subtitle calls it the saga of the Jeannette. The book is dedicated to Emma Wotton De Long, still waiting after sixty years to rejoin the man who sailed away in command.

The first chapter opens in 1909 as the battle fleet steams into Hampton Roads, then turns back to the lost Arctic expedition. De Long's ship and her sledging parties became one of the famous disasters of polar exploration. Readers get a naval officer's retelling of the Jeannette tragedy.
7278-horace:
Theodore Martin's Horace, from the series Ancient Classics for English Readers, follows the Roman poet from birth and schooling. His campaign with Brutus and Cassius, return to Rome after Philippi, and early poems come next. Martin then traces the introduction to Maecenas, the journey to Brundusium, the first book of Satires, and the gift of the Sabine farm.

Life in Rome, Horace's famous bore, and the extravagance of Roman dinners fill the later chapters. Love poetry, poems to friends, praise of contentment, astrology, views of a hereafter, and relations with Maecenas close the survey. Martin writes a clear, friendly life for English readers, letting Horace's wit and moderation shine through.
72786-of-holy-disobedience:
Of Holy Disobedience is a pamphlet by Muste, issued as Pendle Hill number sixty four in January 1952. Pendle Hill at Wallingford in Pennsylvania published the tract at thirty five cents. It opens with a long quotation from the novel Bread and Wine by Ignazio Silone. 

In the scene, slogans against the war and against Fascism have been written on walls in the night. The girl Bianchina cannot understand the fuss about a few inscriptions, and Don Paolo explains it to her. The land of propaganda, he says, is built on unanimity, and one man saying no breaks the spell. Even a poor, solitary, sick man, even a peaceful thinker, must be stifled in that order. Muste sets that fiction at the head of his tract because it states the stakes of disobedience to a regime that demands total assent.
72898-the-winners-in-life-s-race:
The Winners in Life's Race, or The Great Backboned Family, is a natural history book by Arabella Buckley, published by Appleton in New York in 1883. Buckley had written The Fairyland of Science. This volume gives an account of the vertebrate animals. It is a natural sequel to her earlier book, Life and Her Children, which treated the invertebrates, though she calls it a more independent work.

The lower forms of life, she explains, can be treated almost without geology. The vertebrates cannot: their groups are closely linked yet sharply separated, so she must carry readers into the past to make the present clear. Her frontispiece shows a luminous fish of the deep sea. Her object, a note says, is to follow the tide of life.
72967-chalk-face:
Waldo Frank wrote Chalk Face for his father, a fellow lover of mystery tales, and says so in a letter at its front. The book, out in 1924 from Boni and Liveright, is part crime tale, part parable, as he warns. Its three parts name a man with a white head, another room, and a challenge.

Frank asks what tale is not a mystery tale, and calls life itself the great one. The narrator, a man of science who failed in his sphere, tells his own dark story. Frank, a seeker after America's soul in his essays, here turned inward to conscience and desire. A verse from Job stands at the head of the tale.
73048-towards-an-enduring-peace:
Randolph S Bourne compiled a symposium of peace proposals and programs from 1914 to 1916, with an introduction by Franklin H Giddings. The American Association for International Conciliation issued the book. Part one treats principles of a settlement, first in economic terms. John A Hobson writes on economic opportunity, and H N Brailsford on trade as a cause of war.

Walter Lippmann treats diplomacy, and Arnold J Toynbee writes on nationality. A second part argues for a league of peace, with pieces by Charles W Eliot and A Lawrence Lowell. A third part looks toward the future. Jane Addams is among the contributors listed.
73059-my-four-weeks-in-france:
Ring Lardner wrote this comic account of his four weeks in France as a war correspondent, printed at Indianapolis in 1918. Wallace Morgan drew the pictures, and Lardner had written Gullible's Travels before it. Chapter heads promise dodging submarines, strange sights in Paris, and mishaps on the way to the American camp. A stop in London and a round of questions at home close the trip.

The diary opens on July 18, when a man from Connecticut asks if he would like to go to France. Lardner, thirty-two years old with a wife and three children, pleads that he knows nothing about war. That, he is told, has frequently been proved to have nothing to do with it.
7307-the-precipice:
Ivan Goncharov's Precipice, Obryv in Russian, comes here in a condensed translation whose translator is not named. Its preface places Goncharov among the great circle of Russian writers gathered around the Contemporary under Nekrasov, beside Turgenev, Dostoevsky, Tolstoy, Belinsky, and Herzen. Goncharov, born in 1812, lacked the marked genius of the first three, the preface admits, yet his obscurity in the West owes something to a life with nothing sensational in it.

The novel's power lies instead in steady observation of Russian society, love, and moral falling, told without scandal's aid. This condensed text keeps the story's shape while shortening its long, patient scenes. Readers get a classic Russian novel in a briefer, still serious form.
73226-the-wellsprings-of-space:
The Wellsprings of Space is a science tale by Teichner, with art by Adkins, first set in a big pulp sheet in the early nineteen sixties. A head note sets its world: like wells in the waste, they were spaced through the void. Their task is to feed the spark thirst of the giant ships.

A note tells that no proof was found its rights were made new in law. But one old man had seen the catch, that note warns. What coin serves to buy stuff from such wells? Its first scene brings three top men of lore to a sage of three hundred years. They come to tell him their great win: the world of star lore at last holds one view.
73557-the-principles-and-objects-of-geol:
Hume's Principles and Objects of Geology, with special reference to the geology of Egypt, was printed at Cairo in 1911. Hume directed the Geological Survey of Egypt, and the work began as technical lectures delivered at Giza in January and February 1910. It was issued by the Survey Department of the Egyptian Ministry of Finance.

Figures show two anticlines and a syncline, overfolding strata, an unconformity in the Fayum and a fault in a coal seam. Hume notes that thirteen years of survey work have mapped Egypt's varied surface of limestones, sands, clays, sandstones, granites and schists. He reads the Moqattam hills behind the Citadel as a lesson in how those rocks weather, and traces the change from Cairo toward Aswan.
73586-an-enemy-of-peace:
Ralph Burke wrote a science fiction tale printed in a magazine dated February 1957. A head note says foes of peace who threaten the System must be wiped out, one way or another. If all else fails, the note adds with a shrug, a man can always go to war with them.

Center City belongs to Lloyd Riddell, who held it together while atomic fire laid waste the horizon in years past. A young spy, Len Colter, brings word that David Barr in Northburg calls for Center City to be wiped out. Riddell sends the boy back to scout when the attack will come, and calls for a man named Naylor.
7364-the-albany-depot-a-farce:
W. D. Howells's Albany Depot, a farce published by Harper and Brothers in 1892, sets its action in Boston, in a ladies' room opening from a public hall. Mrs Edward Roberts enters laden with proofs of an afternoon's shopping and studies the room with a searching gaze. She finds suburban shoppers on settees with bags and packages, old ladies in rocking chairs, and a chorewoman mopping the floor between expresses.

Mrs Roberts appeals to the chorewoman in anxiety: her husband was to meet her at ten minutes past three, yet no gentlemen seem to be about. From that small missed meeting Howells spins a one-act comedy of manners, misunderstandings, and married talk. The farce plays briskly, all talk and timing in a waiting room.
73662-the-eyes-of-innocence:
Maurice Leblanc wrote The Eyes of Innocence, shown here in English by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos at New York in 1920. Leblanc had writ Arsene Lupin and The Golden Triangle. Eleven chapters carry the tale. Gilberte leads the plot and gives the first chapter its name. A front print shows a faint sound heard behind a woman.

The tale opens at the Villa pension des Deux Mondes at Dieppe. A waiter asks two travellers for their names for his book. Gilberte writes Mme Armand and daughter, from London. Her mother is too tired to say where they go next. Gilberte laughs that they come from England, Germany, and Russia to a France she does not yet know. Her mother asks in a sad voice if she will find happiness there. Love and suitors drive the tale.
73675-a-jest-and-a-vengeance:
A Jest and a Vengeance, a story by E Hoffmann Price, first reached print in Weird Tales in September nineteen twenty nine. The hosted text opens in a sultan's palace in a land called Angor lana. A bullet flattens on the carved wall behind Sultan Schamas ad Din and sprays him with lead and marble bits.

The sultan, calm, notes that the shooter is a poor marksman. He moves his cushions a sword's length aside to sit safe from the mosque tower. His old wazir Amru brings his pipe to the new place. The sultan thinks the shot came from his brother's son. Drums in the hills mutter of revolt, so danger presses from outside and inside at once.
7371-a-sicilian-romance:
Ann Radcliffe helped invent the Gothic romance, and this early novel, published in 1790, shows the form taking shape. A traveler hears of a castle with a solemn history, preserved in a manuscript kept by monks, and the novel that follows is that history retold. The scene is Sicily near the close of the sixteenth century, under Ferdinand, fifth marquis of Mazzini.

Inside the marquis's castle, family secrets, hidden rooms, and long-buried wrongs drive the plot, as the Mazzini household unravels around its daughters. Radcliffe builds suspense through landscape and atmosphere: dark corridors, distant music, and a past that will not stay buried. The book is shorter and swifter than her later romances, and a clear starting point for her work.
73724-the-alien-intelligence:
Jack Williamson wrote The Alien Intelligence, a science fiction story run in Science Wonder Stories for July and August nineteen twenty nine. An editor note ranks it beside A Merritt Moon Pool as a remarkable story. Williamson science, while fantastic, stays within the realms of possibility, the note holds. Chapter one is The Mountain of the Moon. A narrator crosses a sandy waste after noon under a red sun.

Before me, not half a mile away, rose the nearest ramparts of the Mountain of the Moon, he says. The air was still and intolerable, he adds. A plate shows the hero firing at a vessel and splashing liquid over a foe in a purple robe. The flesh was dyed deep purple and partially consumed, the caption says. Adventure on the Moon, with a strange intelligence, follows. Fans get early Williamson space romance.
73750-the-prince-of-space:
Jack Williamson wrote this science fiction tale, first printed in Amazing Stories in January 1931, with pictures by Morey. Williamson had written The Metal Man and The Green Girl. An editor's note at the head argues that even great observatories cannot satisfy the astronomers. An observatory twice as high, fitted with a far more enormous telescope, would be more likely to hit the mark. What may be seen then calls for imagination joined to science.

The first chapter is headed Ten Million Eagles Reward. A headline cries that a space flier was found drifting with two hundred dead. The notorious pirate called the Prince of Space is believed to have committed the ghastly outrage. William Windsor, a newspaperman of forty, rides a moving walk down Fifth Avenue, listening to speakers shout his own story. Bill had risked his life in a mad flight on a sunship to beat his rivals.
73793-the-lost-race:
Robert Howard's The Lost Race, printed in Weird Tales in January 1927, follows Cororuc, a Briton, hurrying home through a dark Cornish forest. He has been on a secret mission to the wild Cornish tribesmen and wants no more of their country. In the mountains lurks Buruc the Cruel, a bandit chief who falls on travelers, and the forest itself seems empty of birds, beasts, and men.

Howard builds his man carefully: six feet tall, lean and strong, with gray eyes and long yellow hair. He wears dressed deerskin and carries a yew bow, a bronze broadsword and dagger, and a small round shield rimmed with bronze. Then, rounding a great tree, he hears the sounds of a fight. The tale is an early Howard piece of ancient Britain, mixing history and adventure.
73812-the-boy-who-never-lost-a-chance:
Annette Lyster wrote The Boy Who Never Lost a Chance, a tale put out in London by a tract group. Lyster had told tales of small maids and of Clarice Egerton. The list of parts is built on the word chance. Chance by sea and chance by land lead the set.

The tale opens when rail roads were still new in England. Men from Birmingham lay rails to link a port in Essex with a town inland. The salt trade gave the line its cause. Salt marsh spread wide near the port, which the tale calls Sandsea. The meal for the work gang came by foot, with no cart to bear it. Best chance of all, a new chance, a fish shop man, and a night school fill the parts that trace the boy rise.
73921-domestic-service:
Domestic Service, by Lucy Maynard Salmon, reached a second edition at New York in 1901. Macmillan issued it with an added chapter on domestic service in Europe. Copyright was first taken in 1897 for the study of household work. A long line from Emerson heads the contents as the book motto.
