Reform of the household must not be partial, that motto from Emerson insists. It must correct the whole system of social living, come with plain living and high thinking. It must break up caste and put domestic service on another foundation, the quote holds. Historical aspects of domestic employments fill the second chapter in her plan. A college teacher brought history and economics to the servant question in this study.
73976-air-service-boys-flying-for-france:
Charles Amory Beach wrote Air Service Boys Flying for France, dated nineteen eighteen, with pictures by Robert Gaston Herbert. The book forms part of a boys' series on the air service. Beach had written a mate volume on flying over the enemy's lines.

The airplane chums say goodbye to their flying school and sail in secret for France. Perils come within and without, and a submarine is sunk on the way. A Zeppelin raid on London and a French flying school follow. The boys join the Lafayette Escadrille and hover over Verdun. A bombing unit wrecks a munition plant, as the front picture shows. One boy is lost in a sea of clouds.
74120-the-hairy-ones-shall-dance:
The Hairy Ones Shall Dance is a novel of horror by Gans T. Field. The text was taken from Weird Tales, where it ran in the first three months of 1938. The tale is billed as one of stark horror that struck in the midst of a spirit seance. It tells of terror and sudden death, and of a frightful thing that made its lair in a place called the Devil's Croft.

The tale is framed as a note to whom it may concern. The writer says he sets his account down as a challenge to the great army of doubters, of which he once was one. He writes it brief and plain, by his own word. He warns that the tale may shake in spots. The hand that writes it, he says, still quivers from his recent ordeal.
74272-the-charm-of-venice:
The Charm of Venice is an anthology of writings on Venice, compiled by Alfred Hyatt and published in London by Chatto and Windus in 1908. Hyatt's note sets out the plan. It is always delightful, he says, to read about Venice. The praise of London is sung by Londoners and of Paris by Parisians. But the beauty of Venice has been written by members of every nation, more than by the Venetians themselves.

From those praises Hyatt chose prose and poems that paint the city's charms briefly. The contents divide the city by its spells. Venice from the sea comes first, then the sea spell, gondola and gondolier, island and lagoon, and canal and bridge. Later parts treat architecture and art, a Venetian day, the seasons, and Venice of the past. The book is a garland of other men's raptures, arranged by a lover of the city.
74275-theology-in-romance:
Madeline Leslie and Baker wrote Theology in Romance, or The Catechism and the Dermott Family, printed at Boston in 1859. Baker had earlier issued The Catechism Tested by the Bible, which sold out in weeks. More than two hundred thousand copies of the catechism works had been printed by this date.

The volumes are given to young converts of the great revival of 1858, to aid their growth in Christian knowledge and grace. Story form carries doctrine: a family catechising scene heads the book as its emblem. Translations into foreign tongues, including Arabic for use in Syria, spread the method abroad. Sunday school and family readers get teaching wrapped in domestic tale.
74276-arthur-s-inheritance:
Emma Leslie wrote this tale for the young, printed by Blackie and Son of London, Glasgow, and Dublin in 1901. Paul Hardy drew its three plates. Leslie had written Gytha's Message and How the Strike Began. The front plate shows Mr Bristow stopping to look hard at Arthur.

The tale opens in a county family, where a tall lad of fifteen owns to a bold act and begs his sisters to shield him from their mother. His father's death has changed all their lives, and he knows a lad like him must now help earn their keep. Chapters move through ends that will not meet, a new railway, a black eye, and a missing letter. The subtitle asks how Arthur conquered, and the story answers by work.
74479-because-of-conscience:
Because of Conscience is a novel of Huguenots in old New York by Amy Blanchard, printed at Philadelphia and London in 1901. Lippincott issued it. Blanchard also wrote Two Girls and Betty of Wye. She dedicates the book to Eliza Elvira Kenyon, whose example had been her stay for many years. Twenty chapters carry the tale.

Nothing in the world smelled so sweet as fresh sun-dried linen, Alaine thinks, watching Michelle heap the white pile on her arms. A loaf baking in the oven comes second in her thoughts. Chapters ahead promise a cider frolic, plot and counterplot, and a night in May. General Jacques and Pierre the engagé cross the tale. Blanchard tells of French settlers holding their faith in a new land.
74544-aldyth-s-inheritance:
Eglanton Thorne wrote Aldyth Inheritance, a tale put out in London by a tract group. Thorne had told tales of an old jug and of two crowns. The tale opens with the Bland family, met in a new and strange way.

Guy Lorraine enters in the third part, as a key man of the cast. A maker of strife, talk in the town, and wrong reads of each heart fill the midst. Stephen Lorraine comes to terms with his heir, then calls in his law man. A feast at Wyndham, grief and joy side by side, and a long deferred hope mark the turn. Aldyth wakes from a dream to face a call to the great house. A crash in the hunt field and a wrong laid bare close the list of parts.
74588-the-boys-of-columbia-high-on-the-i:
Graham B Forbes sent his schoolboys Out for the Hockey Championship in The Boys of Columbia High on the Ice, issued by Grosset and Dunlap at New York in 1911. The series also covers the diamond, the river, and the gridiron, at fifty cents a volume. Chapter one is called Rule or Ruin.

Frank Allen locks a skate to his shoe when Lanky tempts him with a spin on a new ice-boat, the Humming Bird. The Clifford seven get a challenge, an athletic committee meets, and Brutus changes his mind. A mystery, a volunteer fire brigade, and an old farmer's secret fill the middle. The campfire on Rattail Island and a great victory close the tale.
74625-cinderella-s-prince:
Cinderellas Prince is a tale for the young by Marian Hurrell. A faith tract house in London put the small book out. Its title casts a poor girl in the glass slip mould of the old tale. No year is shown in the front pages of the hosted text.

Ella, the slighted girl, bears loads at home and shame at school in turn. A dog named Bruno comes to her aid in an early part of the tale. A godmother in plain form, a pet ape, and a house fire mark the turns. Truth comes out, a school mate owns her fault, and peace is won. The last part gives Ella the prince of the title in her own life.
74654-essays-on-the-use-and-limit-of-the:
Essays on the Use and Limit of the Imagination in Science is a small book by John Tyndall, published in London by Longmans in 1870. Its core is a discourse on the scientific use of the imagination. Tyndall gave it before the British Association at Liverpool in September 1870. An address on the limit of the imagination, given at Norwich in 1868, stands beside it. A short essay of earlier thoughts completes the set. Both pieces treat the bond of life and mind to matter and force.

The book opens with the press storm the discourse raised. The Times is quoted on the glory of the natural philosopher. Newton's fame, it says, rests not on the leap from apple to moon but on patient proof. Tyndall answers his critics in kind. The essays are a Victorian scientist's plea for bold thought held in by fact.
74798-tolerance:
Hendrik Willem van Loon published 'Tolerance' with Boni and Liveright of New York in 1925, opening with Spinoza's words that the true end of the state is liberty. He dedicates the book to the memory of John Nichols. A prologue tells a fable: mankind lived happily in the peaceful Valley of Ignorance, where a little stream of Knowledge trickled through a gully from the Mountains of the Past.

In that valley whatever was old was venerable, and the Old Men Who Knew mumbled holy words from a book written a thousand years before. The chapters then march through the tyranny of ignorance, the Greeks, and the Inquisition. Erasmus, Rabelais, Montaigne, Bruno, and Spinoza each get a chapter, and the survey ends with Voltaire, the Encyclopedia, Lessing, Tom Paine, and the last hundred years.
74814-justin-morgan-founder-of-his-race:
Justin Morgan, Founder of His Race is, in its author's words, the romantic history of a horse. Eleanor Waring Burnham wrote it, and the Shakespeare Press of New York published it in 1911. Her husband, Roger Noble Burnham, modelled the frontispiece. Burnham's foreword admits the record of Justin Morgan's life and origin is full of contradictions.

She chose from the conflicting material what best kept the story whole. The tale is told through True, the great horse's son. Chapters follow True broken to harness, his meeting with his father, and Mistress Lloyd of Maryland, who gives him his first ribbon. True then goes to found his race. The book is a foundation legend for the Morgan breed, written as fiction with a breeder's devotion behind it.
74826-the-sea-charm-of-venice:
The Sea-Charm of Venice is a prose study of Venice by Stopford Brooke. Dutton published it in New York in 1907. Brooke begins with the coming of Attila into Europe. He argues that the Hun's conquests gave rise to two great sea powers. One was England. The other was Venice.

The opening chapter traces the city's birth. Roman nobles fled the mainland towns for the lagoon islands. They settled at Torcello and Rialto. From that flight grew Venice, Queen of the Sea. Brooke stresses her pure Roman character. The Goths changed Italy but never touched Venice. Byzantium, not Rome in Italy, was her nursing mother. Her sea position shaped her art, her trade, and her customs.
74830-in-sargasso-missing-a-romance:
Missing, a romance by Julius Chambers, tells the tale of Captain Austin Clark of the tramp steamer Caribas. Chambers had written A Mad World and Its People before this book, which bears a copyright of 1896. Clark, the title page says, spent two years as a captive among the people of the seaweed sea.

The preface paints the Sargasso Sea as a vast waste of weed, vines, and bloom a week's sail from New York. Lost ships drift there, and a nation of castaways has grown up among the hulks. Chapters treat Sargasson manners, an attack on the Caribas, and a girl named Fidette. Clark cooks for all, joins a spar fight, and in time becomes a Sargasson himself. Escape comes only at the end.
74848-the-donovan-chance:
The Donovan Chance is a railroad adventure novel by Francis Lynde, published in New York by Scribner in 1921. Thomas Fogarty illustrated the book. Lynde wrote many tales of western railroading, and this one opens on a locomotive.

Ten chapters carry the action. Tourmaline Canyon, a breach of discipline, a tunnel, and a crawling shale slope mark the route. Illustrations show a timber raft with a bomb swinging into a current, prisoners hauled out of wreckage, and a locomotive rushing down on a masterless Pullman car. Chapter one, The Bug and the Elephant, starts with Engine 331. The frontispiece shows a man told he can find his own way from here. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
7486-the-master-of-silence-a-romance:
Irving Bacheller's romance opens with a boy's apprenticeship. Near the end of his fourteenth year, the narrator is apprenticed to Valentine, King and Company, cotton importers of Liverpool, as a pair of legs, a runner for the firm. His father has died suddenly, leaving him and his property in the hands of a stepmother and a guardian, and London, where his life was never happy, lies behind him.

Into that new life comes a stranger who does not speak. His clothes drip, his hair is snow-white, and his deathly pallor frightens the boy as he stands blinking with strange, gleaming eyes. Who is the master of silence, and what secret keeps him mute? Bacheller's 1892 romance builds its mystery from that silent entrance, in the counting houses and docks of Liverpool.
74864-the-principles-of-science:
The Principles of Science, a treatise on logic and scientific method by W Stanley Jevons, was published by Macmillan of London in 1883. A picture of the logical machine stands as frontispiece. Jevons was a logician and economist who held that reasoning itself could be studied, and in part mechanised, like any other work of the mind.

This text of the treatise carries notes from its makers. Jevons used letters and signs of his own devising, and the imperfect fonts of the time forced him to shape some symbols by hand. His sign for factorial numbers belongs to a later notation. A warning marks a misleading calculation on page 194, where marks of addition stand in place of multiplication. The book treats evidence, inference, and the methods by which science builds laws from facts.
7492-the-fighting-chance:
Robert W. Chambers, author of Cardigan and The Maid at Arms, sets this novel in the fashionable world of the American season. Sunshine blazes on foliage plants arranged geometrically, on scarlet stars of geraniums, and on thickets of flame-tinted cannas. Around that triumph of landscape gardening, phaetons and motor cars circle and toot, while gaily gowned women, whips aslant, greet expected guests.

The chapters trace a season of acquaintance, imprudence, persuasion, and confession, through the seamy side to the asking price and the selling price of love and marriage. A woman stands beside the fire with Quarrier, one foot on the fender, in the novel's most pictured scene. Chambers writes society romance with a sharp eye for money, manners, and the fighting chance every lover takes.
75077-the-structure-of-the-english-sente:
Lillian Kimball, an instructor in English at the State Normal School in Oshkosh, Wisconsin, wrote this grammar text in 1900. The American Book Company published it for classroom use. Chapter one takes up the proposition, and chapter two sorts propositions into their classes.

Sentences are then sorted by structure and by form in the next chapters. Adjective clauses, noun clauses and adverbial clauses of time, place and manner each get a chapter. Clauses of cause, purpose, result, condition, concession and degree follow in order. Worked analysis of whole sentences runs through the book, giving students a steady method for parsing.
7513-o-t-a-danish-romance:
Hans Christian Andersen, author of The Improvisatore and The Two Baronesses, wrote O. T. as a Danish romance of youth. Its opening celebrates a happiness no poet has yet properly sung. It is the spring-day of life, when the ice-covering of school is broken, the tree of hope puts forth its buds, and the sun of freedom shines. With Danish students, Andersen notes, that spring day falls in October, just as nature loses its foliage and winter clouds gather.

The romance follows a young man through that critical moment, when pious mothers and loving sisters have prayed through sleepless nights for a son or brother facing his examinations and his future. Andersen writes of student life, friendship, and first love with the warmth of his fairy tales and the realism of his novels. O. T. shows the storyteller of children writing for grown readers too.
75339-stories-of-charlemagne-and-the-twe:
Church, once professor of Latin at University College, London, retold these tales from the old romances. Seeley printed Stories of Charlemagne at London in 1902, with plates by George Morrow. Oliver and Fierabras fight on the front plate.

The Slaying of Lothair opens the set, then the end of Duke Benes. The Coming of Roland brings the great hero in. Mawgis the crafty wizard works his tricks in three tales, then turns hermit. What befell at Montalban and Reynaud's end fill the middle. Fierabras defies King Charles, and Oliver fights him in the tale's bright core. Floripas, Guy of Burgundy, and Richard of Normandy share the later deeds.
75366-woman-s-voice:
Josephine Conger-Kaneko shaped Woman’s Voice, an anthology of women’s words in war time. The Stratford Company issued the book in Boston in nineteen hundred eighteen. She gives it to the splendid women of all lands and ages. Their fight was for broader fields of thought and act, she writes.

One woman’s book, however strong, could not sound like a crowd’s. So crowds of women speak here, through their chiefs and pens. Heads of great bands of women, speaking for thousands, stand here. Writers, artists, teachers, stage folk, and speakers share the pages. On the verge of vast change, a land must hear its women, she holds. Woman’s work may bear the race’s saving in the strait, she warns. The book aims at the homes of folk of modest means most of all. Later forms, grown and mended, should make it a household classic.
75383-the-dangerous-inheritance:
The Dangerous Inheritance, or The Mystery of the Tittani Rubies, by Izola Forrester, was published by Houghton Mifflin Company at Boston and New York in 1920. The first chapter sets the scene in the town studio of Signor Jacobelli, on the top floor of an old eight-storied building in the West Fifties.

The signor has kept the studio over twenty years while the building broke up into semi-commercial rooms around him. Dust lies unnoted on bookshelves and music-racks, and the Turkish rug has lost all outline of pattern. Carlota stands in a window recess, tying and untying a faded purple silk cord.
76357-blind-mice:
Kay Scott wrote a novel printed at New York in 1921. Scott gives the book to Otto Frederic Theis, friend of the book and of its author. Thirty six chapters make the tale, though two of them share one number in the contents. The suburban train was crowded and the stops were frequent, the tale opens.

Two young men had secured seats near the end of their car. One read an evening paper and the other made calculations in a note book. The reader stopped often to quote a news item to his companion or to make some remark. This was John Winter, rather short and well nourished, one of the men who indicate that in later years they will grow stout. He had very blue eyes and fair hair. Commuters, marriages, and money fill a plain novel of the new suburbs.
76546-the-corbin-necklace:
Henry Kitchell Webster wrote a novel dated 1926 that turns on a pearl necklace of great worth. A boy called Punch asks what the piece is worth and how a thief could sell such a known gem. Talk in the papers that his grandmother will give it to Judy as a wedding gift vexes him.

Pearls, he learns, are a trade of their own, and a known string can not be sold whole with ease. Chapter heads hint at tricks, watch kept by night, and a point of honor to come. The tale mixes youth, wealth, and risk, with the necklace as the prize all eyes rest on.
76621-sergeant-dick-of-the-royal-mounted:
John Rowe wrote this boys' adventure, copyrighted in 1929 by Cupples and Leon of New York. Its subtitle calls it a thrilling story of the Canadian woods. Rowe had earlier written 'Crusoe Island,' 'Lightship Pirates' and 'The Mystery of the Derelict' for the same house.

The contents open with hooded rustlers, then bring in Muriel Arnold as the second chapter. A house in the lake and the inside of a place called Water Castle follow in the list. Sergeant Dick of the Royal Mounted Police works the case in deep woods, where cattle theft and hidden houses drive the plot.
76673-the-history-of-the-south-african-f:
The History of the South African Forces in France is the state tale of those troops in the great war, by John Buchan. It was put out at London and New York by a great house. The front plate shows a famed wood of the war. The first words of the hand tell how the work was bid. That bid came in the fall of nineteen sixteen.

I was ask by the state of the south land, those words say, to take in hand the state tale of its troops in the war. At that time I was at work in France. There I had a chance to see some what of the foot corps. For more counts than one I could not start the work till past the truce.
76706-the-wonders-of-science:
Henry Mayhew wrote a life of Humphry Davy for boys, and Harper of New York published it in 1878. Davy is named on the title page as the Cornish apothecary's boy who taught himself natural philosophy and rose to head the Royal Society. A letter gives the book to Michael Faraday.

Davy, Mayhew tells Faraday, was the foster father of his genius. The letter retells how Davy befriended the young bookseller's apprentice who loved science and hated trade. Knowledge, Mayhew argues, is the one wealth that grows by being shared. A chemist alone in his room adds his mite of truth to a store meant for all ages. Davy's own rise is the proof held up to young readers.
76717-the-history-of-fashion-in-france:
The History of Fashion in France is a study of womens dress by Augustin Challamel. Two hands turned the French text into English for this print. Its span runs from the Gallic age to the days of its own print. The book came out in London in the year eighteen eighty two.

Poet lines and grave thought on dress open the wide survey in front. Paris is named the shrine of taste, with the shires in its wake. Dolls as dress posts and the first dress sheets earn notes in the plan. Then come Gaul garb, dyed cloth, and the clean ways of Gallic wives. Gown by gown the book walks France through all its past ages.
76925-elementary-lathe-practice:
Palmateer wrote Elementary Lathe Practice, a shop textbook of 1917. He was instructor in machine work at Stanford's junior university. It adapts lathe work to the teaching of technical schools. Nolte Brothers at San Jose printed this first edition for him. An opening exercise is headed: fit shaft to collar, running fit.

Cut a piece of steel six inches and a fraction from a one-inch bar. Allow a margin for finishing the ends and turning. An experienced hand would use smaller stock for the piece. Beginners do better with larger stock, to allow for practice turning. Centering both ends in the centering machine comes next in order. The center in this shaft runs a set size in diameter, it rules. Dividers, punch, and a combination drill do it by hand. Palmateer gives shop craft in exact, numbered practice.
76931-false-face:
False Face is a western story by Ernest Haycox. It opens in a frontier town where Sheriff Bart McKenzie needs a deputy. He picks old Dave Budd, a storekeeper who wants no part of the job.

Budd argues that his fighting days are past. McKenzie pins the star on his vest anyway. Budd warns that a badge will turn his own folks against him. He claims he settles local trouble fine without one. Haycox became one of the most respected western writers of his century. This scene shows his gift for dialogue, humor, and quiet menace.
76969-jock-s-inheritance:
Amy Le Feuvre wrote a novel issued in London and Melbourne by Ward, Lock and Company. Oriss waits in her flat on a cold January day for her sister-in-law and small niece. A letter brings bad news before the guests arrive.

The sister-in-law had meant to wed Captain Arteris at Cannes, but she put all her cash into his oil well and lost it. The firm failed, he left for California, and she fell ill, left with a small pension and a child named Pippa. Later chapters bring an old house, a full cupboard, a farm, a lost girl named Venetia, and the gift that gives Jock his due.
76989-aspects-of-science:
Sullivan wrote a set of essays on science dated 1923, on what science is and why it draws the mind. The lead essay holds that men still balk at the use of reason in fields where passion runs strong. Sure claims are prized and fresh truth feared, he says, when the stakes touch the heart.

Parts treat a life of James Clerk Maxwell, the base claims of science, and how science should be learned. Star lore for the lay fan, joined work with France, and the bond of maths and music fill late pages. Hope of science and the back rush of mystery close a clear, cool survey.
77003-with-the-indians-in-france:
With the Indians in France, by General Sir James Willcocks, was published by Constable and Company at London in 1920. Willcocks dedicates the book to his brave comrades of all ranks of the Indian Army, recording their loyalty and unperishable valour on the battlefields of France and Belgium.

The volume opens with his poem Hurnam-Singh, from Blackwood's Magazine of December 1917. A Khalsa soldier sits beneath a pipal tree by the Jhelum, his empty sleeve his pride, telling villagers of Messines, Festubert, and Neuve Chapelle. The tales of gods and ghouls, he says, are true after all.
77075-man-s-supreme-inheritance:
Alexander's book argues that man's supreme inheritance is conscious guidance and control of himself, set against the strain civilization lays on human nature. John Dewey's introductory word praises the argument warmly.

Dewey says Alexander grasped the crisis of modern life: a conflict between brain and nerves on one side and digestion, breathing, and muscle on the other. Chapters move from primitive remedies and their defects to inhibition, habits of thought and body, and the training of children. A third part gives a method of respiratory re-education. Dutton published the book in 1918, with a second printing that May. A second part sums up the claim, the argument, and the processes in practice.
77076-classics-of-modern-science:
Classics of Modern Science gathers great writings of science from Copernicus to Pasteur. Knickerbocker, professor of English at the University of the South, chose and edited the pieces. Alfred Knopf published the book at New York in 1927. Its opening quote, from Ernst Mach, praises the first great seekers who had no ready methods and made their own.

The contents begin with Bacon on the method of inductive science, then Copernicus on the new idea of the universe, then Kepler. Short prefaces frame each man's work and place. The book lets students read the founders of modern science in their own words, with a teacher's guidance.
77146-buddhism-science:
Paul Dahlke wrote 'Buddhism and Science,' translated from the German by the Bhikkhu Sīlācāra and published by Macmillan of London in 1913. His opening pages sort books into three kinds. First come those that give nothing and are empty entertainment, then manuals that give the unfamiliar and demand only memory. Third come books that give themselves and demand ourselves. Dahlke claims the third kind for his own, as mental nutriment and stimulus.

The contents then build the comparison in order: what a world-theory is and whether it is necessary. Faith and science as world-theories follow, then an introduction to the thought-world of the Buddha Gotama. The doctrine of the Buddha and Buddhism as a working hypothesis follow. Dahlke then tests the doctrine against the problems of physics, physiology, and biology, the cosmological problem, and the problem of thought, before a conclusion.
77161-sophie-kennedy-s-experience:
Lucy Ellen Guernsey wrote Sophie Kennedy's Experience, or The Stepmother, printed in New York in 1856. A picture at the front shows Sophie taking Carrie's outstretched hand, saying she has nothing to forgive. A preface states the aim. The story was written to do something, if possible, toward beating down the dislike felt by children and grown people against stepmothers.

That most useful and sorely tried class of women, the author holds, has hardly had fair play from writers, from the days of Cinderella down to the present. The station is a very hard one. A woman takes at once the whole charge of a family of children, with kin and neighbors watching her every act. As many stepmothers, the author believes, err on the side of softness as on that of strictness. She hopes the little book may make matters easier for some good women.
77224-a-noble-sacrifice:
A Noble Sacrifice is a novel by Emily Grace Harding, the author of A Mountain Daisy and Hazel. It came out in London from Walter Scott, in its thirty-eighth thousand, with pictures by T. Eyre Macklin. A front picture shows a woman spellbound on a threshold at the sight of Lady Bryn upon her knees upon the floor.

The contents set out a tale of castle life and gipsy lore. The Gipsy's Warning stands first, then Little Miss Primrose and The Star in the East. The Earl's Visit, A Mysterious Journey, and Within the Castle stand next in the list. Shadows, Fortune-Telling, and Sir Galahad stand there too. The Lady of the Castle, A New Name, and A Glimpse of the World carry the list on. The Legend of the Pool and The Subterranean Passage stand later.
77246-safe-foundry-practice:
The Travelers Insurance Company of Hartford issued a manual of safe foundry practice, printed in 1920. Pages at the front tell why an employer should choose the Travelers for workmen's compensation and liability cover. The company had spent more than six million five hundred thousand dollars on the prevention of accidents by inspection, it says. The rules then begin with the worker's own dress.

Clothing, shoes and leggings, eye protectors, gloves, aprons, and the rest of the gear take set sections. About eighty per cent of the injuries received in foundries are burns of greater or lesser severity, the text states. The remaining twenty per cent come from defective hooks, chains, and slings. Ladles, cranes, and molten metal fill a plain book that saved hands and eyes in hard shops.
77317-justice:
Hutton wrote this science fiction story about a time traveller on trial. Urs, a Third Level Time Explorer, stands before the System Policy Board while billions watch on life-view screens. The board is no small court of discipline: it is the ultimate court, and its one motive, the story says, is absolute justice.

The charge is read out by the white-haired chairman. Urs is accused of breaking the rule that no visitor to a previous time shall let the knowledge or methods of the future become part of that earlier culture. He learned the rule in his first week of training. Before the hearing, his bureau director told him the bureau would not blame him, and hoped for the best.
77321-vive-la-france:
Vive la France, by E Alexander Powell, was published by Charles Scribner's Sons in December nineteen fifteen. Powell was war correspondent for the New York World, the London Daily Mail, and Scribner's Magazine with the Allied armies. He dated his acknowledgment from the Hotel de Crillon in Paris in November nineteen fifteen.

The chapters take the reader in the field with the French and onto the British battle-line. Campaigning in the Vosges and the retaking of Alsace follow. The fighting in Champagne and the conflict in the clouds come next. The red badge of mercy closes the book. Powell dedicates it to France, whose courage in a conflict she did nothing to provoke won the world's admiration. His photographs show trenches, seventy-fives, and infantry going into action.
77508-the-women-of-the-renaissance:
The Women of the Renaissance, a study of feminism by de Maulde, draws praise in its front pages. French papers of the day called it a bible of feminine life in one notice. The Revue des Deux Mondes held that its author had exhausted the subject. Other journals found no work on feminism more complete or more entertaining in print.

It draws the completest picture of French and Italian society of its age, one notice holds. Finished portraits of women are grouped with accomplished art in the praise. The charm and influence of women at that curious epoch form its theme. Fifteenth and sixteenth century courts, salons, and homes fill the social canvas. A French study of women power in the age of the Medici reached English readers here.
77580-lost-in-the-land-of-ice:
Captain Ralph Bonehill wrote Lost in the Land of Ice, or daring adventures around the South Pole, printed in New York in 1902. Bonehill had written Boys of the Fort and For the Liberty of Texas. A front picture shows a diver diving straight into the spume. Contents open in a cold-storage warehouse, with Barry to the rescue. In the grasp of the enemy and a prisoner on the Vixen follow.

Off for South America, five stowaways, and prisoners in the hold fill the middle heads. The wild Patagonians, a fight, a strange meeting on the beach, and adrift in a storm come next. Three polar bears and adventures on the big iceberg lead toward the South Pole. A meeting of father and son and home again close the tale. The first chapter opens with a fire gong at midnight in New York.
77610-the-color-of-space:
Charles Tanner wrote a science fiction tale that won first prize in a magazine cover contest. Judges praised how well he built his tale and thought hard on what the cover art could mean. His ending, they said, was set up fairly by all that went before it in the tale.

Doctor Henshaw wakes to face a captor who has held him, drugged, for a week in a strange room. Metal walls, two doors, and a huge round shuttered window fill the place. Henshaw thinks he was seized for a secret process that Russia and France both tried to buy, and swears he will not sell.
77611-courses-of-study-in-library-scienc:
Reginald Williams, deputy librarian of the Bolton Public Libraries, wrote this assistants' guide to librarianship as a set of courses of study in library science. The second edition, revised and enlarged, is dated 1926.

Eight courses cover practical bibliography, book selection, classification, cataloguing, English literary history, legislation and equipment, administration, and the history of libraries. Williams advises students to take notes in their own words and answer the tests without books. The memorial page records that the author died at Bolton on March 11th, 1926. Grafton of London and Bowker of New York acted as agents. Williams also wrote graded courses of reading on the civil war and the French Revolution.
77633-servants-and-service:
Servants and Service, by Ruth Lamb, was published at London by the Religious Tract Society. The chapters first ran as a series in the Girl Own Paper, the preface states. Lamb also wrote Only a Girl Wife and Girls Work and Workshops. Some years had passed since those chapters first appeared when the book came out.

Letters since then told her the papers had not been written in vain, she says. Mistresses and maids alike commended them in those messages to the author. Both classes bore witness to the fairness of her treatment, she reports with thanks. A difficult social question gets even handling in this guide for both sides of the hall door. Victorian households bought counsel on duty, wages, and conduct in such little books.
77775-sworn-to-silence: Miller's Sworn to Silence, or Aline Rodney's Secret, is a novel in the Sweetheart Series from George Munro's Sons of New York. The copyright is 1898, and the price was twenty-five cents. The head keeps the title page and the publisher's adverts for cheap Fashion Bazar guides. None of the story's own pages survive in it, so the bare record is all that can be grounded: a sensation tale built on its heroine's secret.
78107-body-build-and-its-inheritance:
Body-Build and Its Inheritance is a research study by Charles Benedict Davenport. Davenport directed the Department of Genetics at the Carnegie Institution of Washington. The study was published by that institution in December 1923. It is paper number 35 of his department. The preface explains how the work began in the World War. Davenport was then in charge of anthropology for the Surgeon-General. The examination of thousands of young men struck him.

Those men showed an extraordinary diversity of build. The question of its genetic basis arose from that fact. Some physiologists explained all variation by food and activity alone. Davenport set out to test whether heredity also played a part. Family data at the Eugenics Record Office swelled the task. Checking and correcting those records took years of correspondence. The book stands as a record of that period's genetics. Its methods and setting belong to the eugenics era.
78211-circe:
Isaac Flagg wrote Circe, a dramatic fantasy issued in nineteen fifteen with a front picture by Bernard Maybeck. The Roycrofters printed and bound the book at East Aurora, New York. Flagg kept the stage rights for himself.

An argument retells Homer's tale before the play begins. Ulysses, sailing home from Troy, lost all but one of his twelve ships. On Circe's isle, the enchantress turned twenty-two of his men into swine. Warned by Mercury and armed with a cure, Ulysses forced her to free them. The crew then feasted at her palace for a year. Flagg builds his drama on that stay.
78246-wild-volatile-oil-plants-and-their:
Wild Volatile-Oil Plants and Their Economic Importance is Bulletin Number 235 of the Bureau of Plant Industry in the United States Department of Agriculture. Frank Rabak, a chemical biologist on the bureau's drug-plant staff, wrote the study. The Government Printing Office issued it in Washington in January 1912.

The bulletin treats three wild plants in turn: black sage, wild sage, and swamp bay. Its concern is supply. The industries that use volatile oils and their derivatives, the bureau notes, draw those materials from Old World plants grown in foreign lands. In some cases supply is hard to obtain. A home-grown source of flavouring and scent oils, if the wild plants proved rich enough, would free American makers from foreign harvests. Rabak reports what the plants yield and what the oils are worth.
78480-a-battle-piece:
Ernest Haycox wrote this story of the American Revolution, set on the night of August 26, 1776. Haycox had earlier written 'With Grape and Bayonet' and 'A Cup of Sugar' in his list. The sun set blood red beyond the Jersey palisades that night, touching British ships in New York harbor as it dipped.

Nine thousand Continentals camped on Brooklyn Heights, their backs to the East River. Their gun muzzles pointed toward the rugged hills that masked Flatbush in the dark. Spruce Marylanders grumbled for Washington and mocked old Uncle Putnam, galloping in shirtsleeves and a dirty leather jacket, while Howe moved twenty thousand troops beyond the hills.
78509-sex-at-choice:
Cicely Erskine, wife of a member of parliament for Westminster, wrote a book on choosing the sex of children, printed at New York and London in 1925. Her husband James Monteith Erskine wrote the introduction. Sex determination opens the book, then the eugenic point of view and the selection of the fit. The mothers' responsibility and a chapter on early births follow.

The superfluous female, sterility, and sex causation come next. For a boy and for a girl take set chapters, with the blank week, the freak ovary, and lying on one side weighed as means. Signs and after effects, twins of mixed sexes, and the length of bearing close the scheme. Sex is the central problem of life, Havelock Ellis is quoted at the start. The book shows its age's faith and its age's errors.
78512-the-golden-fleece:
Golden Fleece, or Who Wins the Prize, is a tale by the writer known as ALOE, issued in 1897. Nelson and Sons published the book in London, Edinburgh, and New York that year. The author is named as writer of The Shepherd of Bethlehem, The Young Pilgrim, and Wings and Stings. A frontispiece shows the prize of the golden fleece for the tale.

Contents list ten chapters of an archery of life in the book in order. Owls and Eagles, Ladies in Council, and A Shot at the Owl open the tale. Aim Higher, Will It Strike, and A Slackened Bow fill the middle chapters in the list.  The fleece of the title is the prize of the Christian life, figured as a contest of bows and aims, in the allegory manner of the author Sunday school classics for girls.
78559-wonders-of-physical-science:
Wonders of Physical Science is a school science book by E E Fournier, printed at London in 1910 in the series Readable Books in Natural Knowledge. The publishers' note warns that the valuable influence of descriptive scientific literature is apt to be overlooked. In an age of practical and systematic study in schools, such books still have their place.

An intimate knowledge of the simplest fact in nature, the note says, can be got only by personal observation or experiment. But broad views of scientific thought and progress are secured best from books. In them the methods and results of investigation are stated in language simple without being childish. The keynote of such a book should be inspiration rather than information. Its execution should awaken appreciation of the scientific method and a desire to emulate the men whose labours built the knowledge of nature.
78652-a-fisher-girl-of-france:
Fernand Calmettes's tale of a French fishing family, in English from Dodd, Mead and Company at New York in 1892, with the author's own illustrations. Elise Hénin and her little brother Firmin put on their Sunday clothes to bid farewell to their mother. She has lain nine years in the old graveyard on the slope of the dune.

Their father, a skipper, was swallowed by the sea with his boat and six companions, caught in a fatal current at the most dangerous shoal on the coast. His death brought ruin, since the boat was all he owned. The plates carry titles like A Sad Return and Father, If You Will Help I Will Find You, over thirty chapters.
78668-when-canada-was-new-france:
When Canada Was New France, by George Locke, was published at Toronto in 1919. Dent issued the book in Canada and France. Locke was chief librarian of the public library at Toronto. Seven pictures go with the text. A front plate shows Canadians landing in France in 1915. The introduction ties the old story to the Great War. Canadian soldiers, Locke notes, sailed from the same French ports as the first explorers. Love of country, his motto runs, is born of knowing its past.

Thirteen chapters carry the tale of two centuries. Cartier, Champlain, Joliet, and La Salle open the line of discovery. Radisson, Montcalm, and Pontiac follow. Missionaries, Iroquois, voyageurs, and habitants fill the later chapters. Stories and poems at the end gloss the main text.
78678-outline-of-a-natural-system-of-med:
Alexander Walker wrote an Outline of a Natural System of Medical Science, printed at Edinburgh in eighteen oh eight. The small book forms the first lectures for two courses. One course treats anatomy and physiology, and the other treats pathology and the practice of medicine. Walker taught physiology and edited the Archives of Universal Science. He gave the book to Alexander Monro, a teacher of medicine, anatomy, and surgery at Edinburgh.

Walker says his aim is not to fight one settled fact of medical science. He wants to show how the parts link, and so make the whole more simple and firm. Anatomy, physiology, pathology, and materia medica stand as one chain in his plan. A line from Lord Bacon heads the book, blaming doctors who call diseases incurable to shield neglect. Students of old medicine get a neat map of an early system.
787-the-man-between-an-international-rom:
Amelia E. Barr wrote this international romance about Ethel Rawdon, a woman whose beginnings the narrator admits she hardly knows, so many picturesque ways are there to introduce her. The tale moves between America and Europe, where love, money, and social rank pull Ethel in different directions, and a man stands between her and her hopes.

Barr writes with warmth for her heroine and a keen eye for society on both sides of the Atlantic. The novel turns on choices of heart against duty, and on the price of a good match. It offers readers a late Victorian romance of manners, full of feeling and of the world its people inhabit.
78735-the-hand-of-providence:
Tuttle returns to Piperock in this western tale, and his regulars are on hand: Ricky Henderson holding forth on the saloon steps, Magpie Simpkins agreeing with someone for once in his life. The year is 1895, and the town is dull: even the broncos have forgotten how to pitch. Then a popping, roaring thing comes down the street with nothing pushing it and nothing pulling it, and the hitched broncos tear the rack loose and sweep the town.

The cause of the cyclone is an early motor car, shaking in the street with Scenery Sims of Curlew at the wheel. Tuttle, who wrote of Tombstone and the Piute country, builds the comedy on cowboys meeting the machine age. The dialect is thick, the pace fast, and the joke is on the old West itself.
78795-number-three-winifred-place:
Agnes Giberne wrote this novel, published at London by James Nisbet and Company with a frontispiece showing Rhona dropped into a man's arms. Twenty-six chapters run from A Stranger through Fire and The Three Aunts to Rhona's Real Uncle and Together Again.

Chapter one opens on a dismal November afternoon at Mrs Burrell's shop, number three in a row off a great thoroughfare. The shop is stocked with wools, Shetland shawls, and work-baskets, and lodgings are also let. Mrs Burrell, fifty, tall and unsmiling, snaps at her dawdling girl Bertha when the doorbell rings, hoping for somebody after lodgings. The contents promise a mother and child, another lodger, Colonel Smyth and his arrangements, a bunch of grapes, and a disappearance in the fog. A chapter is called Number Three, and Number Three, before the threads are gathered up.
78855-the-story-of-the-diamond-necklace:
The Story of the Diamond Necklace is a work of history by Henry Vizetelly. His own firm issued the third edition in London in 1881. It tells the tale in detail for the first time, he claims. Memoirs, letters, and official papers back the account. The Countess de la Motte fronts the book in portrait. She posed as the queen's close confidant. A drawing shows the necklace itself in full.

The fraud shook the French court in the 1780s. A cardinal was duped into buying the necklace. Marie Antoinette's name was used without her knowledge. Vizetelly reworked his book from the French archives. Two costly editions had sold out years before. The scandal still reads like a novel. It helped blacken the queen before the revolution.
78930-taught-by-experience:
Ruth Lamb wrote this story for young readers, printed in London by the Religious Tract Society. The opening scene sets two housemaids in a large country house against each other. Fanny Ellis, the upper housemaid, has given notice after three months, calling the house rules too strict. Kate, the under housemaid, defends their mistress and means to stay.

Mrs Bateson runs a house where family and servants alike keep the Sabbath and attend worship once each Sunday. Fanny calls this being kept in leading-strings, and holds that a servant is no slave. Kate answers that the mistress takes trouble for their good, at no gain to herself. The chapter list points ahead: bad company, misunderstandings, a mistake confessed, and hope deferred. The tale teaches its lesson through the clash of two servants in one house.
79381-evidence:
Evidence is a western tale by Murray Leinster of Texas heat. The text comes from All Story Weekly of July 12, 1919. It was hot, the narrator begins, as his pony jogged listlessly on. He cared only for the problem of getting to shade and water. His saddle burned his hand where the sun struck it hard.

Perspiration trickled down either cheek and a third stream down his nose. He smudged dust across his face to stop those streams in vain. In that Texan air he came upon Jimmy Calton by a car. Calton held a sooted spark plug of his tin lizzy in cloth. He cleaned it while swearing in English and in dobe Spanish.
79415-mrs-grey-s-strange-silence:
Ruth Lamb wrote a story printed in The Girl's Own Annual for 1891 at the Leisure Hour office in London. The Greys are an elderly couple seldom seen apart. If one is missing, it is the lady, who sometimes stays in her own room. Whenever she is visible, he is sure to be close at hand. The narrator meets them under the roof of a Swiss mountain pension.

They are only items in a long list of guests there. The wife's strange silence is the story's puzzle. Lamb wrote improving fiction for girls and women. The annual gathered such tales for the year's reading. Her couple's devotion hides the reason for the silence.
79536-the-story-of-the-world-a-thousand-:
Professor Henry Olerich's The Story of the World a Thousand Years Hence was published by the Olerich Publishing Company of Omaha in 1923. Olerich, author of A Cityless and Countryless World and Modern Thought, bills the book as a scientific forecast of the changes likely to come over the earth in the next thousand years. Twenty-four chapters run from foretelling the future to a closing survey of immediate improvement.

The forecast is co-operative in shape. Chapters take up outside ownership, cityless and countryless living, co-operative farms and mansions, cottage sites, and adjoining paradises. Motive power and coming electricity sit beside vegetarianism, honest money, education, marriage and divorce, and aluminum buildings. Chapter one promises to show, in simple words, how posterity will live, work, play, and travel.
79597-beyond-the-end-of-space:
Beyond the End of Space is a science fiction novel by John W Campbell Jr, printed in Amazing Stories across March and April 1933, with illustrations by Morey. The magazine's editors promised readers the work of a great inventor, with interplanetary or even space travel to come in the second part. Campbell was already a leading name in the field.

The tale opens in the laboratory of Dr Randolph Warren. Electroscopes, a recording bolometer, and a thermopile crowd the work, and a three-inch tube of fused quartz rises forty feet to a huge aluminum sphere. Tom Blamen waits inside the sphere, watching a needle quiver at seventeen on the dial, and asks if he might try the thing on low voltage. The experiment aims at forces no laboratory had handled, and the story builds from its gauges outward.
79745-new-discoveries-in-science:
New Discoveries in Science, by Hereward Carrington, author of The Coming Science and Modern Psychical Phenomena, is Little Blue Book number 493. Haldeman-Julius edited the series; his company published the booklet at Girard, Kansas, with copyright in 1924. Short question and answer essays fill it, each headed by a query.

The first asks why you cry. We cry when hurt, in joy, at tender feeling, at fine music, or at a brave deed, Carrington notes, and from plain bodily causes too: onions, dust, coughing. The tear glands above the eyes keep them moist; strong feeling raises the pressure of the blood and overfills them. Tears then relieve the crowding in the head, a safety valve of nature. The next asks why you frown. Worry, anger, and the hunt for a lost thought all knit the brows. The corrugator muscles draw them together and down, whatever the feeling behind the frown.
809-holiday-romance:
Charles Dickens wrote this holiday tale in four parts, each told as if by a child. William Tinkling, Esq., edits the set, and insists that the opening part is real, not made up, so that readers may grasp how the rest came to be written. The children tell of holidays, games, and small romances in their own voices.

Dickens delights in the child's view, with its solemn rules and sudden fancies. The tale is slight, but it shows his humour and his ear for young speech. It makes a pleasant short read, and a window on how Victorians imagined childhood at play, told by children who take their games very seriously indeed.
8115-authors-of-greece:
The Reverend T. W. Lumb, M. A. , wrote this introduction to Greek authors, with an introduction by the Reverend Cyril Alington, D. D. Lumb argues that Greek literature feels more modern than Latin, medieval, or Elizabethan writing, because it speaks for a society much like our own. Mainly democratic, full of free inquiry, troubled by feuds and stubborn problems, and familiar with militarism, nationalism, and socialism. The defence of a maritime empire against a military oligarchy was twice attempted by the quick-witted Greeks.

The book guides readers through the great names, from epic and drama to history and philosophy, showing why they still speak directly. It suits students meeting Greek literature for the first time, and general readers who want the map before the journey. Lumb's parallel between ancient and modern politics gives the survey lasting freshness.
82-ivanhoe-a-romance:
Norman lords rule Saxon England a generation after the Conquest, and old hatreds still burn. Sir Walter Scott's Ivanhoe follows the disinherited knight Wilfred back from the Crusades in disguise. Tournaments, sieges, and outlaws fill his road home.

Ivanhoe aids King Richard, loves Rowena, and rescues the Jewish healer Rebecca from trial and fire. Robin Hood's men, the Black Knight, and the Templar Bois-Guilbert cross his path. Scott's notes defend his blend of history and romance. The novel set the pattern for historical fiction in English. Scott's blend of Saxon and Norman conflict gave later writers a model for national romance.
8203-a-modern-instance:
William Dean Howells, born at Martin's Ferry, Ohio, on March 1, 1837, wrote A Modern Instance as a realistic novel of American marriage and divorce. Its hero is Bartley Hubbard, a young journalist whose charm carries him from a small town into Boston newspaper life. And whose marriage to Marcia Gaylord slowly breaks down under ambition, jealousy, and incompatible temper. The novel follows the couple to separation and to the divorce court.

Howells called his subject modern because divorce, once scandalous, was becoming a fact of American life, and he treats it without melodrama. The book's moral seriousness made it famous and controversial. For readers of American realism, it remains the classic novel of a marriage failing in plain sight.
8295-through-the-eye-of-the-needle-a-rom:
William Dean Howells frames this 1907 romance as the letters of Aristides Homos, an envoy from the imaginary commonwealth of Altruria, visiting America. Homos had already reported on the United States in Howells's earlier Altrurian tale. Here he turns his eye to wealth itself, to New York society, and to a love affair tested by money. The famous needle's eye of the title is the gospel warning about rich men and heaven.

Through Homos's puzzled, earnest questions, Howells asks whether a society built on getting rich can also be good. The romance is gentle satire rather than polemic, and its heroine must choose between a fortune and a conscience. Readers of Howells's social novels will find his reform hopes here at their most open.
8383-monsieur-maurice:
Amelia B. Edwards sets this story more than fifty years before its 1873 telling, as remembered by a white-haired old woman who was a little girl of ten when the events happened. Monsieur Maurice, the figure at its center, moves through a world the narrator recalls more vividly than the present, with places and people from her childhood standing close in memory.

Edwards, best known for her travel writing on Egypt and her ghost stories, writes here in a quieter, retrospective key. The tale's charm lies in memory itself: how childhood scenes keep their color while later years fade. Readers who like Victorian stories told by an older voice looking back will find the book gentle and atmospheric.
8449-a-traveler-from-altruria-romance:
W. D. Howells sends a traveler from Altruria, an imaginary commonwealth, to visit America, and the romance follows his puzzled impressions. The narrator confesses he was in no hospitable mood when the Altrurian finally presented himself. Yet curiosity wins, and the visitor's questions about American money, work, and manners become Howells's satire of his own country.

Howells, the dean of American letters, uses the visitor's innocent eye to ask whether a society built on competition can be just. The book, published by Harper in 1908 in this edition, pairs with its sequel, Through the Eye of the Needle. Readers of utopian fiction get a gentle, questioning classic, more interested in argument than in adventure.
854-a-woman-of-no-importance:
Oscar Wilde wrote this play about Mrs Arbuthnot, a woman of no importance in society's eyes, and her son Gerald, a young man on the rise. Lord Illingworth, a witty lord, offers Gerald a post, while Mrs Arbuthnot hides a secret: Illingworth is Gerald's father, who wronged her years before. The truth breaks at a country house party.

Wilde's epigrams glitter, but the play turns grave on a mother's shame and a son's choice. First printed in 1894, it shows Wilde moving from pure comedy to moral drama. The play remains a powerful study of respectability, sin, and the price women paid for men's freedom.
8660-woman-and-the-new-race:
Margaret Sanger argues in this 1920 book, with a preface by Havelock Ellis, that women must control childbearing if they are to be free. Dedicated to her mother, who bore eleven living children, the book moves from woman's error and debt, through her struggle for freedom. To the material of the new race and the wickedness, in Sanger's blunt phrase, of creating large families. Later chapters ask when a woman should avoid having children, and whether birth control is a parents' problem or a woman's.

Sanger also weighs continence, contraceptives against abortion, the certainty of preventive means, and birth control's effect on labour. Her eugenic language and some of her claims are now rightly contested, and readers should meet the book as a historical document.
8673-a-columbus-of-space:
Garrett P. Serviss dedicates this space romance to readers of Jules Verne, insisting that the world of imagination is as legitimate a domain of the mind as the world of fact. He does not flatter himself that he can walk in Verne's footsteps, but he shares Verne's faith that a bold idea, worked out carefully, makes a story. An illustration shows a creature shaped like a man, but more savage than a gorilla, waiting on steps.

A marvellous invention launches a trip of terror aboard a planetary limited, through the caverns of Venus, off for the sun lands, and lost in crystal mountains. The children of the sun and a language without speech await the travellers. Serviss, a popular astronomy writer, fills the adventure with then-current ideas about other worlds. Early science-fiction fans will enjoy a pioneering American voyage story, earnest, inventive, and very much of its age.
8686-the-delicious-vice:
Young E. Allison celebrates novel reading itself in this second, revised edition of 1918, first published in 1907 and first printed in the Louisville Courier-Journal. The subtitle calls it pipe dreams and fond adventures of a habitual novel-reader among great books and their people. Allison opens with a rhapsody on the noble profession of novel reading, using Thomas Moore, the Irish poet, as an example of turning a sigh into marketable copy.

Later chapters wander through favourite novels, their heroes and heroines, and the pleasures of living inside other people's stories. The tone is genial, bookish, and deliberately old-fashioned, defending light reading against sterner critics. Readers who love books about books will enjoy a warm, funny companion, and a snapshot of what a well-read American enjoyed, and defended, in the years around the First World War.
8690-american-institutions-and-their-inf:
Alexis de Tocqueville's study of American democracy appears here in the 1851 school and library edition issued by A. S. Barnes and Company, with notes by John C. Spencer. The publishers explain that they were often asked for a cheaper form of Democracy in America, suited to seminaries and school district libraries, so that more readers could own it. Spencer's notes guide students through Tocqueville's argument.

Tocqueville, a French visitor to the young republic, asked why democracy worked in America when it had failed elsewhere in his experience. He pointed to local government, voluntary associations, the jury, and habits of equality as the supports of free institutions. This edition remains a clear way into a classic of political thought, trimmed for classroom use but keeping the Frenchman's central, still-debated claims intact.
880-my-garden-acquaintance:
James Russell Lowell wrote this essay about the birds and beasts that visit his garden, and about the books that taught him to love them. White's Natural History of Selborne, a delight of his father's library, gains charm with years, he says, as he learns the simple secret of its pleasure: close, patient looking.

Lowell sketches robins, orioles, and other garden guests with humour and learning, mixing natural history with personal memory. His prose is urbane and witty, the essayist at ease outdoors. The piece delights readers who keep a garden, or who love the older tradition of nature writing that watches before it judges.
8936-holidays-in-eastern-france:
M. Betham-Edwards records holidays in eastern France as travelling without hotels or guide-books, or very nearly so. Visiting charming French people in delightful places out of the ordinary tourist track. Her preface lists the route: the valley of the Marne, French Protestants at Montbeliard, Besancon amid the beautiful scenery of the Doubs, Lons-le-Saunier with excursions into the Jura. The heart of the Jura highlands at Champagnole, Morez, and St Claude. Illustrations show the chateau of Montbeliard and Ornans, valley of the Loue, country of the painter Courbet.

Betham-Edwards writes as a guest rather than a sightseer, staying with families and learning local life. Her eastern France is Protestant, industrial, and mountainous by turns, far from Parisian polish. Readers planning a Jura journey, or simply enjoying Victorian travel writing at its most companionable, will find a warm, well-observed book that still suggests routes worth following.
8940-an-essay-on-the-evils-of-popular-ig:
John Foster argues against popular ignorance in this revised and enlarged essay, praised by Dr J. Pye Smith as popular and admired yet never receiving a thousandth part of the attention it deserves. Smith calls the present moment a crisis in country and world that makes Foster's reasonings and exhortations applicable and urgent beyond expression. Foster's advertisement explains that the work grew out of topics from a discussion, in a manner of introduction somewhat different from what essay readers might expect.

The essay itself contends that an uneducated people cannot sustain free institutions, sound religion, or honest public life. That education must reach the poor as well as the privileged. Foster writes with evangelical earnestness and reforming zeal. Readers of nineteenth-century social thought will find a classic statement of the case for popular education. A reminder that debates about ignorance, democracy, and schooling are far older than our own.
9152-imogen-a-pastoral-romance:
William Godwin translated this pastoral romance from ancient British, as the work of Cadwallo, an old bard. The preface claims the Welsh original is elegant and pure, with much novelty of conception and classical taste. Its manners claim to show primitive times as one who knew them well might paint them.

Imogen moves through a Britain of bards, love, and old customs, in a style both simple and high. Godwin's version helped shape the Romantic taste for ancient song. The book remains a curious, lovely relic of the age that dreamed of bards.
9199-monism-as-connecting-religion-and-s:
Ernst Haeckel gave this address as a man of science, translated from German by J. Gilchrist. He spoke on the seventy-fifth anniversary of a society for the study of nature, choosing a theme of the highest general import. His theme is monism, the view that nature and mind form one whole, joining religion and science.

Haeckel laments that learned meetings now favor narrow topics of small interest. He urges a return to great questions and truth-seeking. The address remains a bold statement of nineteenth-century scientific faith, confident, sweeping, and open to debate.
9251-an-old-woman-s-tale-from-the-dolive:
In the house where Hawthorne was born, an old woman crouched all day over the kitchen fire, elbows on knees and feet in ashes. Now and then she turned the spit, and always a coarse gray stocking lay in her lap, half finished. It tapered with her waning life, and she knit its toe on the day she died.

Her business and sole amusement was telling stories from morning till night, in a mumbling, toothless voice, to a child grasping her apron. Her memory spanned near a hundred years, jumbled with tales of the dead. The sketch is a fond tribute to oral tale-telling itself.
9259-charlotte-s-inheritance:
Mary Elizabeth Braddon wrote this long sensation novel in seven books, from De Profundis to Diana in Normandy. It opens with Lenoble of Beaubocage, a man who stands alone in the wide world, past hope and in despair, under a decree of banishment. Downhill follows, with the fate of Susan Lenoble and Gustave the Second.

Later books bring Captain Paget, paternal and plotting, Diana's holiday, and assurance doubly sure. Braddon keeps secrets, wills, and love affairs spinning to the end. The novel is full Victorian melodrama, rich, tangled, and hard to put down.
935-self-help-with-illustrations-of-cond:
Samuel Smiles wrote this famous Victorian manual on self-help, with illustrations of conduct and perseverance drawn from the lives of engineers, inventors, and workers. He quotes Shakespeare's counsel to be true to oneself, and he argues that character, thrift, and steady work matter more than birth or luck.

Smiles tells brief lives of men who rose by effort, from humble shops to great works, and he draws lessons for readers of every rank. His tone is earnest and encouraging, the voice of an age that believed in improvement. The book shaped a generation, and it remains a landmark of Victorian moral advice.
943-misalliance:
George Bernard Shaw wrote this play about misalliance, the clash of classes, ages, and ideas in love and marriage. A country house party brings together parents, daughters, and suitors, and Shaw turns their talk into a debate on sex, money, and freedom, with his usual wit and paradox.

Shaw's characters argue as much as they love, and the play's famous long scenes test every convention of courtship. His spelling and punctuation, kept as printed, add to the flavour. Misalliance is a bold Shaw comedy of ideas, for readers who like theatre that thinks as hard as it laughs.
978-the-yates-pride-a-romance:
Mary E. Wilkins Freeman wrote this romance about the Yates pride, centred on Miss Eudora Yates's old colonial mansion. Opposite stands the perky modern Queen Anne house of Mrs. Joseph Glynn, whose daughter Ethel and unmarried sister Miss Julia Esterbrook love to talk, with many callers who like to hear them.

Freeman sets old pride against new money in a New England village, where family honour, gossip, and love pull neighbours apart and together. Her prose is precise and wry, with a keen ear for village talk. The novel charms readers who enjoy Freeman's New England, where a house can hold a family's whole history.
9835-martin-conisby-s-vengeance:
Jeffery Farnol's 1921 novel is told by a man whose quiet solitude is broken by trouble, and who sets out to settle a score. Martin Conisby, the title figure, moves through a world of songs half remembered, sudden danger, and old wrongs that will not stay buried.

Farnol writes in his familiar romantic manner, with swordplay, country roads, and strong feeling. The story's drive comes from its first-person voice: a man pushed from peace into action, learning who his enemies are as he goes. It is a sturdy adventure for readers who like Georgian romance with spirit.
993-malbone-an-oldport-romance:
Thomas Wentworth Higginson wrote this romance of Oldport, the old name for Newport, Rhode Island, opening with a prelude and an arrival. A drive on the avenue, Aunt Jane, and the place aux dames follow, as the tale moves through society, love, and loss in a seaside town of old families and new wealth.

Higginson quotes Thoreau on nature, asking what nature is unless an eventful human life passes within her, with joys and sorrows as its lights and shadows. His romance is gentle and literary, full of sea air and social nuance. Malbone delights readers who love old Newport, in a tale of manners and feeling.
9982-philothea-a-grecian-romance:
Lydia Maria Child's Philothea is a romance set in ancient Greece, written by the author of Letters from New York and Flowers for Children. Child takes her epigraph from Coleridge, on the fair humanities of old religion: power, beauty, and majesty that once haunted dale, mountain, and stream.

Her heroine moves through a Greece of poets, temples, and old faiths, where reason has not yet banished wonder. Child writes with moral earnestness and classical feeling. Readers get a nineteenth-century American's Greece, romantic and thoughtful, and a heroine who seeks truth among gods and philosophers.
a-belated-guest-from-literary-friends-an:
William Dean Howells reflects on the duty of remembering the famous dead in this piece from Literary Friends and Acquaintance. It is sweet at first, he writes, to sit by the fire and recall names, looks, and tones from the past, and to bask in borrowed lustre. But the pleasure soon becomes a grievous obligation, as more shades claim their right to be recorded.

The belated guest of the title arrives late into Howells's company of memories and takes his place among the writers of an older America. Howells sketches talk, character, and the rooms where they met. The essay is literary history at its most personal: a survivor's roll call, written with affection and honest weariness.
a-bibliographical-antiquarian-and-pictur: Thomas Frognall Dibdin records a tour of France and Germany in a series of letters. The first volume follows his passage to Dieppe and on through towns, churches, castles, and libraries. He notes local manners, customs, worship, and amusements alongside books, art, and old buildings. The result is both a travel record and a study of the printed treasures and antiquities he meets on the road.
a-chance-acquaintance: William Dean Howells tells of a chance acquaintance on a boat up the Saguenay. Miss Kitty Ellison waits on the forward deck at Quebec, eager for the voyage and patient with its delay. The journey brings her together with fellow travelers whose talk and manners fill the tale. Howells writes a light novel of travel, character, and American social life.
a-cigarette-maker-s-romance: Francis Marion Crawford tells a romance centered on a cigarette maker. The novel follows its hero through love, work, and the social world of its setting across twelve chapters. Crawford, known for vivid tales of many lands, builds the story on character and feeling. The romance moves from workshop to drawing room with steady dramatic interest.
a-columbus-of-space: Garrett Putman Serviss sends his heroes to the planets in this romance of space travel. A marvelous invention launches a trip of terror aboard a planetary limited bound for Venus and the sun lands. Chapters visit caverns, crystal mountains, and children of the sun, with a language without speech. Dedicated to readers of Jules Verne, the tale honors imagination as a true domain of mind.
a-golden-book-of-venice: Lawrence Turnbull writes a golden book of Venice as a romance of the city. The prelude sees Venice, her life and glory now a memory, still floating like a mirage between blue water and sky. Turnbull inscribes the book to his father's memory and his gift of vivid historic narration. The romance follows Venetian moods, beauty, and mystery.
a-honeymoon-in-space: George Chetwynd Griffith sends a couple on a honeymoon in space aboard the Astronef. The prologue gives the first cruise of the strange vessel, and chapters follow its voyage. Griffith, author of Valdar the Oft Born, writes an early romance of space travel. The book belongs to the first age of scientific romance.
a-little-tour-in-france:
Henry James travels slowly through provincial France and writes up what he sees, town by town. He begins at Tours and works through the Loire country of châteaux, then east and south to places such as Bourges, Dijon, and the old cities of Provence. Churches, inns, markets, and pictures fill his days.

James writes as a novelist on holiday: alert to manners, light, and the look of streets, and honest about boredom where he finds it. He compares French provincial life with American and English life as he goes. The sketches are easy in manner and exact in observation, and they have kept their place as a model of the literary travel book.
a-minstrel-in-france: Harry Lauder recalls his wartime years in France in this memoir, written in memory of his son John, a captain killed in France in 1916. The book blends verse and recollection from a popular entertainer who carried his stage act to the country where his only boy had died for liberty. Pride in that service runs through songs of loneliness, parting, and duty, alongside the humour of a performer among soldiers.
a-modern-instance: William Dean Howells builds this novel around a marriage tested by ambition, journalism, and small-town expectation, following a young couple from courtship into a union that begins to crack. The story is told through the daily pressures of newspaper work and domestic life, where pride and misunderstanding widen into estrangement. Its interest lies less in any single quarrel than in how ordinary choices, repeated over time, undo a bond.
a-rogue-by-compulsion-an-affair-of-the-s: Victor Bridges tells a secret service affair in this novel, opening with a bolt for freedom and a hero disguised in a bicycle and overalls. The chapter titles promise a dubious refuge, an offer without an alternative, a man with a scar, and a palmist named Vivien. A workshop on the marshes and a new clue to an old crime carry the intrigue forward. Through Sonia's visits, police action, and a last-minute rescue, the rogue moves toward exoneration.
a-short-history-of-france: Mary Platt Parmele writes this short illustrated history of France, opening with early conditions in Gaul and Caesar's conquest, including Lutetia. The chapters pass the birth of Christianity, the Franks under Clovis and Charles Martel, Charlemagne, Northmen invasions, and feudalism's decline under Hugh Capet. Free cities, crusades, Philip Augustus, and the Albigensian war carry the narrative toward a kingdom gathering its provinces under one crown.
a-sicilian-romance:
Ann Radcliffe wrote A Sicilian Romance as a Gothic tale framed by a found manuscript. A traveller admires the ruined castle of the house of Mazzini on Sicily's northern shore, and a friar offers him the family's recorded history. tells how luxury and vice brought that proud house to ruin and left its halls to decay.

Inside the manuscript, the Marquis Mazzini rules his castle and daughters with cold cruelty, and lights and sounds in the deserted apartments suggest someone hidden within the walls. Julia Mazzini's flight from a forced marriage drives escapes, pursuits, and revelations through convents, wild country, and dungeons. Radcliffe helped fix the Gothic recipe here: terror, scenery, and a heroine in flight.
a-strange-disappearance:
Anna Katharine Green's detective novel begins with talk of sudden vanishings, as the young detective called Q agrees to tell of a case stranger than most. A young woman has disappeared from a wealthy New York house, and no one will speak plainly about her. The contents promise clues in a bureau drawer, a bit of calico, and a few golden hairs.

Twenty chapters follow secrets in Mr. Blake's studio, a house at a crossroads, a capture, and long explanations. Green builds her case from small physical clues and guarded witnesses. The book is an early American detective story, written before the genre had settled rules, and it shows her gift for slow, careful suspense.
a-traveler-from-altruria-romance: William Dean Howells imagines a traveler from Altruria in this romance, opening with a narrator interrupted in his own story by an unexpected guest. A friend's letter of advice announces the Altrurian. The narrator engages a hotel room, ready to tell the clerk that the visitor's money is not good if he tries to pay. When the traveler steps from the train, the narrator finds himself gladder to see him than expected, and the utopian's American education begins.
a-wanderer-in-florence: Edward Verrall Lucas wanders in Florence in this volume of May 1912, opening with a historical chart of Florence and Europe from 1296 to 1564. The colour illustrations show the Duomo and Campanile, the cloisters of San Lorenzo, the Via Calzaioli, the Palazzo Vecchio, and the Loggia de' Lanzi. Fiesole, the Badia and Bargello, Santa Croce, the Ponte Vecchio, the Piazza della Signoria on a wet Friday afternoon, and evening from the Piazzale Michelangelo complete the wander.
a-wanderer-in-venice: Edward Verrall Lucas wanders in Venice in this 1914 volume, with sixteen illustrations in colour by Harry Morley, thirty-two photographs from paintings, and a map. The frontispiece shows the Grand Canal from the steps of Santa Maria della Salute. An old traveller quoted at the opening preferred the sight of Venice, with her resplendent beauty, antiquities, and monuments. He preferred that sight to four of the richest manors of Somersetshire bestowed gratis on condition of never seeing her.
a-woman-of-no-importance:
Oscar Wilde's play is set at Hunstanton Chase, a grand country house, and later at Mrs. Arbuthnot's home nearby. The title page of this edition notes the play was first printed in 1894. Guests trade sharp talk about love, marriage, and society while a hidden past waits offstage. Mrs. Arbuthnot guards a secret about her son Gerald and the man who fathered him.

Across four acts the polite party talk gives way to shame, anger, and a hard choice about honor. Wilde mixes bright epigrams with a serious attack on rules that punish women and excuse men. The ending refuses the easy pardon the guilty man expects.
abc-s-of-science:
Charles A. Oliver sets out the ABCs of science for young readers in a short primer of seven chapters. The book aims at beginners, as its title promises, and keeps its lessons elementary. It introduces the natural world in simple language meant for a child's first steps into the subject.

Short chapters and plain statements carry the whole design; there is no apparatus of notes or advanced terms. The primer belongs to the age when popular science for children was a new and hopeful trade. Read today, it shows what a young reader of its time was first taught about how nature works, and in what order the wonders were presented.
abe-lincoln-gets-his-chance: Frances Cavanah tells how Abe Lincoln gets his chance in this children's book, a Weekly Reader Book Club edition of 1959 illustrated by Paula Hutchison. Dedicated to her grandnephew Philip Jan Nadelman, the story depends primarily on Lincoln's own statements and on family and friends with firsthand knowledge of his everyday life. Where dialogue had to be imagined, the author notes, the imagined talk fits what is known of the circumstances.
active-service:
Stephen Crane sends a young newspaper correspondent, Rufus Coleman, to cover the war between Greece and Turkey. Crane had reported that war himself, and the novel draws on what he saw: bad information, big talk in cafés, and danger that arrives without ceremony. Coleman goes to rescue a professor and his family caught behind the lines.
