The rescue becomes a tangle of cavalry, comic opera soldiers, and a running fight. Through it Coleman carries on a duel of pride with the professor's daughter. He had once courted her at home. Crane writes the war scenes with his sharp, color-struck eye and treats the heroics with irony. The book mixes adventure, satire of journalism, and a hard-edged romance.
american-institutions-and-their-influenc: Alexis de Tocqueville examines American institutions and their influence, in a work whose American edition carries its own preface and advertisement. The study weighs democracy, law, and local government, asking how a new republic holds together. Tocqueville's analysis remains a classic account of American political life and its tensions, still read by students of democracy.
an-accursed-race:
An Accursed Race is a short work of 1855 by Elizabeth Gaskell, the English novelist often called Mrs Gaskell. Gaskell, best known for her novels of Victorian society and her biography of Charlotte Brontë, here turns to a stranger subject: the Cagots, a despised outcast people of the Pyrenees region. Her piece asks how a whole group could be shunned for centuries without a known crime.

She gathers what history and tradition say about the Cagots: the separate church doors, the badges, and the bans forced on them. The tale is part inquiry and part protest against inherited prejudice. It shows Gaskell's social conscience at work on a small, haunting case, told with the detailed sympathy that marks her fiction.
an-essay-on-the-evils-of-popular-ignoran: John Foster writes an essay on the evils of popular ignorance, in sections that build a sustained case for education. He argues that ignorance harms both the individual and the commonwealth, and that learning is a public duty. Foster's earnest prose made the essay a classic plea for popular schooling.
an-introduction-to-chemical-science:
Rufus P. Williams wrote his textbook, by his preface, for the average high school: simple, practical, experimental, and inductive, not a cyclopaedia of chemical information. He insists above all on the writing of equations, which he calls the multum in parvo, the much in little, of chemical knowledge. Questions throughout call attention to what the pupil should observe.

Chapters build from first experiments with air, water, and common substances toward the metals, acids, and organic compounds, with an appendix of tables. The book belongs to the years when laboratory teaching was entering American schools. Its clarity and order made it a standard beginner's chemistry for a generation of students.
an-old-woman-s-tale-from-the-doliver-rom: Nathaniel Hawthorne tells an old woman's tale, drawn from the Doliver Romance and other pieces of tales and sketches. The fragment carries Hawthorne's familiar mood of guilt, memory, and New England gloom in brief compass. Even unfinished, it shows the master's hand in atmosphere and moral shadow. The sketch form suits its mood of loss and recall.
angelic-wisdom-about-divine-providence: Emanuel Swedenborg writes on angelic wisdom about divine providence, in an edition from the Swedenborg Foundation in New York, established in 1850, with a version by William Frederic Wunsch. The work explains how providence guides human life toward good, even through evil and suffering. Swedenborg's system joins theology to a vision of spiritual order.
atma-a-romance:
Caroline Augusta Frazer, signing herself A. C. F., published this romance at Montreal with John Lovell and Son in 1891. Her preface borrows Max Muller's note on the Sanskrit word atman, usually rendered soul or self, and adopts Self as the least misleading term. The title thus promises a story with a philosophical spine.

Atma and his friend Bertram move through an India of maharanees, shrines, and pilgrimage. Tired of splendour, Bertram rides with Atma toward a sacred well on the southern border of Kashmir, attendants bearing gifts behind them. Their roadside talks weigh the self, duty, and desire. Frazer wraps Vedantic ideas in the dress of a colonial romance, with Kashmir's mountains closing round the seekers.
augustus-does-his-bit-a-true-to-life-far:
George Bernard Shaw wrote Augustus Does His Bit, a short wartime farce first performed by the Stage Society at London's Court Theatre in January 1917. Shaw's preface explains his target: Lord Augustus Highcastle, a well-meaning, patriotic, self-important official. Government departments, Shaw says, knew the type well. Their problem was winning the war with Augustus on their backs.

Lord Augustus sits in a mayor's parlor in Little Pifflington, heels on the writing table, reading his newspaper. A mysterious lady visitor and a clerk named Horatio Floyd Beamish draw him into intrigue over secret papers. Augustus blunders through every exchange while believing himself indispensable. Shaw squeezes a full satire of wartime bureaucracy into one act. Readers get a brief, sharp comedy about the governing class at its most confidently useless.
authors-of-greece:
The Reverend T. W. Lumb wrote this survey of Greek writers, with an introduction by Cyril Alington. Lumb argues in his preface that Greek writing sounds more modern than Latin, medieval, or Elizabethan work. Greece, he says, was mainly democratic, full of free inquiry, and troubled by feuds and problems still familiar: militarism, nationalism, and loud popular preachers included.

Poets, historians, and playwrights pass in review with their plots and merits plainly told. Euripides' Helen gets a full retelling: Helen devises the escape, passing Menelaus off as a messenger of her husband's death until Greek sailors overpower the rowers and sail home. Lumb teaches as a schoolmaster would, keen that readers see their own age in the Greek mirror and draw the lessons waiting there.
avril-being-essays-on-the-poetry-of-the-:
Hilaire Belloc published these essays on French Renaissance poetry with Duckworth of London in 1904. Part of the book had run in The Pilot. Belloc dedicates it to F. Y. Eccles, admitting the essays owe more to his friend's learning than to his own enthusiasm. Six poets carry the volume: Charles of Orleans, Villon, Marot, Ronsard, Du Bellay, and Malherbe.

Belloc reads the Pléiade as a Catholic and a craftsman, praising tunes, clarity, and devotion. On Ronsard he finds a unique illusion of distance, a chastity or weakness of soul that watches itself as it writes. The great picture opening the fifty-eighth sonnet of the second book shows visions rising that Cassandra never gave. French verse gets a champion's brief, written with swagger and song.
back-to-the-woods-the-story-of-a-fall-fr:
George V. Hobart wrote these slang comedies as Hugh McHugh, publishing the book in 1902. His hero John Henry narrates in racetrack American, dedicating the volume to the boys of the Hammer Club: get together and hit hard, for the Devil loveth a cheerful knocker. Clara J., Uncle Peter the trust tamer, Aunt Martha, and Tacks the boy disaster fill the cast list.

Seven stories follow John Henry's luck through a ghost story, a burglar, a country cop, and two queens. One trip lands the party in the Jiggersville calaboose, a little brick jail its town is proud of. A five-dollar bill buys Bunch Jefferson a stay of proceedings while John Henry sweats on the court-room bench. Hobart's John Henry books sold on voice alone: breezy, crooked, and proud of it.
baron-trigault-s-vengeance:
Emile Gaboriau published this crime novel in 1870 as a sequel to The Count's Millions. Vengeance is its first word and ruling passion: a man victimised by conspiracy, his honour and fortune wrecked, finds his torment eased only by picturing it returned a hundredfold. Gaboriau, founder of the French detective novel, builds the reprisal as carefully as any Lecoq investigation.

Around the baron gather the ruined and the scheming. One woman, still young, appears old and haggard from days of hard work for a miserable living and nights of weeping, her magnificent hair and big black eyes the ruins of beauty. Inheritance, disguise, and slow revenge interlock across twenty chapters. English readers took Gaboriau neat in translation, and this late volume shows his machinery of conspiracy at full stretch.
beatrice:
H. Rider Haggard's novel Beatrice appears here in Dutch, in C. Baarslag's version, printed at Amsterdam by Holdert in 1890. The title page names Haggard as the author of Jess. Autumn dusk opens the tale over a still sea on the Welsh coast. Beatrice stands at the far point of the Dog Rocks, watching the brown weed sink under the green tide while mist creeps in.

Geoffrey, the wedded lawyer who loves her, drives the later drama. In one scene he speaks with stern force about little Effie. The child told tales of railway men, and some would beat her for it. He warns that any who touch her will answer to him. A jealous voice replies that she will not stay for such talk. Haggard's story of a schoolmistress, a drowning, and a love that could not be, reads in Dutch just as its first readers knew it.
benita-an-african-romance:
H. Rider Haggard sets this African romance on the Zambesi, where Portuguese gold was said to lie hidden for three centuries. His opening note describes treasure buried near the river in the sixteenth century and a child's trance account that led searchers to a few old coins. The heroine, Benita Clifford, has the gift that found them: under mesmeric trance she sees what is hidden.

Benita sails for Africa on the mail steamer Zanzibar, and the story follows her into the ruins where the gold is believed to rest. Haggard mixes treasure hunting with her unwilling second sight, which draws fortune seekers toward her as much as toward the gold. Love, greed, and the dead hand of the old Portuguese builders drive the plot to its end among the ruins.
brandes-main-currents-2-the-romantic-sch:
French Romantic writers take the stage in the second book of Brandes's Main Currents, here in English. Hugo, Lamartine, and Musset lead a revolt against the stiff classical rules of the old stage and page. Brandes writes of them with heat and flair.

He paints the Romantics as fighters for freedom of the mind. Their poems, plays, and novels broke forms open and let raw feeling in. Brandes tells literary history like a gripping story, with heroes and foes. Readers meet the French movement through a critic who loved bold art and hated dull obedience.
brandes-main-currents-3-the-reaction-in-:
Writers who fought back against the French Revolution fill the third book of Brandes's Main Currents, here in English. Catholic and royalist voices raised altar and throne against the new ideas. Brandes, a liberal, gives even these foes a fair and vivid hearing.

He tracks how fear of chaos fed faith, order, and longing for the old world. Strong minds on the losing side get sharp, honest portraits. The volume shows Brandes at his most generous as a critic. To grasp the century, he insists, one must grasp the reaction as well as the revolt.
britannica-1911-abdera-thrace:
Abdera in Thrace receives a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The coastal town near the Nestos mouth, facing Thasos, claims Heracles as mythic founder. A colony from Clazomenae in the seventh century B.C. gives its history a start.

Teos's folk, fleeing Persia after the Ionian revolt, swelled it in 544 B.C. and brought the gryphon coin type with them. Coin reverses from Abdera win praise for beauty and variety in the entry. Importance faded after the mid-fourth century. A proverb blamed the town air for stupidity, yet Democritus the philosopher was its citizen. Ruins on Cape Balastra cover seven hills and two harbours, with medieval Polystylon on the south-west heights.
britannica-1911-abeyance:
Abeyance receives a law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, signed by John Horace Round and read here inside a shared chunk of text. The word, from Old French abeance, gaping, names a state of waiting in property, titles, or office. Right rests in no one till the true owner appears.

Future estates supply the stock case: a life grant with remainder to a living man's heir hangs in abeyance till that man dies. A benefice's freehold waits the same way between incumbents. Peerages give the common use: a barony by writ falling among sisters sleeps till one line gathers all claims, or the crown calls it out for one heir. Dormant, meaning merely unclaimed, is not abeyance, the entry warns.
britannica-1911-absence: Absence is the headword of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives the word, from Latin absentia, as the fact of being away, in body or in mind. Absence of mind names the state where thought withdraws from what is passing. Eton College calls its special roll-call Absence, boys attending in tall hats. A soldier needs leave of absence before quitting his regiment. Seven years gone with no sign of life stands in law as presumptive evidence of death, the entry closes.
britannica-1911-abstinence: Abstinence is the headword of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives the word, from Latin abstinere, to abstain, as the fact or habit of refraining from anything. Common use narrows it to the indulgence of appetite, and above all to strong drink. Total abstinence and total abstainer belong with taking the pledge against alcoholic liquor, the entry notes, sending readers toward Temperance. In church discipline abstinence names a form of fasting less severe than the full fast, and the notice closes with that distinction.
britannica-1911-acceptance:
Acceptance, in law, is the act by which a person binds himself to comply with a bill of exchange addressed to him by its drawer. The 1911 Britannica entry treats it as a promise to pay the bill in money, and in money only. Signing the bill, with or without the word accepted written across it, makes a general acceptance, an engagement to pay strictly as the bill reads.

Qualified acceptance changes the terms: payment on a condition, of part of the sum, or at a different time or place. A holder need not take such an acceptance, and takes it at his own risk. If the drawee refuses, another person may accept supra protest, for the honour of a party to the bill.
britannica-1911-accidence:
Accidence is a term of grammar, a mis-spelling of accidents, from a Latin word for casual events. The 1911 Britannica entry defines it as the changes words undergo in their inflections, their altered endings and forms, as to gender, number, tense, and case. Those small changes carry much of the meaning in inflected languages.

Usage widened beyond grammar. Accidence also came to denote a book containing the first principles of grammar, the beginner's starting point. From there it stretched further, to the rudiments of any subject or art at all. Readers meeting the word in older schoolbooks should hear that beginner's sense first: accidence is where a subject starts.
britannica-1911-accomplice:
Accomplice, in law, is one who is associated with others in committing a crime, whether as principal or accessory. The 1911 Britannica entry explains why the word matters most in the courtroom. An accomplice who turns king's evidence, testifying against his partners in hope of a pardon, gives evidence tainted by self-interest, since he speaks to save himself.

Juries are therefore warned. Practice directs a jury to acquit where an accomplice's evidence is not corroborated, backed up by independent proof both of the offence and of the accused person's part in it. An accomplice who turns evidence usually receives a pardon, but he has no legal right to escape punishment until that pardon is actually granted.
britannica-1911-ace: Ace names the number one at dice, or the single point, or pip, shown on a die or a playing card. This entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the word through the Latin as back to a Tarentine form of the Greek word for one. The term reaches beyond cards and dice: an ace is also a point in the scoring of racquets, lawn tennis, tennis, and other court games. A single mark, a single point, and a single winning stroke share the same small name.
britannica-1911-adolescence:
Adolescence is the span between childhood and full growth, when traits that make or mar a person emerge. A 1911 Britannica entry gives the Latin root as to grow up, kin to the word adult. Growth in height, weight, and strength speeds up and may even double its rate. In the man it runs toward strength, in the woman toward fitness for motherhood.

Love of nature and religion wakes in this span, with a hunger to know all things. That mix of power for good and ill makes the years hard to guide well. Parents and teachers face their toughest task in this stage of life. The entry treats it as the most weighty passage in human growth.
britannica-1911-aguilar-grace:
Aguilar, Grace, an English writer who lived from 1816 to 1847, is the subject of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the daughter of a Jewish merchant in London and was born there in June 1816. Her writing career was brief, since she died at thirty-one. It still produced a shelf of books, mostly religious fiction written from within her own faith.

Her best known works named here are The Vale of Cedars, published after her death, and Home Influence, which appeared in her final year. In The Spirit of Judaism and other books she defended her faith and its people against attack. Jewish women honoured that service with a testimonial presented shortly before she died at Frankfort-on-the-Main in September 1847.
britannica-1911-albacete-province:
Albacete is an inland province of south eastern Spain, formed in 1833. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica cut it from the north half of Murcia. High plains of New Castile fill its north part in full. Hills and the Sierra de Alcaraz rise in the south part instead.

Rivers Segura and Júcar water its two ends on their way to the sea. Fruit rich glens in Alcaraz stand out amid bare dry tracts nearby. Wheat, olives, vines, and saffron lead its farm output in trade. Bulls for the ring and horses for the cavalry win wide fame. Sparse people and poor roads held back its mines and mills.
britannica-1911-allowance:
Allowance is an English word with two Latin roots behind it, one meaning to praise and one meaning to assign a place. The entry therefore reads its general sense as assigning something with approval. In ordinary use it means the act of allowing, or the thing allowed, especially a limited share of money, food, or diet given to someone.

Commercial usage gives the word a narrower meaning: a deduction from the gross weight of goods. The deduction covers the box or package, plus waste and breakages expected in handling. Practice varies by trade, district, and country. The coal trade supplies the worked example, in which a merchant receives twenty-one hundredweight from the pit for every ton bought, the extra hundredweight covering waste from transhipment, screening, and cartage.
britannica-1911-alma-tadema-sir-laurence:
Sir Laurence Alma-Tadema (1836– ) was a British artist born at Dronrijp, a Frisian village near Leeuwarden, on 8 January 1836. His father, a notary who died when the boy was four, had intended him for the law. A strong leaning toward art won out, and in 1852 he entered the Antwerp academy under Gustav Wappers, later passing to the atelier of Henri Leys.

Early success came with The Education of the Children of Clovis in 1861, the first of a Merovingian series drawn from early Frankish history. The entry follows his collected exhibition in London in 1882–1883, gold medals at Amsterdam and Paris, and works such as Fredegonda, which it treats as the finest of that romantic series. Memberships and honours, including the Royal Society of Water-colours, round out the career as it stood when the entry was written.
britannica-1911-almeria-province:
White table grapes star among Almería's exports: over two million barrels leave each year, despite steep transport costs, and the mild climate also suits oranges, lemons, almonds, and vines. Silk comes from the west, the central districts raise cattle praised for size and quality, and the ground is rich in minerals, iron above all.

Almería is a sea-facing province of southern Spain, carved in 1833 from the eastern lands of the old kingdom of Granada. Across its 3,360 square miles, where 359,013 people lived in 1900, mountain ridges rise to peaks of six to eight thousand feet, cut by fertile valleys. The Adra, Almería, and Almanzora rivers run from the hills to the Mediterranean. Set against these gifts are backward schooling, a low standard of comfort, and steady emigration to Algeria.
britannica-1911-almuce:
Two shapes of almuce stood side by side by the fourteenth century. One was a plain cap dropping just over the ears. The other, hood-like over back and shoulders, was kept for weightier canons. At first the garment had covered the head alone, and lay clergy and lay folk alike wore it. Records from the twelfth to the fifteenth centuries name it often, now as a hood, more often as its own kind of cap.

The almuce is a fur cape, hooded or fur-lined, worn in choir by some high officers of the Western Church; amice is another spelling. Where the word comes from is a puzzle, though its first part likely keeps the Arabic article, the term having risen in the south. In England the garment was put down in 1559 and barred for good by canons drawn up in 1571.
britannica-1911-audience:
Audience is the subject of a word and custom entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from the Latin for to hear. It first means the act of hearing, and then the people who hear. That covers crowds at a theatre, a concert, or a public meeting.

The entry then turns to more formal senses of the word. Audience can mean the right of peers and of the Commons to reach the sovereign. It also names the rite by which envoys are admitted to meet a ruler and present their papers. In France the word names a sitting of a law court. In Spain a like word names certain courts.
britannica-1911-avila-province:
Ávila, a province of central Spain, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It is one of the modern divisions of the old kingdom of Castile. Valladolid bounds it on the north. Segovia and Madrid bound it on the east. Toledo, Cáceres, and Salamanca bound it on the south and west. Its people numbered just over two hundred thousand in 1900.

The province splits by nature into two parts. They differ fully in soil, climate, produce, and way of life. The north is mostly level. Its soil is poor, strong and marly in a few places, but rocky in the valleys. The climate swings from hard cold in winter to great heat in summer. The folk of the north work the land. The south is one mass of rugged granite hills. Sheltered valleys are set among them. The article gives a land of sharp contrasts in a small compass.
britannica-1911-avoidance:
Avoidance, in word history, comes from avoid, properly to make empty or void, from an Old French verb for emptying out, linked to Latin vacuus, empty. In current use avoid means to keep away from or shun, and avoidance is that action of keeping away.

Law gives the word sharper senses, and the entry sets them out in order. In law generally, avoidance means making a thing void or null: invalidation or annulment, as in the plea called confession and avoidance. In church law it means a benefice falling vacant, empty of an incumbent, a living without a holder. One root idea, being empty, thus covers shunning, cancelling, and a post left open.
britannica-1911-aymer-of-valence:
Aymer of Valence (d. 1260), bishop of Winchester, was a half-brother of Henry III, son of Isabelle of Angoulême and Hugo of Lusignan, count of La Marche. His family came to England in 1247 hoping for court favor, and in 1250 strong royal pressure on the electors won him the Winchester see.

The choice was, by the entry's plain judgment, wholly unsuitable: Aymer was illiterate, knew no English, and lived a secular life. Hatred of foreign favorites centred on him. At the Oxford parliament of 1258 he and his brothers rejected the barons' new constitution; pursued to Winchester and besieged in Wolvesey castle, he surrendered and left England. Never consecrated, he won papal backing and was returning when fatal illness struck at Paris.
britannica-1911-badajoz-province:
Badajoz is a frontier province of western Spain, formed in 1833 from districts of Estremadura and bounded west by Portugal. At 8,451 square miles it is the largest province in the kingdom, with 520,246 people in 1900. Much of it is a bare, monotonous plain crossed by the Guadiana river.

Climate swings between fierce summer heat, with fevers in the river valley, and cold winter winds; rain is scant and little land is watered. Farming lags, yet Badajoz keeps more livestock than any other Spanish province, its acorn-fed swine famed across Spain for hams and bacon. Lead mining struggles for want of water and roads, while transit trade through seven custom houses with Portugal matters more than local industry.
britannica-1911-bagration-peter-prince:
Bagration, Peter, Prince (1765-1812), was a Russian general from the noble Georgian Bagratides family who entered the army in 1782 and served years in the Caucasus. He fought at Ochakov's siege in 1788 and in Poland in 1794, then won Suvarov's eye in the Italian and Swiss campaign of 1799, taking Brescia.

In 1805 Bagration's small rearguard held off forces five times its size at Hollabrunn, losing half its men but saving Kutusov's retreating army. He fought doggedly at Austerlitz, Eylau, and Friedland, seized the Åland Islands by a daring march over the frozen Gulf of Finland in 1808, and beat the Turks in 1809. Leading the left wing at Borodino in 1812, he took his mortal wound; a tsar's monument marks the field.
britannica-1911-balance:
Balance, in the 1911 Britannica entry, starts as a word for a weighing tool. It comes from a late Latin word for an apparatus with two pans. The entry covers beam and spring balances, and also torsion balances, which measure force by the twist they give to a wire.

Beyond tools, the word means making things equal. The entry points to balance in bookkeeping, where debit and credit accounts are made to match. It also names the balance wheel of a clock or watch, and the balancing of engines, where added masses cut down shaking while the engine runs.
britannica-1911-barcelona-spanish-provin:
Barcelona is a maritime province of north-eastern Spain, formed in 1833 from districts of the old kingdom of Catalonia. Gerona bounds it to the north-east, the Mediterranean to the south, Tarragona to the south-west, and Lérida to the west. Its population in 1900 was 1,054,541, and its area 2,968 square miles.

Apart from level tracts along the coast and near a few inland towns, the province is mountain through and through. Its ranges are outliers of the Pyrenees, often thickly wooded, rich in minerals, and cut by deep ravines. The Sierra del Cadi lifts the peak of Tosa to 8,317 feet, while Montserrat and Monseny rise alone nearer the sea. The 1911 Britannica entry follows the rivers, led by the Llobrégat, and the province's three climate zones.
britannica-1911-barres-maurice:
Maurice Barrès (1862– ), a French novelist and politician born at Charmes in the Vosges, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. Educated at Nancy, he went to Paris for legal studies in 1883, wrote for journals, and briefly ran his own periodical. A stay in Italy produced Sous l'œil des barbares in 1888, the first book of a trilogy completed by Un Homme libre and Le Jardin de Bérénice.

Early Barrès praised the self above all, dividing the world into himself and the barbarians outside him. Politics pulled him toward General Boulanger, and he sat as deputy from 1889 to 1893. Then came a second trilogy, Le Roman de l'énergie nationale, urging love of home province and country. Later books on nationalism, Alsace, and Sparta are listed, and the entry closes with his admission to the French Academy in 1906.
britannica-1911-barrett-lawrence:
Lawrence Barrett (1838–1891), an American actor born in Paterson, New Jersey, to Irish parents, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His family name was Brannigan. He first acted at Detroit in 1853, reached New York in 1856, and joined the Boston Museum company in 1858. During the Civil War he served with distinction as a captain in the 28th Massachusetts infantry, then helped manage the California Theatre in San Francisco.

Barrett's stage range fills much of the entry. He played Hamlet, Lear, Macbeth, Shylock, Richard III, and Wolsey, and acted Othello opposite Booth's Iago. London audiences saw him several times, and his Richelieu was judged his finest part. He also wrote lives of Edwin Forrest and Edwin Booth and their circle. Barrett died in March 1891.
britannica-1911-baryatinsky-alexander-iv:
Alexander Ivanovich Baryatinsky, Prince (1814–1879), a Russian soldier and governor of the Caucasus, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Privately educated, he joined the Guards at seventeen and won a gold sword for valour in the Caucasus in 1835. Back there in 1845 he distinguished himself again in the attack on Shamyl's stronghold, earning the order of St George. He also helped crush the Cracow rising in 1846.

Command in the Caucasus defines Baryatinsky's fame. His energetic yet systematic tactics opened, the entry says, a new era in mountain warfare. As commander-in-chief and governor from 1856, he subdued the eastern Caucasus within three years and finally captured the long-elusive Shamyl himself. He also conquered tribes in the west and was made a field marshal. Broken health forced his resignation in 1862, and he died at Geneva.
britannica-1911-bayonne-france:
Bayonne is a fortified town of south-western France, set where the Nive joins the Adour, about three miles from the sea. It is the capital of an arrondissement in Basses-Pyrénées, sixty-six miles from Pau. The two rivers split it into Grand Bayonne, Petit Bayonne and Saint Esprit, linked by bridges.

Grand Bayonne holds the Gothic cathedral of Ste Marie, built across the 1200s to 1400s, while a citadel by Vauban guards Saint Esprit. The town began as Lapurdum, a Roman post of the third century and chief port of Novempopulana. Its later story includes long English rule and fighting in the Peninsular War.
britannica-1911-beccafumi-domenico-di-pa:
Domenico di Pace Beccafumi, a painter of Italy born in fourteen eighty six, is set in his school in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was of the school of Siena. In the early days of the free towns of Tuscany, Siena stood as a match for Florence in art skill.

A great plague in thirteen forty eight set the city on a fall. Its folk still held a host of skilled hands in all crafts. Yet its school did not share in the broad rise of Italian art in the next age. By fifteen hundred Siena had no home son of the first rank in art. Its great jobs went most times to men of other towns. Then the works of two giants at Rome were laid bare in fifteen hundred and eight. That sight stirred all the schools of Italy to match them.
britannica-1911-benefice:
Benefice, from the Latin beneficium, a benefit, began as a Roman term for land whose use emperors granted to soldiers for life. It rewarded past service and bound the man to future service. A Book of Benefices kept the list of all such grants at Rome.

Feudal lords copied the pattern, granting land to vassals for upkeep in return for military service, the land returning at death. Bishops did the like for clergy, a practice the council of Orleans recognised in 511. In canon law a benefice always ties to a church office. Later sections treat plural holding, first fruits and tenths, and the ways a benefice falls vacant.
britannica-1911-benevolence:
Benevolence, from Latin words for wishing well, in plain use means a kind act or a gift of money or goods. English history gives it a sharper sense: sums dressed up as gifts that kings squeezed from subjects without parliament’s consent. Forced loans under Edward II and Richard II came first.

Edward IV dropped even the pretence of repayment, and in 1473 the word was first used for such a royal demand. He got away with it, but when Richard III copied him, protest won an act of 1484 wiping out benevolences as “new and unlawful inventions.” Richard still demanded one, and later kings kept testing the device the law had condemned.
britannica-1911-bethune-france:
Béthune, a town of northern France in the Pas de Calais, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on a low hill where the Lawe meets a canal, north west of Arras, with a little over twelve thousand people in 1906. Once strongly fortified, it is now ringed by wide boulevards, with new quarters grown up outside.

The old town is a maze of winding streets and blind alleys, lined with old houses in the Flemish style. In the central square stands one of the finest belfries of northern France, a square tower from the thirteen hundreds topped by a wooden campanile. The chief church, Saint Vaast, dates from the fifteen hundreds. Béthune sits amid the richest coal mines in France. Its work includes oil distilling, tanning, salt refining, brewing, and the making of earthenware and casks.
britannica-1911-bice:
Bice is a term for certain dark shades of green or blue pigment. It comes from the French word bis, of doubtful origin, meaning dark-coloured. The 1911 Britannica entry says the English use is in fact an error. English speakers took it from the French phrases vert bis and azur bis. Those phrases mean dark green and dark blue in French. The English word then settled on the pigments themselves.

The colours are generally prepared from basic copper carbonates. Sometimes they are made from ultramarine and other pigments instead. The entry is a short note on a painter's term, not a full account of pigment making. It gives the word's French source, the mistake in its English use, and the usual base materials. No makers, dates, or trade details are supplied in the text.
britannica-1911-binney-horace:
Horace Binney (1780–1875) was an American lawyer, born in Philadelphia on 4 January 1780. He graduated at Harvard College in 1797 and studied law under Jared Ingersoll. Admitted to the bar in 1800, he practised with great success for fifty years. He was counted among the leaders of the American bar in his time. He sat in the Pennsylvania legislature in 1806 and 1807. As a Whig he served in Congress from 1833 to 1835.

There he defended the United States Bank against President Jackson's policy. His most famous case was Bidal versus Girard's Executors, over Stephen Girard's fortune. Daniel Webster argued against him in that case, and lost the verdict to Binney's side. The 1911 Britannica entry says his argument shaped charity law deeply. During the Civil War he published three pamphlets backing Lincoln's suspension of habeas corpus. His grandson's life of him appeared in 1904.
britannica-1911-binyon-laurence:
Laurence Binyon (1869– ) was an English poet, born at Lancaster on 10 August 1869. He was educated at St Paul's School, London, and at Trinity College, Oxford. There he won the Newdigate prize in 1890 for his poem Persephone. In 1893 he joined the printed books department of the British Museum. In 1895 he moved to the prints and drawings department. His Catalogue of English Drawings there began in 1898.

The 1911 Britannica entry lists his poems volume by volume. Lyric Poems came in 1894, and London Visions filled two volumes by 1898. The Death of Adam, Penthesilea, and the drama Attila followed in the 1900s. As an art critic he wrote on the Dutch etchers and on John Crome and John Sell Cotman. In 1906 he began a Blake reproduction series with his own critical introduction. Critics of the new century are cited at the close.
britannica-1911-bio-bio-province:
Bio-Bio is an inland province of southern Chile. Concepción, Arauco, and Malleco bound it north, west, and south, and Argentina lies east. Its area is 5,246 square miles of well-wooded, mountainous country. Timber is exported from the province to a large extent. The great trunk railway from Santiago south to Puerto Montt crosses its western part. That line also links the province with the port of Concepción.

The capital is Los Angeles, with an estimated 7,777 people in 1902. The 1911 Britannica entry places the town 152 miles east of this railway, a figure as printed in the text. A branch line connects the capital with the trunk route. The entry is a short province gazetteer of a few lines. Area, bounds, timber, and the railway carry its whole picture. No towns besides the capital are named in the text.
britannica-1911-blaye-et-ste-luce:
Blaye-et-Ste Luce is a fortified town in south-west France on the right bank of the Gironde, 35 miles north of Bordeaux by rail. The river there is over 2 miles wide. The town held 3423 people in 1906, and the wider commune 4890.

Vauban built its citadel on a rock by the river, around the ruins of a Gothic castle holding the tomb of Caribert, king of Toulouse. Fort Pâté on a river island and Fort Médoc on the far bank complete the defences. Blaye traded in wine, brandy, grain, fruit, and timber, and built small boats and milled flour. In ancient times, as Blavia, it was a port of the Santones, and tradition buries the hero Roland in its old basilica.
britannica-1911-bloomfield-maurice:
Maurice Bloomfield, an American Sanskrit scholar born in 1855, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Austrian Silesia and came to the United States in 1867. Ten years later he graduated from Furman University in South Carolina. He then studied Sanskrit at Yale and at Johns Hopkins.

After two years of study in Berlin and Leipzig, Bloomfield returned to Johns Hopkins in 1881. He soon rose to professor of Sanskrit and comparative language study. He is best known as a student of the Vedas. He rendered the Hymns of the Atharva Veda into English in 1897. He was the first to edit a key ritual text, and in 1907 he issued a full Vedic concordance. A study of Cerberus, the dog of Hades, shows his range into myth as well.
britannica-1911-bone-lace: Bone-lace is a kind of lace worked by hand on a cushion with linen thread, in this very short 1911 Britannica entry. The pattern is first marked out with pins stuck into the cushion. Each thread is wound on its own bobbin, and the threads are twisted round the pins to build the design. The name has a plain cause. In the early days of the craft, the bobbins used for the work were made of bone, and the lace took its name from them.
britannica-1911-bouchor-maurice:
Maurice Bouchor (born 1855) was a French poet who also carved and staged his own marionette plays. Born in Paris, he published in turn Chansons joyeuses (1874), Poèmes de l'amour et de la mer (1875), a modern Faust in prose and verse (1878), and Paris tales in verse (1880). His Aurore (1883) turned toward religious mysticism.

That strain flowered in Les Symboles (1888, new series 1895), called his most interesting work. Bouchor sculpted the figures for small sacred dramas, Tobie, Noël, and Sainte Cécile, staged at the Théâtre des Marionnettes with voices spoken or sung from behind the scenes. A verse Christmas play reached the Théâtre Français in 1895. With Julien Tiersot he also worked to save French folk songs, printing a school collection in 1897.
britannica-1911-brown-william-laurence:
William Laurence Brown (1755–1830) was a Scottish divine born on 7 January 1755 at Utrecht, where his father ministered to the English church. When his father became professor of ecclesiastical history at St Andrews the family returned to Scotland in 1757. The son passed through St Andrews grammar school and university, then divinity classes, before going back to Utrecht in 1774 for theology and civil law.

He was appointed to the English church at Utrecht in 1777 and about 1788 to chairs of moral philosophy and ecclesiastical history there, with the law of nature soon added. War following the French Revolution drove him to London in January 1795, where Aberdeen's magistrates gave him the chair of divinity and the principalship of Marischal College. Chaplain in ordinary to the king in 1800 and dean of the chapel royal in 1804, he died on 11 May 1830.
britannica-1911-bruce:
Bruce is the name of an old Scottish family of Norman descent, taken from Bruis between Cherbourg and Vallonges, with name forms Braose, Breaux and Brus. The first Robert de Brus, a follower of William the Conqueror, was rewarded with many manors, chiefly in Yorkshire, of which Skelton was the principal. Land and marriages built the line step by step.

His son, the second Robert, received the lordship of Annandale from David I. His comrade at the court of Henry I. The fourth Robert married Isabel, natural daughter of William the Lion. Their son, the fifth Robert, married Isabel, second daughter of David, earl of Huntingdon and niece of the same Scottish king, the marriage that grounded the family's royal claim. The most famous member is the eighth Robert, the Bruce, who became king of Scotland in 1306, and readers are sent to his own entry for the reign.
britannica-1911-budgell-eustace:
Eustace Budgell, an English man of letters who lived from 1686 to 1737, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Saint Thomas near Exeter, the son of a doctor, he entered Trinity College at Oxford in 1705 and then joined the Inner Temple in London. Instead of studying law, he gave his whole mind to literature.

Addison, a first cousin of his mother, befriended him. When Addison went to Ireland as secretary to the lord lieutenant in 1710, Budgell went with him as a clerk. He worked with Steele and Addison on the Tatler, and he wrote for the Spectator and the Guardian as well, his pieces marked. Posts in Ireland followed, and he sat in the Irish parliament. In 1717 Addison won him a revenue post there. A lampoon against a secretary cost him that post the next year, and he came back to England.
britannica-1911-buenos-aires-province:
Buenos Aires is a province study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a province of Argentina in South America. It is the largest province of the republic, at 117,812 square miles. It is also the most full of people, with an count in 1903 of 1,251,000, apart from the federal district.

The article describes a great treeless plain that runs from the coast to the Andes. Few good ports break its long shore, Bahia Blanca chief among them. Much of the middle and south east lies low and marshy. Two low ranges cross the south of the province. Lakes and small rivers water the land well. The chief river, the Salado, flows right across it. Herding of cattle came first as the chief work, with sheep raising added later.
britannica-1911-burgos-province:
Burgos is a province of northern Spain, and a gazetteer entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lays out its bounds and heights. Biscay and Álava bound it to the north east, and Logroño to the east. Soria, Segovia, Valladolid, Palencia, and Santander close the ring. The count for 1900 came to 338,828 people.

The province covers 5,480 square miles in area. It takes in the small county of Treviño, shut in on all sides by Álava. The north and north east districts are mountain country. The centre and south belong to the vast high plateau of Old Castile. Part of the great Cantabrian chain crosses the far north. The highest peaks stand in the east, in the Sierra de la Demanda. The Cerro de San Millán there rises to 6,995 feet.
britannica-1911-cadiz-province:
Cadiz, a sea province in the far south of Spain, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was formed in 1833 from districts taken from the province of Seville. Seville bounds it on the north and Malaga on the east. The Mediterranean, the Straits of Gibraltar, and the Atlantic wash its other sides. It covers 2,834 square miles and held 452,659 people in 1900.

The article gives most of its opening to the coast. The broad mouth of the Guadalquivir marks the Seville border. Farther south the Guadalete river falls into the grand double bay of Cadiz. Then comes Cape Trafalgar, famed for the British naval victory of 1805. Near it a marshy lagoon spreads by a river mouth. The southernmost point of the mainland of Europe stands on the straits.
britannica-1911-calais-france:
Calais (France) is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a seaport and manufacturing town of northern France. It stands eighteen miles from Dover, and its population in 1906 was 59,623. Once a celebrated fortress, it keeps a citadel of 1560 and four older forts. The old town stands on an island between canal and harbour basins.

The article describes the town and its trade. The old town hall stands in the Place d'Armes, near the watch tower. The church of Notre-Dame, built under English rule, has a tower that is a landmark for sailors. Calais is the chief port for passenger traffic with England. Its imports run to coal, iron, cotton goods and timber.
britannica-1911-carapace: Carapace is the name for the upper shell of certain animals. This 1911 Britannica entry is a single short definition. The word is French in form and comes from a Spanish word, carapacho, meaning a shield or armour. The shell of a crustacean bears the name, and so does the shell of a tortoise or turtle. The hard covering of the armadillo is called a carapace too. The term also covers the hard case enclosing certain of the Infusoria, minute water creatures. Nothing beyond the definition and the origin is given.
britannica-1911-carleton-place:
Carleton Place is a town of Lanark county, Ontario, Canada. It stands 28 miles south-west of Ottawa. It lies on the Mississippi river of that province. Two Canadian Pacific lines meet at the town in a junction. This very short 1911 Britannica entry gives its industries. The town is a port of entry for customs purposes. Its population in 1901 was 4059.

Water-power privileges at Carleton Place are abundant, the entry says. Extensive railway-repair shops employ many of its people. Woollen mills also operate in the town. The whole notice runs to a few lines only. It gives the river, the railway junction and the two industries. A reader gets the town's place and character in brief. Nothing more is attempted in the text of the entry.
britannica-1911-cassel-france:
Cassel is a town of northern France, in the department of Nord, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its hilltop place. It stands on an isolated hill 515 feet high, thirty-four miles north-west of Lille, with 1,844 people in 1906. From its top, parts of France, Belgium, and England can be seen.

The entry names its historic buildings, among them the old town hall and the hotel of the Noble Court, once the seat of justice for maritime Flanders. The town is thought to sit on a Roman station and road center. It saw great battles in 1071, 1328, and 1677, the last a defeat for William of Orange.
britannica-1911-castellon-de-la-plana-pr:
Castellón de la Plana is a coastal province of eastern Spain, and this 1911 Britannica entry describes its land and waters. It was formed in 1833 out of districts once part of Valencia. Teruel and Tarragona bound it on the north, the sea on the east, and Valencia on the south. Its people numbered 310,828 in 1900, over an area of 2,495 square miles.

The surface is mountainous almost everywhere, flat only near the coast and along some river valleys. Even the coast has two clear ridges, the Atalayas de Alcalá and the Desierto de las Palmas. The Mijares is the chief river, running down from the Teruel highlands to the sea just south of the capital, which shares the province's name. Other streams, among them the Monlleo, the Bergantes, and the Cenia, water the land well and make it rich for farming.
britannica-1911-cavallotti-felice:
Felice Cavallotti (1842–1898) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an Italian politician, poet, and dramatic author born at Milan. He fought with the Garibaldian corps in 1860 and 1866. He first won notice with anti monarchical lampoons in Milanese papers between 1866 and 1872. In 1872 he entered parliament as deputy for Corteolona. He took the oath of allegiance only after publicly attacking its validity.

On Bertani's death in 1886 Cavallotti took the leadership of the extreme Left. Under him the party grew from twenty members to seventy. His eloquence and combativeness made him a power in the house. The entry also notes his defamatory methods, which sometimes smacked of political blackmail. He fought thirty three duels and many lawsuits. Service in the cholera epidemic of 1885 added to his fame. On 6 March 1898 Count Macola, a conservative editor he had attacked, killed him in a duel.
britannica-1911-cenci-beatrice:
Beatrice Cenci (1577–1599) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Roman woman famed for her tragic story. Poetic fancy wove a halo of romance round her. Modern research, the entry says, has destroyed much of it. She was the daughter of Francesco Cenci, a rich man of violent temper. Tradition blamed him for monstrous cruelty to her. The entry calls that tradition legendary.

The facts it gives are grim enough. Francesco quarrelled with all his children. Two sons were killed in brawls. Another son once tried to murder him. At last his wife Lucrezia and his children Giacomo, Bernardo, and Beatrice plotted his death. They hired two bravos for the work. Francesco was killed in his sleep at his castle of Petrella. The entry weighs the legend against the documented record and finds the family disreputable on all sides.
britannica-1911-chaderton-laurence:
Laurence Chaderton (about 1536-1640), a Puritan churchman, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Lees Hall in Lancashire, he was the second son of a rich old family and a firm Catholic father. Taught by a priest, he became a sound scholar. At Cambridge he took up the reformed faith, and his father cut him off for it.

The article says he became a fellow of Christ's College in 1567 and a much heard preacher at a Cambridge church for many years. His views were moderate, though his friends included men of stronger stamp. When Emmanuel College was founded in 1584, its founder chose him as the first master. In 1604 he was one of four men picked to plead the Puritan cause at the Hampton Court meeting.
britannica-1911-chance:
Chance, the fall of things unseen, is weighed in an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word runs through French to a Latin word for things falling out. A chance thing is one with no cause that men can see. It is an event no one has looked for or set up. Good luck and bad luck both wear the name in plain talk.

From that talk men made chance a thing with power of its own. What had no known cause was held to have no cause at all. In the sums of odds the word works in two set ways. In the strict way chance is the same as probability itself. In the looser way it sets ways to win against ways to lose. Law splits games of chance from games of skill apart.
britannica-1911-charles-iii-king-of-fran:
Charles the Third, called the Simple, king of France, born in eight seventy nine, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a son born past the death of his father, Louis the Stammerer. When the fat king was cast down, Charles was kept from the throne by his youth. A new king took the crown in his stead.

In the reign of that king, Charles won the nod of a part of the great men. He was crowned at Reims in eight ninety three. He won the bond of the emperor and forced his rival to yield part of a great tract. When that rival died, the whole realm came to him. His chief act was a pact with the Normans in nine eleven. The land that grew into the duchy of Normandy was given to them in fee.
britannica-1911-charles-iv-king-of-franc:
Charles the Fourth of France, called the Fair, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1294, he was the third and youngest son of Philip the Fourth. He became count of La Marche in 1316 and king of France and Navarre early in 1322.

The article stresses his harsh search for funds. He pressed royal power over the nobles, but his strong central rule cost more and more. To fill the gap he recast the coinage, sold offices, and laid duties on trade. He took a church tithe raised for a crusade and kept its yield. He also seized the goods of Lombard bankers his father had called in. In foreign affairs he kept close ties with the pope. A pact with England was followed by a feudal war in Guienne.
britannica-1911-charles-ix-king-of-franc:
Charles the Ninth, king of France, gets a frail reign life in the 1911 Britannica. Born in fifteen fifty, he was the third son of Henry the Second. His mother was Catherine de Medici of Italy. At first he bore the title of Duke of Orleans as a boy. He took the throne at age ten when his brother died in fifteen sixty.

Real rule lay with his mother while he was still a child king. Spoilt by whims and wild sport, he wrecked his health in youth. He was named of age in fifteen sixty three but still bent to his mother. Warmth to the chief Coligny drew him toward a war in the Low Lands. Dread acts of that age broke his mind and mood for good.
britannica-1911-charles-v-king-of-france:
Charles the Fifth of France, called the Wise, lived from 1337 to 1380 and ruled a land at war. The 1911 Britannica entry places his birth at Vincennes as son of John the Second. In 1349 he became dauphin and in 1355 duke of Normandy as well. At Poitiers in 1356 his father ordered him off the field before capture.

While his father sat prisoner in England, Charles in effect ruled France himself. He called the states general to Paris to raise men and money for war. Merchant leader Etienne Marcel and allies pressed hard claims in that assembly. The entry opens a reign of strain, revolt, and slow recovery for France.
britannica-1911-charles-vi-king-of-franc:
Charles the Sixth was king of France, son of a wise king and his queen, born in Paris in the late thirteen hundreds. At his birth he was granted the land of the Dauphine. He was thus the first prince of France to bear the title of dauphin from his first days.

His father had set his schooling in the hands of a trusted aide and fixed the age at which he would rule in his own right. He came to the throne at age twelve. Real power split at once among his uncles and his mothers brother, the 1911 Britannica entry says. One uncle took the role of regent. Two more took the guard of the boy king and the rule of Paris and the north, while the last uncle, shut out, was paid off with a rich province.
britannica-1911-charles-vii-king-of-fran:
Charles the Seventh, king of France, was born in Paris on 22 February 1403 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the fifth son of Charles the Sixth and Isabeau of Bavaria. As a boy he was count of Ponthieu. He was promised in marriage to Mary of Anjou in 1413 and spent two years at the Angevin court.

Death of a brother made him dauphin in 1417. Murder of the duke of Burgundy in his presence at Montereau in 1419 wrecked his cause for a time. The treaty of Troyes cut him off in 1420. When his father died in 1422 he held court near Bourges. The south owned him as king, while English power grew in the north.
britannica-1911-charles-viii-king-of-fra:
Charles the Eighth, who lived from 1470 to 1498, was a king of France and the only son of Louis the Eleventh. The 1911 Britannica article says the boy grew up far from his father, at the castle of Amboise. That place stayed his love all his life. When Louis died in 1483, Charles was thirteen and of age in law. He was quite unfit to rule, the piece says. Till 1492 his sister Anne of Beaujeu held the reins.

In 1491 Charles wed Anne of Brittany, though she was pledged to Maximilian of Austria. At twenty-two he cast off his sister's rule and her wise course with it. Dreams of old Angevin rights drew him to Naples, as a step to the throne of the East. He marched into Italy in 1494 and took Naples in pomp. A league of foes then drove him home in haste.
britannica-1911-chimneypiece:
Chimneypiece is the term for the projecting hood built over a medieval fireplace to catch the smoke, and later for the decorative frame around a fireplace, often carried up to the ceiling. Mantelpiece is now the general term for the jambs, shelf and outer fittings of a fireplace. For many centuries the chimneypiece was the most ornamental and artistic feature of a room. Smaller fireplaces and modern heating have since cut both its art and its use.

Before the 12th century rooms were warmed by braziers or open hearths, and the earliest known chimneypiece, at Southampton, dates from the first half of that century. Great timber hoods, the vast 30 foot example at Poitiers and Piranesi's designs of 1765 mark the growth the entry traces. Inigo Jones brought a simple classic type to England, bolder mouldings followed at Hampton Court, and the Adam brothers' designs ruled the late 18th century.
britannica-1911-circe:
Circe, a famed sorceress of Greek legend, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the daughter of Helios, the sun, and the ocean nymph Perse. After murdering her husband, a prince of Colchis, she was driven out by his people. Her father set her on the lonely island of Aeaea, off the coast of Italy.

By drugs and spells she changed human beings into wolves, lions, and swine. Those beasts prowled around her palace on the island. Odysseus came to her shore, and she turned his companions into swine. Guarded by the herb moly, a gift of Hermes, he forced her to restore them. She then kept him with her for a year in love. Before he left, she taught him how to reach the land of shades. There the prophet Teiresias would tell him his fate.
britannica-1911-ciudad-real-province:
Ciudad Real is a province of central Spain, formed in 1833 from districts of New Castile and holding 321,580 people in 1900 over 7,620 square miles. Toledo, Albacete, Jaén, Córdoba and Badajoz bound it on all sides. Most of its surface is a level or slightly undulating plain, with the Sierra de Alcudia and Sierra Madrona rising in the south-west. The Guadiana drains almost the whole province from east to west.

The eastern part forms part of La Mancha, a flat, thinly peopled plain with meagre vegetation often ravaged by locusts. Drought is common and summers are oppressively hot, while winter winds strike the plains bitterly cold. Grain, vine and olive growing suffer from poor irrigation and barren soil, yet sheep, goats and forest swine thrive. Coal at Puertollano, lead in various districts and mercury at Almadén are mined, and no great manufacturing towns exist.
britannica-1911-clairvoyance:
Clairvoyance, French for clear-seeing, is a term in psychical research, much the same in strict use as lucidity. It names a power of gaining knowledge where the normal senses play no part at all. Talk with other minds, living or dead, must also play no part in the strict sense. The word is also used, at times with telepathic, for gaining such knowledge from another mind. Spiritualists use it for seeing spirit forms.

Few tests have tried this claimed power, the entry says. In practice no proof sets facts gained this way apart from facts gained by telepathy from the living. Three accounts are offered for the few good trials, the power itself, telepathy and a sharpening of the senses. Richet's card tests are faulted for missing the telepathy point. His subject named twelve cards out of sixty-eight under weak guards.
britannica-1911-cloots-de-grace:
Cloots, Jean Baptiste du Val de Grace, Baron von (1755–1794), better known as Anacharsis Cloots, was a figure in the French Revolution, born near Cleves at the castle of Gnadenthal. He belonged to a noble Prussian family of Dutch origin and, heir to a great fortune, was sent at eleven to Paris for his education. There he took in the theories of his uncle, the Abbé Cornelius de Pauw. He left the Berlin military academy at twenty and traversed Europe preaching revolutionary philosophy.

On the Revolution's outbreak he returned to Paris in 1789, seeking his dream of a universal family of nations. On 19 June 1790 he appeared at the bar of the Assembly heading thirty-six foreigners. That embassy of the human race adhered to the Declaration of the Rights of Man. He dropped his baron title and took the name Anacharsis. In 1792 he gave 12,000 livres for arming fighters against tyrants.
britannica-1911-cockatrice:
The cockatrice is a fabulous monster that men believed in through ancient and medieval times. Writers such as Pliny and Aldrovandus described and pictured it in books on nature. Aldrovandus published as late as the start of the 1600s. The beast was said to hatch from a cock's egg, brooded by a serpent.

Its powers were said to be deadly. Plants shrank at its touch. Men and beasts died from its look alone. Yet the beast feared the cock, whose crow could kill it. Travellers thus carried a cock through lands where the monster was feared. The weasel alone could face its eye and attack it. When bitten, the weasel cured itself with rue. That herb was the one plant the cockatrice could not wither.
britannica-1911-cognizance:
Cognizance means knowledge or notice, above all notice taken by a court of law. The word comes from a Latin verb for knowing. In law it names the right to hear and judge a case. It also names the use of that right by a court. One short entry holds both the legal sense and a second, quite apart sense.

In heraldry, a cognizance is an emblem, badge or device. Retainers of a royal or noble house wore it as their mark. It told at a glance which lord a man served. The entry gives no list of houses or badges. It fixes the two meanings and stops. A lawyer and a student of arms each gain their own sense from the same few lines. Brevity is the point here.
britannica-1911-commerce:
Commerce, from Latin roots meaning trade goods together, is used here for trade between nations, and this 1911 Britannica entry opens a long history of it. The word in its broad sense covers the foreign trade of all lands, set apart from trade inside one land. To trace the roots of such dealing, the entry goes back to the oldest records in the Hebrew Scriptures.

It reads Abraham's purchase of a field for four hundred shekels of silver as a sign of a grown trading world. That one act points to owned land, sale of land, mined and refined metal, and silver used as a shared means of payment. The entry names the southern Arabs as the first foreign merchants it can find, and the Phoenicians as the first great sailors and carriers of goods by sea.
britannica-1911-commonplace: Commonplace is traced as a word in a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It renders a Greek phrase for a passage or line of proof that fits many cases. A commonplace book was a store of such passages and quotes, sorted under broad heads for quick use. From that first sense the word slid toward its modern one, a thing said so often that it sounds stale or flat. The entry also gives the Latin name adversaria for notes written on one side of a page.
britannica-1911-conference:
A conference is a bringing together for talk, from a Latin word for that act. It may join members of a society for shared work. It may join men from law-making bodies or from split states. Talks between the two houses of the British parliament take this name. Talks between the two houses of the United States congress take it as well.

Colonial prime ministers met the home government in this form at set times. In 1907 the title Colonial Conference gave way to Imperial Conference. A move to swap conference for council fell through at the same time. Council smacked too much of rule and office work. Conference kept the pure sense of talk and counsel. In diplomacy the word marks a meeting of state agents on set points. A congress stands above it in rank. Early talks before a congress take the same name.
britannica-1911-conscience:
Conscience is a philosophy article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a Latin term for knowledge shared with another, or full knowledge. In its derived sense it means awareness in general. As a term of thought, it names the mental power that decides between right and wrong in our acts.

In common use, the entry says, conscience is taken to give direct and binding verdicts on single acts. That use assumes each act has an inborn goodness or badness of its own. Conscience then discerns that quality much as the eye sees or the ear hears. Moral thinkers, though, mostly agree on a further point. Such judgments rest on moral laws behind them, and the place of conscience shifts with the view taken of those laws.
britannica-1911-constance:
Constance is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town in Baden, in Germany. In German it is Konstanz. It stands on the left bank of the Rhine, just where the river leaves the Lake of Constance. In 1905 it held 24,818 people, most of them German-speaking Catholics.

A fine bridge crosses the Rhine to the suburb of Petershausen. To the south, the town shades into the Swiss suburb of Kreuzlingen. Steamers link it to all the towns on the lake shore. The article calls it a pretty town with fine old buildings. Its former cathedral was built mostly from 1069 to 1089 and later made Gothic. A plate in the floor marks the spot where Huss stood when he was condemned to death.
britannica-1911-conveyance:
Conveyance is first of all the act of conveying a thing, as the 1911 Britannica entry explains. The verb to convey now means to carry, send, pass on, or hand over. It once held the same sense as convoy, to go with or guard on the way. That sense lived on into the eighteenth century. Both words spring from a late Latin root through old French forms.

Apart from the broad sense, the word now serves in three set uses. It names a carriage or other means of transport. In law it names the passing of goods or land by deed between living men. Last, it names the written deed by which such a passing is made.
britannica-1911-copper-glance:
Copper-glance is a mineral made of cuprous sulphide, with the formula Cu2S. It is also called chalcocite, redruthite and vitreous copper. Agricola gave it the German name Kupferglaserz in 1546. Its crystals form in the orthorhombic system as six-sided tables or prisms. The angle between the prism faces is 60 degrees and 25 minutes.

Twinning on those prism faces is a common trait. Twin crystals fake a sixfold symmetry, as aragonite and chrysoberyl do. Two more twin laws give crystals that pierce each other at set angles. The mineral also forms in compact masses of great extent. Its colour is dark lead-grey with a metal sheen. Light blackens and dulls that sheen with time. The stuff is soft and can be cut with a knife, like argentite. Its weight runs 5.7 times that of water.
britannica-1911-coppice:
A coppice, or copse, is a small plantation or thicket of trees grown to be cut on a set cycle. The trees may be planted by hand or sown by nature. Cutting comes before they grow into large timber. The word runs back through Old French to a Late Latin term for a blow. That root fits a wood ruled by the axe.

English law treats the yield of such a wood in a set way. The produce counts as fructus industrialis, a fruit of labour rather than of the soil alone. A tenant for life or for years may take that produce as his own. The entry cites a case of 1891 for that rule, Dashwood against Magniac. It gives no list of tree kinds or cut cycles. Form, word root and one point of law form its whole matter.
britannica-1911-cordoba-province:
Cordoba is a large central province of the Argentine Republic, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It is bounded by Santiago del Estero, Santa Fe, Buenos Aires, La Pampa, San Luis, Rioja, and Catamarca. Its count was 351,223 in 1895 and an estimated 465,464 in 1904. Its area is 62,160 square miles in all.

The greater part of the province belongs to the pampas, though less fertile and grassy than the plains farther east and south. It also includes large saline and swampy areas in its extent. The north west part is traversed by an isolated mountain system of three sierras. Those ranges run for some 200 miles from north to south in line. They intercept the moist winds from the Atlantic and receive abundant rainfall on their eastern slopes. That rain gives them a strikingly green look against the surrounding plains.
britannica-1911-cordova-province:
Cordova, an inland province of southern Spain, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It is bounded by Ciudad Real, Jaén, Granada, Málaga, Seville, and Badajoz. Its people in 1900 numbered 455,859. Its area is 5,299 square miles. The river Guadalquivir divides the province into two unlike parts.

On the right bank lies the mountain region of the Sierra Morena. It is less peopled and less fertile than the left bank. On the left bank stretch the great plains of La Campiña. The ground there rolls gently toward the south and south-east. There the surface grows mountainous again, with the outer ridges of the Sierra Nevada. The Guadalquivir waters the richest districts of Cordova. It has many tributaries, of which the Bembezar is named. The article sets a province of plain and sierra side by side, cut by one great river.
britannica-1911-cornice: Cornice is a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on a part of a building. A cornice is the lip that juts out at the top of a wall. Its use is to throw rain water off the roof, clear of the face of the house. In the classic orders it forms the top part of the entablature, split into three bands with set names. In a wider sense the word covers any crown moulding, on doors, on windows, or on household goods.
britannica-1911-corpulence:
Too much fat on the body is the theme of a medical entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The piece calls the state corpulence or obesity. Some fat is normal and serves the body well under the skin. A good deal of fat can still go with health and strength. Only fat in great excess, or fast growing, counts as a disease state.

To show how far excess can go, the entry cites famed cases. A grocer of Maldon who died in 1750 weighed over six hundred pounds. Daniel Lambert of Leicester, who died in 1809, weighed still more. He is called the heaviest man who ever lived. The piece warns that great bulk makes exercise hard and health hard to keep.
britannica-1911-correspondence:
Correspondence is a word article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tracing the senses of one term. Strictly, the word means a fitness of parts, one thing answering to another. Now it chiefly means the exchange of letters, or the letters themselves.

The article then gives two special uses. In Swedenborgian teaching, every natural object typifies some spiritual truth. In mathematics, correspondence names a relation between two groups of objects. When each member matches one and only one of the other, it is one to one. Wider cases, where members match in stated numbers, are also defined.
britannica-1911-corrientes-province:
Corrientes is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a province in north-east Argentina. The text bounds it by Paraguay, Brazil, Entre Rios, and Santa Fe. It gives an area of 32,580 square miles. The count for 1895 is 239,618, with a higher guess for 1904.

Near a third of the land is swamp or lagoon, the entry says. The great Ibera lagoon fills much of the centre and north-east. Streams flow from these lagoons to the Parana and Uruguay rivers. The south, by contrast, is high rolling land fit for stock and crops. Heat, woods, and farm goods are also covered.
britannica-1911-credence:
A credence is a small side-table that began as a place where food and drink were tasted for poison. In royal and noble houses an officer called the praegustator performed this assay near the high table. The rite and the table both took their name from the Latin credere, to believe or trust. When the tasting lapsed, the table gained a back and shelves for plate and merged into the buffet.

The name survives chiefly as church furniture. A credence table of wood or stone stands near the altar, usually on the south side. On it rest the cruets of wine and water, the chalice, and other items used at Mass. A special table on the Gospel side serves when the pope celebrates, and the old tasting of the elements is still kept there. Old stone examples survive in England, as at St Cross near Winchester.
britannica-1911-crest-france:
Crest is a town of south east France in the department of Drôme. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica counts 5,660 people in its commune in 1906. It stands on the right bank of the river Drôme. Silk worm breeding and silk spinning are its chief trades. It also makes woollens, paper, leather, and cement. Truffles pass through its markets. A rock above the town carries a huge keep.

That keep is all that left of a twelfth century castle. On that castle Crest owed its weight in the middle ages and the wars of religion. The rest was destroyed in the early 1600s, and the keep became a state prison. Crest once ranked as capital of the duchy of Valentinois. Its town charter, cut in stone in the 1100s, survives in the archives. Ten miles south east lies the Forest of Saon.
britannica-1911-cromagnon-race:
The Cromagnon race is a name Paul Broca gave to a type of early man drawn from remains found in the Cromagnon cave at Les Eyzies. Workmen found the small cave, nearly filled with debris, in 1868. Near the top lay three skeletons, one a woman whose skull bore a severe wound. Their skulls showed such marked traits that Broca took them as types of a race.

The skulls were long-headed, with a mean cephalic index of 73.34, which first suggested a palaeolithic date. The entry notes that long heads persist far into neolithic times, so the race may instead be early neolithic. It may have spread over much of Europe at the close of the Pleistocene period. Some writers see in it the base of the present peoples of western Europe. Quatrefages matched its type with the tall, fair Kabyles of Mauritania and traced its coming from Siberia.
britannica-1911-czartoryski-adam-george-:
Adam George Czartoryski, who lived from 1770 to 1861, was a Polish statesman, son of Prince Adam Casimir. The 1911 Britannica article says he was schooled at home by fine French tutors. He first went abroad in 1786. At Gotha he heard Goethe read a play, and met Herder and Wieland. In 1789 he saw the trial of Warren Hastings in England. A second visit in 1793 let him study the English constitution.

In the war of the second partition he fought for Poland. Austria seized him on his way to join Kosciuszko. After the third partition the family lands were taken. In 1795 Adam and his brother were called to Saint Petersburg and made to enter Russian service. Catherine was so pleased with the youths that she gave back part of their estates. A strong bond of mind grew between Adam and the grand duke Alexander.
britannica-1911-deems-charles-force:
Charles Force Deems is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an American clergyman. He lived from 1820 to 1893. He was born in Baltimore, Maryland, in December 1820. He was a precocious child by the entry's account. He delivered lectures on temperance before he was fourteen. He also lectured on Sunday schools at that age. He graduated at Dickinson College in the year 1839.

He taught and preached in New York city for a few months. In 1840 he took charge of a Methodist church at Asbury. The next year he removed to North Carolina. There he was general agent for the American Bible Society. He was professor of logic and rhetoric at North Carolina university. That post ran from 1842 to 1847. He then taught natural sciences at Randolph-Macon College. After preaching at Newbern, he led a women's college at Greensboro. That presidency ran from 1850 to 1854.
britannica-1911-defeasance:
Defeasance is a law article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In law, a defeasance is a deed that undoes the force of another deed. Its name comes from a French word meaning to undo. What one deed grants, its defeasance can take away.

The entry marks the term off from a near neighbour. A condition sits inside the same deed it limits. A defeasance does its work from a separate deed of its own. Rules govern the making of a valid defeasance. It should recite the deed it defeats, with that deed's date. It must be made between the same parties as the first deed. The thing undone must be of a kind that can be undone. Every condition in it must be strictly carried out before it takes effect. The article closes with the looser use of the term in bills of sale.
britannica-1911-defence:
Defence means a keeping off, a guard, or a plea that answers a charge, as a 1911 Britannica entry explains. In daily life it covers the right to ward off an attack with force. A person under attack may use the force he thinks needful, even to killing. The same right guards a spouse, parent, child, master, or servant.

In court use, defence is the denial of a charge or the steps an accused person takes. In civil suits the statement of defence answers the claim point by point. Each fact must be admitted or denied, and new facts may be added in reply. A set off or counter claim may also be raised at that stage.
britannica-1911-elie-de-beaumont-jean-ba:
Leonce Elie de Beaumont, who lived from 1798 to 1874, was a French geologist. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica honors his map work and theory. He was born at Canon in Calvados in September 1798. Top prizes at school led him to the mines college in Paris.

In 1823 he toured England and Scotland to study mines and maps. That trip aimed at a like survey map for France. He took the geology chair at the mines school in 1835. High posts and academy seats followed in France and abroad. He became a senator and a fixed secretary of the sciences academy. His fame turns on a theory of how ranges of hills arose. Ranges on one great circle, he held, rose at one time.
britannica-1911-esperance: Esperance is a small seaport on a fine natural harbour on the south coast of West Australia. It lies 275 miles north-east of Albany. The town is a summer resort, and caves of note stand near it. Its weight as a port comes from its place on the main road between the eastern states and the gold-fields. It is the nearest place for the shipment of gold from the Coolgardie fields.
britannica-1911-eugene-of-savoy-prince:
Prince Eugene of Savoy is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a famed soldier who lived from 1663 to 1736. He was born in Paris in October 1663. He was the fifth son of a prince of Savoy. His mother was a niece of Cardinal Mazarin. He was meant for the church and called the little abbe. His own wish ran strongly to a life in arms.

His mother fell from favour at the French court. The king refused his pleas for a post more than once. That slight bred in him a life long grudge. In disgust he quit France and went to Vienna. The emperor there took him in with kindness. He served against the Turks in the drive of 1683. Brave acts in fights for Vienna won him a regiment. Wounds in siege work did not halt his rise in arms.
britannica-1911-falconet-etienne-maurice:
