The 1911 Britannica article on Étienne Maurice Falconet (1716-1791) gives the life of a French sculptor born in Paris. His parents were poor. He was first apprenticed to a carpenter. Clay figures he made in his free hours caught the eye of the sculptor Lemoine. Lemoine took him as a pupil. Falconet also studied Greek and Latin. He wrote several pamphlets on art.

The article judges his work with care. His statue of Milo of Crotona won him a place in the Academy in 1754. In 1766 the empress Catherine called him to Saint Petersburg. There he made a huge bronze statue of Peter the Great. Many of his church works were destroyed in the Revolution. His writings were later gathered in six volumes.
britannica-1911-fluorescence:
Fluorescence is the glow some substances give out under light, the subject of a long scientific article. It opens with Sir David Brewster's paper to the Royal Society of Edinburgh in 1833. Brewster passed a condensed beam of sunlight into a solution of chlorophyll, the green matter of leaves. The path of the rays inside the fluid shone bright blood-red against the green. He named the effect internal dispersion and found it in other vegetable solutions, essential oils and solids such as fluor-spar.

Sir John Herschel found the same effect independently a few years later. The article then follows the study of the phenomenon through the century. It treats Stokes's law, the rule that fluorescent light is of lower refrangibility than the light that excites it. It also treats Lommel's work showing the law fails for some bodies. Kinds of fluorescence, absorption bands and spectra come under review.
britannica-1911-francis-i-of-france:
Francis I (1494-1547), king of France, was the son of Charles of Valois, count of Angouleme, and Louise of Savoy. He was born at Cognac on 12 September 1494. His father, great-grandson of Charles V, died in 1496, and Louise watched over her son with passionate tenderness. On the accession of Louis XII in 1498 Francis became heir-presumptive to the throne. Louis gave him the duchy of Valois and set tutors over him, first Marshal de Gie and then Artus Gouffier.

Louise herself taught Francis and his sister Marguerite Italian and Spanish, while an abbot taught them Latin and history. The library at Amboise was stocked with romances of the Round Table, which fired the boy's imagination. He loved violent exercise still more: hunting was his ruling passion, with tennis close behind. The long entry follows the king into Italy, to Pavia and captivity.
britannica-1911-francis-ii-of-france:
Francis II (1544-1560), king of France, was the eldest son of Henry II and Catherine de' Medici. He was born at Fontainebleau on 19 January 1544. On 25 April 1558 he married Mary Stuart, daughter of James V of Scotland, the famous queen whose name clings to his short reign. He ascended the French throne on 10 July 1559, a boy of fifteen succeeding a father killed in the lists, and France passed at once into the hands of his wife's uncles.

The young king, sickly and of feeble understanding, was the mere tool of Francis, duke of Guise, and Charles, cardinal of Lorraine. Into their hands he virtually delivered the government. Their favour and their high-handed rule roused the princes of the blood, Anthony of Navarre and Louis of Conde, who backed the conspiracy of Amboise with the Protestants. It was discovered in March 1560, shortly before the day fixed for the rising.
britannica-1911-frederick-charles-prince:
Prince Frederick Charles (1828-1885), Prussian field marshal, was born in Berlin on 20 March 1828, son of Prince Charles and grandson of King Frederick William III. He entered the army at ten, read at Bonn with Major von Roon at his side, and fought in Schleswig in 1848. Wounded leading a charge at Wiesenthal in 1849, he traded wild daring for the fixed resolve that marked his later command.

From 1860 he trained the III Corps for ten years to a pitch few troops matched. In 1864 he stormed the Düppel lines and took Alsen. In 1866 his I Army drove into Bohemia and bore the brunt at Königgrätz. In 1870 he led the II Army in France, held the field at Vionville, won at St Privat, and closed the war with the victory of Le Mans. The Red Prince, named for his hussar uniform, died in 1885.
britannica-1911-gelderland-province:
Gelderland is a province of Holland between great rivers. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica contrasts its sand north and clay south. Its area is about nineteen hundred square miles. About five hundred sixty-seven thousand people lived there in 1900.

North of the Rhine the land is sand and gravel waste. Dark heaths and fen patches cover that poor ground. South of the river line the soil turns to rich clay. The north splits into the Veluwe and the old Zutphen county. Veluwe means bad land, and its heaths stay thinly peopled. Rye, buckwheat, and sheep scrape a living on those wastes. River banks in the south hold the fat farms and towns. Fine country houses line the scenic Rhine strip there.
britannica-1911-gerard-etienne-maurice:
Etienne Maurice Gerard (1773-1852), count and French general, was born at Damvilliers on 4 April 1773. The 1911 Britannica entry has him joining volunteers in 1791 and serving under Dumouriez and Jourdan. He rose fast: colonel by 1800, general of brigade after Austerlitz and Jena, and a baron for his conduct at Wagram.

In Russia he won a division at Borodino, and he fought through the retreat and the 1813 campaign, wounded at Leipzig in command of a corps. Napoleon made him a count, then a peer, and gave him the IV corps for the Waterloo campaign. There he shone at Ligny and urged Grouchy to march to the guns on 18 June. After 1830 he was war minister and a marshal of France, drove the Dutch from Belgium in 1831, and besieged Antwerp in 1832. He died on 17 April 1852.
britannica-1911-ghost-dance:
Ghost Dance, a rite dance of American Indians, is the subject of a brief faith entry in the 1911 Britannica. Dancers wore a white cloak for the rite, also called the Spirit Dance. The dance ties to a faith in a coming savior for the tribes. That faith rose in Nevada with the Paiute tribe in eighteen eighty eight. A young Paiute healer named Wovoka spread the word of it.

He taught that if the dance and rites were done with care, the tribes would be rid of the white men. The faith spread fast from tribe to tribe as a kind of craze. In eighteen ninety it was one cause of the Sioux rise, the text says. A source note points to a report by Mooney for the Bureau of American Ethnology.
britannica-1911-golden-fleece: Golden Fleece, in Greek mythology, is the fleece of the ram on which Phrixus and Helle escaped. The 1911 Britannica entry is a pure cross-reference, only a few lines long. For the myth itself, readers are sent to the article on the Argonauts. For the modern order of knighthood of the same name, they are sent to Knighthood and Chivalry, to its section on orders of knighthood. The name thus stands as a signpost, its two stories told elsewhere.
britannica-1911-grace:
Grace is a word of many shades, all tied to the idea of favor. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica groups its senses under three main heads. They are pleasing quality, favor or goodwill, and thanks in return. The word comes through French from Latin gratia, from gratus, beloved.

Favor bestowed holds the weight of the account by far. Rulers grant acts by way of grace as free concessions, it says. Papal letters of grace grant special rights and relief from rules. In universities a grace began as relief from degree rules there. Days of grace for paying a bill extend the same idea to law.
britannica-1911-granada-province:
Granada is the subject of a province article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Granada is a coastal province of southern Spain, formed in 1833. It matches the central parts of the old kingdom of Granada. By 1900 its people numbered near half a million. Its area is near five thousand square miles. The sea bounds it on the south and Malaga on the west.

The article describes the Sierra Nevada, a vast ridge running beside the sea. Its highest peaks rise over eleven thousand feet and look over the city of Granada. Three main rivers rise on this watershed and flow to larger rivers or the sea. The coast has three small harbours of little trade weight. Climate runs from warm in the low valleys to severe on high ground. The plain of Granada, watered since Moorish days, is called the richest soil in the peninsula.
britannica-1911-granville-france:
Granville, a fortified seaport and bathing resort of north west France, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the department of Manche, at the mouth of the Bosq river. The entry gives it 10,530 people in 1906. The upper town is built on a headland jutting into the sea, ringed by ramparts.

Below it lie the lower town and the harbour, with a tidal basin, two floating basins, and a dry dock. Its fleets fish deep sea grounds, including the cod banks off Newfoundland, and oyster fishing goes on as well. Regular sailings link it with Guernsey, Jersey, and the islands of Saint Pierre and Miquelon. Eggs, vegetables, and fish are its chief exports, while coal and timber come in. Trades include shipbuilding, fish salting, and the making of cod liver oil.
britannica-1911-greene-maurice:
Maurice Greene (1695-1755) was an English musical composer, born in London, the son of a city clergyman. The 1911 Britannica entry has him a chorister at St Paul's cathedral, studying under its organist Richard Brind, whom he succeeded in 1718. In 1727 he became organist and composer to the Chapel Royal, on Croft's death.

In 1730 Cambridge elected him professor of music and gave him the doctorate. He was a voluminous composer of church music, and his Forty Select Anthems became a standard work of its kind. Oratorios, a masque, the pastoral opera Phoebe of 1748, and glees and catches fill out the list. Master of the king's band from 1735, he wrote many pieces for the king's birthday. The entry ends with his broken friendship with Handel, lost through his equal closeness to Handel's rival Buononcini, and his part in founding the Society of Musicians.
britannica-1911-groningen-province:
Groningen is the most northerly province of Holland. Drente and Friesland border it to the south and west. The North Sea and Prussian Hanover bound it elsewhere. Its area is 887 square miles. Its population in 1900 was 299,602. The sandy Hondsrug links it to the Drente plateau. Elsewhere sea-clay and fen cover a flat surface. Successive lines of sea-dikes mark its growth.

Agriculture is the main industry of the province. Landownership is unusually widespread there. The beklem-recht explains much of that spread. Under it a tenant holds his lease in perpetuity. He can even bequeath the farm. Barley, oats and wheat are the chief crops. Flax grows in the north-east. The higher clay supports cattle and horses. Butter and cheese making matter there too. Delfzyl, Appingedam and Winschoten are the chief smaller towns. Heavy emigration to America reflected seasonal shortages of farm work.
britannica-1911-ground-ice:
Ground-ice is ice formed at the bottom of streams while the water above it is still above freezing-point. Radiation is given as the prime cause: it forms only under a clear sky, most readily on dark rocks, and never under a bridge or other covering. Professor Howard T. Barnes of McGill argued that a river bed radiates heat upward through the water on cold clear nights far more freely than the sun's rays penetrate downward.

Spongy masses of anchor-ice grow on the bottom overnight, then sunlight loosens them and they rise with force, often carrying gravel, which is said to strew the bottom of Lake Erie. Caught masses can dam narrow stretches of river. The account also covers frazil-ice, surface crystals swept downward in turbulent water, and the Scottish, French, German and French-Canadian names for these formations.
britannica-1911-ham-france:
Ham is a small town of northern France, in the department of Somme. Amiens lies 36 miles to the west-north-west. The Northern railway runs through it toward Laon. Its population in 1906 was 2,957. It stands on the Somme in a marshy district. From the 9th century Ham was a lordship's seat.

Notre-Dame church dates from the 12th and 13th centuries. Lightning fire gutted its wooden parts in 1760. The castle is the town's great sight. Louis of Luxembourg rebuilt it massively between 1436 and 1470. Its great tower's walls run 36 feet thick. Viollet-le-Duc judged it able to resist artillery. The castle long served as a state prison. Joan of Arc and Louis Napoleon were held there. Louis Napoleon escaped after six years, disguised as a workman. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Ham entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-hanover-province:
Hanover's end as a kingdom fills this account. Hanoverian troops won at Langensalza on 27 June 1866. Fresh Prussian forces still compelled capitulation two days later. The king could not reside in Hanover under the terms. His officers were barred from further war service. Prussia took his ammunition and stores. A decree of 20 September 1866 annexed Hanover outright. It became a Prussian province from that date.

King George appealed in vain from exile at Hietzing. Many Hanoverians stayed loyal to him. Their Guelph Legion served in France at his expense. Prussia sequestrated his compensation money in 1868. That fund, the Welfenfonds, financed secret service against Guelph intrigue. George died in June 1878, still unreconciled. His son Ernest Augustus kept the claim alive. Berlin therefore barred him from Brunswick in 1884 and again in 1906.
britannica-1911-home-office:
The Home Office is a principal government department of the United Kingdom, dating from 1782. In that year foreign affairs, once split between northern and southern secretaries, passed wholly to the northern department. The home department kept Irish and colonial affairs, and war business until 1794. In 1801 colonial business left it too, and it has attended only to domestic affairs since.

Its head, the home secretary, sits in the cabinet on a salary of £5,000 a year. He is the channel between sovereign and subject and receives petitions to the crown. He answers for the king's peace, and oversees criminal justice, police and prisons; through him the sovereign's mercy is exercised. Lunatic asylums, reformatories and industrial schools also fall under his eye, as does the safety of workers in special and dangerous trades. A permanent under-secretary and other staff assist him.
britannica-1911-horn-dance: The horn dance is an old folk rite kept at Abbots Bromley, a town by Needwood Forest in Staffordshire. The 1911 Britannica note sets out the rite in a few plain lines. Six or seven men wear deer skulls with antlers for the dance. They move through the streets while a mate rides a sham horse. That mate whips the dancers to keep them on the move. The dance falls on the Monday next past the fourth of September.
britannica-1911-housman-laurence:
Laurence Housman (1867– ) is an English writer and artist, born on the 18th of June 1867. He studied at South Kensington and first made his name as a book illustrator. His best designs appear in editions of Meredith's Jump to Glory Jane (1892), Jonas Lie's Weird Tales (1892) and Christina Rossetti's Goblin Market (1893). His sister Clemence Housman engraved his designs on wood, and also wrote the Werewolf (1896) that he illustrated.

Housman's verse volumes include Green Arras (1896), Spikenard (1898), Rue (1899) and Mendicant Rhymes (1906). The mystic cast of the devotional poems in Spikenard returns in his half-allegorical tales: All Fellows (1896), The Blue Moon (1904) and The Cloak of Friendship (1906). His nativity play Bethlehem was staged in the great hall of London University. The entry catches a living author mid-career, known as much for the look of his books as for their words.
britannica-1911-hughes-hugh-price:
Hugh Price Hughes, a British Nonconformist divine who lived from 1847 to 1902, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Carmarthen, the son of a surgeon. He began to preach at the age of fourteen. In 1865 he entered Richmond College to train for the Wesleyan Methodist ministry, and he took a London degree in 1869.

In 1887 he set up the West London Mission, with full Sunday services in a hall in Piccadilly. There he spoke on the housing of the poor, on sweated work, and on gambling. His wife led a sisterhood for the social side of the work. In 1885 he had started the Methodist Times and made it a chief voice of Nonconformist thought. He fought the drink trade and backed causes of reform. His sharp words gave rise to the phrase the Nonconformist conscience.
britannica-1911-humphrey-lawrence:
Lawrence Humphrey, head of Magdalen College at Oxford, born about fifteen twenty seven, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Newport Pagnell, he won posts at his college in his late teens. He took his first degree in fifteen forty nine and rose step by step. He was marked as a bright pupil of a famed teacher of the faith.

When Mary came to the throne, he won leave to travel abroad. He lived in Basel, Zurich, Frankfurt, and Geneva. There he met the lead Swiss church men and took up their views of the church. His leave ran out and he lost his college post. When Elizabeth took the throne, he came home. In fifteen sixty he was made royal teacher of the faith at Oxford. High church men urged the fellows to pick him as head of the college. They at first said no.
britannica-1911-ice:
Ice is the solid form that water takes when it is laid open to cold strong enough to freeze it. The word is shared by the Teutonic tongues. Ice is a clear crystal stuff whose forms belong to the hexagonal system. It has a marked habit of twinning. That habit gives rise to the fair ice flowers shown by hoar-frost.

Ice falls from the sky as hoar-frost, snow, or hail. In the glaciers and snows of high ranges and of lands far north or south, ice stands on a huge scale. It marks the seas and lands round the poles above all. In some regions, France and Italy among them, much ice forms in caves. Depth, height, or winds that fit the cave keep such caves cold all year, so ice can form and last.
britannica-1911-ignorance:
Ignorance is a 1911 Britannica article on a state of mind with weight in law. The word comes from a Latin root that means not to know. A famed legal maxim runs that ignorance of the law does not excuse. A second maxim is often paired with it. It runs that ignorance of the fact does excuse.

The text defends the first rule as a needful one. Each person with the capacity to grasp the law is presumed to know it. Without that rule, courts would face endless probes into what a man truly knew. Such probes would be near impossible to settle. The work of justice would grind to a halt. The article thus shows how a hard rule keeps the courts able to act at all. Law students meet here a base rule of the system, stated plainly.
britannica-1911-impotence:
Impotence, from the Latin impotentia, want of power, is the legal term for the inability of a husband or wife to have marital relations. In English marriage law, if that inability exists when the marriage is made, the marriage can be set aside from the start.

Only the injured spouse may bring a suit to annul the marriage on this ground. Other people, however strong their interest, cannot sue, and the marriage cannot be attacked after one spouse has died. The old church court rule asked for three years of living together before a suit, but that rule had fallen away in practice. Medical proof is required, and two medical inspectors are usually named to examine the parties, with the case heard in private. Most American states also treat it as a ground for annulment, as does Germany, but France does not.
britannica-1911-indulgence:
Indulgence is a term of church study, and the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica gives the set form of its sense in the Roman Church. It is the waive of the time bound pain that oft stays due to sin past the waive of its guilt. That waive may be in full, and then it is called full in name. Or it may be in part, as the terms of the grant lay down.

In the speech of the middle ages such a waive was called a pardon in street use. That name lives on in at least one tract of France in the day of the book. The law of the rite is laid by church men on more than one text of the holy book, named in the piece.
britannica-1911-jaundice:
Jaundice, in the 1911 Britannica, is a medical entry on the yellow staining of the skin and body. The French name ties it to the word for yellow, and its Latin name to a golden bird. The colour comes from bile, or parts of it, loose in the blood. The entry is firm that jaundice is a sign of some deeper ill, not a disease in itself.

In blocked jaundice, bile cannot pass from the liver to the gut and is soaked back into the blood. Blocks come from gallstones, swelling or closing of the duct, growths, or pressure from outside. The liver first swells with held bile, then shrinks if the block lasts. Signs vary by cause, and the yellow of the eye white is most often the first seen.
britannica-1911-john-i-of-france:
John the First (born and died 1316), king of France, is the subject of a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Louis the Tenth, born after his father's death, on the fifteenth of November 1316. He lived just seven days. His mother was Clemence, daughter of Charles Martel, who claimed the crown of Hungary.

The article records the dark tale that clung to the brief reign. His uncle, later Philip the Fifth, was accused of causing the child's death. A second tale said the uncle had swapped in a dead child in his place. Nothing, the entry stresses, was ever proved. In the reign of John the Second, a man in Provence claimed to be the lost John the First. He was seized and died in prison. The piece is a study in how a seven day reign can breed a lasting legend.
britannica-1911-justice-of-the-peace:
A justice of the peace is a lesser magistrate in England, appointed by special commission under the great seal to keep the peace in the area named for him. The title is shortened to J.P. after a man's name. Coke praised the office as without match in the Christian world when well done.

The truth, as the long article presents it, lies between. Justices do a large mass of work needful to the running of the law, for no reward but the standing the office gives. Most are not trained lawyers, and their rulings can be ill informed, yet on the whole they act with sense and fairness. For centuries they came chiefly from the landed gentry. A royal commission of 1909 asked how the best men might be chosen without regard to creed or party. In large towns, paid magistrates do the heavy court work.
britannica-1911-kendall-henry-clarence:
Henry Clarence Kendall (1841–1882) was an Australian poet, son of a missionary, born in New South Wales on the 18th of April 1841. He had only a slight schooling. In 1860 he entered a lawyer's office in Sydney, and in 1862 he sent some of his verses to London, where they appeared in the Athenaeum.

The next year he took a clerkship in the Lands Department at Sydney, moving later to the Colonial Secretary's office. He joined that work with poetry and journalism. His chief books of verse were Leaves from an Australian Forest in 1869 and Songs from the Mountains in 1880. His feeling for nature, in Australian landscape and bush life, is judged very true and full of charm. In 1869 he left the public service for a time in business with his brothers. Sir Henry Parkes took an interest in him and in time made him an inspector of forests.
britannica-1911-kerman-province:
Kerman, the ancient Karmania, is a province of Persia. It is bounded east by Seistan and Baluchistan, south by Baluchistan and Fars, west by Fars, and north by Yezd and Khorasan. Its shape is highly uneven, wide toward Khorasan in the north and narrowing southward to a wedge between Fars and Baluchistan. Its length is about 400 miles, its breadth about 300, and its area is put at about 60,000 square miles.

Kerman is often described as two parts: a desert region in the north where no one can live, and a mountainous region in the south that can be lived in. Recent exploration has shown that view needs much softening. Mountains and desert tracts occur in all parts of the province. Much of what maps show as the western share of the great Kerman desert is in fact the fertile uplands of Kuhbanan.
britannica-1911-knight-service:
Knight-service was the main form of land tenure under the feudal system. It grew with the kind of warfare that made the mailed horseman the chief force in battle. Older writers derived it from the old English rule that every five hides owed one soldier. Instead, the Normans brought it in after the Conquest as a new system. The knight's fee matched the Norman fief du haubert, named for the hauberk, or coat of mail.

The Conqueror shared the lay lands of England among his followers on these terms. Each share was held by the service of a fixed number of knights, in units of ten. A baron could meet his quota by granting parts of his fief to under-tenants on the same terms. The surviving records include the barons' returns of 1166, scutage payments, the Testa de Nevill and Feudal Aids.
britannica-1911-kuban-province:
Kuban is a province of Russian Caucasia. It has the Sea of Azov on the west, the Don Cossack territory on the north, Stavropol and Terek on the east, and Kutais and the Black Sea district on the south. Its area is 36,370 square miles. It takes in the marshy lowlands by the Sea of Azov, the rich steppes of northern Caucasia, and the north slopes of the Caucasus up to Elbruz.

North of the river Kuban, wide treeless plains stand 1000 to 2000 feet high, watered by the river and its many rushing branches. The lower delta is a rush-covered waste, haunt of wild boar and full of malaria. Coal and oil are found, the best oil wells in the Taman Peninsula, though output is still small. In 1897 the Kuban Cossacks numbered 804,372, and Russian peasants over a million. Wheat is by far the chief crop.
britannica-1911-la-grace: La Grâce, or Les Grâces, is a game invented in France in the first quarter of the 19th century, called there le jeu des Grâces. It is played with two light sticks, about 16 inches long, and a wicker ring. The ring is laid over the crossed sticks and shot into the air by parting them fast. Another player catches it on a stick and throws it back. The aim is to keep the ring from falling to the ground.
britannica-1911-laurium-greece:
Laurium, a mining town in Attica, Greece, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its modern name is Ergastiri. The town was famed for silver mines that ranked among the chief revenues of Athens. Their metal fed the coinage of the state.

After the battle of Marathon, Themistocles persuaded Athens to spend the mine revenue on ships. That choice laid the base of Athenian sea power and made the win at Salamis possible. The mines were state property, farmed out for a fixed sum and a share of the yield. Slave labour alone worked them, the article states. Output fell late in the fifth century, hurt by a Spartan post at Decelea. In Strabo's day men were reworking the old waste heaps. Ancient shafts, galleries, and washing pans can still be seen. French and Greek firms work the ground still, chiefly for lead and other metals.
britannica-1911-lecce:
Lecce is a town of Apulia in Italy and chief town of its province. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica praises its ornate old churches. It lies southeast of Brindisi by rail. Its count in 1906 was about thirty-five thousand.

Most fine buildings date from the 1600s in a rich rococo style. The cathedral and three churches lead that showy group. A town museum holds Greek vases and other finds. One older church shows a fine Romanesque door from 1180. A large state tobacco factory works in the town. Rich farm land spreads around it on all sides. The site stands near ancient Lupiae of Roman times. A small harbor linked by tram serves the town trade.
britannica-1911-lee-james-prince:
James Prince Lee (1804-1869) was an English churchman and schoolmaster, and this 1911 Britannica entry gives his career in brief. He was born in London and schooled at St Paul's and at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he shone as a classical scholar. After taking orders in 1830 he taught under Thomas Arnold at Rugby. In 1838 he became headmaster of King Edward's school in Birmingham.

Among his pupils there were three boys who grew into leading churchmen of the next age. In 1848 he was named first bishop of the new see of Manchester. His schoolroom manner could grate on his clergy, the entry admits. His great work was church building: in twenty-one years he consecrated one hundred and thirty churches. He also helped found the Manchester free library and left his own fine book collection to Owens College.
britannica-1911-lens-france:
Lens is a town of northern France in the department of Pas-de-Calais, thirteen miles north-east of Arras. The 1911 Britannica article gives its count as 27,692 in 1906. The town stands on the river Deûle and on the Lens canal. It holds large iron and steel foundries. Its works make machines and steel cables. Lens sits at the heart of the coal field of the department, and coal is the base of its trade.

Two and a half miles to the west-south-west lies Liévin, with a count of 22,070, also a coal town. The land near Lens holds a place in French military history. In 1648 the prince of Condé won a famed victory there over the Spanish. The short entry thus joins an old battle fame to the smoke and pits of a modern coal town.
britannica-1911-locri-greece:
Locri names a Greek people split in two lands. One band held ground from Parnassus north-east to the Euboean channel. Boeotia and Malis flanked that strip. The other band sat south-west of the mount, on the Corinthian Gulf's north shore. Phocis and Aetolia were its neighbours.

East Locri split again in name: Epicnemidii by Mount Cnemis, and Opuntii from their chief town, Opus. Homer knows the east band alone. Ajax Oileus stands as their Troy hero, and his face marks their coins. Old mother-rule held on among them past most Greek lands. West Locri, called Ozolian, were held a rough folk. Greek wars bring them into view late. One root stock, split by fresh folk moving in, is the guess made here. A Locrian colony in Italy, planted late in the 700s B.C., closes the tale.
britannica-1911-lothair-king-of-france:
Lothair, king of France, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Lothair was born in 941 and succeeded his father, Louis the Fourth, in 954. As a boy king he stood under the guardianship of Hugh the Great. His uncle Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, also guided him.

The article tells of a reign spent in war. Early fights with his vassals, above all the duke of Normandy, filled his first years. Then Lothair set his sights on winning back Lorraine. In 978 he nearly captured the emperor Otto the Second at Aix-la-Chapelle. Otto struck back that autumn, marching as far as Paris. He failed to take the city and retreated with heavy loss. Peace came in 980, and Lothair was later chosen guardian of the young Otto the Third. The entry shows a king still able to shake an empire.
britannica-1911-louis-ii-of-france:
Louis II (846-879), king of France, called the Stammerer, is the subject of an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Son of Charles the Bald, emperor and king of the West Franks, he was born on 1 November 846. On his elder brother's death in 866 he became king of Aquitaine.

The entry says he succeeded his father in October 877 as king of the West Franks, though not as emperor. He bought his crown with large grants to the nobles, lay and clerical, and was crowned by Hincmar at Reims. After a feeble reign of eighteen months he died at Compiegne in April 879. He is described as a simple, gentle man, loving peace, justice, and religion.
britannica-1911-louis-iii-of-france:
Louis the Third, king of France, who lived from about 863 to 882, is treated in a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a son of Louis the Second, and with his brother Carloman he followed his father on the throne in 879. A strong party doubted the young princes' right, since their parents' marriage had not been accepted by Charles the Bald.

A plan to offer the crown to an East Frankish Louis came to nothing. In September 879 the brothers were crowned at Ferrières. A few months later they split the kingdom, and Louis took the part of France north of the Loire. The two acted as one against the Northmen, whom they beat in a famed fight in August 881. They also moved against Boso, set up as king in Burgundy and Provence. Louis died at Saint Denis in August 882, leaving no sons.
britannica-1911-louis-ix-of-france:
Louis the Ninth of France, Saint Louis, opens a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1214, he lost his father the king in 1226. His mother Blanche of Castile then held the realm for the boy. She won his crowning at Reims that same year of grief. Great lords rose to test the crown in that weak hour.

Pierre of Brittany and Philippe Hurepel led that feudal push. With help from Rome and Champagne, Blanche beat their plans down. Not till 1234 was the duke of Brittany tamed in full. Then Thibaut of Champagne turned and raised a new league too. The king's host at Vincennes cowed that league with no blow struck. Louis kept deep trust in his mother to her last days.
britannica-1911-louis-v-of-france:
Louis the Fifth was king of France, who lived from nine sixty-seven to nine eighty-seven. He took his fathers throne in March of nine eighty-six at age nineteen. His one year of rule held no great deed of note. Old tale men thus gave him a name that means the man who did naught.

He died in May of the next year, and his mother was charged with his death by sap. He had wed a count of Anjous kin but left no young. His heir by blood was a duke of a low land. Church men who broke faith gave the crown to a new line.
britannica-1911-louis-vi-of-france:
Louis the Sixth of France is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a French king. He lived from 1081 to 1137. He was surnamed the Fat in history. He was son of Philip the First and Bertha of Holland. He lost none of his energy when he earned the fat nickname. In 1098 he was made a knight of the realm.

About that time he was joined with his father in government. Philip's growing infirmities left more and more to the son. The queen Bertrada opposed that rise in power. From 1100 to 1108 Louis won victorious wars. His foes were the English and the brigands of the land. Those wins secured the army on his side. The court, by contrast, supported Bertrada against him. Unable to beat him in war, she tried poison. Chroniclers blamed that poison for the pallor of his face.
britannica-1911-louis-vii-of-france:
Louis the Seventh, king of France, who lived from about 1121 to 1180, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Louis the Sixth and was anointed as co king in 1131. He succeeded his father in 1137 and wed Eleanor of Aquitaine that same year. Early in his reign he was vigorous and jealous of his rights.

Soon Louis clashed with the pope over a vacant archbishopric and drew an interdict on his lands. War with the count of Champagne followed, marked by a church burning at Vitry. In 1145 he declared a crusade, and Saint Bernard preached it to great effect. The crusade of 1147 was a disaster, and Louis came home in shame in 1149. After that his piety grew to the point of weakness. His council annulled his marriage to Eleanor in 1152, a grave political blunder.
britannica-1911-louis-viii-of-france:
Louis the Eighth of France is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Louis was born in Paris in 1187, the eldest son of Philip Augustus. The entry paints him as short, thin, and pale, with studious tastes. He left the name of a saint, yet he was also a warrior prince.

Much of the article covers his bold bid for England. Rebel barons asked him to free them from King John. Louis landed in 1216 and gained a strong hold in the east. John's death and the rise of the child Henry the Third undid his claim. Beaten at Lincoln, he gave up the claim by treaty in 1217. The entry then turns to his crusade in the south of France and his short reign after 1223.
britannica-1911-louis-xiii-of-france:
Louis XIII (1601-1643) was king of France, the son of Henry IV and Marie de' Medici. He became king when his father was killed in 1610. His mother at once took the full powers of regent. She set out to undo her husband's course and to bind France to Spain and the Austrian house.

Two marriages were planned to seal the new bond. Louis was to wed Anne of Austria, daughter of the king of Spain. The Spanish prince was to wed the king's sister in turn. In spite of protests, the queen had her way, and both weddings took place in 1615. The years after were full of civil war and court intrigue. Louis was a backward boy whose schooling had been much neglected.
britannica-1911-louis-xiv-of-france:
Louis the Fourteenth, king of France from 1638 to 1715, is the subject of a long life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, the long-awaited son of Louis the Thirteenth. His birth was hailed as a win for the crown. A childless king had left the throne open to a hostile brother.

His father died when Louis was still a small boy, in 1643. Rule passed to his mother and her chief helper, Cardinal Mazarin. The court twice fled Paris during the revolts called the Fronde. Crowds were once let in to see the young king in his bed. The entry says those shames helped breed his later iron grip on rule. By 1659 peace with Spain set him free to rule in fact.
britannica-1911-louis-xv-of-france:
Louis the Fifteenth, king of France who lived from 1710 to 1774, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the great grandson of Louis the Fourteenth and third son of the duke of Burgundy. Deaths in his family in 1712 swept away his father, his mother, and his elder brother. Louis was thus brought into the line of succession without warning as a child.

He was only five years old when Louis the Fourteenth died in his turn. The dead king had tried by his will to bind the government after his death. A council of regency was to rule, with the duke of Orleans as its nominal head. With help from the parlement of Paris that plan was set aside at once. The duke was declared regent with full powers in the traditional form.
britannica-1911-maccarthy-denis-florence:
Denis Florence MacCarthy was an Irish poet born in Dublin in the early eighteen hundreds. He was schooled in his home city and at a college for priests. His first verses ran in a Dublin paper, and he soon wrote verse on public affairs for a new national paper.

The 1911 Britannica entry lists his work as an editor of Irish poets and ballads, then his own book of songs and lyrics. That book won his countrymen by its strong love of Ireland. More verse books came, and a life of the poet Shelley. His renderings of Spanish stage plays won him a medal from the royal school of Spain. He held a state pension for his work in letters, and died in Ireland in his sixties.
britannica-1911-macdonald-lawrence:
The 1911 Britannica article on Lawrence Macdonald (1799-1878) gives the life of a British sculptor. He was born at Findo-Gask in Perthshire, Scotland. He first served as a mason's apprentice. His gift for stone carving soon showed. He became an art student at the Trustees' Academy in Edinburgh.

Friends helped him visit Rome. There he helped found the British Academy of Arts with other artists. He returned to Edinburgh in 1826. He joined the Scottish Academy in 1829. From 1832 until his death his home was in Rome. The article lists his ideal works. They include Ulysses with his dog Argos. They include Andromeda chained to the rock. They also include a Siren and a Bacchante.
britannica-1911-maeterlinck-maurice:
Maurice Maeterlinck (1862-) was a Belgian-French playwright and poet of Flemish stock, and his early fame is traced in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Ghent, he studied law there and was enrolled as a barrister at twenty-four. In 1887 he settled in Paris and met the leaders of the symbolist school.

The entry says his writing life began in 1889 with a book of verse and a play, La Princesse Maleine. A glowing piece by Octave Mirbeau in the Paris Figaro, calling him a Belgian Shakespeare, made him the talk of the town. More plays followed fast, among them L'Intruse and Les Aveugles in 1890.
britannica-1911-making-up-price: Making up Price is a short term entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It explains a phrase used on stock markets in London and other British towns. The phrase names the price used when open deals are carried from one market period to the next. A buyer who holds on sells for cash and buys back at that same price. It is set at noon on roll over day, by the market price at that hour. New York uses the phrase too.
britannica-1911-malleson-george-bruce:
George Bruce Malleson (1825–1898) is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an Indian officer and writer, born at Wimbledon. Schooled at Winchester, he won a cadetship in the Bengal infantry in 1842 and served through the second Burmese War. His later posts were on the civil side, the last as guardian to the young maharaja of Mysore. He retired with the rank of colonel in 1877.

Malleson wrote a great deal. The work that first drew eyes was the famous Red Pamphlet, put out at Calcutta in 1857 while the Mutiny was at its height. He took up the History of the Indian Mutiny that Sir John Kaye had begun and left undone, and rewrote it in six volumes. Among his other books, the most valued are his History of the French in India and The Decisive Battles of India.
britannica-1911-mangan-james-clarence:
James Clarence Mangan (1803-1849) was an Irish poet, and his hard life is told in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Dublin, son of a grocer ruined by wild spending, he took the added name Clarence himself. At fifteen he entered a scrivener's office and drudged as a copying clerk for ten years.

The entry follows his posts in the Trinity College library and on the Irish Ordnance Survey from 1833. Disappointed in love and dogged by ill health, he turned to opium and suffered vivid fancies. He wrote for several Dublin journals, sent translations from the German poets to one magazine, and made versions of old Irish poems as well.
britannica-1911-margaret-of-provence:
Margaret of Provence, who lived from 1221 to 1295, was a queen of France. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells her strong willed story. She was a daughter of the count of Provence. In 1234 she wed King Louis the Ninth at Sens and was crowned next day.

The queen mother treated Margaret with cold envy for years. Margaret still sailed with the king on crusade. She bore herself with courage at Damietta in Egypt. Her push and her feuds could harm the realm, the entry says. She fought her brother in law over rights in Provence. Only in 1285 did she trade that claim for income from Anjou. She died at the end of 1295.
britannica-1911-marie-de-france:
Marie de France (fl. c. 1175–1190) was a French poet and writer of fables. Denis Pyramus, in a note of about 1240, says she was one of the most loved authors of her day. Counts, barons, and knights read her, and ladies read her most of all. The writer of the Couronnement Renart also names her. Her lays were turned into the tongue of Norway by order of Haakon IV. Thomas Chestre later gave a form of her Lanval in English.

Very little is known of Marie's life, and the age in which she lived was in doubt till late times. In the close of her fables she says that her name is Marie and that she is of France. Men have read that to mean that she came from the Île de France.
britannica-1911-maritime-province:
Maritime Province, a Russian province in East Siberia, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It forms a long strip of land along the Pacific coast. The strip runs from Korea all the way to the Arctic Ocean. It also takes in the Kamchatka peninsula, part of Sakhalin island, and several small islands.

The article gives the province a vast area of more than seven hundred thousand square miles. Its northern part is a barren plateau, cut by rivers and long inlets. Only lichens, mosses, and dwarf trees grow in that cold district. Yet its animal life is richer than a reader might expect. A few American birds and beasts cross the frozen strait from Alaska. For two centuries the region and its seas fed the Siberian trade in furs and like goods.
britannica-1911-mary-queen-of-france:
Mary, queen of France, who lived from 1496 to 1533, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was a daughter of Henry the Seventh of England and Elizabeth of York. At first she was to wed Charles of Austria, the future emperor Charles the Fifth. A treaty of 1507 set the match for when he turned fourteen, and she was wed to him by proxy in 1508.

The plan fell apart as the emperor Maximilian held back and looked to a French match instead. Wolsey moved first, and peace with France was signed in August 1514. A treaty of the same date gave Mary to Louis the Twelfth of France, who had just lost his wife. They were wed at Abbeville in October. He was a worn man of fifty two, and she a girl of eighteen whose heart was already given to Charles Brandon.
britannica-1911-mayor-of-the-palace:
Mayor of the palace, an office found among the Franks in Merovingian times, is explained in a 1911 Britannica article. The post grew from the chief steward of a large estate. A steward ran the land and took in its rents. The king's chief steward took his name from the royal house, called the palace.

The job soon grew past house work. A mayor kept order in the palace and judged those who lived there. If the king was a child, the mayor raised him and ran state affairs. By the seventh century the mayor led the whole rule of the realm. He helped pick counts and dukes and often led armies.
britannica-1911-medical-jurisprudence:
Medical jurisprudence, also called forensic medicine, is the branch of state medicine that applies medical knowledge to points of civil and criminal law. This 1911 Britannica article notes that the tie between medicine and law was seen long before the subject had a name. It first rose in Germany, and was taken up more slowly in Great Britain.

The field covers all points that bring a medical man into contact with the law. These fall into two groups: points touching the civil rights of persons, and injuries to the person. The article first takes up the growth of the human frame. Age and growth bear on guilt and on the power to make valid contracts. They also bear on naming a living person or a corpse.
britannica-1911-monstrance:
Monstrance is a term entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names a vessel used in the Roman church to show the sacred host. The host is shown at a set rite and borne in street marches. The word comes from a Latin root that means to show or display.

The entry traces the shape of the vessel from old relic cases. First forms used a glass tube set in rich gold work and gems. Some took the shape of a small tower with a dome on top. A later form uses a flat glass disk ringed with gold rays. That form fits the round shape of the wafer it holds for view.
britannica-1911-morris-dance:
Morris-Dance is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on an old English dance. The name comes from a Spanish word that means Moorish. Some say John of Gaunt brought the dance in from Spain. Others say it came by way of France or Flanders.

It grew from the morisco dance, a solo Spanish dance form. By the reign of Henry the Eighth it was a chief part of village feasts. In old times five men and a boy in girl's dress danced it. The boy was called Maid Marian in the old custom. Two musicians played, and one dancer led as foreman of the set. Bells on the clothes rang in tune as they danced and stepped.
britannica-1911-museums-of-science:
Museums of Science is a 1911 Britannica article on what a science museum should be. The ideal museum, it says, should cover the whole field of human knowledge. It should teach the truths of all the sciences. Anthropology, the science of man and all his works, belongs in it too.

All the sciences and all the arts are linked, the text argues. So the wide split between art collections and science collections is a false one. That split is the rule, not the exception, in its day. It came from how many collections began. In other cases, poverty or lack of space forced it. The article notes that many national museums of Europe had mixed starts. Readers get a plea for one house of knowledge, not two kept apart by habit.
britannica-1911-negligence:
Negligence is a 1911 Britannica article on a key idea in law. The word comes from a Latin root that means, in plain terms, not to pick up. In civil law, it is a ground for being held liable for harm. In criminal law, it plays a part in some crimes, most of all manslaughter by negligence.

The article sets out what must be proved to win a civil case. There must be a duty to take care, a lack of due care, and real harm caused by that lack of care. Mere carelessness is not enough on its own. The person harmed must show that a legal duty was owed. The text then works through how that duty can arise, such as when an act puts the public at risk.
britannica-1911-nonfeasance:
Nonfeasance is a law article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a trio of terms in English law: nonfeasance, misfeasance and malfeasance. The words concern the discharge of public duties owed by common law, custom or statute. The rule laid down is sharp: no action lies for nonfeasance, the mere failure or refusal to perform the duty.

The article shows where the distinction bites. Today the terms are used most often of town authorities and their statutory duties. A person hurt by negligence can sue, but for simple failure the remedy is indictment or mandamus. The rule is firmest for unrepaired highways, though the article notes that courts are quick to find carelessness and award damages. The piece adds that misfeasance is also used of company directors, and malfeasance sometimes of bad medical practice.
britannica-1911-north-west-frontier-prov:
North West Frontier Province was the most northerly province of British India. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lays out its parts and borders. It was created in October 1901 as a new province. It lies between the Indus River and Afghanistan.

One part is the Hazara district toward the Himalaya hills. A second part is a narrow strip of settled districts. Peshawar, Kohat, Bannu, and Dera Ismail Khan sit in that strip. The third part is rough mountain land held by free tribes. Five agencies watch that tribal belt for the governor general. In all the province spans near thirty-nine thousand square miles. Only a third of that land was British ground outright.
britannica-1911-notice:
Notice is a law word that starts from the idea of knowledge. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces it from the Latin notitia. It can mean the knowledge itself, as in judicial notice. It can mean the means of bringing knowledge, as in notice to quit. At last it can mean the very paper that carries the word. Courts take judicial notice of facts they need not have proved. Those facts include the dates of the calendar and where parliament sits.

The doctrine of notice in equity gets the most space. A buyer who pays full price but knows of an earlier claim loses. He cannot use his legal title to defeat that claim. A buyer in good faith with no notice is as a rule protected. Stock phrases fill the tail of the entry. Notice of dishonour, of action, and of trial are each glossed.
britannica-1911-nuisance:
Nuisance in English law is set out as a wrong of two kinds in a 1911 Britannica law entry. The word comes through French from a Latin verb for to hurt. A public wrong blocks or harms folk in a right shared by all. Such an act counts as a breach that the law can punish. A boss bears blame for acts of his staff done in their work.

A private wrong harms one person or one plot of land. Courts ask if the harm cuts the ease or worth of the land in a real way. Long use can make a private wrong lawful in time. No lapse of time can do the same for a public wrong. Cures span court claims, charges, and direct clearing of the block.
britannica-1911-orsini-felice:
Italian patriot Felice Orsini, born at Meldola in eighteen nineteen, is given a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was meant for a church career, but he gave that up. He became a keen liberal and joined the Young Italy society of Mazzini.

In eighteen forty four he was seized for his part in plots and given life in prison. A new pope set him free. He led young men in the first war for Italian freedom in eighteen forty eight. He sat in the Roman assembly the next year. After its fall he plotted again for the cause. A secret trip to Hungary ended in his arrest in eighteen fifty four.
britannica-1911-pabianice: Pabianice is a town of Russian Poland, in the government of Piotrkow. It lies thirty miles north west of the town of Piotrkow and ten miles from Lodz station. Its people numbered eighteen thousand two hundred fifty one in eighteen ninety seven. The town stands amid wide forests round the head waters of the Ner river. Those woods were once the hunting grounds of the Polish kings. Pabianice has woollen mills, cloth mills, and paper mills. It also makes tools and machines for farm work.
britannica-1911-pace: Pace is the subject of a short word article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes through French from a Latin word for a step. It means one movement of the leg in walking. It also means the ground covered by each step, or the speed at which a thing moves. As a measure, a pace runs from a short military pace to a full yard. The Roman pace counted from one foot back to the same foot. A thousand such paces made the Roman mile.
britannica-1911-palace:
Palace first named the home of a king or prince, from the home set up by Augustus on the Palatine Hill. In some lands the word grew to cover the home of a bishop or a house of law. In Italy it can name a great town house as well. The entry then gives a world tour of such homes.

First come the halls of Egypt by the great shrines at Thebes. Greek halls in Crete and at Tiryns come next, then those of the kings of Assyria and Persia. Rome fills a long stretch, with homes that sprawled past a vast floor count. Later styles in France, Venice, and England close the sweep.
britannica-1911-patents-of-precedence:
A patent of precedence is a grant that lifts a man's rank. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as a gift by letters patent. It gives a higher place than a man's ordinary standing allows. The chief modern use was at the English bar. Taking the rank of king's counsel once barred a lawyer from acting against the crown. It also cost a member of parliament his seat.

A patent gave the same honour with none of those bars. Mansfield, Erskine, Scott, and Brougham all held one on that ground. Serjeants at law later got such patents as their old rights faded. By 1897 only one judge and one dying serjeant held the grant. Canada also grants such patents, by its governor general and its provinces. A court ruling of 1898 upheld the provincial power to grant them.
britannica-1911-penzance:
Penzance, a town and port in Cornwall, England, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the end point of the Great Western railway and the westernmost port in England. It stands on the west shore of Mount's Bay, facing Saint Michael's Mount. The entry gives it 13,136 people in 1901.

The old town slopes sharply up from the harbour, with a modern quarter and promenade to the west. Its mild climate has made it a favoured health resort. A statue of Sir Humphry Davy, born here in 1778, stands by the market house. The town has a fine public library and museums of geology and natural history. Its harbour covers twenty four acres behind a breakwater. Fish, tin, copper, granite, and early vegetables are its chief exports to London and beyond.
britannica-1911-phosphorescence:
Phosphorescence is the subject of a science entry in the 1911 Britannica. The name covers acts where things give off pale light. That light is faint and not from plain burning. The word was first used for one such trait. Some stuffs glow on their own after light has hit them. Old writers noted gems that shone with their own light. One sage knew a diamond glows when warmed a bit.

A stone found near Bologna drew the first keen study. A cobbler there found it in about 1602. More stuffs that glow were found in its wake. Some glow after light, some with heat, some with rubbing. All such stuffs were called phosphori at first. Later use cut the word to the glow after light. A broad term, luminescence, was put forth for all such cases. Kin terms and sub kinds are set out from there.
britannica-1911-pinnace: Pinnace names two kinds of craft, as the 1911 Britannica article explains in a short entry. One was a light sailing ship with two masts rigged in schooner style. The other was a heavy boat with eight oars, carried by a man-of-war for work about the ship. The word is most often traced to the Latin word for pine, but the older form of the word, spinace, does not fit that source well.
britannica-1911-plaice: The plaice is a flat fish of northern Europe, from Iceland to the Bay of Biscay. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica picks it out by its yellow or orange spots. Those spots run in a row along the back and belly fins. More spots scatter over the body. Its eyes sit on the right side, and its scales are minute and smooth. Plaice favour a sandy sea floor over rocky ground. They spawn early in spring. A fish of seven or eight pounds counts as large.
britannica-1911-police:
Police, a word for law keeping and for the force that does it, is treated in a 1911 Britannica article. The term came into English in the 1700s and was disliked as a sign of foreign rule. Its first known official use was for Scotland in 1714. The piece gives the word two senses, crime work and wider public order.

The growth of a set police force in England was slow, the text shows. France had such a force far earlier, but it turned into a tool of harsh rule. Old English steps, such as the Watch and Ward law of 1285 for London, are traced as early roots. Later acts for Westminster are also noted.
britannica-1911-potemkin-grigory-aleksan:
Grigory Aleksandrovich Potemkin, a Russian statesman born in seventeen thirty nine, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at a town near Smolensk, he was schooled at the high school of Moscow. In seventeen fifty five he joined the horse guards. His part in a coup drew the eye of the new empress.

She made him a court aide and gave him a small estate. The tales of his next years are dim and most of them not firm in fact. In seventeen sixty eight he left the guards for a court post. The next year he went to the war with the Turks. He stood out at more than one great fight in that war. In seventeen seventy one he rose to be the chief love of the empress.
britannica-1911-poultice:
Poultice is defined in a very short entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a mass of meal, bread, or like stuff, at times with healing herbs. The mass is mixed with hot water. It is then wrapped in thin cloth and laid on the skin.

The aim is plain in the text. A plain pack is used to cut red sore skin or to bring warmth to a spot. Mixed with mustard, the same pack works as a counter rub that draws blood to the skin. The word is traced to a Latin word for thick soup or pulse food. Though the note is tiny, it gives form, stuff, wrap, and use in one clear sweep. A reader who meets the old home cure in a book or a case note will place it at once from this text.
britannica-1911-precedence:
Rank at court and in public life is mapped in an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word for that rank order is precedence, from a Latin root. It means who goes first and who holds the higher place. Such order rules state rites and the forms of private life. In Britain no one code fixes the whole scale for good.

Rules grew at sundry times and came from sundry sources. The Crown stands as the spring of all honour in the land. It may grant titles, rank, and place as it sees fit. That power is broad at common law, the entry notes. Old disputes of rank went to the court of chivalry. Heralds and kings of arms served as its staff there.
britannica-1911-recognizance:
Recognizance is the subject of a law entry in the 1911 Britannica. The term comes from a Latin word for owning a fact. In English law it names a bond of record. A man enters it before a court or a justice. In it he owns that he owes a debt to the Crown. A clause can void that debt if he does a set act. Such acts span court shows, peace keeping, and the like.

That plan took the place of old pledge ways in law. One old gloss stretched the term to bonds for private men. Present use ties it near sole to crime steps in court. Guards of wards once gave such bonds in Chancery. Those bonds barred secret wedlock or flight of the ward. A court receiver still gives his bond in this form. Old acts gave justices wide power to call for such bonds.
britannica-1911-reconnaissance:
Reconnaissance, from a French word meaning to recognize, is a term of war set out in this 1911 Britannica article. It denotes the scouting or examination of an enemy's position or movements, or of a tract of ground. Such work varies without limit according to the purpose for which it is undertaken.

A survey type of this work is in effect a survey of a stretch of country or a route, with a map and a report on its good and bad points. All such work is done by officers with small patrols or helpers. The strategic kind is done by squadrons sent forward to find the enemy. The tactical kind falls to troops of all arms, in contact with the enemy or for their own protection. A test by a large force of all arms, meant to make the enemy show his hand, is called a reconnaissance in force.
britannica-1911-rice:
Rice is the subject of a grain entry in the 1911 Britannica. Rice is a well known cereal grown across warm lands. Word forms in Greek, Latin, and French are listed first. Its plant name is given in Latin form in the text. One view holds that crop rice sprang from a wild plant. That wild plant grows by lakes in India, the text says. It is also native to warm parts of Australia.

The plant is a grass that grows for one year. Its leaves are long, straight, and smooth to touch. Its grains grow on a branched spike head. Each small spike holds one flower in its husk. Kinds of rice are very many in number. Some kinds suit marsh land and some suit hill sides. Growers split the kinds by early or late growth. A rite in China from deep past is then noted.
britannica-1911-ricold-of-monte-croce:
Ricold of Monte Croce, an Italian Dominican missionary who lived from 1242 to 1320, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Monte Croce, near Florence. In 1267 he entered the Dominican house of Santa Maria Novella in Florence. In 1272 he joined the house of St Catherine in Pisa.

He set out for Acre with a papal commission to preach. The year was 1286 or 1287. Soon after, he began to keep a record of his travels in the Levant. That record he most likely put in book form at Bagdad. His route crossed Galilee to the Sea of Tiberias. He went down the coast to Jaffa, then up to Jerusalem. He visited the Jordan and the Dead Sea as well. The piece follows a friar whose notes became a window on the East.
britannica-1911-robert-i-king-of-france:
Robert the First, king of France, born about eight sixty five, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the younger son of Robert the Strong, count of Anjou. His brother rose to be king of the western Franks in eight eighty eight. That brother made Robert the ruler of more than one county, Paris among them.

Robert held as well the post of duke of the Franks, a war rank of high weight. When his brother died, he did not claim the crown. He owned the sway of the old line king and was kept in his posts and lands. He then kept north France safe from the raids of the Normans for years. Calm held between king and great vassal till about nine twenty one. Then the rule of the king, and his fondness for one court friend, bred heat in the land.
britannica-1911-robert-ii-king-of-france:
Robert II (about 970-1031), called the Pious, was king of France. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica presents him as son of Hugh Capet, born at Orleans. Gerbert, later Pope Silvester II, taught him at Reims in youth. His father crowned him as joint king in 987, and he ruled alone from 996.

His marriages drive most of the drama in the account. He left an older first wife to wed Bertha, a kinswoman, in 996. The pope banned him and set seven years of penance for that step. After five years he gave Bertha up and wed Constance. Burgundy was the chief gain for France in his reign.
britannica-1911-robertson-william-bruce:
William Bruce Robertson lived from 1820 to 1886 and was a Scottish divine. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Greenhill in Stirlingshire, where he was born. He studied at Glasgow and at the Secession hall in Edinburgh. There he met Thomas de Quincey, who urged him to study at Halle. He worked there under Tholuck and then toured Italy and Switzerland.

Licensed to preach in 1843, he soon took charge at Irvine in Ayrshire. He stayed in that post for a full thirty five years. From his pulpit he held crowds with a rare, warm force. Health failed from 1871 despite trips to Florence and the coast. He gave up his charge in 1878 and died eight years later.
britannica-1911-rochefort-france:
Rochefort is the subject of a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Rochefort is a town in western France, southeast of La Rochelle. It stands on the right bank of the Charente river, nine miles from the Atlantic. By 1906 its people numbered over thirty six thousand in the wider commune. The town is laid out with wide, straight streets around a central square.

The article stresses its role as a naval port. It holds both a naval and a trading harbour with deep, safe anchorage. The naval yard has covered building slips, repair docks, and timber basins on both banks. It also has a rope walk from 1668 and a school of navigation. Other navy sites include barracks and a hospital with a school of medicine. A deep artesian well in its grounds yields warm water.
britannica-1911-rollinat-maurice:
French poet Maurice Rollinat, born at Chateauroux in eighteen fifty three, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His father sat in the National Assembly of eighteen forty eight. His father was a friend of George Sand, whose sway marks his first book of verse in eighteen seventy seven.

That first book drew little notice. A second book, very different in manner, made his name. In it he showed himself a follower of Baudelaire. He returned again and again to the horrors of death, with grim images. Later books were less extreme, and one was verse for children. He was a musician as well as a poet, and set many of his songs. He lost his reason after his wife's death and died in nineteen oh three.
britannica-1911-rouvier-maurice:
Maurice Rouvier, a French statesman born in 1842, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He spent his early manhood in business at Marseilles. He backed Gambetta there and in 1870 founded a journal against the empire. He then served as a senior officer of the local prefecture.

Rouvier entered the National Assembly in 1871 and voted with the Republican party. He soon became a known voice on finance and led the Budget Commission more than once. He served as minister of trade and the colonies under Gambetta and under Ferry. In May 1887 he became premier and finance minister. His cabinet fell in a scandal over honours sold by the presidents son in law. Later he held the finance post through a run of cabinets, and again from 1902.
britannica-1911-salamanca-province:
Salamanca is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a frontier province of Spain. It was formed in 1833 from the south part of old Leon. Portugal bounds it on the west, Zamora on the north. The count for 1900 is 320,765, on 4,829 square miles.

Most of the land drains to the Duero river and its streams. The Tormes runs north-west for 135 miles to join it. The north of the province is flat and low in height. Ranges in the south rise to near 5,692 feet at the top peak. Rain is uneven, but good soils yield wine, oil, and grain. Oak, pine, and chestnut woods cover a wide tract.
britannica-1911-salamis-greece:
Salamis is a Greek island in the Saronic Gulf of the Aegean Sea. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its place and past. The island lies along the coasts of Attica and Megaris. It closes in the Bay of Eleusis between two narrow straits. Its bent shape gave it a folk name that means a baker crescent.

Ancient tales made Salamis the home of Telamon and his sons Ajax and Teucer. Athens won the island from Megara after a fight near the year 600 before Christ. In 480 the Greek fleet made its base there against Persia. Greek ships trapped the larger Persian fleet in the straits and won a famed sea fight. Later notes track coins, garrisons, and Athenian settlers on the island.
britannica-1911-samarkand-province:
Samarkand, a province of Russian Turkestan, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the ancient Sogdiana, known to the Muslims of the middle ages as Sughd. Bokhara bounds it on the west and Ferghana on the east. It covers 26,627 square miles. The south is very hilly, cut by ranges of the Alai system.

The article names three great ranges. One forms the watershed between two river systems. A second runs between two parallel rivers, and a third stretches west to east along a north bank. All three are clad in snow. Their highest peaks reach 18,500 feet in the west and 22,000 feet in the east. The passes over them are hard as a rule and lie at some 12,000 feet. Alpine lakes dot the high ground. The entry warns that the ranges are most likely far more tangled than the simple scheme suggests.
britannica-1911-samothrace:
Samothrace, an island in the north of the Aegean Sea, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies nearly opposite the mouth of the river Hebrus. Its people numbered about three thousand five hundred, nearly all Greek. The island is still called Samothraki by its folk.

Though small, Samothrace towers over its part of the Aegean. Its mountain mass rises to more than five thousand feet. In the Iliad, Poseidon takes his post on that summit. From there he surveys the plain of Troy and the war below. The island has no tolerable harbour, a want that barred it from power. Pliny called it the most harbourless of all the Aegean isles. Its fame came instead from religion, from the worship of the Cabeiri. Those mysterious gods were a survival of older Pelasgian faith. Herodotus ties their rites at Samothrace to that ancient people.
britannica-1911-saragossa-province:
Saragossa, an inland province of north Spain, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is one of the three parts into which Aragon was split in 1833. In 1900 it held over four hundred and twenty thousand people. The whole province lies in the basin of the river Ebro.

High sierras bound the main valley, and side streams feed the Ebro from both banks. Wide tracts of land are barren, but where water is at hand the soil is rich. Wheat, rye, barley, hemp, flax, oil, and wine lead the crops. Sheep graze the high ground, and silk worms are bred in the low. Trade in goods made by hand and mill has grown since 1885. Wine, flour, oil, and fruit head the goods sent out.
britannica-1911-sauce:
Sauce is a flavouring for food, most often in liquid or near-liquid form. The 1911 Britannica article says it may be served apart or mixed in the dish. Good sauces are counted one of the core skills of fine cooking. The word came through French from a Latin term for salted or pickled food. That term grew from the Latin word for salt, used as seasoning.

Kindred words fill the rest of the short piece. Saucer first meant a dish for sauce, before it shrank to the small plate set under a cup. Sausage traces to a Latin phrase for minced, seasoned meat stuffed in skins. The slang sense of saucy, meaning cheeky, came from the sharp bite of a sauce. A quote from Latimer shows the word in that use long ago.
britannica-1911-sceve-maurice:
Maurice Scève, French poet born at Lyons in about 1500, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His father worked in the law there, and Scève followed that trade too. He was also a painter, a builder, and a musician. At Lyons he stood at the centre of a circle of writers.

That circle shaped a theory of spiritual love drawn from Plato and from Petrarch. His chief work is Délie, from 1544, in praise of his mistress. It holds 450 ten line verses and about fifty other poems. Two eclogues and a long poem on the fall of man round out his work. Even his great fan Étienne Dolet said he could not grasp the poems, so obscure was their sense.
britannica-1911-science:
Science, from a Latin word for knowing, is defined here as ordered knowledge of natural events and the ties between them. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica essay takes the word in its modern narrow sense, as a short name for natural science. It then asks how such knowledge began among early peoples.

Physical science grew, the essay says, from slow watching of the skies and from growing skill with rude tools. Life science began with noting which plants and animals served man, and with rough medicine and surgery. Only after much knowledge was stored did men ask after causes and links. The first answers were myths that gave each event to an unseen being much like man himself. Such tales still served inquiry, since a false view that can be tested beats none at all.
britannica-1911-sconce: Sconce is a short word study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, tracing one term through many senses. Its best known sense is a wall light, a metal bracket with socketed branches for candles. The word also names the socket of a candlestick and the rim set round a candle to catch grease. Older senses reach as far as the head or skull. At the English universities, to sconce a man is to fine him a quart pot of beer or cider at dinner.
britannica-1911-seville-province:
Seville, an inland province of southern Spain, is the subject of a regional entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was one of the eight provinces into which Andalusia was divided in 1833. The entry gives it 555,256 people in 1900 and an area of 5,428 square miles. Badajoz, Cordova, Malaga, Cadiz, and Huelva bound it.

The navigable Guadalquivir river cuts the province in two and takes in the Genil and other streams. West of the river the land is broken by low ranges of the Sierra Morena. The eastern districts are flat and fertile, with wide marshes near the river mouth. Coal, copper, iron ore, and marble are its chief mineral products. The province is famed for oranges and exports grain, olives, oil, and wine. Cattle breeding is a key trade in the plains. Seville city is the capital and chief river port.
britannica-1911-solstice: Solstice, from Latin words for the sun and for standing still, is the name in astronomy for two points in the sky. At each point the sun reaches its greatest tilt north or south. The 1911 Britannica entry places each solstice on the sun path midway between the two equinoxes, and so ninety degrees from each of them. The word is also used for the exact moment at which the sun arrives at that point. Together the two solstices mark the turning points of the solar year.
britannica-1911-soria-province:
Soria, a province of Spain formed in 1833 from districts of Old Castile, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Logroño bounds it to the north, Saragossa to the east, and Burgos to the west. Its people numbered 150,462 in 1900, over an area of 3,983 square miles. Soria is a bleak and lofty region, ringed on three sides by mountains. Peaks in the north reach above 7,000 feet.

Those ranges part the valley of the Duero from that of the Ebro. The Duero rises on the slopes of Urbion and crosses the province in a winding course. The soil is not noted for fertility, since barren mountains cover much of the area. Yet some districts hold wide forests of pine, oak, and beech. Others hold pasture where cattle, sheep, and swine are reared.
britannica-1911-spheres-of-influence:
Spheres of influence are terms used in law between nations. A set of like phrases names tracts where states have agreed that one of them may act with a free hand. Other states agree to stay out of those tracts. The phrases came into wide use after 1882. That was when the rush by European powers to seize land in Africa began.

The article quotes views from men of the time to pin the term down. Lord Knutsford, as colonial secretary in 1890, said it meant that no foreign state would be let to settle in the tract or take it over. The rest of the piece works through what such a pact binds each side to do. It treats the term as a deal between two states about a third tract of land.
britannica-1911-st-vitus-s-dance:
Saint Vituss Dance, or chorea, is an ill of the nerves seen most in the young. Its chief mark is jerk moves of the flesh past near the whole frame, with no will in them. Age counts much, since the ill is one of youth most of all. It strikes most in the years of the next teeth.

Girls take it twice as oft as boys. A bent to nerve ills in the blood can show in this ill when health runs low. Fright, harsh use, poor food, and strain are named as sparks. Its tie to joint fever is now held as sure by all.
britannica-1911-sterne-laurence:
Laurence Sterne was an English humorist who lived from seventeen thirteen to seventeen sixty eight. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Roger Sterne, an English officer in Ireland. Most facts on his first forty six years come from his own brief memoir.

Sterne was born at Clonmel on the twenty fourth of November seventeen thirteen. For ten years he moved with his father regiment from place to place. That roving life taught him army ways he later used in fiction. His famed book Tristram Shandy drew on Uncle Toby and Corporal Trim. Kin at Cambridge helped him study at Jesus College after his father died.
britannica-1911-surface:
Surface is a geometry article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It treats the surface as the bounding or limiting part of a body. The entry sets its topic beside the companion article on curves. Ideas first traced there, it says, carry over to the study of surfaces.
