The article explains why surfaces get a lighter historical treatment. The ideas peculiar to surfaces are less basic in nature. They are rather developments of the curve ideas, applied to a higher part of geometry. Curves in space are left to the earlier article and not taken up again. The piece then sets out the basic figures of solid geometry. In plane geometry those figures are the point and the line. The curve may be viewed as a system of points or of lines. Readers get a careful doorway into a hard branch of mathematics.
britannica-1911-temperance:
Temperance, in the limited sense of the fight against drink, is the vast topic of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word strictly means moderation, but groups formed to cut or end the use of strong liquor took the name Temperance Societies. Their work made temperance stand, in common speech, for the whole drink question.

The entry opens with a long view. Ever since man first found how sugar ferments into alcohol, and felt its power, there has been a drink question of some kind. Old records from India, Persia, China, Palestine, Egypt, Greece and Carthage all touch on it. Priests, sages and lawgivers in those lands tried to fight drunkenness from very early times. Yet the entry holds that the evil had never drawn so much notice as in its own age, when it had set terms in French and German as well as English.
britannica-1911-terek-province:
Terek, a province of Russian Caucasia, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies north of the Caucasus chain and covers 23,531 square miles. The government of Stavropol bounds it on the north, and the Caspian Sea and Daghestan on the east. Its southern border follows the main range from Mount Elbruz to Kasbek, taking in some of the highest peaks.

The article divides the land by its shape. Near one third is hilly tract. The rest is rolling and flat land in the low basin of the Terek river. Half of that flat part, on the left bank, is sandy desert, salt clay steppe, and dry ground unfit for crops. Old rock beds spread wide under the plains, and mineral springs rise near Pyatigorsk. The climate is of the inland kind, with a mean yearly heat given for that town.
britannica-1911-terence:
Terence is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Terence was the famed Latin playwright Publius Terentius Afer. What we know of his life comes chiefly from a fragment of a lost work by Suetonius. That fragment is kept in a commentary by Donatus. Both his birth date and the manner of his death are uncertain. His last play was shown in the year 160 before Christ.

The article says he was born in Carthage and brought to Rome as a slave. In Rome he was schooled like a free man in a senator's house. That senator soon freed him, and Terence took his master's name. He was taken into the circle of the best young men of Rome. If he was born in 185, he wrote his six plays between the ages of eighteen and twenty five.
britannica-1911-teruel-province:
Teruel is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a province in the north east of Spain. The province was formed in eighteen thirty three from part of the old kingdom of Aragon. High ranges cross its centre and south, and its north drains toward the Ebro river.

The entry lists the main rivers and the chief goods of the land. Farms yield grain, wine, oil, cheese, fruit, and wool. Forests and coal beds are noted, but trade is held back by poor roads and few rail lines. Only one rail line serves the whole province. The account gives a clear picture of a rich but cut off rural region.
britannica-1911-thackeray-william-makepe:
William Makepeace Thackeray, an English novelist who lived from 1811 to 1863, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the only son of Richmond and Anne Thackeray and was born at Calcutta. Both his father and grandfather had been Indian civil servants. His mother was nineteen at his birth and was left a widow in 1816.

The young Thackeray was brought home to England from India as a child. He went to private schools in Hampshire and at Chiswick, then to Charterhouse in 1822. A school friend later recalled him as a pretty, gentle, and rather timid boy at school. The entry finds traces of that sensitive nature all through his writings. In the boy who does not understand it, such a nature can look like shyness. In the man, the entry argues, it was a source of creative power.
britannica-1911-toole-john-lawrence:
John Lawrence Toole (1832-1906) was an English actor, and his comic career is traced in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London, son of an East India Company man long famed as a City toast-master, he started life in a wine merchant's office. A natural bent for comic acting pulled him to the stage in 1852.

The entry follows his London start in 1854, his hit as Paul Pry in 1857, and his lasting friendship with Henry Irving, whom he urged to come to London. At the Adelphi from 1858 he fixed his fame as a comedian. In 1879 he took over the Folly theatre in London, renamed Toole's in 1882.
britannica-1911-tourneux-jean-maurice:
Jean Maurice Tourneux was a French man of letters and maker of book lists. He was the son of an artist and author. Born in Paris in the mid eighteen hundreds, he began his work in a plain way. He helped on new texts of two famed guides. Those guides dealt with false named books and with books that bear no name.

His chief work, the 1911 Britannica entry says, was a vast list of books on Paris in the revolt years. It ran to three thick parts and was crowned by a great learned body. That work serves as a guide to the tale of the city far past those years. He made like lists for famed authors. He also put out sound texts of letters and tales by great French writers.
britannica-1911-trance:
Trance, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, names a sleep like state that plainly differs from normal sleep. The word came through French from a Latin term for a crossing or passing over. In its first use it hinted that the soul had left the body for a time. That belief was held by peoples in many parts of the world.

The entry warns that the term is used loosely in common speech. Medical and scientific writing defines it little better. The word now covers a range of states with no such soul theory implied. Sleepwalking is one case named. Deep melancholic lethargy and stupor are others. The deeper stages of hypnosis and the cataleptic state also fall under the term. So do the ecstasy of religious devotees and the dream like state of medicine men.
britannica-1911-tucuman-province: Tucuman is the subject of a short province article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Tucuman is a northern province of Argentina. Salta bounds it on the north and Catamarca on the south and west. Its area is near nine thousand square miles. Its people numbered near two hundred sixteen thousand in 1895. A high range stands on its western edge, while the east is flat, rich, and fertile. The Sali river is its one large stream. Exports include sugar, rum, timber, hides, leather, and fruit.
britannica-1911-twiss-horace:
Horace Twiss is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an English writer and law maker born at Bath in seventeen eighty seven. His father wrote on the plays of Shakespeare and wed into a famed stage family. The son had a quick wit and wrote light pieces for the press.

The entry follows his work at the bar and his long years in parliament. He held a junior post in charge of war and the colonies. He wrote the daily sum of house debates for a great London paper. His best known book is a life of a famed lord chancellor. He died without warning in London in eighteen forty nine.
britannica-1911-united-states-the-financ:
Finance is a section of the long 1911 Britannica article on the United States, dealing with taxes and public revenue. It sets out the taxing powers at each level, starting with the national state. That power is limited only by a ban on duties on exports and by a rule that direct taxes be levied in line with population.

The states hold wide revenue powers, limited by their own constitutions and by United States law. Within each state, counties, cities, boroughs, and smaller districts hold tax powers for strictly set purposes. The article notes that state and local revenues came mainly from a general property tax on land and goods. More than eighty-two per cent of their tax revenue came that way in 1902, a system it calls rare in the wider world.
britannica-1911-united-states-the-indust:
Industries and Commerce is a section of the long 1911 Britannica article on the United States, dealing with manufactures and trade. It opens by noting that in the colonial period there were only small starts in making goods, and that British policy was in general hostile to their growth. After independence, the nation's strength went into taking up the land and farming it.

So long as land was plentiful, the article argues, there was little push toward a factory system, which in the main grew after the Civil War. It then traces the record of the census: no counts of manufactures in 1790 or 1800, weak returns in 1810, 1820, and 1840, and full ones from 1850 on. A new special count of true factories began in 1905.
britannica-1911-uralsk-province:
Uralsk was a province of Asiatic Russia north of the Caspian Sea. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica maps its land, weather, and people. Its area is given as about one hundred forty thousand square miles. It sat among Russian governments such as Astrakhan, Samara, and Orenburg.

Most of the land is dry steppe and desert that slopes toward the Caspian. Much of it lies below sea level. The Ural River drains the province on a long course to the sea. Winters are cold and dry, and summers are hot and still drier. The count for 1906 was about seven hundred thirty thousand people. Ural Cossacks, Russian peasants, and Kirghiz herders made up the mix.
britannica-1911-valencia-province:
Valencia, a sea side province of eastern Spain, is set out in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Teruel and Castellon bound it north, the sea east, Alicante south, and two inland provinces west. Its count in nineteen hundred was past eight hundred thousand. Its area is four thousand one hundred and fifty square miles.

Along the coast the land is low and flat. Rich farm plains lie here, in places just above sea level. West of them table lands rise to a mean height of a thousand feet. Those climb in turn to hills that rim the high plain of New Castile. The top height nears four thousand feet. Sand dunes fringe the coast and cut off a famed lagoon from the sea.
britannica-1911-vendace:
Vendace is the name of a freshwater fish of the genus Coregonus, covered in this 1911 Britannica article. Two other species of that genus live in the fresh waters of the British Islands, the gwyniad and the pollan. The vendace itself is confined to some lochs in Dumfriesshire, Scotland, though it is very like a species found in the large deep lakes of northern Europe.

Its name came, the article says, from the French word for the dace, passed on in the days when French was the tongue of the Scottish court. Local fame is so great that a tale credits Mary Queen of Scots with bringing the fish to the Lochmaben lochs. It is counted a great delicacy, and on good days, when the shoals rise near the edges of the loch, great numbers may be taken. It spawns in November and scarcely exceeds eight inches in length.
britannica-1911-veterinary-science:
Veterinary science, the science of care for farm beasts, is laid out in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its Latin root ties it to beasts of burden and draught. In broad terms it deals with the build and frame of tame animals, the horse above all. It takes in how their bodies work and what marks each breed.

Breeding, feeding, and clean care of stock fall inside its scope. So do the sickness and hurts to which animals are prone, and how to ward them off or cure them. Work by drug and by knife both count in that care. The science also weighs how stock can be raised and made better over time. Its links to human health count too, since some ills pass between beasts and men. Food and goods drawn from animals close the wide field.
britannica-1911-voice:
Voice is the sound made by the quiver of the vocal cords, two bands of springy fibrous stuff in the throat. The 1911 Britannica entry draws the word from French and Latin roots. It parts voice from speech with care: speech is the making of jointed sounds meant to carry thought.

Many beasts below man have voice, the entry says, but none has speech as man has it. Speech can stand with no voice, as in a whisper. Voice can stand with no speech, as when a singer runs a scale of pure tones. The piece then points to heads on song and on the sounds of speech, and shows plates of the throat parts, each part named and placed.
bruce:
Albert Payson Terhune dedicated Bruce to his ten Sunnybank collies, the best friends of his famous dedication, and the novel follows a collie family at his New Jersey kennels. It opens with Rothsay Lass, a beautiful collie bitch marked down as a second because her ears prick up instead of tipping as show fashion demands. Her son Bruce inherits her brains and courage rather than her fault.

Chapters carry Bruce through puppy trouble to service as a war dog, with episodes titled When Eyes Were No Use and The Werewolf. Terhune tells dog stories as biography, crediting his collies with loyalty, humor, and moral sense. Readers of Lad will find the same Sunnybank world here, deepened by a harder, stranger tale.
burke-reflections-revolution-france:
Edmund Burke published his Reflections on the Revolution in France in November 1790, while the revolution was still young. The book is framed as a letter to a young French friend who had asked his views. Burke, a Whig statesman, shocked old allies by attacking a cause many of them cheered.

Burke warns that tearing up a whole society by abstract rights ends in chaos and tyranny. He defends slow reform, inherited custom, and respect for church and crown. His praise of Marie Antoinette and his dread of paper money made the book famous at once. Paine's Rights of Man answered it, and the two books still argue across the centuries.
california-1849-1913-or-the-rambling-ske:
L. H. Woolley's California, 1849-1913 records sixty-four years of one pioneer's residence. Woolley, a member of the Society of California Pioneers and of the Vigilance Committee of 1856, wrote for his descendants. He left the Green Mountains of Vermont for the El Dorado in 1849. His train left Independence, Missouri, on the fourteenth of May.

Forty wagons, one hundred and fifty mules, and as many passengers made the Pioneer Line's first train. Woolley tells of wild mules, burnt bacon, and a cook dancing furious around the fire. Plains hardships give way to mining camps, vigilance days, and settled life. The sketches ramble as his title promises, anecdote after anecdote. Such plain memoirs are the ore from which California history is refined, and Woolley knew their worth.
cambridge-neighbors-from-literary-friend:
William Dean Howells wrote Cambridge Neighbors as part of Literary Friends and Acquaintance, his memoir of American literary life. Howells arrived in Cambridge, Massachusetts, at twenty-nine to work on the Atlantic Monthly. Poets and scholars filled his days. He recalls feeling practically immortal among them, with endless hours to read and dream of writing.

Francis J Child, the Harvard ballad scholar, opens his gallery of portraits. Howells describes Child's refined face, gold-rimmed spectacles, and unfailing sweetness. Other neighbors from Harvard and Boston literary circles follow. Howells writes freely because most of his subjects had died by publication. Readers get warm, precise recollections of the generation that made Cambridge a center of American letters, recorded by a younger writer who loved them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abstinence:
Abstinence means abstaining from food, and the entry traces the history of church legislation on it and the motives behind that legislation. Its first instance under law is Genesis 2:16-17, where a mandate taught the moral head of humanity dependence on the Creator. Fasting laws chiefly fix the quantity of food allowed on fast days, while abstinence laws fix its quality. Fridays of Lent are days of both fasting and abstinence, while ordinary Fridays bind to abstinence alone.

From that starting point the long entry works through abstinence in the Old Testament and the early church, then through councils, theologians, and later discipline. It examines why the church shaped the rule as it did and how custom and desuetude bear on obligation. Sources run from the Fathers and Duchesne to Hefele, St. Thomas, and Thomassin on fasting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acceptance:
In canon law, acceptance means taking a thing with approval. A benefice's collation stays incomplete until the person accepts it. Acceptance links benefice and benefited. It grounds a right in the thing itself. Acceptance is likewise needed to make an election valid.

Acceptance is also of the essence of a gift, a free gift of property. For goods, giving with words of gift suffices, and for land a deed is mostly needed. Acceptance of a law, however, is not needed to impose submission to it. Even where people vote, they may not refuse laws once made and published. Otherwise the power to make laws would be a mockery. Custom and disuse can end duty only for merely church law, never against natural or divine law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-accomplice:
An accomplice is a partner in some form of evildoing, one who cooperates in the wrongful act of another counted as the principal. Moral theology does not judge every such association unlawful at once. It first distinguishes formal from material cooperation. Formal cooperation shares the perverse frame of mind of the principal, as in persuading another to skip Sunday Mass without reason. Material cooperation shares only the physical act, as in selling a revolver in an ordinary deal to a man who then kills himself.

Cooperation is also proximate or remote, by closeness to the principal's act. Formal cooperation can never be lawful, since it presupposes a sinful attitude of will. The entry also treats restitution among partners. It covers the constitution of Benedict XIV, which bars a priest who shared a sin against the Sixth Commandment from validly absolving that person, except in danger of death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-actual-grace:
Actual grace is treated here as distinct from sanctifying grace, a distinction seldom drawn before Trent but made necessary by modern disputes. Grace in general is God's supernatural gift to men and angels for eternal salvation, whether by salutary acts or a holy state. Actual grace is the transient help to act, while sanctifying grace is the permanent state of grace. This article treats only actual grace.

The name actual comes from Latin actualis, toward an act, since the grace is granted for performing salutary acts and is present and gone with the action itself. Its opposite is not possible grace but habitual grace, which makes for holiness, so the two relate as action to state, not as act to potency. The entry examines its nature and properties, then grace and liberty, and closes on the heathen who cooperates with vocation's grace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altarpiece:
An altarpiece is a sacred picture on the wall or framed behind the altar, or statuary grouped on the altar. In the Middle Ages some churches used embossed silver or gold, enamelled and jewel-set work, instead of picture or group. Sometimes the piece stood upon the altar itself, rather than behind it, for all to see.

Where the altar stood free in the choir, visible from behind just as from before, both sides bore painted work. The decorated screen, retable, or reredos also carries the name of altarpiece today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amice:
The amice is a short linen cloth, square or oblong, blessed before use like other sacerdotal vestments, and first put on by the priest vesting for Mass. It covers the shoulders and originally the head. Many older orders still lay it first over the head, ends falling on the shoulders, then vest from alb onward. Only flax or hemp linen is permitted, as for the alb, and a little cross must be sewn to it.

Tracing its history meets the same difficulty as the alb's: early writers' expressions vary, and the word amictus shifts meaning. The amice thus opens the vesting, a plain linen square with a long, tangled name history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-chu:
The Apostolic Church Ordinance is a third-century collection, falsely claiming apostolic authorship, of moral and hierarchical rules drawn mainly from ancient Christian sources. Initially published in Ethiopic by Ludolf in 1691 with a Latin translation, it served as a law code among the Egyptian, Ethiopian, and Arabian churches. It rivalled the Didache, the Teaching of the Twelve Apostles, under whose name it sometimes passed. Though of undoubted Greek origin, it survives chiefly in Coptic, Arabic, Ethiopic, and Syriac versions.

Bickell of Marburg first published it in Greek in 1843 from a twelfth-century Vienna manuscript and gave it its usual German name, Apostolische Kirchenordnung. After a short introduction inspired by the Letter of Barnabas, it falls into two parts, the first adapting the Didache's first six chapters. The entry introduces a code that governed eastern churches while wearing apostolic dress it never owned.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assessor-of-t:
The Assessor of the Holy Office is a functionary of the Congregation of the Inquisition, also called the Congregation of the Universal Inquisition. Its present functions are to watch over matters of faith and examine suspected tenets of persons or books. The office-holder ranks next after the congregation's cardinals, and is a secular churchman or an honorary chamberlain of the pope.

His duty is to make the report of the Holy Office in a particular case. When consultors alone meet, he presides and then lays their ballots before the cardinal inquisitors. When the congregation decides, he reports the result to the pope that same evening, if the pope has not presided. He must attend all four meetings of the congregation, and on Saturdays he examines matters laid before the Holy Office with four fellow officials.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-association-o: The Association of Priestly Perseverance is a priests' association founded in 1868 at Vienna and first confined to that archdiocese. In 1879, mainly through its journal La Correspondance, it extended into other dioceses and countries. In 1903 it counted 14,919 living members in 150 dioceses across Austria, Germany, Switzerland, and other countries. Its structure closely matches the Apostolic Union of Secular Priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-avarice:
Avarice, from the Latin avarus, greedy, is the inordinate love for riches. Its special malice lies in making the getting and keeping of money and possessions a purpose in itself to live for. Such things, the entry insists, are worth only as tools for a rational and harmonious life, with due regard for one's social condition. Avarice forgets that limit and treats wealth as an end.

It ranks as a capital vice because many other sins are committed to gain or hold its object. It is more to be dreaded because it often cloaks itself as a virtue. It slips in under the pretext of decent provision for the future. Where it drives injustice in gaining or keeping wealth, it is often a grievous sin. In itself, as mere excess desire or pleasure in riches, it is commonly not a mortal sin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-avempace:
Avempace, also called Ibn Bajja or Ibn Badsha, was an Arabian philosopher, physician, astronomer, mathematician, and poet. He was born at Saragossa toward the end of the eleventh century and died at Fez in 1138. In 1118 he stood at Seville, writing treatises on logic, and later he moved to Granada and to Africa. Arabian accounts say rival physicians poisoned him.

He wrote on mathematics, medicine, and philosophy, and he commented on Aristotle's Physics, Meteorology, Generation and Corruption, and parts of his animal works. His philosophical books include logical treatises, a work On the Soul, The Hermit's Guide, a work on the intellect's union with man, and a Valedictory Letter. Most of his writings are lost or still undiscovered, though his logical treatises survive at the Escorial. Moses of Narbonne's account of The Hermit's Guide lets us trace its aim: the mind's union with the Active Intellect.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benefice:
Benefice, a central term of church law, receives a long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. In strict use it means a permanent right granted by the Church to a cleric. That right lets him draw income from church property in return for a spiritual service, such as the care of souls. Popular speech often confuses it with the property itself or with the office alone.

Four marks define it: a right to revenue without ownership of its source, a twofold permanence in both income and holder, and a spiritual duty attached. The entry then works through kinds of benefices, how they are gained and lost, and who may hold them. It is a lawyer's map of how clergy were once paid.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berenice:
Berenice, a titular see in Egypt, is the subject of this brief 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. It stood at the end of the Greater Syrtis, where Benghazi stands today, first named Euhesperides until Ptolemy III renamed it for his wife Berenice. A Jewish colony there helped make it an early Christian centre.

Its bishops appear in ancient records, including Ammonas, to whom Dionysius of Alexandria wrote in the third century. Another bishop, Daces, attended the Council of Nicaea in 325. The entry is a short note tying a classical town, a royal name, and a line of early bishops together.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernold-of-co:
Bernold of Constance, a historian and theologian, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Swabia about 1054, he died at Schaffhausen in 1100 after study at Constance under Bernard of Constance. He was present at Rome's Lenten Synod in 1079, where Berengarius retracted his errors on the Eucharist.

Back in Germany he defended Bishop Gebhard's enforcement of Gregory VII's reform decrees and served as counsellor to King Herman at the battle of Bleichfeld in 1086. His chronicle and theological writings make him a key witness to the Gregorian reform. The entry presents a partisan scholar writing history as it happened.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bigamy-in-civ:
Bigamy in civil jurisprudence, marrying while a former marriage still stands, receives a long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Definitions from Bishop, Murray, and Coke agree that it is a species of polygamy, the having of two or more spouses at once. The entry surveys its punishment across legal systems.

Polygamy, though legal among some peoples, proves rarer than custom suggests: early Babylon, Assyria, and Egypt leaned to monogamy, and China forbade a second wife. The entry follows English and American law on the crime, its defences, and its proof. It is a comparative study of marriage law's oldest offence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-candace:
Candace was the Ethiopian queen whose eunuch Saint Philip baptized. The name appears in a ruined pyramid near ancient Meroe. Another queen of the same name, named by Strabo and Dion Cassius, revolted against Rome. She was beaten by Petronius at Napata in 22 B.C.

Pliny reports that Nero's explorers, crossing Nubia, found a Queen Candace on the throne of the island of Meroe. Pliny adds that the name had long passed to all queens of that country. The Ethiopia of Candace is not modern Abyssinia, but the region of Meroe at the meeting of the Nile and the Taccasi. Pliny's queen may be the queen of the Acts, but no direct proof settles it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chalice:
The chalice ranks first among sacred vessels. By a figure of speech, the cup itself often stands for the Precious Blood. St. Paul calls it the communion of the blood of Christ. No reliable tradition survives about Christ's Last Supper vessel. In the sixth and seventh centuries pilgrims at Jerusalem were shown a chalice said to be the actual one. It was kept in the Holy Sepulchre with the sponge offered to the Saviour on Calvary.

Later claimants fared no better under scrutiny. Antoninus of Piacenza called the Jerusalem vessel onyx. Adamnan, less than a century later, called it a silver cup with two handles holding a Gallic sextarius. Two more vessels were later venerated as the Last Supper chalice: the sacro catino of Genoa, a green glass dish long taken for emerald, and an agate cup at Valencia. The article judges the tradition untrustworthy and late.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-church-mainte:
An entry on church maintenance, the support of church buildings, institutions, and clergy, always both a necessity and a problem. Since the Church is visible, with priesthood, worship, and temples, it must hold property, movable and immovable, and that requires generosity from the faithful. To strip the Church of all property, the entry argues, is both error and absurdity.

Under the Old Law the priesthood held towns through Israel and received firstfruits, tithes, and shares of sacrifices, while kings and people maintained the Temple and its treasury. In the New Testament, Christ and the apostles kept a common purse. The first Christians sold lands and laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet, and Christ told His preachers to accept support from those they served. The entry follows that principle through later offerings, endowments, and laws.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-civil-allegia:
Civil allegiance means the loyalty and obedience owed by a person to his State as citizen. The word comes from liege, a free man's service to his lord. Catholic teaching grounds that duty in nature and religion. As children owe dutiful conduct to parents, so citizens owe obligations to country and rulers: patriotism and obedience.

Patriotism asks esteem and love for one's country, interest in its history, and readiness to sacrifice life for the commonwealth. Obedience asks respect for rulers as God's ministers for the common good and observance of just laws. The article meets the charge that Catholics cannot be good citizens while obeying a pope who may be foreign. It answers that the Church is a separate spiritual society. The State has no competence in religion, and when it oversteps its bounds, obedience ends: God, rather than men, ought to be obeyed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-d-espe:
Claude d'Espence, a French theologian, was born in 1511 at Chalons-sur-Marne and died at Paris on 5 October 1571. He entered the College de Navarre in 1536 and became rector of the University of Paris in 1540, before his doctorate in 1542. Cardinal de Lorraine's court called him, and he saw propositions from his 1543 Lenten sermons referred to the Sorbonne. He joined the Melun consultation of 1544 on Trent and was sent to the council at Bologna in 1547.

At Poissy in 1561 he argued against Beza for tradition, the infallibility of the Church, and the Sacrament of Order. An anonymous work on image veneration, censured by the Sorbonne and believed his, forced him to subscribe the faculty's sixteenth article against Protestants. His collected works of 1619 include a treatise against the Predestinarians and an Institution of a Christian Prince. They also include a work on parents' consent in marriage and commentaries on Timothy and Titus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-concupiscence:
John Ming's entry defines concupiscence broadly as any yearning of the soul for good. Strictly it means desire of the lower appetite against reason. The senses seek gratification, while reason seeks the good of whole nature in subordination to God. Left alone, the lower appetite chases sensuous pleasures without regard for higher faculties. Desires against reason's good may thus rise before the mind attends, then stir the body to pursuit. This clash is natural in man, an imperfection rather than corruption.

Paul's voice sounds the law: when he wills good, evil stands present. Christ's death freed mankind from sin's bondage. Sixteenth-century Reformers, above all Luther, taught anew that concupiscence itself is sin, the corrupt state of nature, and that original justice was due to man by nature. The Catholic Church condemns these views as erroneous or heretical, a line later drawn by Pius VI against Pistoja in 1794.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conscience:
John Rickaby's entry opens with the name. English doubled a Latin word: conscience for morals, consciousness for the universal field. Cicero leaves the ethical limit to context, valuing his own conscience above all men's talk. Hamilton weighed consciousness of outer objects, and German keeps Bewusstsein apart from Gewissen.

Origin follows in race and individual. Some anthropologists accept the Biblical account, others do not. Ethics means regulated life, beginning crudely in animal life as stimulus response, reflex action, and adaptation. Customary rules gain ethical character through principles and ideals. Conscience is no distinct faculty, but intellect judging right and wrong, aided by good will. History moves from pre-Christian testimonies through patristic Scripture and pagan classics, each Father characteristic without system, into scholastic times. Merit begins once duty stands fulfilled, goodness beyond duty meritorious too, virtue prized for itself and God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-constance:
Michael Ott's entry on Constance, Latin Constantia, German Konstanz, Czech Kostnitz, presents a town formerly seat of a diocese. Very ancient, it sits where the Rhine leaves the Bodensee, in Baden's south-east. A lake-dwellers' village first, it gained Roman fortification in 304. Legionaries likely brought Christianity by the second century's end or the third's start. The see first stood at Vindonissa, now Windisch in Aargau, Switzerland, its erection date unknown.

Bubulcus, present at Epaon's Burgundian Synod in 517, stands as the first bishop history records. Diocesan limits were fixed in the seventh century, and decline began with the Reformation. The city won municipal rights in 780, became a free imperial city in 1192, and ranked among Germany's largest medieval cities. Chronicles from Merck and Neugart to Eiselein and Beyerle carry the record through war, property, and civic rights.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-continence:
John Melody's entry defines continence as abstinence from even licit marriage gratifications. It forms part of temperance, though Aristotle denied it virtue's high character, since it involves conflict with wrong desires, an element foreign to virtue in the strict sense. Continence bears a narrower sense than chastity, which finds place within marriage. The abstinence discussed belongs to celibacy's state, though celibacy's notion does not necessarily involve continence.

Practice treats continence as a state of life. Even among peoples where early marriage rules, continence frequently appears. Two general objections face the state of continence, answered in turn. The entry closes by weighing social service. Critics may doubt such lives make desirable citizens, yet the example's service, given every person's duty of absolute chastity for longer or shorter periods, holds highest value.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-controversies:
Joseph Pohle's entry treats controversies on grace. How can grace's potent influence on the will, eliciting good works, reside with free will's simultaneous consent? Merely sufficient grace, gratia mere sufficiens, implies withheld consent, hence inefficiency, gratia inefficax. The question reduces to free will versus efficacious grace, gratia efficax, by which free will does grace's desire. The radical solution cuts the knot, setting aside supernatural grace with the Pelagians.

Heretical solutions follow, including Luther's theory: original sin so impaired free will that, like a horse, it acts only as ridden by God or the devil. Faith's sources protest free will's subjugation. Catholic systems start from grace or free will. Thomism rests on Saint Thomas, with premotion as Divine knowledge's medium for foreseeing. Objections press freedom's survival, the efficacious-sufficient distinction, sin's demand for first-mover predetermination, and premotion's infallibility. Linking two kinds of efficacious grace deepens difficulties, ending in mystery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cornice:
Thomas Poole's entry defines the cornice as an entablature's uppermost division, the roof's representative within an order. It consists of projecting mouldings and blocks, usually divisible into bed-moulding, corona, and gutter. In classic architecture each order possesses its own peculiar cornice, distinct in profile and proportion from the others.

More widely, any moulded projection crowning or finishing the part it adorns counts as a cornice. Examples include a façade's coping, the moulding running round an apartment beneath the ceiling, and mouldings surmounting a door or window. The term thus spans both the strict classical member and every comparable crowning moulding in building.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-co:
The Council of Constance, a partly ecumenical council held from 5 November 1414 to 22 April 1418, faced three tasks. It had to end the Western Schism, reform church government and life, and repress heresy. Pisa's council of 1409 had only added a third pope to the two it tried to remove, leaving Christendom with three claimants.

Across forty-five general sessions the council secured resignations and depositions, then elected Martin V, restoring a single head. Reform decrees and action against Wycliffite and Hussite teaching accompanied the settlement. Attendance and procedure receive their own closing survey in the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-fl:
The Council of Florence, the Seventeenth Ecumenical Council, continued the Ferrara assembly after plague forced its move to Tuscany, and behind Ferrara stood Basle, convoked in 1431. Eugene IV proclaimed the transferred council the lawful continuation, and its ecumenical standing rests on that claim. Greek and Latin differences, above all the Filioque, dominated debate.

On 6 July the union decree Laetentur Coeli was proclaimed in Florence cathedral, and the Greeks departed at once. Latin members stayed on to pursue reunion with Armenians, Syrian Jacobites, Mesopotamians, Chaldeans, and Maronites of Cyprus, ending at the Lateran in Rome. Papal supremacy emerged strengthened, winning back men like Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini, later Pius II.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-a:
The Councils of Aix-en-Provence span seven meetings, in 1112, 1374, 1409, 1585, 1612, 1838, and 1850, a long provincial thread rather than a single event. Each gathering answered its own century, from medieval discipline to nineteenth-century doctrinal defence, and the entry picks out the meetings with lasting marks.

In 1612 the fathers censured Edmund Richer's Gallican work on ecclesiastical and political power. In 1838 they asked Gregory XVI to add Immaculate to Conception in the Mass preface for the Blessed Virgin's feast, and he did. In 1850 they condemned rationalism, pantheism, communism, and arbitrary interpretation of Scripture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-credence:
A liturgical entry describes the credence, or credence table, a small table placed in the sanctuary near the Epistle side of the altar. It holds the cruets, acolytes' candles, and other utensils needed for the celebration of Mass. In solemn Masses the chalice, paten, corporal, and veil rest on it until the Offertory.

Size and covering follow the occasion: about forty inches long for ordinary use, larger when a bishop celebrates, and draped to the ground on very solemn feasts. For low Masses the rubrics allow a wall niche or bracket instead, though custom now favours a credence table. The entry cites the Ceremoniale Episcoporum and standard manuals of Mass celebration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daughters-of-:
A congregational entry traces the Daughters of Providence, founded at Paris by Madame Polaillon, born Marie de Lumague, a pious widow. In 1643, with letters patent from Louis XIII, she opened a home to protect and instruct young girls. Beauty, poverty, or parental neglect exposed them to loss of faith and other perils. She named the home the Seminary of Providence.

Seven women of religious vocation among the inmates formed a community under rules drawn by Saint Vincent de Paul at Archbishop Gondy's direction in 1647. Louis XIV's mother gave them the Hospital de la Sante in 1651, confirmed by royal letters in 1667. After two years' probation, members took simple vows of chastity, obedience, service, and perpetual stability, and houses spread to Metz, Sedan, and across Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-divine-office:
The divine office, also called the Liturgy of the Hours, is the set of prayers said at fixed hours of day and night. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains the name as a duty done for God, laid by church law on priests, religious, and clerics. It covers only the prayers of the Breviary, not the Mass or other liturgical rites. Other names for it include canonical hours, diurnal and nocturnal office, and simply cursus.

The entry traces the obligation of clerics to recite the office and the growth of the Roman Breviary. It cites the great histories of the Breviary and studies of the personal duty of recitation. For readers new to the hours, it offers a clear door into the daily round of prayer that orders clerical life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-divine-provid:
Providence in general is foresight, the practical reason that fits means to an end. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry applies the word to God, in whom providence is the act by which his wisdom orders all events of the universe toward the end of creation. That end is that all creatures should show forth the glory of God, and that man in particular should glorify him, serve him in love, and reach eternal happiness in him.

The universe forms a system of real beings that God both made and guides, and his concurrence is needed for each natural working. The entry defends this ordering against chance and fate, drawing on the moral order of the world. It closes with a long shelf of writers on divine government, from Lacordaire to modern English theologians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-divorce-in-ci:
Divorce in civil jurisprudence is defined as the ending or partial suspension by law of the marriage bond. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry distinguishes the absolute form, divorce from the bond itself, which ends the marriage wholly where the law allows it. Beside it stands a limited form, divorce from bed and board, which suspends common life for a time or without limit. Courts also grant decrees that declare a marriage void from the start.

Such marriages, never valid, leave the parties free as though no bond had existed. The entry surveys these forms across the states and the wider literature of marriage law. It points readers to the proceedings of the National Divorce Congress of 1906 and to a world bibliography of marriage and divorce, a guide for lawyers and moralists alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-donation-in-c:
Donation in civil jurisprudence is the free transfer, or gift, of ownership of property. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that the Latin munus meant a gift for a special occasion, such as a birth or marriage. The giver is called the donor and the receiver the donee. In law, donation rests on the basic right of each person to dispose of his property as he wills, a right long held fit for legal regulation and restraint.

Donation needs the consent of both sides, the donor to give and the donee to take. The entry draws on Story, Parsons, and the court reports to set out the rules. It serves as a compact guide to a simple act, giving, that the law has fenced about with care since Babylonian times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
An ecclesiastical province is an administrative district under an archbishop. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that provinces first took fixed shape in the Eastern Roman Empire. The great centers, Antioch for Syria, Ephesus for Asia, Alexandria for Egypt, and Rome for Italy, sent out missionaries and became mother churches of new Christian communities.

From the later second century, bishops within the same natural bounds met for common counsel in synods on weighty occasions. By the end of that century the bishop of the state capital commonly summoned these synods and presided over them. The entry cites Sieke, Werminhoff, and Phillips on the growth of the metropolitan system from those gatherings.

Ecclesiastical residence means abiding where one's duties lie, as a bishop in his diocese, a rector in his benefice, or a canon in his cathedral church. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry sets it against non-residence or absence. Residence exists to guarantee service and the fulfillment of duty, and mere bodily presence does not satisfy the law. Vigilance and solicitude must go with it, and only a laborious residence counts.

Residence differs from domicile, since domicile turns on the intent to remain. By a fiction of law, one lawfully absent fulfills the residence rule, while one unlawfully absent counts as present. The entry cites Trent, Urban the Eighth, and Benedict the Fourteenth on a duty that keeps shepherds with their flocks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-ignati:
Edmund Ignatius Rice founded the Irish Christian Brothers, living from 1762 to 1844. Born at Callan, he grew rich as a Waterford merchant, known for honesty, charity, and piety. About to enter a convent abroad, he was stopped by the sight of ragged boys in the street. A friend challenged him: why bury himself in a cell when poor youths needed him at home?

He opened his first school at Waterford in 1802, and Bishop Hussey laid the stone of Mount Sion schoolhouse that June. His first paid helpers fled, but young men from Callan took their place, and more schools followed. The entry tells how a businessman turned his wealth and life to free schooling for poor boys, and how a small start grew into an order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-egyptian-chur:
The Egyptian Church Ordinance is an early Christian set of thirty-one canons ruling ordinations, worship, and the main lines of church life. It takes its name from Egypt because the West first met it in languages tied to Egypt. In 1677 the Dominican Wansleben gave a short account of the canons as found in the Ethiopic Synodos, and in 1691 Ludolf printed a fragment with a Latin version.

Later finds filled out the text. Tattam printed all the canons in Bohairic, the lower Egyptian tongue, with English in 1848. Lagarde printed them in Sahidic, the upper Egyptian tongue, from a manuscript of 1006. In 1900 Hauler found a very old Latin version from the fifth or sixth century, prized because it keeps the liturgical prayers missing elsewhere. The lost original was doubtless Greek, and the work belongs to a chain of church-order books linked to Hippolytus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-essence-and-e:
Essence and existence are transcendentals, so no strict definition of either is possible. Essence is properly described as what makes a thing what it is. Existence is what makes the essence actual in the order of being. The essence is the ground from which a thing's properties emanate. Essence is the abstract counterpart of the concrete entity, pointing to the reason why a thing is precisely what it is.

Answering the question What, essence is equivalent to quiddity: the essence is what a thing's definition expresses. As essence is what makes a thing what it is, nature is what makes it act as it does. Hence Saint Thomas says nature is the essence as it relates to its proper operation. Essence is also in a manner synonymous with form, since beings are sorted into species chiefly by their formal principle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-examination-o:
Examination of Conscience means looking back over one's past thoughts, words, and deeds to judge them against the moral law. It concerns the will above all, the good or bad aim behind each thought, word, and deed. The Stoics practiced such self-scrutiny, and Scripture enforces it, from God's word to Abraham to Jeremiah's call to search our ways. Saint Paul then commanded it before Holy Communion, saying a man must prove himself before eating the bread and drinking the chalice.

Early Christians, who received Communion often, made it a familiar exercise, and saints such as Anthony, Basil, Augustine, and Bernard made it a daily rule for their followers. The entry separates the devotional examen from the examen before confession. In the latter, the penitent reviews the Ten Commandments, the Church's precepts, the seven capital sins, and the duties of his state of life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-final-perseve:
Final perseverance means keeping the state of grace from the last conversion until death. The phrase comes from Matthew, chapter ten, where endurance to the end brings salvation. It differs from mere continuance in grace, since lost grace can be won back again. Theologians view it both as a power to persevere and as the fact of persevering.

Catholic teaching, shaped by Augustine and the Council of Trent, joins divine grace with human will. Neither grace alone nor will alone suffices; the two must work together, Trent held. The gift lies beyond certain knowledge and beyond strict merit, yet prayer can seek it. A good death crowning a life of well-doing is the normal form the gift takes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-florence:
Florence stands on the Arno in Tuscany, at the foot of the Fiesole hills. Destroyed by Sulla in 82 B.C., it was rebuilt by Caesar in 59 B.C. as a military post. Its wealth began in the eleventh century, when it backed the papacy against the emperors. By 1155 it could shut its gates against Frederick Barbarossa.

The commune grew under consuls, then a podesta, with guild priors holding legislative power. Guelphs and Ghibellines, born of a broken engagement and a murder in 1215, split the city for centuries. In 1250 the people deposed the podesta and set up a Captain of the People with elders. Trade, guilds, and civic pride made Florence a great republican power in Italy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-france:
France is treated here in a vast survey article, one of the longest in the encyclopedia. It covers a country of 207,107 square miles with coasts on both the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. It opens with descriptive geography, tracing the hexagon of France from Dunkirk to the Pyrenees and the Alps, its cliffs, dunes, river mouths, and mountain frontiers. It notes that France alone in Europe touches both seas.

From geography the survey moves through the nation's history, its church, religious orders, charitable and social organisations, and contemporary Catholic life. It closes with long lists of sources on French charity and religious movements. Readers looking for a single reference point on France's land, people, and Catholic institutions will find the article's scale matches its subject. Individual sections now read as history in their own right.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gebhard-iii-o:
Gebhard III of Constance, a bishop of the Investiture struggle, defended papal rights against emperors for twenty-six years. Born about 1040 to Duke Bertold I of Zähringen, he served as provost at Xanten. He became a Hirschau monk and was consecrated bishop in December 1084 by the legate who became Urban II. An imperial anti-bishop, Otto, held the see by force.

An imperial synod at Mainz deposed Gebhard in 1085, but Otto's death in 1086 let him take his see. He reformed Petershausen, consecrated a new cathedral in 1089, and served with Passau's bishop as papal vicar for Germany. Driven out again in 1103, he returned with Henry V in 1105, freed the king from the ban, and, after a papal rebuke for siding with the emperor, withdrew to diocesan care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerace:
Gerace, a diocese in Calabria's Reggio province, stands on a height above the Ionian Sea near Cape Spartivento. Its importance rose from the ruin of Locri Epizephyrii, an early Greek colony founded by Ozolian Locrians about 684 to 680 before Christ and law-given by Zaleucus. Locri flourished by trade and culture, suffered under Dionysius the Younger and Pyrrhus, and passed to Rome in the Second Punic War, keeping Zaleucus's constitution as it decayed.

Before Locri's total ruin its bishop's see moved to Gerace in 709 under Bishop Gregory. Gerace likely takes its name from Saint Cyriaca, whose church Saracens wrecked in 915; they seized the town in 986 and Normans took it in 1059. The Greek Rite held until 1467, despite a Latin-Greek schism about 1250 to 1253. Barlaam II, bishop in 1342, taught Greek to Petrarch and Boccaccio. The see, suffragan of Reggio, counts sixty-nine parishes and 132,300 souls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ghost-dance:
The Ghost Dance was the rite of a Native American religion that arose about 1887 around Wovoka, also called Jack Wilson, a Paiute man in Nevada. In a vision he claimed to have spoken with God. God promised a new earth where dead Indians, buffalo, and game would return and white settlers would be pushed back across the ocean. A Catholic Encyclopedia article recounts the teaching and the dance meant to hasten it.

Believers held hands in a circle, sang ghost songs without instruments, and danced while priests brought dancers into trances. The faith spread to nearly all tribes east of the Missouri and stirred years of excitement, until set dates passed without result. In Dakota it fed the Sioux outbreak of the winter of 1890-91, marked by the killing of Sitting Bull and the massacre at Wounded Knee. Its doctrine of human brotherhood barred all warlike acts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-croc:
Giovanni Croce was a composer born at Chioggia near Venice in 1557, who died on 15 May 1609. Under Zarlino's tutelage at Venice he became one of the noted composers of the Venetian school. After entering the priesthood he served at Santa Maria Formosa. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows him to the top post at St. Mark's.

In 1593 he took charge of the choir boys at St. Mark's as vice-director. On the death of Baltazzaro Donati in 1603, he succeeded him as choirmaster. He wrote much secular music, madrigals and canzonettas, but his chief works served the Church. Their marks are clarity of form and a devotional spirit, and three of his motets appear in Lueck's collection.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grace:
Grace is a teaching article in four parts: actual grace, sanctifying grace, the controversies on grace, and supernatural adoption. Actual grace is a help from God for good acts, granted through Christ's merits. A Catholic Encyclopedia article moves from first meanings to the schools that divided Catholics.

Sanctifying grace is treated with justification and its preparation. The controversies section covers the Reformers' and Jansenists' heresies and the Catholic solutions of Thomism, Augustinianism, Molinism, Congruism, and Syncretism. The closing part presents adoption as God's children, the gracious raising of man to share the inner life of the Most Blessed Trinity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-greece:
Greece is treated under seven heads. They cover the land and people, the Church before the schism, the Orthodox Church, the Church's constitution, the Catholic Church, Protestants and other sects, and the Church in enslaved Greece. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows Hellenism as a force unbroken for nearly thirty centuries.

The Greeks first appear as small states bound by language, religion, and civilization in the southern Balkans, the islands, and the Asia Minor coast. For three centuries they reached a perfection in civilization that gives them the first place in European history. Hellenism then spread over Asia, Egypt, and Italy. Greece swallowed the eastern Roman Empire from Constantinople for nearly ten centuries. At last, chiefly by the magic of her name, she shook off the tyrant to become free Greece again.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guardianship-:
Guardianship, the lawful care of someone too young, inexperienced, or weak in mind or will to act for themselves, is traced here from Rome through England to modern law. Roman tutela gave a tutor authority over a free minor, boys to fourteen and girls to twelve, with a curator to age twenty-five. The office could arise by will, by law among relatives, or by a magistrate's appointment.

English law added guardianship by nature for parents, feudal wardship that tied a landholding orphan to the lord of the fee, and socage guardianship kept deliberately from the next heir. A statute of 1660 let fathers name testamentary guardians. The lord chancellor stood as paramount guardian of all infants, with the Court of Chancery carrying out what the sovereign, as father of the country, owed minors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gulf-of-st-la:
Quebec's Vicariate of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, erected on 12 September 1905 from a prefecture of 1882, covers the province's north-east beyond the Diocese of Chicoutimi as a suffragan of Quebec. Eudist Fathers staff all its missions except the Montagnais, Naskapi, and Eskimo stations, which belong to the Oblates of Mary Immaculate.

Its first vicar apostolic, Gustave Blanch, born at Josselin in France in 1849 and ordained in 1878, took up residence at Seven Islands after his consecration at Chicoutimi in October 1905. The vicariate then counted 9,650 Catholics, including 2,000 Indians, served by 20 priests across 12 missions with residences, 28 stations, and schools teaching 950 pupils.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-harbor-grace:
Newfoundland's Diocese of Harbor Grace, erected in 1856, gathers the northern bays from Conception to White Bay with the Labrador coast under Newfoundland's rule. Its coastline of five hundred miles is served by twenty-three priests for 29,000 Catholics. Forty-nine churches, eighty-five stations, five convents, and a hundred schools with 4,500 pupils fill that scattered charge.

John Dalton, its first bishop, built the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception in a peaceful thirteen years, while his Italian successor Carfagnini doubled the clergy but battled faction near schism. Ronald MacDonald restored peace across twenty-five years and rebuilt the fire-ruined cathedral. John March, consecrated in 1906, opened a fund for church students as his first act.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hector-boece:
Scottish chronicler Hector Boece, born at Dundee about 1465, helped found the University of Aberdeen and wrote the history that reached Shakespeare through Holinshed. A student and then professor at Paris's College of Montaigu. There he befriended Erasmus and joined Bishop Elphinstone from about 1495 in winning a bull for an Aberdeen university. King's College opened its teaching in 1505.

Boece served as principal, lecturing in divinity and medicine, and published Lives of the Bishops of Murthlack and Aberdeen in 1522 and his seventeen-book History of Scotland in 1527. Admired for grace, love of country, and love of freedom, he was attacked even by contemporaries for credulity about origins. Yet Bellenden's Scots translation of 1536 carried his tales into Holinshed and so into Shakespeare's plays.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hendrik-consc:
Antwerp novelist Hendrik Conscience, born in 1812 to a French father and Flemish mother, became the father of Flemish prose literature. A cripple until seven, raised on his mother's fairy tales, self-taught by reading, he quit tutoring for six years as a private soldier, learning peasant life in northern Belgium at first hand.

Advised to write in Flemish, then scorned as too rude for letters, he failed with two romantic books. He then triumphed in 1838 with The Lion of Flanders, and never stopped, leaving more than a hundred volumes. Drawn from fatherland, family, and loyalty to the Church, his historical novels, village tales, and studies of manners won translation across Europe. Antwerp raised his monument weeks before his death in 1883.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-de-sain:
Carmelite theologian Henri de Saint-Ignace, born at Ath in 1630, was a learned moral theologian whose Jansenist leanings coloured a long controversial career. Professor of moral theology, he professed Augustine and Aquinas while favouring Baius and Jansenius. A long Roman stay under Clement XI saved his orthodoxy without cooling his lifelong antipathy to the Jesuits.

His chief work, Ethica amoris of 1709 in three volumes on human acts, laws and virtues, and sacraments, drew on a fellow Carmelite's Tempestas. It adopted novel views on the Eucharist that Rome forbade in 1714 and 1722 and Paris condemned, its venom earning it the nickname Ethica odii. A 1713 defence of efficacious grace provoked a Jesuit reply. His Molinismus profligatus of 1717 closed a life spent in doctrinal war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-william:
Henry William Wilberforce, born at Clapham in 1807, was the famous William Wilberforce's third son and Robert's younger brother. Entering Oriel College, Oxford, in 1826 as a pupil of Newman, he took a brilliant degree, studied law at Lincoln's Inn, and was persuaded by Newman to leave law for the Church. He took Anglican orders in 1834 and served as curate of Bransgrove, vicar of Walmer, and vicar of East Farleigh.

On 15 September 1850 Wilberforce and his wife entered the Catholic Church. He then turned to journalism, owning and editing the Catholic Standard, afterwards the Weekly Register, from 1854 until 1863. His books include The Parochial System of 1838 and Reasons for Submitting to the Catholic Church of 1851, which ran through several editions and stirred much controversy. Proselytism in Ireland, an essay on events before the English Reformation, and The Church and the Empires, published after his death in 1873, complete the list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-alliance:
The Holy Alliance was a treaty signed on 26 September 1815 by Emperor Francis I of Austria, King Frederick William III of Prussia, and Tsar Alexander I of Russia. Though a political act, its wording is purely religious in character. After Napoleon's fall, the three monarchs resolved in gratitude to God to take Christian principles, justice, love, and peace, as the only rule of their rule, at home and abroad.

They declared Christian morality the best guide in public life, not only in private life. They pledged brotherly feeling, mutual support, and abstention from war with each other, and promised to guide subjects and armies in a fatherly manner. Christ, they said, remained the rightful Lord of nations. The entry traces the treaty's terms and its place in post-Napoleonic Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hospice:
A hospice, from the Latin hospitium or guest house, was in early Christian centuries a shelter for the sick, the poor, orphans, the old, travellers, and needy people of all sorts. It dates back to Constantine's reign. Originally all hospices stood under bishops, who named priests to run their spiritual and temporal affairs.

About 436, a statute from Carthage's so-called Fourth Council ordered bishops to keep a small hospice near their churches. In time the general hospice gave way to special establishments for particular needs, and the term came to mean houses where travellers were harboured. Such hospices rose in wild regions and on mountain passes, run by hermits or monks, and multiplied as pilgrimages to the Holy Land, Rome, and Compostela grew.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-human-race:
This article asks whether mankind forms one race or several species. Some have treated human varieties as distinct species, while others defend human unity, judging the differences too small to split species. The apparently unlimited fertility of crossed races supports unity, and the gaps between darkest and lightest peoples are bridged by many intermediate stages.

Intellectual likeness between the most primitive peoples and the most cultured also supports unity, the entry argues. Various living types are only different races. Schwalbe proposed splitting an early Quaternary type, homo primigenius, with heavy brow ridges and chinless jaw, from homo sapiens, but Klaatsch's study of aboriginal Australian skulls challenged that split. The article surveys the evidence for unity against the case for division.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ignorance:
To be ignorant is to lack knowledge about something, in a being that can know. Fundamentally it comes from the limits of our intellect or the obscurity of the matter itself. This article treats its ethical aspect and consequences. Only free, voluntary acts count as imputable, so ignorance that kills or weakens that freedom has to be reckoned with.

Here the word narrows to mean missing information that one ought to possess. Mere want of knowledge, without any requirement to possess it, may be called nescience. For fixing human responsibility the chief division is invincible versus vincible ignorance: invincible when a person cannot rid himself of it despite moral diligence, vincible when he could have removed it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-immanence:
Immanence comes from the Latin in manere, to stay within. It names the quality of an act that starts and finishes inside the agent. Living action counts as immanent in body, mind, and morals alike, since it flows from the spontaneity at the heart of a living subject and works out that subject's own powers. Such action begins and ends inside one being, like a closed system.

Yet is that system sealed off, able to stand alone and take in nothing from outside? Or can it grow by absorbing things around it, sometimes things it needs, just as food feeds the body's inward activity? Philosophies of immanence raise this question and try to answer it, for individual people and for the whole universe. The teaching itself arose as soon as people began to philosophize.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-injustice:
Moral theology gives injustice a narrow sense here, apart from its broad use for any breach of the virtue of justice. In this narrower sense it means breaking another person's strict right against that person's reasonable will. A right, the entry explains, is the moral power to hold, do, or claim something that serves one's own good.

Goods tied to the person stand apart from goods outside the person. The first kind includes life, limb, liberty, and good name. The second kind includes property of any kind. Harm to the first kind counts as personal injury, harm to the second as real injury. The entry sorts those cases and the forms of wrongdoing that follow, giving readers a working map of how moralists graded offenses against what others are owed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-armand-l:
Jean-Armand Le Bouthillier de Rancé, born in Paris in 1626 and dead at La Trappe in 1700, became abbot of Notre-Dame de la Trappe and its reformer. A child prodigy, he published an edition of Anacreon with Greek notes at twelve. His brother's death left him canon of Notre-Dame, abbot of La Trappe, and holder of rich benefices.

Ordained in 1651, Rancé lived at first as a wealthy man of the world, fond of feasting and hunting. Conscience at last turned him: he gave up his wealth and ease, took up strict monastic life, and remade La Trappe under a hard rule of silence, labour, and penance. That reform, born from his own conversion, shaped the Trappist way of life that still bears the abbey's name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jeanne-mance:
Jeanne Mance, foundress of Montreal's Hôtel-Dieu, was born at Nogent-le-Roi in 1606 and died at Montreal in 1673. Daughter of the king's attorney, she lived with her father until his death in 1640, when she met Dauversière and first heard of New France and its mission women.

Sailing from La Rochelle in June 1641, Mance reached Quebec that August and nursed settlers all winter. In May 1642 she went upriver with Maisonneuve to Montreal, dressed the altar for its first Mass on 18 May, and founded a hospital in her own home that year. A larger hospital on Saint Paul Street followed in 1644, which she ran alone for seventeen years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-boyce:
John Boyce, writing as Paul Peppergrass, was an Irish priest, novelist, and lecturer who carried his countrymen's stories to America. Born in Donegal in 1810 to a wealthy hotelkeeper and magistrate, he studied at Navan and Maynooth. He was ordained in 1837 and labored eight years on the Irish mission before emigrating in 1845. From Eastport, Maine, he moved in 1847 to St. John's Church, Worcester, Massachusetts, where he stayed until his death in 1864.

His novels, Shanty Maguire, The Spaewife, and Mary Lee, or the Yankee in Ireland, show a keen observer's humor and pathos rather than his full scholarship. One was dramatized. He also wrote for the Boston Pilot and published sketches and criticism. He lectured in New York on the satisfying influence of Catholicity on intellect and senses, winning fame as an eloquent speaker.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-chetwode:
John Chetwode Eustace was an Irish antiquary whose Classical Tour made him suddenly celebrated in 1813. Born in Ireland about 1762 to an English family, he was educated at Sedgley Park and the Benedictine house at Douay. He taught rhetoric at Maynooth and was ordained there. He then returned to England as tutor and chaplain, traveling through Italy in 1802 with three pupils and keeping the journal that became his famous book.

In 1805 he became tutor at Jesus College, Cambridge, to George Petre. That post was unusual for a Catholic priest. It drew charges of indifferentism from Bishop Milner, who accused him of laying aside distinctive priestly worship to please Protestant company. Friends insisted he never lost sight of his sacred character. Later tours took him to Greece, Sicily, Malta, and France. A final Italian journey ended with malaria at Naples, where he died in 1815, lamenting errors in his writings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-ponce:
John Ponce was an Irish Franciscan philosopher and theologian of the Scotist school. Born at Cork in 1603, he entered the Irish Franciscans at Louvain young, studied philosophy at Cologne and theology at Louvain under Hugh Ward and John Colgan. He was called by Luke Wadding to Rome's new College of Saint Isidore in 1625.

Teaching philosophy and then theology at St. Isidore's, Lyons, and Paris, he won great repute for learning. His Course of Philosophy of 1643 drew opposition from Mastrius. He answered in 1645 by accepting Scotus's conclusions without adopting all his proofs, a reply Mastrius acknowledged as illuminating. His Complete Course of Theology of 1652 and his great Commentary on the Sentences of 1661 explain Scotist teaching with clearness and precision. He also aided Wadding's edition of Scotus and served Irish Confederate Catholics at Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-justice:
Justice, in the sense used here, is the cardinal virtue that perfects the will and moves it to give each person what belongs to them. Prudence perfects the intellect, fortitude steadies anger and daring, and temperance moderates appetite. Fortitude and temperance look inward; justice looks outward to others, sharing that field with charity. Charity gives from one's own stores to a neighbor in need; justice hands over what is already his.

Human beings hold God-given rights prior to the State, as free, intelligent persons made to know and love their Creator. Those natural rights, with rights from Church, State, or one's own work, form the object of justice. Justice therefore requires that everyone be left in free enjoyment of their rights. Claims like a needy man's call for help count here as charity, not justice, unless a strict right stands behind them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kielce:
Kielce is a diocese in the south of Russian Poland, covering the province of Kielce and part of Piotrkow. This entry describes its cathedral town, where the Assumption church, now the cathedral, dates to 1173, alongside a Holy Trinity church from 1646 and a St. Adalbert church on the saint's traditional martyrdom site.

First raised in 1807 by Pius VII and made subject to Cracow, the diocese was suppressed after its first bishop clashed with the Russians. Leo XIII restored it on 26 December 1882 as a suffragan of Warsaw. By 1910 it counted 944,604 Catholics, 242 parish churches, and 339 secular clergy. Its seminary had ten professors and 79 seminarians, and Sisters of Charity ran a hospital and ten houses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lace:
Lace, from Latin laqueus, a noose, is hand-made openwork in two great families: needle-made and bobbin-made. Needle lace splits into lacis, stitches on knotted netting, linen lace by drawn or cut work, and punto in aria, lace worked in the air with no foundation at all.

Bobbin lace, made with bobbins on a pillow or by crochet, tatting, and knotting, takes three chief forms. First comes early peasant tape lace. Then finished sprays joined by brides or net ground. Last comes the all-in-one method of Mechlin, Binche, and Valenciennes. History reaches back to Egyptian knotted netting found in 1909 at Qurneh, covering vases beside a seventeenth-dynasty burial of about 1600 before Christ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lecce:
Lecce, in Apulia's Terra d'Otranto, is the capital of its province, seven and a half miles off the sea. It is an industrial and trading city of tobacco, grain, wine, oil, and woven goods, with marble quarries nearby. Megalithic ruins prove very ancient settlement, and ancients knew it as Lupiae, with a port Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius enlarged.

Under the Normans it became a countship, with famous counts like Tancred, who contested Henry VI for the Two Sicilies, and Gautier de Brienne. Charles V gave it new life, and its uniform baroque style endures: the cathedral of St. Oronzio, first built in 1114, the seventeenth-century St. Domenico, sixteenth-century St. Croce, and a 240-foot cathedral tower still serving as a lighthouse between Otranto and Brindisi. Its first named bishop appears in 1057.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leuce: Leuce was a Thracian see, known to no old writer on history or place. Yet its bishop Symeon sat at the Council of Constantinople. Lists of sees from the tenth to the thirteenth centuries put Leuce under Philippopolis. It is likely today's village of Copolovo, south of Philippopolis, or Plovdiv, in Bulgaria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mace:
A mace is a short, richly ornamented staff, often of silver, topped with a knob or head-piece. It bears a coat of arms and is borne ahead of high church bodies, magistrates, and learned institutions as a sign of authority.

More strictly, the mace is the club-shaped beaten silver stick, mazza. Papal mazzieri, Swiss Guard vergers in papal chapels, and papal messengers, cursores apostolici, bear it at bishops' consecrations. Carried on the right shoulder with head upward, it descends from the twelfth century, when mazzieri, once servientes armorum or halberdiers, formed the pope's bodyguard.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manifestation:
Manifestation of conscience was a practice in many religious orders, by which members told their superior the state of their conscience. The aim was close knowledge of each person, so the superior could guide spiritual growth. It belonged to domestic, paternal rule, needing no church jurisdiction, so even a lay or female superior might receive it.

Such knowledge let a superior judge how often a member should receive communion, what reading suited them, what penances fit, and what counsel met their doubts and temptations. Its first object was the member's own good, its second the institute's good. A superior could not use it to harm the member or betray the secret. Leo XIII's decree Quemadmodum of 17 December 1890 ended compulsory manifestation and barred superiors from pressuring members toward it. It required the decree to be read aloud once a year. Voluntary sharing for help stayed lawful.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marianus-of-f:
Marianus of Florence was a Friar Minor and historian, born at Florence about the mid-fifteenth century and dead there on 20 July 1523. Little is known of his life, and his writings share that obscurity, not because they lack worth but because none was ever published and copies are hard to get.

His chief work, the Fasciculus Chronicarum, tells Franciscan history from the order's start to 1486. Writing three centuries after St Francis, he still merits trust, since he used original sources now lost, whose precious fragments reach us through him. He died of plague while giving last sacraments to Florence's stricken people. Besides the Fasciculus, he wrote a catalogue of over 150 famed women of St Clare's order. He also wrote histories of Mount Alvernia and the Tuscan province, a Rome itinerary, and a history of St Francis's habit moving to Florence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marie-de-fran:
Marie de France was a French poet of the twelfth century, known almost only by inference, since no biography survives. Her lays honour a King Henry, and her Ysopet a Count William, long a puzzle for scholars.

Careful study of her language settled both figures. She was Norman, writing in the pure Norman dialect of the later twelfth century, and her patrons were Henry II of England and his son William, Count of Salisbury. Her works comprise fifteen lays of the Breton cycle's love group, short octosyllabic tales of knights braving deeds for their ladies, told with rare feeling, simple grace, and clear brevity. Her Ysopet holds 103 fables from Henry Beauclerc's English version, and her Purgatory of St Patrick sends an Irish knight through a cavern of torments and joys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-master-of-the:
Master of the Sacred Palace, Magister Sacri Palatii, is the pope's theologian, an office always held by a Friar Preacher. St Dominic, appointed in 1218, was the first holder. Among eighty-four Dominican successors, eighteen later became cardinals, twenty-four archbishops or bishops, and six generals of the order. 

Dominic's work included teaching St Paul's letters to church leaders and their aides, who had idled gossiping in waiting rooms. The office's work continues today: by 1409 records show the Master lecturing on set days and answering questions at theological conferences. Before the Inquisition congregation of 1542 and Index of 1587, he condemned books and banned reading under censure, a task fading by 1604. Pius V made him canon theologian of St Peter's in 1570, though Gregory XIII revoked that bull. Since Rome's 1870 occupation he examines Italian bishop candidates and confers the doctorate from his Vatican apartment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maurice:
Maurice, Roman emperor from 582 to his death in November 602, was born in 539 to an old Latin family settled in Cappadocia. He began as a soldier and served well against the Persians under Tiberius II, who gave him his daughter Constantina in marriage and named him successor. Tiberius died almost at once, and Maurice took the throne peacefully.
